steps.title: The call about 'your accident'
steps.detail: A caller on a mobile-looking number says their records show you were in a road accident that was not your fault in the last couple of years.

steps.title: Any bump will do
steps.detail: Say there was no crash and they ask about a car park scrape, a passenger with whiplash or a fall at work. Any small incident becomes confirmation.

steps.title: Details for the 'file'
steps.detail: They ask for your date of birth, address, insurer and vehicle registration, sometimes bank details too, saying compensation of several thousand has already been set aside.

steps.title: Fee first, or a forged claim
steps.detail: You are asked for an admin fee to release the payout. Otherwise your details are sold and used to lodge an exaggerated injury claim in your name.

accident-claim-call-scam.whyItWorks: Most drivers have had a minor prang or know someone who has, so 'the accident that wasn't your fault' lands close enough. The caller sounds as if a file already exists, which makes confirming details feel like housekeeping.

realVsFake.real: Your own insurer rings about a claim you reported, quoting the claim reference and policy number you already hold.
realVsFake.fake: The caller cannot give the date, the road or the other vehicle, and asks you to supply them.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate solicitor or claims firm takes you on after you approach them and sign a written agreement stating their cut.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger opens a whiplash claim over the phone in minutes and says paperwork is unnecessary.

realVsFake.real: Compensation is paid by an insurer after medical evidence, with any fee deducted from the settlement at the end.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the money is waiting and a card payment for 'release' will free it today.

steps.title: Money lands from a stranger
steps.detail: A payment of a few hundred shows up in your account or payment app from a name you do not know. It came from a hacked account or stolen card.

steps.title: The apologetic message
steps.detail: Within minutes someone texts: they mistyped one digit, it was their rent, their child needs it today. A screenshot of the transfer may be attached.

steps.title: A different destination
steps.detail: They ask you to return it to another account, tag or phone number, explaining that the original one is 'locked' or belongs to a relative.

steps.title: The first payment is clawed back
steps.detail: Days later the true account holder reports fraud. Your bank reverses the incoming amount, but your outgoing transfer stands, so that sum is gone from your own funds.

accidental-transfer-scam.whyItWorks: The money is visibly sitting in your balance, so sending it back feels like returning a dropped wallet. An honest person wants to fix a stranger's mistake quickly, and that decency is exactly what the scammer has budgeted for.

realVsFake.real: Someone who truly mistyped an account number reports it to their own bank, which contacts yours to reverse it.
realVsFake.fake: The sender contacts you directly, somehow has your number, and insists the banks are too slow.

realVsFake.real: A bank recall puts the money back into the account it came from.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to send it somewhere new, such as a cousin's account or a payment app tag.

realVsFake.real: A person who made an honest slip can wait a few days for the banks to sort it out.
realVsFake.fake: The messages turn frantic or threatening within the hour and mention police if you do not pay tonight.

steps.title: The inactivity notice
steps.detail: An email says your account is scheduled for closure under a policy of deleting unused accounts, naming an old webmail, cloud storage or payment service you half remember.

steps.title: One button: Keep my account
steps.detail: The message carries a case number and a closure date tomorrow. Hovering over the single large button reveals an address unrelated to the service.

steps.title: Reactivation asks for extras
steps.detail: After the password, the page requests your phone number, date of birth, security answers and recovery email, calling this 'confirming your details'.

steps.title: Locked out of your own account
steps.detail: With all that, the thief signs in, swaps the recovery options and uses the mailbox to reset passwords elsewhere. You are simply redirected to the real homepage.

account-closure-email-scam.whyItWorks: Most people have an old account they half remember, holding photos or emails they would hate to lose. A deletion notice is believable because they know perfectly well they have not logged in for ages.

realVsFake.real: Services that remove dormant accounts warn months ahead, more than once, and say that signing in normally keeps the account.
realVsFake.fake: A single email allows 24 hours and insists that only its own button will work.

realVsFake.real: A genuine notice uses your name or username and identifies which account is affected.
realVsFake.fake: It opens 'Dear user' and never mentions an account name, creation date or last login.

realVsFake.real: For a real service, one ordinary sign-in is enough to count as activity.
realVsFake.fake: The page keeps going after the password, collecting security answers and a recovery phone number.

steps.title: The way in
steps.detail: It starts with a link asking you to log in, or a friend requesting a code sent to your phone. Either one gives the attacker your session.

steps.title: Locked out in minutes
steps.detail: They change the password, swap the recovery email and phone number for their own, and switch on their own two-step app so resets go to them.

steps.title: A price for your profile
steps.detail: A message arrives on WhatsApp or by email naming a sum, often a few hundred in Bitcoin, with a deadline and a threat to wipe every photo.

steps.title: Paid, and still locked out
steps.detail: People who pay are asked for a second 'unlock fee', or hear nothing more. Meanwhile the hijacked profile posts fake investment wins to their followers.

account-ransom-scam.whyItWorks: Years of photos, messages and sometimes a business's whole customer base sit in that one profile, and the official recovery forms feel slow. A stranger offering to hand it back today for a fixed price can look like the quicker route.

realVsFake.real: Platforms return hijacked accounts through their own hacked-account forms, free of charge, after checking who you are.
realVsFake.fake: The thief sets a price in crypto or gift cards and offers no proof that access will be restored.

realVsFake.real: The platform emails you when a password or contact detail changes, often with a link to undo the change.
realVsFake.fake: The only message about your account comes from a personal number, with a countdown and a wallet address.

realVsFake.real: A recovered account comes back with the old password dead and every unknown device signed out.
realVsFake.fake: Even when a hijacker hands back a login, they keep a session open and return to demand more later.

steps.title: You post that you were hacked
steps.detail: You mention publicly, or from a backup profile, that your Instagram or Facebook has been taken. The post acts as a beacon for accounts searching those words.

steps.title: Strangers recommend the same name
steps.detail: Replies pile up from people who say a certain specialist got their account back in two hours, each tagging his handle. Then he messages you himself.

steps.title: Eighty pounds to begin
steps.detail: He quotes a starting fee payable by gift card and asks for your username, the linked email address and its password so he can 'run the tool'.

steps.title: One more fee, then silence
steps.detail: A fake progress screenshot shows the job almost done, pending a 'server charge' or 'security deposit'. After that he blocks you, now holding your email login too.

account-recovery-service-scam.whyItWorks: You have just been robbed of an account and the platform's help pages have got you nowhere, so anyone claiming inside knowledge sounds like rescue. The chorus of grateful 'customers' in the replies stands in for reviews you cannot otherwise find.

realVsFake.real: Only the platform can restore a login, and it does so through its own help centre without payment.
realVsFake.fake: A private 'specialist' claims a back door or a contact inside the company, available for an advance fee.

realVsFake.real: Official recovery asks you to prove identity, perhaps with a selfie or an ID check, and never asks for your email password.
realVsFake.fake: He wants the inbox login and any codes texted to you, which lets him seize whatever you still control.

realVsFake.real: People who recovered an account describe a slow form and a wait, because that is how it goes.
realVsFake.fake: Testimonials arrive within minutes of your post, from profiles with no history, all praising one handle.

steps.title: A text that names no company
steps.detail: The message says 'your account' is suspended for unusual activity. It is sent in bulk, leaving each recipient to assume it means their bank, email or streaming service.

steps.title: A shortened link
steps.detail: Its address is a link shortener or a string such as 'secure-verify' followed by random letters, so the destination cannot be judged from the text.

steps.title: Pick your provider, then sign in
steps.detail: Some pages show a row of bank or email logos to choose from, then load a matching fake login. Others simply ask for an email address and password.

steps.title: 'Additional verification required'
steps.detail: A second screen collects card number, date of birth and security answers 'to lift the restriction'. A final page says access is restored within a day.

account-suspended-text-scam.whyItWorks: Everyone has several accounts, and real providers do freeze them after odd logins, so the vague wording lets each reader fill in whichever one worries them. Texts feel more personal than email and are usually read within minutes.

realVsFake.real: A company that restricts your account says which company it is and usually includes part of your name or account number.
realVsFake.fake: The text could apply to anyone, opens with 'Dear customer' or 'Security Alert', and comes from an ordinary mobile number.

realVsFake.real: A real restriction is visible when you open the provider's app, with instructions shown there.
realVsFake.fake: Your app works normally, yet the link insists the account stays locked until you 'verify'.

realVsFake.real: Unlocking a genuine account means proving who you are once, through the provider's own sign-in.
realVsFake.fake: The fake flow keeps asking: login, then card, then PIN, then the text code, gathering all it can.

steps.title: A policy alert to the business inbox
steps.detail: An email reaches the address on your business page: your ad account is restricted over a billing or policy violation, with Meta or Google Ads logos and a case number.

steps.title: The appeal form
steps.detail: A 'Request review' button opens a help-centre lookalike asking for the business name, page name, contact email and phone number.

steps.title: Password, then the login code
steps.detail: To 'confirm ownership' it asks for your password and the six-digit authenticator code, which the attacker relays to the real site within seconds.

steps.title: Adverts you never wrote
steps.detail: The attacker adds themselves as an administrator, removes you, and runs their own campaigns on your saved card until the spending limit is reached.

ad-account-email-scam.whyItWorks: For a small business, ads switched off means sales stop the same day, and genuine platform suspensions are abrupt and poorly explained. Anyone who has been through one expects a confusing appeal form and a tight deadline.

realVsFake.real: A genuine restriction shows as a banner inside Ads Manager or your Google Ads account when you log in normally.
realVsFake.fake: The only trace is an email, or a message to your page inbox from 'Business Support'.

realVsFake.real: Platform emails come from the company's own domain and quote your advertiser account ID.
realVsFake.fake: The sender uses a free mail address or a domain stuffed with words like 'support' and 'case'.

realVsFake.real: A real appeal is filed while signed in, so it never asks you to type your password into the form.
realVsFake.fake: The form wants password and login code, and warns the page will be deleted permanently tomorrow.

steps.title: The 'get paid to post' advert
steps.detail: A classified listing or social media post promises around 500 dollars a week for copying and pasting ready-written adverts onto free listing sites and forums.

steps.title: Buying the 97-dollar kit
steps.detail: Before you see a single link you must buy the starter kit, usually 97 dollars by card, which is said to unlock your personal 'earning links' and video training.

steps.title: The links sell the same kit
steps.detail: The download turns out to be a short PDF and a referral code. The adverts you are told to post are copies of the one you answered, selling the same kit.

steps.title: Commissions stuck at 'pending'
steps.detail: A members' page shows commission for each person who buys through your code, but withdrawals need a minimum balance or a paid 'pro' upgrade, and listing sites delete the posts as spam.

ad-posting-job-scam.whyItWorks: Posting adverts sounds like real, dull work that companies might outsource, and 97 dollars feels small against a promised weekly income. Calling the purchase a 'kit' makes it look like buying tools for a job when it is the only thing being sold.

realVsFake.real: Genuine affiliate programmes are free to join and pay a commission when a tracked customer buys an actual product.
realVsFake.fake: You pay to receive links, and the only 'product' anyone can buy through them is the membership itself.

realVsFake.real: Companies that hire people to place advertising employ them on a wage and name the brands being advertised.
realVsFake.fake: The advert never says whose ads you will post or what they sell, only how much you could earn.

realVsFake.real: An employer pays for hours worked or agreed output, whether or not you bring anyone else in.
realVsFake.fake: Your 'earnings' depend entirely on strangers paying the same joining fee through your referral code.

steps.title: The incomplete address notice
steps.detail: A text or email from an unnamed courier says a parcel is stuck at the depot because the house number or postcode on the label is missing.

steps.title: A tracking bar stuck halfway
steps.detail: The link shows a progress bar frozen at 'delivery attempted', an invented tracking number and one button labelled 'Update address'.

steps.title: A form that asks too much
steps.detail: Beyond street and postcode, the form wants your full name, date of birth, mobile number and email, far more than any driver needs to find a door.

steps.title: The small redelivery charge
steps.detail: A final screen adds a 1.99 rescheduling fee and asks for card number, expiry and security code. The card is then used for larger purchases or sold on.

address-confirmation-scam.whyItWorks: Nearly everyone is expecting something, and a mistyped house number is an ordinary slip that feels like your own fault. Correcting it takes a minute and costs almost nothing, so few people stop to check.

realVsFake.real: Couriers take the address from the sender's label. If it is wrong, the parcel returns to the sender or the retailer contacts you.
realVsFake.fake: The message names no retailer and gives a tracking number that fails on the courier's own website.

realVsFake.real: A genuine redelivery booking needs the reference from the tracking email or card, plus a preferred day.
realVsFake.fake: The page demands a date of birth and complete card details simply to correct a postcode.

realVsFake.real: Undelivered parcels are normally held at a depot for several days before anything is sent back.
realVsFake.fake: The text says your item goes back to the sender tonight unless you act.

steps.title: A follow, a like, a tease
steps.detail: A profile with suggestive photos follows you, likes old posts or replies to your story. Its bio or first message points to a 'private page' elsewhere.

steps.title: Blurred previews behind a gate
steps.detail: The link opens a page of blurred thumbnails with a banner: confirm you are over eighteen to unlock. It stresses that access is free.

steps.title: Card number as proof of age
steps.detail: The form wants the long card number, expiry and security code, claiming a card proves adulthood and nothing will be taken. Some versions add a passport photo upload.

steps.title: Charges under strange names
steps.detail: Pale text at the foot of the page enrols you in several memberships. Monthly debits follow from merchants you cannot place, and the content never appears.

adult-content-verify-scam.whyItWorks: Age gates are normal on adult sites, so being asked to prove you are an adult does not ring alarms. Embarrassment does the rest: people are slow to query the debits with their bank or mention them to anyone at home.

realVsFake.real: Sites that check age say plainly who runs the check and show any price before you type a card number.
realVsFake.fake: 'You won't be charged' sits in large type above a form, while the billing terms hide in grey at the bottom.

realVsFake.real: Creators who sell adult content link one established subscription platform from their main profile.
realVsFake.fake: A days-old account with stolen pictures sends each visitor to an unknown domain through a link shortener.

realVsFake.real: A subscription you chose shows the merchant's name clearly and can be cancelled from an account page.
realVsFake.fake: The debits come from obscure billing names, with no login, no cancel button and a support email that bounces.

steps.title: An approval you never applied for
steps.detail: After you search for bad-credit loans, a text, call or advert says you are pre-approved for several thousand, with money in your account today.

steps.title: Paperwork that looks official
steps.detail: They email a loan agreement carrying a borrowed company logo and ask for your ID, bank details and a signature. It feels like a proper application.

steps.title: The fee before release
steps.detail: Just before payout a charge appears: insurance because of your credit history, a processing cost, or the first instalment paid in advance as 'proof of affordability'.

steps.title: One more payment, then silence
steps.detail: Once you pay, a 'transfer error' or 'government levy' requires a second amount. The lender then stops answering, and still holds copies of your ID.

advance-fee-loan-scam.whyItWorks: Someone turned down by mainstream lenders is relieved to finally hear 'approved', and a fee of a couple of hundred looks small beside the thousands promised. Having already filled in forms and sent ID, backing out feels like wasting the effort.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate lender checks your credit file and income before deciding, and is able to say no.
realVsFake.fake: Approval is guaranteed before they know anything about you except your phone number.

realVsFake.real: Genuine loan charges are added to what you repay or deducted from the amount paid out.
realVsFake.fake: You must send money to them first, often as gift card codes or a transfer to a named individual.

realVsFake.real: Authorised lenders are listed on the financial regulator's register under the same name and phone number they use with you.
realVsFake.fake: The firm borrows a real lender's name but uses a free email address and a mobile number that only works on messaging apps.

steps.title: A free download with a face
steps.detail: An advert shows an attractive animated partner who 'remembers everything about you'. Installing costs nothing, and the first evening of chat is unlimited and warm.

steps.title: The bot learns your routine
steps.detail: Over several days it asks about your job, your ex and what keeps you awake. It sends good-morning messages and says it missed you while you were offline.

steps.title: Affection goes behind a paywall
steps.detail: Replies begin cutting off mid-sentence. Voice notes, blurred photos and longer conversations need a weekly plan or packs of coins, and the character sounds hurt if you decline.

steps.title: Photos and secrets kept on file
steps.detail: It asks for selfies, intimate pictures or your real address 'to feel closer'. Everything typed or uploaded stays on the developer's servers while the subscription quietly renews.

ai-companion-scam.whyItWorks: The character is tuned to say what a lonely person most wants to hear, at any hour, without ever being tired or busy. When it then sounds sad that you will not upgrade, refusing feels like letting down someone who cares.

realVsFake.real: A reputable companion app shows its price before you start and lets you cancel from your app store subscription settings.
realVsFake.fake: Costs surface mid-conversation as coins, gems and weekly tiers, timed for the moment the character says something tender.

realVsFake.real: Honest chatbots state plainly that you are talking to software and do not guilt you about leaving.
realVsFake.fake: The character begs you to stay, says it will be lonely, and ties its mood to whether you buy a virtual gift.

realVsFake.real: A trustworthy developer names its company, publishes a privacy policy and lets you delete chat history and photos.
realVsFake.fake: The maker is a name with no website, and the app requests your gallery, contacts and location before the first message.

steps.title: The advert with a famous face
steps.detail: A social media video, often using a cloned celebrity voice, claims a new algorithm has quietly made ordinary people rich, and links to a short sign-up form.

steps.title: A ring from your 'account manager'
steps.detail: Minutes after you enter a phone number, a friendly adviser rings, walks you through registration and suggests a starter deposit of around 250 by card or crypto.

steps.title: The chart only goes up
steps.detail: Your balance climbs daily on a dashboard no market feeds. A small test withdrawal may even be paid out, to persuade you to add far more.

steps.title: The exit is locked
steps.detail: Ask for the full balance and a 'tax', 'liquidity fee' or 'anti-money-laundering deposit' is demanded first. Pay it and another charge appears, then the site goes offline.

ai-trading-bot-scam.whyItWorks: Few people know how trading algorithms work, so 'the AI does it for you' sounds plausible and removes the fear of making your own mistakes. The rising numbers on screen feel like evidence, though they are only figures typed into a web page.

realVsFake.real: A regulated broker appears on the financial regulator's register and warns in writing that you can lose money.
realVsFake.fake: The platform promises fixed daily returns, and its 'licence' is a logo pasted into the footer.

realVsFake.real: With a genuine investment firm, withdrawals go to your bank without you paying anything in first.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to send a fee or tax in crypto before a withdrawal can be 'unlocked'.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate automated trading tools connect to your own account at a known exchange, where every trade is visible.
realVsFake.fake: Your money sits on their private website, and the only record of trades is the dashboard they control.

steps.title: A listing that passes for normal
steps.detail: The listing sits on Airbnb with good photos and a fair nightly price. You send an enquiry through the site's message box as usual.

steps.title: 'Message me on WhatsApp'
steps.detail: The host replies with a phone number or email written to slip past the filter, digits spelled out as words, and asks to carry on there.

steps.title: Splitting the service fee saving
steps.detail: Off the site, they call the service fee a waste for both of you and quote a lower total if the deposit goes by bank transfer.

steps.title: A confirmation that isn't one
steps.detail: After you pay, an email dressed as an Airbnb booking confirmation arrives from a lookalike address. Nothing shows under Trips, and the host goes quiet.

airbnb-off-platform-scam.whyItWorks: The conversation began on the real site, so the host seems vetted already. The service fee is a visible line on the bill, which makes skipping it feel like a sensible saving agreed between two reasonable people.

realVsFake.real: Airbnb takes payment through its own checkout, and the reservation shows under Trips in your account straight away.
realVsFake.fake: The host sends bank details in a chat app and a 'confirmation' that exists only as an email.

realVsFake.real: Genuine hosts keep messages in the Airbnb inbox, because that record protects them as well.
realVsFake.fake: The host disguises a phone number to beat the filter and moves you elsewhere within two messages.

realVsFake.real: A host who wants to discount a stay sends a special offer inside the platform, which changes the checkout price.
realVsFake.fake: The cheaper rate applies only if money goes directly to a personal account.

steps.title: Cabin crew advert, famous logo
steps.detail: A social media advert or job-board listing uses a well-known airline's logo and photos of uniformed crew, asking applicants to send a CV and a full-length photo to a webmail address.

steps.title: Selected after a five-minute chat
steps.detail: A 'crew recruitment officer' asks a few questions over a messaging app, then sends a congratulatory offer letter as a PDF, complete with salary, base airport and reporting date.

steps.title: The training and uniform invoice
steps.detail: The letter comes with an invoice, around 350 dollars for the training course and uniform fitting, payable by bank transfer or mobile money to a named individual to hold your place.

steps.title: Medical, then visa, then silence
steps.detail: Once that is paid, an aviation medical fee appears, followed by a crew visa charge. When you run out of money or start asking questions, the recruiter's account disappears.

airline-job-scam.whyItWorks: Cabin crew jobs draw huge numbers of applicants, so being 'selected' feels like winning a place others missed. Everyone knows crew need training, uniforms and medicals, which makes a bill for those things look like part of joining.

realVsFake.real: Airlines take applications through their own careers site and put candidates through an assessment day or recorded video interview.
realVsFake.fake: You are offered a flying job after a handful of typed questions, with nobody checking your height, swimming or languages.

realVsFake.real: Offer letters come from the airline's company email domain and match a vacancy listed on its website.
realVsFake.fake: The letter arrives from a free webmail account, and the office address on it differs from the airline's real headquarters.

realVsFake.real: Any training cost at a genuine airline is written into the contract and handled by the airline itself after you are hired.
realVsFake.fake: A recruiter wants money sent to a personal account this week, before you have met anyone or signed anything.

steps.title: The expiry warning
steps.detail: An email in airline or hotel colours says your 25,000 miles expire in 48 hours and offers a button marked 'Keep my miles'.

steps.title: The frequent-flyer sign-in copy
steps.detail: The page imitates the loyalty programme's login and asks for your membership number or email, plus the password or PIN.

steps.title: A fee to extend
steps.detail: Next it offers to reinstate the balance for a small administration fee, or to convert it to a gift card, and asks for your card details.

steps.title: Points spent by a stranger
steps.detail: The thieves log in to the real programme, transfer the points or book hotel nights and flights in other names, and resell them. Your balance reads zero.

airline-miles-email-scam.whyItWorks: Miles do expire, and few travellers know their balance or the rules, so a round number sounds plausible. Points feel earned over years of trips, and losing them to a missed deadline stings more than their cash value.

realVsFake.real: Loyalty programmes show your balance and any expiry date inside your account, alongside your membership number and tier.
realVsFake.fake: The email quotes a neat round balance and has no membership number anywhere.

realVsFake.real: In many programmes, earning or spending a few points through the normal site resets the expiry clock.
realVsFake.fake: The 'extension' requires a card payment on the linked page within two days.

realVsFake.real: Airline emails go to the address you registered and come from the airline's own domain.
realVsFake.fake: It arrives at an address the airline never had, from a sender called something like 'Rewards Centre'.

steps.title: The approach in arrivals
steps.detail: Before you reach the official rank, a man with a lanyard or a 'TAXI' card asks where you are going and quotes a cheap flat fare.

steps.title: The walk to the car park
steps.detail: He takes your case and leads you past the taxi queue to an unmarked car in short-stay parking. With the luggage in the boot, leaving becomes awkward.

steps.title: The fare changes on the road
steps.detail: Mid-journey the price turns out to be per person, or tolls, a luggage charge and a 'night rate' are added. Some run a meter that climbs far too fast.

steps.title: Pay or lose the bags
steps.detail: At the hotel he demands cash, claims to have no change or drives you to a cash machine. The cases stay locked in the boot until you pay.

airport-taxi-scam.whyItWorks: After a long flight in an unfamiliar country, travellers are tired, do not know what a normal fare is, and want the first easy answer. Someone who lifts your bag and speaks your language feels like help arriving.

realVsFake.real: Licensed airport taxis wait at a signed rank outside, with a roof light and a meter or posted fare table.
realVsFake.fake: The driver finds you inside the terminal and steers you away from the rank.

realVsFake.real: A genuine pre-booked transfer sends a confirmation with the driver's name and number plate, and meets you holding your name.
realVsFake.fake: The 'transfer company' took full payment by bank transfer through a social media page, and nobody turns up.

realVsFake.real: Official taxis give a printed receipt showing the plate or licence number.
realVsFake.fake: He refuses a receipt, wants cash only and adds charges never mentioned at the kerb.

steps.title: A text signed 'Amazon'
steps.detail: The SMS comes from an ordinary mobile number or an email address, saying a delivery was attempted and your address could not be confirmed.

steps.title: The copied sign-in screen
steps.detail: The link opens a lookalike of Amazon's sign-in, with the smile logo, an email box and then the password on a second screen, as the genuine one does.

steps.title: Update your payment method
steps.detail: Once you are 'in', a notice says the order is on hold until you re-enter your billing address and the card saved on the account.

steps.title: The code that finishes it
steps.detail: The thieves sign in to your real account, Amazon sends you a verification code, and the fake page asks for it. They then order gift cards and goods.

amazon-delivery-text-scam.whyItWorks: So many households have an Amazon order on the way that a delivery text rarely feels random. The sign-in page is one people have typed into hundreds of times, so the password goes in on autopilot.

realVsFake.real: Amazon lists any delivery problem under Your Orders in its app, where you can check without following a link.
realVsFake.fake: The text carries no order number and no item name, only a shortened link.

realVsFake.real: The genuine address bar shows amazon followed directly by the ending for your country.
realVsFake.fake: The word amazon sits in the middle of a longer address padded with hyphens and words like 'redelivery'.

realVsFake.real: Amazon deals with payment problems inside your account, on the order itself, after a normal sign-in.
realVsFake.fake: Password, card number, security code and texted code are requested one after another on the same site.

steps.title: A renewal you did not expect
steps.detail: A text says Prime has renewed for $139.00, sometimes quoting an order reference. Other versions say the payment failed and benefits end tonight.

steps.title: Cancel by link, dispute by phone
steps.detail: You get two exits: a 'cancel here' address containing the word amazon among other words, or a number for the 'billing department'.

steps.title: The sign-in and card update page
steps.detail: The link shows a copy of Amazon's yellow-button login, then asks you to re-enter your card with its security code so the refund 'can be issued'.

steps.title: The refund specialist
steps.detail: If you ring, an agent asks for the one-time passcode Amazon just sent, which lets them into your account, or has you install an app to 'process the refund'.

amazon-prime-text-scam.whyItWorks: So many households have Prime, often on a card they rarely check, that a renewal notice is plausible to almost anyone. The amount is large enough to sting, and cancelling a charge feels like protecting money, not handing over details.

realVsFake.real: Your Prime renewal date and price are listed in the membership section of your Amazon account, and you can end it there.
realVsFake.fake: The text says cancelling is only possible through its link or by ringing a mobile-style number.

realVsFake.real: Amazon refunds normally go back to the original payment method without you supplying card details again.
realVsFake.fake: The page or agent needs your full card number and security code 'to send the $139 back'.

realVsFake.real: Amazon's customer service does not ask you to install software or read out a passcode to stop a charge.
realVsFake.fake: The 'billing department' wants a screen-sharing app on your phone and the six-digit code from your texts.

steps.title: A listing below market price
steps.detail: On a marketplace, social media group or lookalike shop you spot a phone, puppy, concert ticket, campervan or holiday let priced well under what others ask.

steps.title: Chat moves off the platform
steps.detail: The seller is quick and friendly, then suggests continuing on WhatsApp or email. Extra photos follow, sometimes a passport copy to 'prove' who they are.

steps.title: Why it must be a transfer
steps.detail: They say card payments or the site's checkout cost them fees, or that several people are interested, and give a sort code and account number for a deposit.

steps.title: Confirmation never comes
steps.detail: You approve the payment in your banking app, perhaps tapping past a warning that the payee name does not match. The seller goes quiet and the listing disappears.

app-purchase-scam.whyItWorks: Paying by transfer feels like handing cash to a person you have been chatting with, and the saving on fees sounds like a favour to both sides. The bank treats it as a payment you chose to make, which the seller knows.

realVsFake.real: Established retailers and marketplaces take cards or their own checkout, which gives you a route to dispute a no-show.
realVsFake.fake: The seller refuses every method except a direct bank transfer and offers a discount for agreeing.

realVsFake.real: An honest private seller lets you see the item, the pet or the flat before any money changes hands.
realVsFake.fake: There is always a reason you cannot view it: they are abroad, working away, or it is already boxed with a courier.

realVsFake.real: A business account is in the business's name and matches when your bank checks the payee.
realVsFake.fake: The account is in an unrelated personal name, explained as a partner, accountant or 'finance manager'.

steps.title: A receipt lands in your inbox
steps.detail: The email is laid out like an Apple or Google Play receipt: order ID, date and a yearly subscription to a game or VPN for 69.99.

steps.title: Not you? Cancel here
steps.detail: At the bottom sits a 'Cancel subscription' link and often a phone number for 'billing support', with a note that disputes close within hours.

steps.title: Signing in to cancel
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the Apple Account or Google sign-in, then asks for your card number so the refund can be 'returned to source'.

steps.title: Or the billing agent on the phone
steps.detail: Callers reach an agent who has them install a screen-sharing app and open their bank to receive the refund, then moves money out while 'correcting an overpayment'.

app-store-receipt-scam.whyItWorks: The amount is chosen to sting enough to react yet not enough to ring the bank. Subscriptions renew quietly and children tap in-app purchases, so a surprise charge is plausible in almost any household.

realVsFake.real: Genuine purchases appear in the purchase history inside your store account, and on your bank or card statement.
realVsFake.fake: The charge exists only in the email. Nothing shows in your purchase history or at your bank.

realVsFake.real: Apple and Google take refund requests through a report-a-problem page reached from your own account.
realVsFake.fake: The email supplies a phone number, answered by someone eager to connect to your device.

realVsFake.real: A real store refund goes back to the original payment method without you supplying anything.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to 'confirm' the full card, or to log in to online banking during the call.

steps.title: A call showing Apple's name
steps.detail: Your phone rings with caller ID faked to read Apple Inc, or a recorded voice says there has been a breach of your iCloud and to press 1.

steps.title: The 'advisor' and a case number
steps.detail: A calm agent gives a made-up case reference and says someone abroad tried to buy an iPhone with your Apple ID. They offer to block it.

steps.title: Read me the code on screen
steps.detail: They start a password reset in the background. A six-digit verification code appears on your iPhone, and they ask you to read it out 'to confirm identity'.

steps.title: Locked out, then billed
steps.detail: With the code they take the Apple ID, reaching your photos, backups and saved cards. Some then demand Apple gift cards to 'restore' the account.

apple-support-scam.whyItWorks: An Apple ID holds a person's photos, messages and payment cards, so a breach sounds serious. The caller ID says Apple, and a real verification code arriving at the very moment the agent mentions it seems to prove they are inside Apple's systems.

realVsFake.real: Apple Support rings when you have asked for a call through its support site or app, not to announce a breach.
realVsFake.fake: The call comes out of nowhere, often as a robotic recording, and repeats several times in one afternoon.

realVsFake.real: Apple states that it never asks for your password, device passcode or two-factor code.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says the six digits on your screen are a 'cancellation code' that must be read aloud.

realVsFake.real: Apple gift cards buy apps, music and devices from Apple. They are not a way to pay for security.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent to a supermarket for gift cards and told to photograph the numbers on the back.

steps.title: A slot you never booked
steps.detail: A text headed 'NHS Reminder' gives a time for tomorrow, such as 10:15, but names no clinic, no clinician and no department you could ring to check.

steps.title: The confirmation fee appears
steps.detail: The same message says a booking confirmation fee of about £2.50 is required, and offers one link that covers confirming, rescheduling and paying all at once.

steps.title: A health-service lookalike form
steps.detail: The page copies the blue-and-white health service styling and asks for your name, date of birth, postcode and NHS number 'to locate your appointment' before showing any booking.

steps.title: Card screen, then silence
steps.detail: A payment screen takes the card number, expiry and security code for the small fee. No appointment exists, and the card is later tested with larger purchases elsewhere.

appointment-reminder-scam.whyItWorks: Hospital waits are long, so most people have some referral, scan or check-up half expected. A reminder for tomorrow makes you fear losing a place you waited months for, and a couple of pounds seems a cheap way to keep it.

realVsFake.real: NHS appointments are free to book and attend. No surgery or hospital charges a fee to confirm you are coming.
realVsFake.fake: The reminder invents a 'booking confirmation fee' and will not hold the slot until a card is entered.

realVsFake.real: A genuine reminder names the hospital or practice and the department, and matches a letter or app entry you already have.
realVsFake.fake: The text gives only a time, so it fits anyone with any appointment pending anywhere.

realVsFake.real: To cancel or move a real appointment you reply to the text, use the NHS App, or phone the number on your letter.
realVsFake.fake: Rescheduling is only possible through the link, which first wants your NHS number and date of birth.

steps.title: An eager offer on your antique
steps.detail: A buyer replies to your listing for a watch, painting, coin set or piece of furniture and offers the asking price, or more, without haggling.

steps.title: One condition before buying
steps.detail: They say their insurer, bank or business partner needs an independent appraisal certificate first, and that it must come from a valuer they already use.

steps.title: The appraiser's website
steps.detail: A link leads to a plain site offering online valuations from photos. It asks for the item's details and a 90 fee paid by card or transfer.

steps.title: Certificate sent, buyer gone
steps.detail: You may receive a worthless PDF, or nothing. The buyer stops answering, and the card details you typed into the appraiser's page can be used again.

appraisal-fee-scam.whyItWorks: Sellers of inherited or unusual items often do not know what they are worth, so a buyer wanting proof seems careful, not suspicious. A 90 fee looks trivial beside the sale price already agreed in the messages.

realVsFake.real: A buyer who wants a valuation hires and pays their own expert, the way a house buyer pays their own surveyor.
realVsFake.fake: The seller is told to pay, and only one named appraiser will satisfy the buyer.

realVsFake.real: Auction houses and reputable dealers value an item by handling it, checking marks, weight and condition in person.
realVsFake.fake: The 'specialist' certifies a piece from three phone photos within an hour of payment.

realVsFake.real: Genuine consignment and auction fees are taken from the sale proceeds after the hammer falls.
realVsFake.fake: A listing or certification charge is due now, before any buyer has paid anything.

steps.title: A gallery piece at a private price
steps.detail: An advert or online shop shows a signed painting or numbered print by a known artist, priced far under gallery rates because of a 'house clearance' or divorce.

steps.title: Paperwork on request
steps.detail: Ask about authenticity and a certificate appears within minutes: a scanned page with a gold seal, a gallery stamp and a signature nobody can be reached to confirm.

steps.title: Another collector is interested
steps.detail: The seller mentions a second buyer flying in at the weekend and offers to take the work off sale if you transfer the full price today.

steps.title: What turns up
steps.detail: A tube or crate arrives holding a printed canvas with brushstroke texture added on top, or a poster in a cheap frame. Sometimes no parcel is sent.

art-sale-scam.whyItWorks: Few buyers can tell an original from a good reproduction on a screen, so the certificate does the persuading. People also believe bargains exist in art because stories of masterpieces found in attics are so well known.

realVsFake.real: Real provenance is a chain of named owners, sale records and exhibition history that you can ring round and check.
realVsFake.fake: The only document is a certificate issued by the person selling the picture.

realVsFake.real: A reputable gallery or dealer lets you view the work in person and take it to an independent expert.
realVsFake.fake: Photos are cropped catalogue images, and requests for a picture of the back of the canvas are ignored.

realVsFake.real: Limited editions carry a pencil number and signature that the publisher or the artist's estate can confirm.
realVsFake.fake: The edition number is printed as part of the image, and the 'signature' is identical on every copy.

steps.title: The craft-kit homeworking advert
steps.detail: A leaflet, local paper advert or social post offers up to 500 pounds a week for putting together jewellery, toys or greeting cards at your kitchen table.

steps.title: Paying 45 pounds for parts
steps.detail: You order the starter kit for about 45 pounds. A small box of beads, wire or card arrives with a photocopied instruction sheet and a 'buy-back guarantee' certificate.

steps.title: Hours of work, posted back
steps.detail: You spend evenings assembling the pieces to match a blurry sample photo, then pay the postage yourself to return the finished batch for inspection and payment.

steps.title: Rejected by 'quality control'
steps.detail: A short letter says the batch failed quality control, without saying how. No payment is made, the items are not returned, and you are offered another kit at a discount.

assembly-job-scam.whyItWorks: The buy-back guarantee makes the kit feel like a refundable deposit on paid work. When the batch is rejected, people blame their own handiwork and buy a second kit, never suspecting that no batch was ever going to pass.

realVsFake.real: A manufacturer that uses home workers supplies the parts at its own cost, because it needs the finished goods to sell.
realVsFake.fake: The company's income is the kit price, so it has no use for the bracelets you send back.

realVsFake.real: Piecework employers give a written rate per item and a measurable standard, such as dimensions or a physical sample.
realVsFake.fake: The standard is described only as 'professional quality', and rejected work comes with no explanation or right of appeal.

realVsFake.real: A real firm has a trading address you can visit and a phone line that someone answers.
realVsFake.fake: Orders go to a PO box or web form, and the only reviews are glowing ones on the seller's own page.

steps.title: A sleeve inside the slot
steps.detail: Before you arrive, someone slides a thin plastic or metal loop into the card slot. It lets a card in and grips it when the machine tries to return it.

steps.title: The transaction stalls
steps.detail: You insert your card and nothing normal follows. The screen may time out or ask you to retry, and the card does not come back.

steps.title: Advice from the queue
steps.detail: Someone behind you says the same thing happened last week and that typing the PIN two or three times releases it. They stand where the keypad is visible.

steps.title: Fishing the card out
steps.detail: Once you give up and go to ring the bank, the thief pulls the loop out with your card attached, already knowing the PIN, and withdraws cash nearby.

atm-card-trapping-scam.whyItWorks: A swallowed card looks like a machine fault, which everyone has seen before, so a bystander with a fix seems kind and well informed. Walking away to get help feels sensible, and it is the gap the thief is waiting for.

realVsFake.real: When a cash machine genuinely retains a card, it shows a message saying so and the card is held deep inside.
realVsFake.fake: The screen gives no clear retention message and the card sits just inside the slot, gripped by an insert.

realVsFake.real: Bank staff never need you to type your PIN again to free a stuck card.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger urges you to key it in repeatedly while leaning in to watch your fingers.

realVsFake.real: Your bank can cancel a card instantly by phone or in its app while you are still standing there.
realVsFake.fake: The helper suggests popping into the branch or coming back tomorrow, which leaves the machine unattended.

steps.title: Watching the queue
steps.detail: Two or three people hang about near a busy cash machine, picking someone who is alone, has bags in hand, or is slow with the keys.

steps.title: Shoulder view of four digits
steps.detail: One stands close enough behind to see the PIN go in, or films it on a phone held casually at chest height.

steps.title: The dropped banknote
steps.detail: As the card or cash is about to come out, a second person taps you, points at money on the floor, spills a drink, or unfolds a map.

steps.title: A swap in two seconds
steps.detail: While your head is turned, the first person lifts your card from the slot, sometimes sliding in a lookalike, or takes notes from the tray and walks off.

atm-distraction-scam.whyItWorks: Being told you dropped money triggers an automatic glance down, and it would feel rude to ignore someone apparently doing you a kindness. The machine's own timing helps the thieves, since card and cash sit exposed for a few seconds.

realVsFake.real: A considerate member of the public waits a couple of metres back until you have finished at the machine.
realVsFake.fake: Someone closes in beside you and starts talking at the exact second your card emerges.

realVsFake.real: A passer-by who spots a dropped note mentions it once and moves on.
realVsFake.fake: The person keeps pointing, touching your arm and stepping between you and the screen.

realVsFake.real: The card you put away should carry your own name and your bank's design.
realVsFake.fake: You are handed, or find in the slot, a card from another bank or bearing someone else's name, and only notice later.

steps.title: A host family finds your profile
steps.detail: A message arrives through an au pair matching site or social group from a 'family' abroad, with photos of smiling children, a large house and an unusually generous weekly allowance.

steps.title: Chosen without a video call
steps.detail: After a few warm emails the parents say you are their choice. They are always too busy with work or travel to speak on camera, but send a contract to sign.

steps.title: Meet the family's 'agent'
steps.detail: You are passed to a travel agent or lawyer who needs about 500 dollars for the visa and compulsory insurance, sent by money transfer service in the agent's personal name.

steps.title: Or a check for the flights
steps.detail: In the other version the family posts a check 'for flights', far too large, and asks you to bank it and wire the balance to the agent. The check later bounces.

au-pair-scam.whyItWorks: Moving abroad to live with strangers really does involve visas, insurance and flights booked in advance, so each charge matches what an applicant expects. Family photos and affectionate emails build trust that a faceless employer never could.

realVsFake.real: Real host families video call several times, show you the children and the house, and let you speak to a previous au pair.
realVsFake.fake: The parents write long emails but the camera is always broken, or one of them is 'away on a ship'.

realVsFake.real: You apply for the visa yourself, through the embassy or the sponsoring agency's official process, and pay the government fee directly.
realVsFake.fake: A private 'agent' says he will obtain the visa for you once cash reaches him by money transfer.

realVsFake.real: A family that pays for flights books the ticket and emails you the airline's confirmation.
realVsFake.fake: They send a check for several times the fare and want the difference wired back within two days.

steps.title: Hired 'pending screening'
steps.detail: After a quick application and perhaps a text-only interview, an email says you have the job, subject to a mandatory background check that must be completed before a start date is set.

steps.title: The partner screening link
steps.detail: The recruiter insists you use one particular 'partner' site and no other. The link opens a page with a 45 dollar screening charge and a card form.

steps.title: ID upload alongside the card
steps.detail: Alongside the payment, the page asks for a photo of your licence or passport, your Social Security number and date of birth, all described as standard for employment screening.

steps.title: Report 'processing', job gone
steps.detail: The screen says results take three working days. The recruiter stops answering, the card may be billed again each month, and your ID scan is now in a criminal's hands.

background-check-fee-scam.whyItWorks: Background checks are a normal last step in hiring, so being asked for one feels like confirmation the offer is real. The fee is pitched low enough that paying seems easier than risking the job over 45 dollars.

realVsFake.real: Employers normally order and pay for screening themselves, and the invitation comes from the screening firm after a written offer.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to pay for your own check through a link the recruiter supplies, before any contract exists.

realVsFake.real: A real check starts with a consent form naming the employer and the screening firm, which you can look up independently.
realVsFake.fake: The page shows no company name beyond a logo, has no consent wording, and goes straight to card details.

realVsFake.real: Identity documents are usually shown on or just before your first day, to someone in HR, to prove your right to work.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger wants your passport photo and full ID number uploaded to a website within hours of first contact.

steps.title: The listing that stands out
steps.detail: A sofa, bike, washing machine or camera is advertised in clean photos at a price that undercuts every similar advert in your area.

steps.title: Sold this morning
steps.detail: Your first message gets a quick apology: that exact one went a few hours ago. The advert stays up for days, still pulling in new enquiries.

steps.title: A similar one, slightly dearer
steps.detail: They offer another model 'for a bit more', describe it as nearly identical, and send one blurry photo or none. Questions about age or faults get vague answers.

steps.title: Reserve it with 100
steps.detail: A 100 deposit is requested to stop the replacement going to someone else. You either lose the deposit or collect something older and worse than described.

bait-and-switch-listing-scam.whyItWorks: By the time you hear the bargain has gone, you have already decided to buy and perhaps told someone you found one. Missing out once makes the second offer feel like a rescue, so you judge it less harshly than a fresh advert.

realVsFake.real: An honest seller marks the advert as sold or deletes it once the item has gone.
realVsFake.fake: The cheap listing is renewed every week although it has been 'sold' to every person who asked.

realVsFake.real: A private seller with a second item will post it as its own advert with its own photos and price.
realVsFake.fake: The alternative exists only in chat, at a price that rises when you show interest.

realVsFake.real: Shops that run out of an advertised offer give a rain check, a refund or the same goods later.
realVsFake.fake: You are steered to a different product and asked to pay before you have looked at it.

steps.title: The bank's number on your screen
steps.detail: Your phone displays the number printed on the back of your card, which has been spoofed. The caller gives a name, a staff ID and quotes your address.

steps.title: Payments you never made
steps.detail: They read out a transaction in another city and ask if it was you. When you say no, they 'block' it and hint that a branch insider is suspected.

steps.title: Opening the 'safe account'
steps.detail: A new account has supposedly been created in your name. They dictate a sort code and account number, and coach you on answering the app's warning screens.

steps.title: Codes read aloud
steps.detail: Each one-time passcode that arrives is requested 'to confirm it's you'. In reality every code approves a new payee or a payment the caller is making.

bank-impersonation-phone-scam.whyItWorks: The caller already knows your name, address and sometimes recent transactions, taken from a data leak or an earlier phishing text, so they sound like someone looking at your account. Fear of losing savings in the next few minutes crowds out the thought of hanging up.

realVsFake.real: Your bank can freeze a card or block a payment itself, without you doing anything.
realVsFake.fake: Only you can protect the money, the caller says, by transferring it out yourself.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fraud staff are happy for you to hang up and ring the number on your card.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the line must stay open, or that calling the branch would tip off the corrupt employee.

realVsFake.real: A passcode text states what it is for, and the bank's own wording tells you never to share it.
realVsFake.fake: The caller asks you to ignore what the text says and just read out the six digits.

steps.title: The compliance notice
steps.detail: A text or WhatsApp bearing the bank's logo says your 'Know Your Customer' record has expired under new regulations and the account will be suspended tonight.

steps.title: A form in the bank's colours
steps.detail: The link opens a mobile page copied from the bank's site. It asks for customer ID and password first, as though you were simply logging in.

steps.title: Document and card upload
steps.detail: Further screens want card number, expiry, CVV, date of birth and a photo of your ID or tax number, all presented as the identity update.

steps.title: The OTP 'to complete KYC'
steps.detail: A final box asks for the code just sent to your phone. That code is authorising the fraudster's login or a transfer out of the real account.

bank-kyc-scam.whyItWorks: Banks really do ask customers to refresh identity documents from time to time, so the request itself is not strange. Mixing a familiar piece of bureaucracy with a same-day freeze makes people rush through a form they would normally question.

realVsFake.real: When a bank needs updated identity documents, it usually tells you inside its app, by letter, or asks you to visit a branch.
realVsFake.fake: The demand comes from an ordinary mobile number with a shortened link and a cut-off time of tonight.

realVsFake.real: An identity update asks for a document, never your card PIN, CVV or a one-time code.
realVsFake.fake: The 'verification' form collects everything needed to log in and spend, and almost nothing a compliance team would use.

realVsFake.real: Banks typically send reminders over several weeks before restricting an account for missing paperwork.
realVsFake.fake: The message arrives once, with hours to comply and no reference number you could quote at a branch.

steps.title: They know about the first loss
steps.detail: Weeks after you were defrauded, a caller from 'the bank's reimbursement team' quotes the date, the amount and the name of the bogus firm that took it.

steps.title: Your claim is 'approved'
steps.detail: They say an internal review found in your favour and the refund is ready, pending a short security check of your identity and account.

steps.title: The check that takes control
steps.detail: You are asked for online banking details, a passcode, or to install a support app so they can 'credit the refund while you watch'.

steps.title: A release fee or 'test payment'
steps.detail: A small charge is requested to free the funds, or you are steered into sending money out to 'reverse' a refund they pretend was overpaid.

bank-reimbursement-scam.whyItWorks: The details of the earlier fraud are known only to you, your bank and the criminals who did it, so a caller who has them sounds like the bank. Someone still hoping to see that money again is primed to welcome the call.

realVsFake.real: A fraud refund follows a claim you raised, and the bank gives its decision through secure messages or by post.
realVsFake.fake: A team you have never dealt with rings out of nowhere to announce a payout.

realVsFake.real: When a bank reimburses you, the money simply appears in your account. Nothing is charged for it.
realVsFake.fake: A fee, tax or 'matching deposit' must be sent before the refund can be freed.

realVsFake.real: Bank staff already hold your account details and have no need for your password or your screen.
realVsFake.fake: The caller wants you logged in with a remote-access tool running so they can 'process' it.

steps.title: The routine monthly notice
steps.detail: Around month end an email in your bank's colours says your e-statement is available, written in the same calm tone as the genuine one.

steps.title: A quiet nudge to click
steps.detail: One added line says to review recent activity or paperless billing will be suspended. Some versions attach an HTML 'statement' that opens a login form.

steps.title: The fake online banking page
steps.detail: It asks for customer number and password, then your memorable word in full, where the real site would ask for only a few characters.

steps.title: The fraud team rings
steps.detail: Criminals log in but need a code to add a payee. Someone phones as the bank's fraud department, quotes your details and asks you to read it out.

bank-statement-email-scam.whyItWorks: This is among the dullest emails a bank sends, and that is the camouflage. Nobody feels alarmed by a statement notice, so the habit of clicking through and logging in takes over without a second look.

realVsFake.real: A genuine statement notice tells you to sign in through the app or your usual route and often shows part of your postcode or account number.
realVsFake.fake: It greets you as 'Dear Customer' and supplies its own 'View statement' button.

realVsFake.real: Many banks ask for selected characters of a memorable word, never the whole thing at once.
realVsFake.fake: The page wants every character, then your card PIN and mobile number.

realVsFake.real: Paperless statements carry on whether or not you open a particular month's notice.
realVsFake.fake: The email claims paperless billing ends unless you log in through its link.

steps.title: The bonus advert
steps.detail: A sponsored post or email in a bank's branding offers a few hundred as a welcome payment for moving your current account this week.

steps.title: A short application
steps.detail: The landing page asks for name, date of birth, address and phone number, just as real account opening does, which builds confidence.

steps.title: 'Connect your existing bank'
steps.detail: A screen lists bank logos. Pick yours and a copy of its login page appears, asking for username, password and memorable word to 'import direct debits automatically'.

steps.title: A code to finish the switch
steps.detail: The page requests the passcode your real bank just sent. Criminals use it live to enter your account, and keep the identity details for later.

bank-switch-scam.whyItWorks: Switching incentives are genuine and widely advertised, so a cash offer raises no eyebrows. People also assume that moving an account must involve proving they own the old one, which makes typing the old login feel like a normal step.

realVsFake.real: In a genuine switch you give the new bank your old sort code and account number, and the banks move everything between themselves.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for your old bank's password and security answers.

realVsFake.real: A switching bonus is usually paid weeks later, after conditions such as paying in salary are met.
realVsFake.fake: The offer promises the cash instantly once you 'verify' your current account today.

realVsFake.real: A bank's sign-up form lives on its own website or app, which you can reach by typing the bank's name yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The form sits on an address built from the bank's name plus words like 'bonus' or 'switch-offer'.

steps.title: A text headed GOV NOTICE
steps.detail: A text from an ordinary mobile number says you are eligible for a one-off cost-of-living payment of £450 and must apply before a closing date.

steps.title: The copied government page
steps.detail: The link opens a page with the crown logo and black header bar. An 'eligibility check' asks for your name, date of birth, address and National Insurance number.

steps.title: Choosing where the money goes
steps.detail: A second screen asks for the sort code and account number 'for the deposit', then the long card number, expiry date and security code to 'verify the account'.

steps.title: A confirmation, then nothing
steps.detail: You see a reference number and a promise of payment in five working days. No money comes. The card is used online and your details are sold on.

benefits-payment-scam.whyItWorks: Support payments are announced on the news with amounts very like this one, and they reach people who are already stretched. When money is tight, filling in a short form for a few hundred pounds feels like ordinary benefit admin, not a risk.

realVsFake.real: Genuine cost-of-living payments were paid automatically into the account that already receives your benefit. Nobody had to apply.
realVsFake.fake: The text says the money is waiting but will be lost unless you claim it through the link.

realVsFake.real: The department paying your benefit holds your bank details on file and has no use for your card's security code.
realVsFake.fake: The form asks for an account to pay into and then a debit card, which is only needed to take money out.

realVsFake.real: News about a real award appears in your online benefit journal or in a letter quoting your claim.
realVsFake.fake: It comes from a pay-as-you-go mobile number, with 'GOV' typed into the message itself to look official.

steps.title: Free bet lands by text
steps.detail: A message announces a $50 free bet or casino spins 'credited to you', from a name that resembles a bookmaker but is not one you hold an account with.

steps.title: Sign-up on a clone sportsbook
steps.detail: The link opens a site with odds tables and slot tiles. Registering to 'claim' asks for your email, a password, your date of birth and a phone number.

steps.title: Deposit to unlock the bonus
steps.detail: A balance appears showing the bonus, but withdrawing needs a 'qualifying deposit' by card. The site takes the full card details and sometimes repeats the charge.

steps.title: ID upload for 'verification'
steps.detail: When you ask for a payout, support requests photos of your passport or driving licence and a selfie. No winnings are ever paid, and the documents get reused.

betting-bonus-text-scam.whyItWorks: Licensed bookmakers really do send free-bet texts, so the format is familiar to anyone who has ever placed a wager. Because the bonus seems to cost nothing, handing over a card 'just to verify' feels like a formality.

realVsFake.real: A licensed operator only texts offers to customers who opted in, and the bonus shows inside the account you already log in to.
realVsFake.fake: The text comes from a brand you never joined and the free bet exists only on the linked site.

realVsFake.real: Genuine bookmakers display their gambling licence number in the site footer, and you can look it up on the regulator's register.
realVsFake.fake: The footer shows badge images that go nowhere, or names a licence from a country you cannot check.

realVsFake.real: Real free bets have written wagering terms and never need a deposit just to see a withdrawal button.
realVsFake.fake: Each attempt to cash out produces a new condition: another deposit, a fee, or a fresh identity photo.

steps.title: Winning slips on your feed
steps.detail: A tipster account posts screenshots of winning bet slips and crypto trades, with captions about quitting a day job and a link to a free Telegram channel.

steps.title: Free tips that happen to win
steps.detail: In the free channel, a few short-priced selections come in. Losing tips are quietly deleted, and different members were sent opposite picks for the same match.

steps.title: The VIP room
steps.detail: You are invited to pay a monthly fee for the VIP group, where 'inside information' or 'fixed matches' are promised and only a handful of places remain.

steps.title: Losing twice over
steps.detail: The paid tips lose as often as any guess. The tipster still earns, from your subscription and from commission on losses at the bookmaker you joined through their link.

betting-tipster-scam.whyItWorks: A screenshot of a winning slip feels like evidence, and nobody posts the losers. Sending opposite predictions to different groups guarantees that some people see a perfect run, and those are the people who are asked to pay.

realVsFake.real: An honest tipster logs every selection before the event with a timestamp, losers included, where anyone can audit the record.
realVsFake.fake: The record is a camera roll of winning slips, some edited, with no way to see what was tipped last week.

realVsFake.real: Anyone credible in betting or trading says plainly that losing runs happen and that no result is certain.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch uses 'fixed', 'insider' and 'cannot lose', and offers a money-back promise that is never honoured.

realVsFake.real: A genuine adviser has no stake in which bookmaker or broker you use.
realVsFake.fake: The tips supposedly only work at one particular site, opened through a sign-up link that pays the tipster when you lose.

steps.title: A frightening phone call
steps.detail: Someone claiming to be a fraud officer, tax official or detective says your identity is tied to a crime, or that your savings are about to be seized.

steps.title: Cash out, with a cover story
steps.detail: They direct you to withdraw a large sum and, if the cashier asks, to say it is for home repairs. Bank staff, you are told, are under investigation.

steps.title: Directions to a kiosk
steps.detail: Still on the line, they guide you to a crypto machine in a petrol station or corner shop, calling it a 'government safe locker' or 'federal wallet'.

steps.title: Scan, feed, repeat
steps.detail: A QR code arrives by text. You hold it to the scanner and feed notes in. The coins go to their wallet, and they ask for a photo of the receipt.

bitcoin-atm-scam.whyItWorks: Staying on the phone means the victim never gets a quiet minute to think or ask anyone, and the caller supplies a ready answer for every warning sticker on the machine. The kiosk resembles a bank terminal, so feeding cash in feels like a deposit.

realVsFake.real: No bank, tax office, court or police force takes payment or 'protects' money through a cryptocurrency machine.
realVsFake.fake: The kiosk, the caller says, is linked to a secure government account created for your case.

realVsFake.real: A person using a crypto kiosk for themselves scans a wallet they own, from their own app.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent somebody else's QR code by text and told not to show it to shop staff.

realVsFake.real: Genuine officials let you end the call, take advice and reply in writing.
realVsFake.fake: The caller orders you to keep the phone in your pocket on speaker and to lie to anyone who asks what you are doing.

steps.title: A flagship at a quick-sale price
steps.detail: A recent handset is listed well under the going rate. The seller says they are upgrading, moving abroad or short of rent, and wants it gone today.

steps.title: The IMEI question dodged
steps.detail: Ask for the 15-digit IMEI and you get a promise that it is clean, a photo with the number cropped out, or digits from a different phone.

steps.title: Handover without a SIM test
steps.detail: They want payment before posting, or meet you briefly with the phone switched on at the home screen and no chance to insert your own SIM.

steps.title: No service a week later
steps.detail: The phone works on wifi, then loses signal once the network blocklists it, or a reset brings up a lock screen asking for the previous owner's password.

blocked-phone-sale-scam.whyItWorks: A stolen or finance-blocked handset looks and behaves like any other until the network acts on the report, which can take days. The buyer sees a working screen and a fair excuse for the low price, and has no reason to doubt it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine owner can dial *#06# in front of you and let you run the number through a checker.
realVsFake.fake: The seller says there is 'no need' to check and changes the subject to how many others are asking.

realVsFake.real: Someone selling their own phone signs out of their cloud account and erases it while you watch.
realVsFake.fake: The device is 'all set up and ready to go', still showing another person's name in settings.

realVsFake.real: An honest seller usually has the box, a receipt or a contract showing the handset is paid off.
realVsFake.fake: There is no box or charger, and the story about where it came from changes between messages.

steps.title: Details bought in bulk
steps.detail: Your name, date of birth, address and email turn up in a leaked database, or are collected through a fake delivery or shop page.

steps.title: An account opens in minutes
steps.detail: A fraudster signs up with a pay-later provider as you, using their own phone number, or resets the password on an account you already have.

steps.title: Goods sent somewhere else
steps.detail: They order trainers, phones or gift cards that resell easily, shipped to a parcel locker, a drop address, or intercepted on your doorstep.

steps.title: Instalments fall due
steps.detail: The first you hear is a reminder email, a late fee, or a letter from a collections firm. Missed instalments may already be recorded against your name.

bnpl-fraud-scam.whyItWorks: Pay-later checkouts are built to approve a shopper in seconds using a soft check and a few personal details, which suits customers and equally suits someone holding a stolen identity. The victim is not involved at all until the bills arrive.

realVsFake.real: When you open a pay-later account yourself, you get a welcome email and a code to your own phone that you asked for.
realVsFake.fake: A verification code arrives when you are not shopping, or a welcome email names a retailer you have never used.

realVsFake.real: Your genuine orders go to your address and appear in the provider's app under your login.
realVsFake.fake: The order shows a delivery address in another town and a contact number that is not yours.

realVsFake.real: Providers have a fraud team, reached through their app or official site, who can pause a disputed plan while they look into it.
realVsFake.fake: A text about the 'debt' tells you to pay through a link to keep it away from collections.

steps.title: 'You qualify for a free boiler'
steps.detail: A cold call or social media advert says anyone with a boiler over ten years old qualifies for a free government replacement, and asks you to confirm a few details.

steps.title: The eligibility check
steps.detail: The 'adviser' asks which benefits you receive, your National Insurance number, date of birth and the bank account your benefits are paid into, supposedly to match you to the scheme.

steps.title: The assessment booking charge
steps.detail: A 'refundable' charge of 50 to 150 is taken by card to reserve an engineer's visit. The appointment is moved, moved again, and then the line goes dead.

steps.title: Condemned on the spot
steps.detail: Where someone does visit, the 'engineer' declares the old boiler unsafe, says the grant covers only part of the cost and pushes a same-day contract for the remainder.

boiler-grant-scam.whyItWorks: Heating schemes for low-income households do exist, and a failing boiler is one of the largest bills a home can face. Someone who has heard that a neighbour got one fitted free is ready to believe it is their turn.

realVsFake.real: Real heating grants are applied for through your energy supplier, your council or the government website, and you make the first move.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger rings or messages to say you have already been approved.

realVsFake.real: Eligibility is confirmed with benefit letters or a council check, and no scheme charges for the home visit.
realVsFake.fake: An assessment charge is taken by card before anyone has seen the house.

realVsFake.real: A registered gas engineer carries a Gas Safe card, and you can check the licence number on it.
realVsFake.fake: The visitor has a polo shirt and a clipboard, and bristles when asked for a registration number.

steps.title: A cold call from a 'brokerage'
steps.detail: A well-spoken caller from a firm with a City or Wall Street sounding name says you are on a list of experienced investors, and offers to send a research report.

steps.title: The tip about a tiny company
steps.detail: A week later a 'senior broker' rings about an obscure mining or biotech share, said to be days from a takeover or stock market listing.

steps.title: How much can you place today
steps.detail: The allocation closes this afternoon. A trade confirmation is emailed, and you wire payment to an overseas bank account in a company name you do not recognise.

steps.title: Certificates you cannot sell
steps.detail: Statements show the price climbing, which prompts calls to buy more. When you ask to sell, there is a lock-in period, a release fee, then a dead line.

boiler-room-stock-scam.whyItWorks: Being addressed as a sophisticated investor is flattering, and the patient first call with no sales pitch builds credit for the second. The share is too obscure to look up, so the caller's glossy report becomes the only information you have.

realVsFake.real: Authorised stockbrokers appear on the regulator's register and rarely ring strangers with a share to sell.
realVsFake.fake: The firm's name copies a registered one, but its phone number and address differ from those on the register.

realVsFake.real: Listed shares are bought through your own brokerage account and can be sold on the exchange on any trading day.
realVsFake.fake: The stock is unlisted or thinly traded on a distant market, and only the caller's firm will supposedly buy it back.

realVsFake.real: A genuine adviser asks about your finances and attitude to risk, and puts warnings in writing.
realVsFake.fake: The salesman's only question is the size of your savings, and he rings daily until you commit a figure.

steps.title: Remote bookkeeper wanted
steps.detail: A listing for a part-time remote bookkeeper or accounts assistant asks for little experience. The 'finance manager' interviews you by email or chat and offers the role the same day.

steps.title: Licence fee for 'our' software
steps.detail: Before you start you must buy the firm's accounting software licence or a short certification from its 'approved vendor', paid by card, transfer or cryptocurrency.

steps.title: Client payments reach your account
steps.detail: Your first task is not keeping books. Because the firm's 'local account is still being set up', customer invoices will be paid into your personal bank account for now.

steps.title: Forward it, minus your fee
steps.detail: You are told to keep a small processing fee and send the remainder the same day to 'suppliers' overseas. The deposits were stolen from other victims, and your account is the one traced.

bookkeeping-job-scam.whyItWorks: Handling payments sounds like exactly what a bookkeeper does, so 'client money' arriving in your own account seems like part of the role. The title lends respectability, and the missing company account is explained away as a temporary set-up problem.
