realVsFake.real: A bookkeeper records transactions inside the client's own accounting system, using a login the client grants.
realVsFake.fake: No ledger or login is ever provided. The only 'bookkeeping' is watching for deposits and passing them along.

realVsFake.real: Business income goes into a business bank account held in the company's name.
realVsFake.fake: Customers are told to pay you personally, and you are coached on what to say if your bank queries it.

realVsFake.real: Firms that need staff on particular software give them a seat on the company's licence.
realVsFake.fake: The new hire is sent to a vendor nobody has heard of to buy a licence key out of their own pocket.

steps.title: An alert with a familiar logo
steps.detail: An email or text styled as a bank, a password manager or a credit agency says your details were found in a breach or on the dark web.

steps.title: A real old password as proof
steps.detail: The message may quote a password you once used, taken from an old leak. Seeing it in print makes the warning feel personal and current.

steps.title: The 'Secure my account' button
steps.detail: The button leads to a copied login page that asks for your current password and the six-digit code your phone has just received.

steps.title: Locked out, or billed
steps.detail: Using what you typed, the criminals sign in to the real account and change the recovery email. Other versions sell 'identity protection' and take a card.

breach-notification-scam.whyItWorks: Real breaches are reported so often that most people have received a genuine notice, and the standard advice is to change your password quickly. The scam gives that same advice and simply supplies the page where you do it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine breach notice says what happened, when, and which data was involved, then tells you to visit the site yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The fake names no incident or date. It offers a red warning banner and a single button.

realVsFake.real: Companies that lose customer data usually offer free credit monitoring through a named provider, using an enrolment code.
realVsFake.fake: 'Protection' is sold for a monthly sum, with your card and national ID number collected on the same form.

realVsFake.real: Password managers and browsers show leak warnings inside the app itself, next to the affected login.
realVsFake.fake: The warning arrives by email from an address unrelated to the brand, and never says which login is affected.

steps.title: Your address is picked up
steps.detail: A seller obtains your name and address from a leaked customer list or a past order, then creates a shopping account in your name on a marketplace.

steps.title: A parcel of cheap odds and ends
steps.detail: A light packet arrives with no invoice: hair ties, seeds, a phone ring holder, a cheap bracelet. The seller needed a real tracking number showing delivery.

steps.title: A five-star review appears
steps.detail: With delivery confirmed, the seller posts a glowing 'verified purchase' review under your name for a much pricier product, lifting its ranking.

steps.title: The card with a QR code
steps.detail: Later parcels may include a card inviting you to scan a QR code to 'find out who sent your gift' or pay a small customs fee. That page asks for logins or card details.

brushing-scam.whyItWorks: A free parcel does not feel like an attack, so most people shrug and keep it. Curiosity about who sent it is the lever: a QR code that promises an answer gets scanned by people who would never click a link in an email.

realVsFake.real: A genuine gift arrives with a gift note or packing slip naming the sender and the shop it came from.
realVsFake.fake: A brushing parcel has a return address that is a freight depot or a jumble of letters, and nothing inside explains it.

realVsFake.real: Any real charge on a delivery is tied to an order you can find in your own account with the retailer or carrier.
realVsFake.fake: A printed card tucked in the packet asks for payment or 'registration' through a QR code, for goods you never bought.

realVsFake.real: Reviews on your shopping profile should match things you ordered, and your order history should hold no surprises.
realVsFake.fake: A profile in your name praises a product you have never seen, or your own account shows an order you did not place.

steps.title: Congratulations on a grant you never sought
steps.detail: An email, social media message or call tells the owner their company has been selected for a government or foundation grant that needs no repayment.

steps.title: A form asking for the company file
steps.detail: The 'grant officer' sends an application asking for the registration number, directors' dates of birth, turnover and the business bank account for the payout.

steps.title: Awarded, subject to a processing fee
steps.detail: An award letter with a crest and reference number confirms the sum. Before release, a processing or legal fee of a few hundred must be paid.

steps.title: Release keeps slipping
steps.detail: After the first fee comes a 'tax clearance' charge, then an anti-fraud deposit. No grant is ever paid, and the company details are reused for other fraud.

business-grant-scam.whyItWorks: Real grant schemes do exist and are poorly publicised, so an owner who has never applied for one has no idea what the process looks like. A few hundred in fees seems trivial against a five-figure award for a firm short of cash.

realVsFake.real: Government and foundation grants are won through a published application with eligibility rules, a deadline and a named scheme.
realVsFake.fake: The business is told it was pre-selected from a database and only needs to confirm details to be paid.

realVsFake.real: Public funders do not charge applicants to receive an award they have been granted.
realVsFake.fake: Each stage has a new fee payable by transfer to a personal account or in cryptocurrency.

realVsFake.real: A real award comes with conditions: what the money may be spent on, reporting dates and often match funding.
realVsFake.fake: The offer letter says the funds are unrestricted and names no project, only a deadline for claiming.

steps.title: A letter weeks after you form
steps.detail: Company filings are public, so soon after you register an LLC a letter arrives quoting your exact business name, filing number and formation date.

steps.title: Dressed as a state form
steps.detail: It carries an eagle or seal-style emblem, a barcode, a 'respond by' date and a tear-off payment slip, sent by something like 'Business Compliance Division'.

steps.title: The fee for a free filing
steps.detail: The slip asks for a three-figure sum for an EIN, a certificate of good standing or 'annual minutes'. A faint line admits it is not a government agency.

steps.title: The cheque goes to a mail drop
steps.detail: You post a cheque or enter a card on the site named in the letter. At best they file a form you could have filed yourself; often nothing is filed.

business-registration-scam.whyItWorks: A new owner has just worked through a stack of unfamiliar filings and fully expects more to follow. A letter that quotes the real entity number, uses penalty language and arrives in that first month looks like the next step on the list.

realVsFake.real: The IRS issues an EIN free of charge through its own online application, usually in one sitting.
realVsFake.fake: A site found through a search advert charges a 'filing fee' to retype your answers into that same free form.

realVsFake.real: Your state's business registry writes under its own name and takes annual report fees on its own website.
realVsFake.fake: The sender's title sounds governmental, but the return address is a rented mailbox and payment goes to a private company.

realVsFake.real: Official filing deadlines follow a published calendar, such as the anniversary of formation, and the fee is listed publicly.
realVsFake.fake: The letter invents its own cut-off a fortnight away and warns of dissolution or fines if the slip is not returned.

steps.title: An offer in your comments
steps.detail: A comment or DM lands on your newest post: ten thousand followers for the price of a coffee, delivered in a day, with a link to a price list.

steps.title: Pick a package
steps.detail: The site lists bundles of followers, likes and views with a countdown discount. Checkout takes a card, a payment app or crypto, and shows no refund terms.

steps.title: Your password to deliver
steps.detail: To 'connect the growth engine', the seller asks for your username and password, and the login code your phone receives when they try to sign in.

steps.title: Bots, a ban or a hijack
steps.detail: Either nothing arrives, or a burst of blank accounts appears and is purged within days. The platform may restrict you, and the seller may now own your login.

buy-followers-scam.whyItWorks: A big follower count looks like success, and for a small creator or shop the shortcut costs less than lunch. Because buying followers breaks platform rules, buyers who get nothing rarely complain, which suits the seller.

realVsFake.real: Platforms sell reach only through their own ad tools, paid for inside the app and reported in your insights.
realVsFake.fake: An outside seller promises a fixed number of 'real, active' followers by tomorrow for a flat fee.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate marketing agency works through delegated access or ad-account roles and never needs your password.
realVsFake.fake: The seller insists delivery is impossible without your login and the six-digit code from your phone.

realVsFake.real: Followers gained from real interest trickle in, comment in their own words and stay.
realVsFake.fake: Purchased followers arrive in one lump, have no posts or faces, and vanish at the next clean-up.

steps.title: The failed instalment text
steps.detail: A text or email using a pay-later brand's name says an instalment of 42.00 was declined and the account is on hold, with late fees starting in 12 hours.

steps.title: A login page in the right colours
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the provider's sign-in screen in its brand colours. You type your phone number or email, then the password.

steps.title: Card details and the texted code
steps.detail: The page then asks you to 'update your payment method' with the full card number and security digits, then to enter the six-digit code just texted to you.

steps.title: Shopping on your credit
steps.detail: That code lets the criminal sign in as you on their own phone. They place orders for electronics and gift cards on your instalment plan, shipped to another address.

buy-now-pay-later-scam.whyItWorks: People running three or four instalment plans rarely remember which payment is due when, so a notice about a failed 42.00 is plausible. Late fees and a mark on a credit file are real consequences, which makes a twelve-hour deadline bite.

realVsFake.real: Pay-later providers show every instalment and its due date inside their app, where a failed payment appears against a specific order.
realVsFake.fake: The message names no shop and no order, only an amount, and the problem is invisible when you open the real app.

realVsFake.real: A genuine sign-in sends a one-time code that you enter in the provider's own app or site, and staff never ask for it.
realVsFake.fake: The copy page asks for the code seconds after you give your number, because the thief is logging in at that moment.

realVsFake.real: When a real instalment fails, providers typically retry the card and send reminders, with days to sort it out.
realVsFake.fake: The scam text gives you until tonight and threatens fees, suspension and debt collectors in a single message.

steps.title: An invitation you never see
steps.detail: Spammers send a calendar invitation to your email address. The email may land in spam, but many calendars add invitations automatically, so the event appears anyway.

steps.title: An odd entry in today's schedule
steps.detail: An event titled 'You have (1) pending payment' or 'iPhone winner, claim today' sits among your real appointments, sometimes repeating every day.

steps.title: Your own calendar buzzes
steps.detail: The reminder pops up on your phone from the calendar app itself, with a link placed in the event's description or location field.

steps.title: Where the link goes
steps.detail: The link opens a fake prize survey, a bogus virus warning or a login form, each ending with a card number or password typed in.

calendar-invite-scam.whyItWorks: A calendar is somewhere only you and people you know write, so an entry there borrows the authority of your own diary. The alert comes from an app you trust, not from a stranger's email.

realVsFake.real: A genuine invitation comes from a person or organisation you recognise, with a time, place or call link that makes sense.
realVsFake.fake: The 'event' is an advert, with a prize or payment warning as its title and a random string as organiser.

realVsFake.real: Real payment reminders from a bank or shop appear in their own app or on your statement.
realVsFake.fake: A calendar alert says money is pending and the only route offered is the link in the notes.

realVsFake.real: Meetings from colleagues list a handful of attendees you could ask about it.
realVsFake.fake: The guest list holds hundreds of unrelated addresses in alphabetical order, with yours among them.

steps.title: An invoice with no link
steps.detail: An email, often with a PDF attached, thanks you for renewing antivirus or a streaming plan for several hundred. There is nothing to click, only a phone number.

steps.title: You make the call
steps.detail: Because you dialled, your guard is down. A calm 'billing agent' with call-centre noise behind them agrees it looks like a mistake and offers to cancel.

steps.title: The cancellation form
steps.detail: They direct you to a website to 'fill in a refund form'. It actually downloads a remote-access program that hands them control of your screen.

steps.title: A refund typed too large
steps.detail: You are asked to enter the refund amount, then they fake an extra zero and plead for the difference back by transfer or gift cards.

callback-phishing-scam.whyItWorks: An email with no links to click slips past spam filters and past the reader's own training about suspicious links. Picking up the phone to dispute a charge feels like the careful, responsible thing to do.

realVsFake.real: A real subscription charge shows on your bank or card statement and in your account with that company.
realVsFake.fake: The 'charge' exists only in the email. Your statement shows nothing.

realVsFake.real: Companies print their support number on their website and often beside the charge on your statement.
realVsFake.fake: The number appears only in the message, and the email comes from a free webmail address.

realVsFake.real: A company cancelling a subscription does it from its own system and refunds the original card.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says cancelling requires their 'refund tool' on your computer and your online banking open in front of them.

steps.title: The right name on screen
steps.detail: Your phone displays your bank's name, or the exact number printed on your card, because the caller has set the outgoing ID to copy it.

steps.title: 'Check the back of your card'
steps.detail: The caller invites you to compare the number on screen with the one on your card. It matches, and that one check does most of the persuading.

steps.title: A payment happening right now
steps.detail: They describe a transaction being attempted this minute, often in a distant city, and say they must stop it while you stay on the line.

steps.title: Codes, transfers or screen access
steps.detail: You are asked to read out a one-time passcode, move your balance to a 'safe account', or install an app so they can 'secure' the handset.

caller-id-spoofing-scam.whyItWorks: People treat the caller display like a signature, yet the phone network simply shows whatever number the calling side supplies. When the digits match the back of your card, doubting the voice feels unreasonable.

realVsFake.real: A bank that phones you is content for you to hang up and ring the number on your card from another phone.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says hanging up will let the fraud go through, and keeps you talking.

realVsFake.real: Banks never ask you to move money to a 'safe account' or to read out a passcode sent by text.
realVsFake.fake: The whole spoofed call builds towards one of those two requests.

realVsFake.real: A genuine fraud team asks you to confirm or deny a payment, and can block the card without your help.
realVsFake.fake: The voice says only you can stop it, by approving a prompt in your banking app or sharing your screen.

steps.title: Looking for a shout-out
steps.detail: You search for a birthday message from an actor or sports star, or comment under their post. An account using their name and headshot replies offering to record one.

steps.title: Cheaper if you book direct
steps.detail: The 'star' or a 'booking manager' says the official site takes a big cut, so paying them directly by gift card or bank transfer costs half.

steps.title: Script taken, rush fee added
steps.detail: They collect the recipient's name and the message you want read out. Then a 'priority filming' charge appears, because the birthday is close and the queue is long.

steps.title: A clip made for nobody
steps.detail: What arrives, if anything, is a generic greeting ripped from someone else's order with no name spoken. Complain and the account blocks you.

cameo-video-scam.whyItWorks: Paid celebrity greetings are a real product, so the offer itself is ordinary. A fixed birthday date creates the hurry, and the idea of cutting out the middleman makes an off-site payment sound like a favour to the star.

realVsFake.real: On a genuine video-greeting platform you choose the person, pay by card on the site and receive the clip in your account.
realVsFake.fake: Payment is steered to gift card codes or a personal transfer, with the order living only in a DM thread.

realVsFake.real: Stars who sell greetings link their booking page from a verified profile and do not chase customers in comments.
realVsFake.fake: A lookalike handle with an extra letter or underscore replies to fans and pitches a discount.

realVsFake.real: A proper personalised clip says the recipient's name and the details you supplied.
realVsFake.fake: The file is a reused 'happy birthday, have a great one' that could be sent to anybody.

steps.title: An instant online valuation
steps.detail: You type your registration and mileage into a car-buying site, add your name, phone and address, and get a figure well above what dealers offered.

steps.title: Booking the inspection
steps.detail: Calls and texts push you to bring the car in quickly because the quote 'expires in days'. You are told to bring the logbook, both keys and ID.

steps.title: The walk-round with a clipboard
steps.detail: An inspector lists stone chips, a kerbed alloy, tyre wear and a missing service stamp, then announces a much lower figure, less an admin or transfer charge.

steps.title: Sign now or drive home
steps.detail: You have taken time off and travelled there, so the cut-price offer is framed as take it or leave it. Bogus sites skip this and sell your details.

car-buyer-scam.whyItWorks: The high quote anchors what you think the car is worth and gets you to stop shopping around. Once you are standing on a forecourt with the logbook in your hand, accepting less feels easier than starting the whole sale again.

realVsFake.real: A fair buyer asks about scratches, service history and tyres before quoting, so the online figure already reflects them.
realVsFake.fake: The form asks almost nothing about condition, which guarantees there will be 'faults' to find later.

realVsFake.real: Reputable car buyers publish their fees up front and hold the quote long enough for you to compare.
realVsFake.fake: Charges appear for the first time on the day, taken off an offer that is valid for ten minutes.

realVsFake.real: A proper trader pays by bank transfer and you can see it arrive before handing over keys.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to sign the logbook over first, with payment promised in a few working days.

steps.title: The mileage is rolled back
steps.detail: Before the advert goes up, a cheap plug-in tool rewrites the digital odometer through the diagnostic port, cutting the displayed mileage in minutes.

steps.title: History tidied to match
steps.detail: Service book pages with higher readings disappear, a fresh book is stamped, or the seller says the paperwork was 'lost in a house move'.

steps.title: Advertised as a low-miler
steps.detail: The listing leads with the mileage and a phrase like 'one careful owner'. At the viewing the seller keeps talk on the dashboard and the price.

steps.title: You pay the low-mileage premium
steps.detail: You hand over a price set by the false reading. The shiny steering wheel, sagging seat bolster and overdue timing belt show up as repair bills later.

car-clocking-scam.whyItWorks: Buyers treat the odometer as a fact because it is a number on the car's own display. Mileage is also the quickest way to compare two similar cars, so a low reading does most of the selling before anyone looks underneath.

realVsFake.real: A straight car has test certificates and invoices where the recorded mileage climbs steadily year after year.
realVsFake.fake: Readings jump backwards between two tests, or several years of records are simply missing.

realVsFake.real: Genuine low-mileage cars have firm seats, textured pedal rubbers and a matt steering wheel.
realVsFake.fake: The clock shows a short life, but the driver's seat is collapsed and the gear knob is worn smooth.

realVsFake.real: A seller with nothing to hide gives you the registration early so you can run a history check.
realVsFake.fake: The number plate is blurred in the photos, and you are told checks are a waste of money.

steps.title: A car priced to move
steps.detail: A tidy hatchback or pickup appears on a classifieds site for much less than others like it. The photos are lifted from an old dealer advert.

steps.title: The deployment story
steps.detail: By email the seller explains they have been posted overseas with the military, or are selling after a bereavement, and the vehicle is sealed in storage.

steps.title: The 'vehicle protection' invoice
steps.detail: An official-looking invoice arrives carrying a marketplace logo, a case number and a money-back guarantee, with instructions to pay the deposit by wire or gift cards.

steps.title: Delivery that never leaves
steps.detail: A 'shipping agent' confirms a delivery date, then asks for insurance or a transport top-up. No transporter is booked and the listing vanishes.

car-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: A soldier posted abroad is a seller people want to help, and it neatly explains both the low price and the missing viewing. The guarantee on the invoice makes paying first feel safer than handing cash to a stranger on a driveway.

realVsFake.real: Classified sites are noticeboards. They do not hold buyers' money, store cars or deliver them.
realVsFake.fake: The seller says the site's 'protection programme' has the car and will ship it once you pay.

realVsFake.real: A private seller meets you with the car and the registration document, and lets you drive it.
realVsFake.fake: Every request to view is answered with the storage unit, the posting abroad and a tracking promise.

realVsFake.real: Normal car sales are paid by bank transfer or banker's draft at handover.
realVsFake.fake: The invoice lists gift card brands or a wire to a named individual in another region.

steps.title: The headline monthly price
steps.detail: A social media advert or a cloned broker site shows a new SUV or electric car at a monthly figure far below any main dealer's.

steps.title: A quick 'credit approval'
steps.detail: You fill in an application with income, address history and bank details. An approval email comes back within the hour, though no lender has searched your file.

steps.title: Reserve it for 500
steps.detail: The broker asks for a 500 admin and processing fee by bank transfer to hold the vehicle, and says the contract follows once the money clears.

steps.title: Delivery dates and more charges
steps.detail: A delivery slot is given, then pushed back for a 'registration' or 'insurance' charge. The phone line stops answering and the advert reappears under a new name.

car-leasing-scam.whyItWorks: Lease pricing is confusing, with initial rentals, mileage limits and broker fees, so few people know what a fair monthly figure is. Real brokers do charge admin fees, which makes this one sound like normal paperwork.

realVsFake.real: A regulated broker shows its authorisation number, and you can look the firm up on the financial regulator's public register.
realVsFake.fake: The number quoted belongs to a different company, or the name on the register has another address.

realVsFake.real: With a real lease you sign a finance agreement with a named funder before any money moves.
realVsFake.fake: Money is wanted first, and the 'contract' is a one-page order form with no finance company on it.

realVsFake.real: Genuine initial rentals are collected by the funder, normally by direct debit after delivery is arranged.
realVsFake.fake: The fee goes by transfer to a personal or unrelated business account, with a deadline of today.

steps.title: A search advert at the top
steps.detail: You search for car hire at an airport and click the top sponsored result, a site with a familiar-sounding name and day rates that undercut every known brand.

steps.title: The reservations line
steps.detail: The site or a search listing gives a 'reservations desk' phone number. The agent who answers uses a real rental brand's name and quotes a special prepaid rate.

steps.title: Prepay to lock the rate
steps.detail: To hold the price you must pay the whole rental now, by bank transfer or by reading out the numbers from prepaid cards bought at a shop.

steps.title: No booking at the desk
steps.detail: A confirmation email arrives with a made-up reference. At the airport counter, staff find no reservation under your name, and the only cars left cost walk-up prices.

car-rental-booking-scam.whyItWorks: Car hire is usually booked in a hurry, late in trip planning, by people comparing on price alone. Sponsored results sit above the real brands, and prepaying for a discount is a genuine industry habit, so the request does not jar.

realVsFake.real: Rental companies take bookings by credit or debit card on their own site and want the main driver's card shown at pick-up.
realVsFake.fake: The fake desk will not accept a card on file and steers you to a transfer or prepaid vouchers.

realVsFake.real: A genuine reservation number can be pulled up in the 'manage booking' section of the rental brand's official site.
realVsFake.fake: The reference you were emailed returns 'not found' there, and the helpline says the system is 'still syncing'.

realVsFake.real: Real rental terms spell out the excess, fuel policy, mileage limit and the address of the pick-up branch.
realVsFake.fake: The confirmation is three lines long and says a representative will 'meet you in the arrivals hall'.

steps.title: Paid to drive with a decal
steps.detail: A text, email or campus flyer offers a few hundred dollars a week for carrying a drinks or tech brand's advert on your car. A short form collects your address and vehicle model.

steps.title: A check lands by courier
steps.detail: Within days an express envelope brings a check for around 2,400 dollars, far more than the first week's pay, with instructions sent separately by text.

steps.title: Pay the 'wrap installer'
steps.detail: You are to deposit it, keep 400 dollars, and send 2,000 to the graphics installer by payment app or money order so he can book your fitting.

steps.title: The installer never comes
steps.detail: No fitting is ever scheduled. About a week later the bank finds the check is counterfeit, reverses the deposit, and the 2,000 dollars you sent comes out of your own balance.

car-wrap-scam.whyItWorks: Wrapped cars are a common sight, so the idea of being paid for it is easy to accept. The deposit shows as available in your account within a day, which looks like proof the check was good when the bank has not yet verified it.

realVsFake.real: Real wrap advertising firms check your mileage and usual routes first, often through an app, and only take drivers who suit a campaign.
realVsFake.fake: You are approved instantly from a form that asked only for your name, address and car.

realVsFake.real: The advertising company books and pays its own installer. The driver never handles that money.
realVsFake.fake: The installer's fee is routed through your bank account, and he can only be paid by app or money order.

realVsFake.real: Drivers are paid modest amounts after the wrap is on and the miles have been driven.
realVsFake.fake: A four-figure check arrives before anyone has seen your car, with a deadline to pass most of it on.

steps.title: A pitch on a real park
steps.detail: A marketplace or caravan forum advert offers a seasonal pitch or static plot on a named holiday park, with annual fees far below what owners there pay.

steps.title: The self-styled park manager
steps.detail: The contact says they handle pitch allocations, and sends photos of the plot with a site map lifted from the park's own brochure.

steps.title: Siting deposit before any visit
steps.detail: They say the plot goes to the next enquirer unless a siting deposit is paid now, and send a one-page 'licence agreement' naming a personal bank account.

steps.title: Reception has never heard of it
steps.detail: You ring the park or turn up with your tourer. The office has no record of the pitch, the agreement or whoever sold it.

caravan-pitch-scam.whyItWorks: Pitches on popular parks have waiting lists and site fees climb each season, so a cheap vacancy feels like a lucky break worth grabbing. Buyers assume anyone holding a site map and plot numbers must work there.

realVsFake.real: Holiday parks let pitches through their own office and will walk you round the plot before any agreement.
realVsFake.fake: The seller says a visit is impossible this week but the siting deposit cannot wait.

realVsFake.real: Pitch fees are invoiced by the park company and paid into a business account in the park's name.
realVsFake.fake: The money goes to an individual's account, or is requested as gift card codes.

realVsFake.real: A genuine pitch licence runs to many pages covering season dates, site rules and annual fee reviews.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agreement' is a single sheet with a logo, a plot number and a signature line.

steps.title: An ethical opportunity by phone
steps.detail: A caller or glossy brochure presents carbon credits as the coming commodity, with companies supposedly forced by law to buy them as climate targets tighten.

steps.title: Certificates from a forest project
steps.detail: You are offered voluntary credits tied to a reforestation or clean cookstove scheme, each with a serial number, at a price per tonne far above the wholesale rate.

steps.title: A buyer is said to be waiting
steps.detail: The salesperson claims a corporate purchaser will take your whole holding at a profit within a year, and urges a larger order to meet their minimum.

steps.title: Nowhere to resell
steps.detail: The promised buyer never materialises. Individuals have no real market for small parcels of voluntary credits, and the firm dissolves or offers an 'exit' for another fee.

carbon-credit-scam.whyItWorks: Carbon markets are real and appear in the news, but almost nobody knows how credits are priced or traded. Buying something that claims to protect rainforest lets an investor feel principled, which dulls the questions they would ask about any other commodity.

realVsFake.real: Carbon credits are bought in bulk by companies offsetting emissions, through specialist brokers and registries.
realVsFake.fake: Retail savers are sold a few hundred credits each as a personal investment, with a brochure about soaring demand.

realVsFake.real: A regulated investment firm states that capital is at risk and names the market where you can sell.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch guarantees double-digit growth and brushes off resale questions with talk of a buyer already lined up.

realVsFake.real: Credits on a recognised registry can be looked up by serial number, showing the project and current holder.
realVsFake.fake: You receive a decorative certificate, but the serials are absent from the registry or already marked as retired.

steps.title: Your card 'switched off'
steps.detail: The text says your debit or credit card was temporarily deactivated for security, without naming the bank or the last four digits of the card.

steps.title: Reactivation page in bank colours
steps.detail: Tapping through shows a 'reactivate my card' form. It often starts by asking which bank you use, then swaps in that bank's logo.

steps.title: Number, expiry, code and PIN
steps.detail: The form collects the long card number, expiry date, three-digit code and then the four-digit PIN, followed by your online banking username and password.

steps.title: A one-time code finishes it
steps.detail: Minutes later a genuine passcode arrives from your bank. The form asks for it, and that code lets the thief add your card to their own phone's wallet.

card-deactivated-text-scam.whyItWorks: Banks do freeze cards after odd transactions, and most people have had a payment declined at a till. The fear of being stuck without a working card before the next shop or bill makes 'reactivate now' sound helpful.

realVsFake.real: Your bank never asks for your PIN on a website, in a text, or over the phone. It is only for cash machines and card terminals.
realVsFake.fake: The reactivation form has a box for the PIN right under the card number.

realVsFake.real: A blocked card is unblocked inside the banking app or by calling the number printed on the back of the card.
realVsFake.fake: The only route offered is a link, with a warning that the card will be suspended for good.

realVsFake.real: Genuine bank alerts usually quote the last four digits of the card they concern.
realVsFake.fake: The message says 'your card' and nothing more, so it can be sent to any phone number.

steps.title: Details copied somewhere else
steps.detail: The long card number, expiry date and three-digit code are captured by a fake delivery-fee page, a hacked shop checkout, or bought from a leaked batch.

steps.title: A tiny test charge
steps.detail: An automated script tries the card for a pound or two at a charity donation page or a digital download store, to see whether it is live.

steps.title: The spending run
steps.detail: If it clears, larger orders follow fast: electronics, food delivery credit, gaming top-ups. Merchants that skip the extra bank approval step are chosen on purpose.

steps.title: Getting past the passcode
steps.detail: Where a one-time code is required, the fraudster rings or texts you posing as the bank and asks you to read it out to 'cancel' the purchase.

card-not-present-scam.whyItWorks: Online shops need only the numbers printed on the card, so the plastic never has to leave your wallet. A charge of a pound or two is easy to overlook among everyday spending, which buys the criminal time.

realVsFake.real: Your own online purchases come from retailers you recognise, at times you were actually shopping.
realVsFake.fake: Charges appear overnight from merchants abroad, or with names made of random letters.

realVsFake.real: A bank's fraud alert asks you to reply yes or no, or to check its app. It does not ask for the code.
realVsFake.fake: A caller says a code is on its way and that reading it back will stop the purchase.

realVsFake.real: If a delivery charge is genuinely owed, the courier's own app or the driver at the door takes it.
realVsFake.fake: A text demands a small redelivery fee, and the page wants every digit on your card plus your date of birth.

steps.title: Points about to lapse
steps.detail: A text or call in the card issuer's name says several thousand reward points, worth a couple of hundred in cashback, will be wiped at midnight.

steps.title: The helpful redemption desk
steps.detail: An agent offers to convert the points into a voucher right now and 'just needs to locate your card', asking for the sixteen digits and expiry.

steps.title: A copy of the rewards catalogue
steps.detail: Alternatively a link opens a page of gifts and vouchers, asking you to sign in with your card login and enter the CVV to 'credit the cashback'.

steps.title: The OTP that 'credits' you
steps.detail: A code arrives and the agent says reading it out confirms the redemption. It is in fact approving a purchase or transfer they have just set up.

card-rewards-scam.whyItWorks: Reward points feel like money you have already earned, so losing them stings more than missing a random prize. Since cardholders rarely check their points balance, almost any figure quoted sounds about right.

realVsFake.real: Card issuers show your points balance and expiry date in their app or on your statement, and you redeem there yourself.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger phones to do the redemption for you and wants the card number read out.

realVsFake.real: Redeeming points never needs a one-time passcode, because nothing is being paid out of your account.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says a code must be shared to 'release' the cashback onto your card.

realVsFake.real: Loyalty schemes that expire points usually flag it on statements well ahead of time.
realVsFake.fake: The first you hear of any expiry is a message giving you until tonight.

steps.title: The overlay goes on
steps.detail: A moulded plastic reader is clipped over the real card slot, or a wafer-thin 'shimmer' is pushed inside it. Fitting takes under a minute.

steps.title: Capturing the PIN
steps.detail: A pinhole camera hidden in a strip above the screen or in a leaflet holder films the keys, or a false keypad laid on top records each press.

steps.title: Your transaction works normally
steps.detail: Cash comes out, fuel pumps, the receipt prints. Nothing seems wrong, because the genuine reader underneath still does its job while the copy is made.

steps.title: Clones and cash-outs
steps.detail: The gang collects the device, writes the stolen data onto blank cards and withdraws cash, often in another country or at machines that still read magnetic stripes.

card-skimming-scam.whyItWorks: Nothing unusual happens at the time, so there is no moment that feels like a scam and nothing to refuse. People trust a machine bolted to a bank wall or a forecourt pump and rarely tug at its parts before using it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine card slot sits flush with the fascia, and its flashing light surround is fully visible.
realVsFake.fake: A skimmer stands proud of the panel, covers the light, and may wobble if you pull it.

realVsFake.real: Factory keypads are firm and sit level with the metal around them.
realVsFake.fake: A false pad feels thick or spongy, and the keys may stand higher than the casing.

realVsFake.real: Many fuel stations seal pump doors with security tape that stays in one piece.
realVsFake.fake: On a tampered pump the tape is cut, missing, or shows a 'void' pattern across the door.

steps.title: Activate secure payments
steps.detail: An email with Visa or Mastercard marks beside a bank logo says new rules require enrolling your card in 3-D Secure, or online purchases will be declined.

steps.title: The enrolment form
steps.detail: The page asks for the sixteen-digit number, expiry date, security code, name and date of birth, and sometimes the card's PIN.

steps.title: We have sent you a code
steps.detail: While you wait, the criminals are entering your card at a real shop or adding it to a phone wallet. The code your bank texts is for that.

steps.title: Successfully verified
steps.detail: You type the code and a green tick appears. Their purchase goes through, or your card becomes active for tap payments on a stranger's phone.

card-verification-email-scam.whyItWorks: Shoppers meet extra bank check screens at checkout without ever being told how they were set up. An email offering to activate that protection sounds like the missing instruction, and it borrows the card schemes' names.

realVsFake.real: Card security checks are switched on by your bank automatically and appear only during a purchase you are making.
realVsFake.fake: An email asks you to enrol in advance by filling in a form.

realVsFake.real: The bank's text states what the code is for, naming the shop and amount or the wallet being set up.
realVsFake.fake: The page calls it a 'verification code' and counts on you not reading the text closely.

realVsFake.real: No bank asks for a card PIN on a website or by email.
realVsFake.fake: The form includes a PIN box, labelled as identity confirmation.

steps.title: Login details phished in advance
steps.detail: A fake bank text or lookalike sign-in page has already captured your username and password. The fraudster now lacks one thing needed to enrol a device.

steps.title: A new handset joins your account
steps.detail: They add your card to a mobile wallet or register the banking app on their phone, which makes your bank text you a verification code.

steps.title: 'Security' on the line
steps.detail: At that moment a caller says a cardless withdrawal is being attempted in another city and asks for the code to block it.

steps.title: Tap and withdraw
steps.detail: With the code, their phone becomes your card. They hold it to a contactless cash machine, or generate a cash code in the app, and withdraw up to the daily limit.

cardless-atm-scam.whyItWorks: The code really does arrive from the bank's usual number at the instant the caller mentions it, which seems to prove the caller is genuine. Most customers have never used cardless cash, so they cannot tell that the code switches it on.

realVsFake.real: A cardless withdrawal starts in your own banking app, on your phone, while you are standing at the machine.
realVsFake.fake: An alert or code about cardless cash arrives while you are at home and have not opened the app.

realVsFake.real: Bank texts carrying a code state its purpose, such as adding a card to a wallet or registering a device.
realVsFake.fake: The caller describes the same code as a 'cancellation reference' and talks over you as you read the message.

realVsFake.real: To stop a suspicious withdrawal, a bank blocks it internally and may ask you to confirm inside the app.
realVsFake.fake: The 'security team' claims the block cannot go through unless you say the digits aloud.

steps.title: The #blessing post
steps.detail: A social media account running a 'Cash App Friday' style giveaway replies that you have won, or a stranger messages that they are 'blessing' followers today.

steps.title: A small send to 'verify'
steps.detail: You are asked to send 20 or so to a cashtag to prove your account is active, with a promise that it will come back multiplied.

steps.title: A screenshot of 'pending' money
steps.detail: They send a doctored image showing hundreds waiting for you, and say a 'clearance fee' or account upgrade is needed to release it.

steps.title: 'Support' wants the sign-in code
steps.detail: When you complain, a fake support account or phone number offers help and requests your sign-in code or PIN, then logs in and empties the balance.

cash-app-scam.whyItWorks: The company has run genuine giveaways on social media, so the hashtag and the format are familiar. Sending twenty to receive hundreds seems a tiny risk, and payments in the app go through instantly with no way to pull them back.

realVsFake.real: Cash App's real giveaways are announced from its verified accounts, and winners are never asked to send money first.
realVsFake.fake: A lookalike profile with extra letters in its name messages you privately asking for a 'verification' payment.

realVsFake.real: Genuine support is reached through the app's own help section, and staff never ask for your PIN or sign-in code.
realVsFake.fake: 'Support' is a phone number from a search advert or a reply under your complaint, and its first request is your code.

realVsFake.real: Someone who really paid the wrong person can ask the app's support team to sort it out.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger sends money from a stolen card, begs you to send it back, and the original is later reversed.

steps.title: The free postal pack
steps.detail: An advert, leaflet or daytime TV spot offers a free prepaid envelope for unwanted rings, chains and broken jewellery, with payment promised the day it lands.

steps.title: Your jewellery goes in the post
steps.detail: You seal the items in the envelope without a written weight or photos. The included cover is small, and nobody independent has seen what you sent.

steps.title: Weighed behind closed doors
steps.detail: The company tests and weighs everything itself, grades it at a lower carat, ignores stones and workmanship, and prices it as scrap.

steps.title: A cheque you must refuse fast
steps.detail: A small payment is sent automatically. The terms give you only days to reject it, and by then the gold may be melted or 'lost in return post'.

cash-for-gold-scam.whyItWorks: Most people have no idea what an old chain weighs or what purity it is, so any number sounds plausible. Once the envelope is posted the buyer holds the gold, and arguing for it back feels like more trouble than accepting.

realVsFake.real: A high-street jeweller or pawnbroker weighs your gold on the counter while you stand there, and states the carat.
realVsFake.fake: Weighing happens out of sight, and the result arrives as a single total with no breakdown.

realVsFake.real: Honest gold buyers quote a price per gram for each purity and let you walk away with your items.
realVsFake.fake: The rate is never published, and declining means paying a return fee and waiting weeks.

realVsFake.real: A reputable postal buyer insures the parcel for its declared value and waits for you to accept an offer.
realVsFake.fake: Money is sent without your agreement, and banking it or staying silent counts as acceptance.

steps.title: An app promising a third back
steps.detail: An advert or a friend's referral link promotes an app paying cashback on every purchase plus bonuses for small tasks such as rating products or watching videos.

steps.title: The balance climbs quickly
steps.detail: After you upload receipts or link a card, the in-app balance jumps to 180 within days. A progress bar shows you close to the 250 needed to cash out.

steps.title: The last stretch costs money
steps.detail: Reaching the threshold now needs 'premium tasks' that require a deposit, or you must recruit friends. Earnings slow to pennies just short of the line.

steps.title: A fee to withdraw
steps.detail: When you finally request a payout, the app asks for a withdrawal fee or 'tax', then your online banking login to 'verify the account'. No payment ever arrives.

cashback-app-scam.whyItWorks: A number rising on a screen feels like money already earned, and nobody wants to abandon 180 when the finish is 70 away. Each new condition looks small compared with what seems to be sitting in the account.

realVsFake.real: Genuine cashback services are paid commission by retailers and pass on a slice, which is why typical rates are a few pence in the pound.
realVsFake.fake: The scam app offers a third back on groceries and fuel, a margin no shop could fund.

realVsFake.real: A real service never asks you to send money in order to receive your own cashback.
realVsFake.fake: A fee, a 'tax' or a deposit is demanded before any withdrawal, and the minimum rises as you approach it.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate apps come from the official app stores and ask for the permissions the feature needs, such as the camera for receipts.
realVsFake.fake: The fake is installed from a link as a loose file and wants access to text messages, contacts and your banking password.

steps.title: A photo chosen to move you
steps.detail: A social media advert shows a veteran, a rescue dog or a sick child beside a T-shirt or bracelet, with a caption saying every sale funds the cause.

steps.title: A shop with a mission statement
steps.detail: The link opens a store with a heartfelt 'our story' page and a counter of money raised, but no charity registration number and no named partner organisation.

steps.title: Checkout with a guilt nudge
steps.detail: At checkout a pre-ticked box adds a 'donation', and a banner says the campaign closes tonight. You pay by card on a page run by the store itself.

steps.title: A thin shirt, or nothing
steps.detail: Weeks later a flimsy shirt with a blurry print arrives from overseas, or no parcel at all. The cause never hears from the shop, and your card details stay on its files.

cause-merchandise-scam.whyItWorks: Buying a shirt feels like giving with something to show for it, so shoppers skip the checks they might make before a donation. Questioning a store that says it helps wounded soldiers or abandoned animals feels mean-spirited.

realVsFake.real: Charities that sell merchandise do it through their own shop, linked from their main website, or name the licensed partner.
realVsFake.fake: The store says 'supporting veterans' or 'for the animals' without naming any organisation that receives the money.

realVsFake.real: A genuine cause partnership states the amount per item that is donated and to which registered charity.
realVsFake.fake: The wording is 'all profits' or 'a portion of proceeds', with no figure and no way to check a single payment.

realVsFake.real: If you ask a real charity whether a shop is fundraising for it, someone there can confirm or deny.
realVsFake.fake: The same shirt designs appear on other sites under different causes, swapped to match whatever is in the news.

steps.title: A livestream with a famous face
steps.detail: A video stream on a hijacked or renamed channel replays old interview footage of a tech billionaire, framed with a banner announcing a giveaway to mark a launch.

steps.title: The QR code in the corner
steps.detail: Viewers are pointed to a site through a QR code or pinned comment. It shows the rules: send between 0.1 and 5 BTC and receive twice as much back.

steps.title: A scrolling list of 'winners'
steps.detail: The page displays a live table of incoming and outgoing transactions and a countdown of remaining places. Chat is full of bot accounts thanking the host.

steps.title: One-way transfer
steps.detail: You send coins to the address shown. Nothing returns, the transaction cannot be recalled, and the page may suggest sending again because the first amount was 'below the minimum'.

celebrity-crypto-giveaway-scam.whyItWorks: The footage is real, the channel may carry a verification badge and a large subscriber count, and wealthy founders are known for publicity stunts. A fake transaction feed showing strangers apparently being paid makes the remaining slots feel like they are slipping away.

realVsFake.real: Real promotions from crypto companies credit existing customers' accounts and never need you to send coins first.
realVsFake.fake: The giveaway only pays after a 'verification deposit' to an address shown on screen.

realVsFake.real: A public figure's genuine announcement appears on every one of their established accounts and in mainstream news.
realVsFake.fake: The event exists on one channel whose older videos are about gaming or music in another language.

realVsFake.real: A live broadcast responds to events and takes questions as they come in.
realVsFake.fake: The 'live' video loops every few minutes, and comments are switched off or limited to long-standing subscribers.

steps.title: The star follows you back
steps.detail: After you comment on a famous person's post, a profile with their photo and a name ending in 'private' or 'official2' follows you and says thanks for the support.

steps.title: Moved to a quieter app
steps.detail: They ask to continue on Telegram or WhatsApp, away from 'management'. Daily chats follow about tour fatigue, loneliness and how refreshing it is to talk to a real fan.

steps.title: The membership card
steps.detail: A 'fan card' or VIP membership is offered for a modest fee, payable in gift card codes, which supposedly unlocks private calls and a backstage meeting.

steps.title: Keep this between us
steps.detail: Bigger asks follow: a charity project, a frozen account, a flight to visit you. You are told not to tell anyone, because the press would ruin it.

celebrity-impersonation-dm-scam.whyItWorks: Fans already feel they know the person from years of interviews and songs, so a warm private message confirms a bond that felt real long before. The secrecy rule keeps away the friends who would point out how unlikely it is.

realVsFake.real: Public figures speak to fans from one verified account, in public posts, and rarely message individuals at all.
realVsFake.fake: A second 'private' or 'backup' profile with few followers starts a one-to-one chat and asks about your day.

realVsFake.real: Official fan clubs take card payments on the artist's own website and send a receipt.
realVsFake.fake: Membership is paid by photographing the back of gift cards and sending the codes in chat.

realVsFake.real: A wealthy performer has agents, accountants and a bank, and no need to borrow from a fan.
realVsFake.fake: The 'celebrity' has cash tied up and needs you, specifically, to cover a fee until Monday.

steps.title: 'Your household is not counted'
steps.detail: A caller, a text or someone on the doorstep with a lanyard and clipboard says your address is missing from the national count and must be verified today.

steps.title: Ordinary questions come first
steps.detail: They begin with what a census really asks: how many people live there, their ages, whether you own or rent. It sounds exactly right.

steps.title: The questions change direction
steps.detail: Next they want your full Social Security or national ID number 'to match the record', then your bank, your income and sometimes your mother's maiden name.

steps.title: A fee to finish the form
steps.detail: Last comes a 'processing fee' or a fine for late response, payable by card on the spot. The card is charged and the identity details go to open accounts.

census-scam.whyItWorks: Answering the census is a legal duty in many countries, and people know that ignoring it can bring a fine, so an official demand to respond feels legitimate. A count comes round so rarely that almost nobody remembers what the last one actually asked.

realVsFake.real: Census field staff carry a photo ID badge and expect you to phone the census office to check them.
realVsFake.fake: The visitor flashes a card too quickly to read and becomes impatient when you say you will ring to confirm.

realVsFake.real: The questionnaire covers who lives at the address, with ages, sex, ethnicity and housing. It is free to complete.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor's version ends with a card number, a PIN or online banking password, or a fee to 'register' your answers.

realVsFake.real: Invitations normally come by post, addressed to the household, with an access code for the official online form.
realVsFake.fake: A text with a link claims to be your only notice and gives no code, only a page of blank fields.

steps.title: Homework on your company
steps.detail: The scammer reads the company website and LinkedIn to learn who the boss is, who handles payments, who has just joined and when the boss is away.

steps.title: Are you at your desk?
steps.detail: A short email arrives under the chief executive's name from a free mail account or lookalike domain, asking only whether you are available for a quick favour.

steps.title: The discreet task
steps.detail: Once you reply, the request lands: buy four gift cards for clients, or pay an attached invoice to a new supplier today, and keep it confidential.

steps.title: Codes photographed, wire sent
steps.detail: You scratch the cards and email pictures of the codes, or finance sends the transfer to a mule account. The 'boss' stops replying and the money moves on.

ceo-fraud-scam.whyItWorks: Refusing the boss carries a cost that agreeing to an odd request does not, particularly for a new starter. The first email asks only whether you are free, so by the time money is mentioned you have already said yes.

realVsFake.real: A genuine payment request from an executive goes through purchasing, with a purchase order and a second approver.
realVsFake.fake: The email asks you to skip approvals 'just this once' and mention it to nobody.

realVsFake.real: Real bosses can be reached on a known number, on the company chat or through their assistant.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is in back-to-back meetings or boarding a flight, and tells you not to phone.

realVsFake.real: Companies buy client gifts on a company card, with receipts filed afterwards.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to pay from your own pocket, scratch the panels and send photos of the codes.

steps.title: Forwarded by someone you know
steps.detail: A relative or group chat passes on a message marked 'forwarded many times'. It says the app will start charging, or delete inactive accounts, unless you send it on.

steps.title: The ten-contact rule
steps.detail: The text sets a quota: forward to ten people, or five groups, and your icon turns blue, your account is spared, or a supermarket voucher unlocks.

steps.title: A progress bar that fills
steps.detail: Versions with a link open a page with a short quiz and a share button. A bar creeps towards full each time you pass it to another chat.

steps.title: The reward page
steps.detail: Once the bar is full, the page asks for your name, mobile number and address, pushes browser notifications, or signs your number up to a paid text service.

chain-message-scam.whyItWorks: Forwarding costs nothing and takes two taps, so 'just in case' wins over checking. The message also arrives from an aunt or a neighbour, not a stranger, and each person who passes it on lends it their own good name.

realVsFake.real: Messaging apps announce changes inside the app or on their official blog, and no setting depends on forwarding anything.
realVsFake.fake: A text signed by 'the director' of the app claims your account survives only if ten contacts receive it.

realVsFake.real: Supermarkets and airlines run voucher offers on their own websites and verified pages.
realVsFake.fake: The 'anniversary voucher' lives on an odd web address and unlocks only after you spam your contacts.

realVsFake.real: A genuine public warning names its source, such as a police force or health body, and can be found there.
realVsFake.fake: The alert cites 'a friend who works in IT' or 'it was on the news' with nothing you can look up.

steps.title: A call after the headlines
steps.detail: Days after a flood, earthquake or wildfire leads the news, a caller says they are ringing on behalf of the relief appeal.

steps.title: A name one word off
steps.detail: They give a charity name that sounds like a household one with a word swapped or added, and describe children without shelter or clean water tonight.

steps.title: 'Can we take a card now?'
steps.detail: You are asked for the long card number, expiry and security code on the spot. Offers to give later through the charity's website are brushed aside.

steps.title: A monthly gift you never agreed
steps.detail: The card is charged more than you pledged, or again each month. Some callers ring back weeks later claiming your promised donation is overdue.

charity-call-scam.whyItWorks: Saying no to a disaster appeal feels mean, and the caller knows the footage is fresh in your mind. Because generosity is the lever, asking hard questions seems rude at exactly the moment they matter.

realVsFake.real: Registered charities give their registration number when asked, and appear on the national charity register under that exact name.
realVsFake.fake: The fundraiser dodges the registration question or reads out a number belonging to a different organisation.

realVsFake.real: A genuine fundraiser will post or email details and let you donate later through the charity's own site.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the appeal line closes tonight and only a card over the phone counts.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate telephone fundraisers will say whether they work for a paid agency and roughly how gifts are spent.
realVsFake.fake: Questions about where donations go get a vague 'it all reaches the families'.

steps.title: Fundraisers wanted, commission paid
steps.detail: An advert seeks street or door-to-door fundraisers for a children's, veterans' or animal cause, offering a share of everything collected and an immediate start with no experience.

steps.title: Buy your collection kit
steps.detail: Before your first shift you pay for a kit: a branded bucket or tin, a lanyard ID with your photo, a tabard and a stack of leaflets about the cause.

steps.title: Cash from strangers, in your hands
steps.detail: You spend days asking shoppers and householders for cash. Each evening the takings go to a 'team leader' in person, or you bank them and transfer the total to the organiser's own account.

steps.title: No commission, no charity
steps.detail: The promised commission is delayed until a 'monthly reconciliation' that never happens. The cause appears on no register, and you were the public face collecting for it without a permit.

charity-fundraiser-job-scam.whyItWorks: People assume a charity must be honest, and paying for a bucket and badge seems a minor cost of doing good while earning. Recruits rarely think to look the cause up on a register because the organiser talks about sick children, not paperwork.

realVsFake.real: A registered charity has a number you can look up on the official charity register, along with its trustees and accounts.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser gives a cause name and a logo but changes the subject when asked for a registration number.

realVsFake.real: Professional fundraising agencies pay a wage, issue ID and materials free, and mostly sign donors up to bank payments.
realVsFake.fake: You buy your own badge and bucket, and your pay is a cut of whatever loose cash you bring back.

realVsFake.real: Collection tins are sealed and numbered, and takings are counted by two people and banked into the charity's account.
realVsFake.fake: Open buckets are emptied into one man's rucksack at the end of the day, with nothing written down.

steps.title: Get paid per message
steps.detail: An advert offers remote work as a 'chat operator' or 'text moderator', replying to members of a dating or fan site under a house persona for about 20 cents a message.

steps.title: Onboarding fee and ID first
steps.detail: Sign-up requires a 30 dollar onboarding or 'platform access' fee, a selfie holding your ID and your bank details for payouts, all before you have typed a single reply.

steps.title: A balance that only grows
steps.detail: You answer messages for hours and the on-screen earnings tick upward. The withdraw button stays grey until you hit a weekly message count and a 'quality score' set by the site.

steps.title: Targets move, payout never comes
steps.detail: Near the target, messages dry up or your score drops without reason. Support suggests a paid 'priority queue' or recruiting three friends, and the balance resets at the end of the week.

chat-operator-job-scam.whyItWorks: Paid chat moderation does exist, which makes the advert plausible, and a rising balance on screen feels like money already earned. Having put in the hours, people keep typing or pay for the upgrade because quitting means abandoning wages they can see.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate moderation contractor signs a written agreement with you and pays on fixed dates for the work already logged.
realVsFake.fake: Pay exists only as a number on a dashboard, released if you clear a target the site controls.

realVsFake.real: Genuine platforms cover their own software and onboarding costs, since they profit from your replies.
realVsFake.fake: You pay to get in, then are offered paid boosts to receive enough messages to qualify for a payout.

realVsFake.real: Bonuses at a real employer reward your own performance against terms stated in writing.
realVsFake.fake: The quickest route to 'unlocking' your balance is bringing in new operators who each pay the joining fee.

steps.title: A lookalike in the store
steps.detail: You search for a well-known AI assistant and the top result is a sponsored app with a near-identical icon and a name one word off.

steps.title: The trial screen with a hidden X
steps.detail: On first launch a full-screen offer appears. The close button is faint or delayed, so most people tap 'Continue' and start a three-day trial.

steps.title: Permissions a chat app never needs
steps.detail: It requests contacts, storage, notifications and sometimes accessibility access. The chat itself gives a few short answers, then hits a daily limit.

steps.title: Weekly billing begins
steps.detail: After three days the store bills you every week, which over a month costs more than the genuine tool's paid plan. Deleting the app does not cancel it.

chatgpt-app-scam.whyItWorks: People have heard of the famous AI tools but often do not know who makes them or what the official app is called. A familiar-looking icon near the top of a store search is enough to pass for the genuine article.

realVsFake.real: The genuine assistant is published under the AI company's own name and linked from that company's official website.
realVsFake.fake: The developer is an unknown studio whose other listings are wallpaper, scanner and phone-cleaner apps.

realVsFake.real: Well-known chatbots have a usable free tier and show monthly pricing on a settings page.
realVsFake.fake: A paywall appears before your second question, with the price in small grey print under a large button.

realVsFake.real: A text chat app needs a network connection, plus a microphone only if you choose voice input.
realVsFake.fake: It wants your contacts, files and permission to draw over other apps before you type anything.

steps.title: A lifetime licence for pocket money
steps.detail: A search result or marketplace listing offers a 'genuine lifetime licence' for an office suite or operating system at the price of a sandwich, with instant email delivery.

steps.title: Paying a shop with no name
steps.detail: You pay a few pounds by card or crypto on a site with no company name. The receipt says 'digital goods, no refunds' and little else.

steps.title: Activate quickly, they say
steps.detail: An email delivers a 25-character key and tells you to activate within 24 hours, sometimes by phoning an automated line or signing in to a stranger's account.

steps.title: The licence switches off
steps.detail: It works for a few weeks. Then the publisher blocks the key because it was bought with a stolen card or taken from a volume licence, and the software locks.

cheap-software-key-scam.whyItWorks: Software is invisible stock, so a huge discount seems possible in a way it would not for a physical product. The key often activates on the first day, which convinces the buyer it was genuine and discourages any complaint.

realVsFake.real: Publishers and their authorised resellers tie a licence to your own account, where it shows up under your purchases.
realVsFake.fake: The grey seller emails a bare code, or a username and password for an account that belongs to somebody else.

realVsFake.real: Authorised sellers can be found on the publisher's partner list, and discounts are modest outside student or seasonal offers.
realVsFake.fake: The listing claims a retail or 'OEM' key at a tiny fraction of list price, with no explanation of where it came from.

realVsFake.real: With a legitimate licence, you download the installer from the publisher's own site and support will help if activation fails.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent a file-sharing link to an installer and an 'activator' tool that your antivirus flags straight away.

steps.title: Cash today, no bank needed
steps.detail: A flyer, shopfront sign or social media advert offers instant money for payroll, benefit or insurance cheques, aimed at people without a bank account or in a hurry.

steps.title: Endorse it and hand it over
steps.detail: You are asked to sign the back of the cheque and post it, photograph both sides, or leave it at a counter, along with a copy of your ID.

steps.title: Deductions nobody mentioned
steps.detail: The payout arrives short. A 'verification charge', a 'same-day premium' and a 'risk fee' have been taken, sometimes swallowing a large slice of the cheque's value.

steps.title: Or no payout at all
steps.detail: In the worst version the phone number goes dead. The signed cheque has been paid into someone else's account and your ID copy is reused elsewhere.

cheque-cashing-scam.whyItWorks: A paper cheque is awkward for anyone with no bank account, or with an overdraft that would swallow it, and waiting days for clearance is hard when rent is due. A stranger offering notes in hand today solves an immediate problem.

realVsFake.real: A licensed cheque casher displays its fee as a clear rate on the wall and on a receipt before you sign anything.
realVsFake.fake: The cost is described as 'a small fee' and only becomes a number once they hold your cheque.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate service pays you across the counter during the same visit, and you leave with paperwork.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to post the cheque or send photos and wait for a deposit that may never come.

realVsFake.real: Your own bank, or the bank that issued the cheque, will usually cash or deposit it for little or nothing.
realVsFake.fake: The service warns that banks will 'hold it for weeks' and pushes you to decide on the spot.

steps.title: Lifted from the post
steps.detail: A thief fishes envelopes from a street postbox with a sticky line, raids a building's outgoing mail tray, or takes bill payments left out for collection.

steps.title: The solvent bath
steps.detail: The cheque is soaked in a household chemical such as nail varnish remover. Ordinary ballpoint ink dissolves, while the printed details and often your signature remain.

steps.title: A new payee, a bigger figure
steps.detail: Once dry, the blank spaces are filled in with a different name and a larger amount, or the cheque is scanned to print further forgeries.

steps.title: Paid in through a borrowed account
steps.detail: The altered cheque is deposited by phone app or at a machine, into an account opened with false ID or lent by a recruited 'money mule', then withdrawn fast.

cheque-washing-scam.whyItWorks: There is no persuasion here at all. The cheque carries your real signature, account number and the bank's own paper, so it passes automated checks, and you only find out when the intended recipient chases you for payment.

realVsFake.real: The cheque image in your banking app should show your own handwriting, the payee you named and the amount you wrote.
realVsFake.fake: A washed cheque shows a different hand or pen in the payee and amount lines, with your signature untouched.

realVsFake.real: A payee who receives your cheque banks it and stops asking for payment.
realVsFake.fake: Your statement shows the cheque as paid, yet the company you posted it to sends a reminder.

realVsFake.real: Ink from a pigmented gel pen soaks into the paper fibres and resists solvents.
realVsFake.fake: Washers look for cheques written in standard ballpoint, which lifts off cleanly and leaves little trace.

steps.title: The number gets out
steps.detail: A child's Social Security number leaks through a breach at a school or clinic, a fake enrolment form, or someone with access to the family's papers.

steps.title: A new adult is invented
steps.detail: The thief pairs the number with a different name and an adult's date of birth. No credit file exists for it yet, so nothing contradicts the invention.

steps.title: Credit built, then drained
steps.detail: A phone contract or store card is opened and paid on time for a while to raise the limits. Then everything is run up and abandoned.

steps.title: Discovered years later
steps.detail: The first sign may be a collection letter addressed to a nine-year-old, or a refused student loan or tenancy when the child turns eighteen.

child-identity-theft-scam.whyItWorks: A child's number is a blank record that nobody checks for a decade or more, which gives a thief years of quiet use. Parents write that number on school, clinic and sports forms so routinely that one more request for it rarely stands out.

realVsFake.real: Schools, clinics and clubs can usually enrol a child without a Social Security number if you ask why it is needed.
realVsFake.fake: A caller or form posing as the school insists on the full number today, to 'update records' or 'confirm benefits'.

realVsFake.real: Lenders send pre-approved offers to adults with a credit history. A young child should have no file at all.
realVsFake.fake: A card offer or debt letter in your child's name means a file exists, built by somebody else.

realVsFake.real: A tax agency accepts a child as a dependant on one return, the return of the family who supports them.
realVsFake.fake: Your own return is rejected because the child's number has already been claimed on a stranger's.

steps.title: Signed up by a neighbour
steps.detail: An agent, often a neighbour or colleague earning commission, signs you up to a hamper or voucher club and hands you a payment card to fill in weekly.

steps.title: Small payments all year
steps.detail: You pay five or ten a week by cash to the agent or by standing order. A catalogue shows the hamper, toys or shopping vouchers you are saving towards.

steps.title: The bonus that keeps you in
steps.detail: Midway through, the club offers 'double value' or a free extra if you raise your payments or recruit two friends. Statements show a healthy balance.

steps.title: November silence
steps.detail: As payout nears, deliveries are 'delayed by suppliers'. Then the phone line closes, the website shows a notice, and the money, never kept separate, has been spent.

christmas-club-scam.whyItWorks: For households that struggle to keep savings untouched, handing over a little each week to someone else feels safer than a bank account they might dip into. The collector is usually a familiar face, and nothing is due back for eleven months.

realVsFake.real: A sound savings club states in writing that customers' money sits in a separate trust account the business cannot spend.
realVsFake.fake: The terms say nothing about where payments are held, and the agent answers that 'the company looks after it'.

realVsFake.real: Banks, credit unions and supermarket stamp schemes return what you put in, perhaps with a small top-up.
realVsFake.fake: The club promises goods worth twice your savings, which could only be paid from other members' money.

realVsFake.real: With an ordinary easy-access account you can check the balance yourself and take the money out before December if needed.
realVsFake.fake: Leaving the club early means losing a cancellation charge, and the only record is a card the agent initials.

steps.title: A normal stay, a quiet checkout
steps.detail: The stay goes smoothly. You leave the keys as instructed, and nobody mentions a problem at checkout or in the hours afterwards.

steps.title: The message days later
steps.detail: A message says the cleaner found stains, a broken lamp or a smell of smoke, and that 300 has been kept from your deposit or charged to your card.

steps.title: Photos that prove nothing
steps.detail: The 'evidence' is a set of close-ups with no date, no wide shot and nothing showing the room is the one you slept in.

steps.title: Pushed to settle privately
steps.detail: When you object, the host offers to halve the amount if you pay directly and leave the booking site out of it, or threatens a damaging guest review.

cleaning-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: By the time the accusation arrives you are home, cannot inspect the room and probably took no photos on the way out. The sum is pitched low enough that arguing feels like more trouble than paying.

realVsFake.real: Honest hosts raise damage promptly through the platform's resolution process, with dated before-and-after photos and a repair quote.
realVsFake.fake: The accusation comes by private message with blurry close-ups and a suspiciously round figure.

realVsFake.real: Where a booking site holds the deposit, a damage claim goes through its process and the guest gets to respond.
realVsFake.fake: The host says the deduction is final and that disputing it will only cost you more.

realVsFake.real: A genuine cleaning fee is shown in the price breakdown before you book.
realVsFake.fake: An extra cleaning charge appears after you leave, for mess nobody mentioned when you handed back the keys.

steps.title: An advert for healthy volunteers
steps.detail: A post on a jobs board or social feed offers a large payment for a four-week sleep or vaccine trial you can complete mostly from home.

steps.title: The screening questionnaire
steps.detail: A 'trial coordinator' emails a form asking for medical history, current medication, photo ID and a tax or Social Security number 'for the payment paperwork'.

steps.title: A fee or an oversized cheque
steps.detail: Either you pay a refundable registration fee for a screening kit, or a cheque arrives for more than agreed, with a request to forward the extra to an 'equipment supplier'.

steps.title: The cheque bounces
steps.detail: Days after you send the difference, the bank reverses the cheque and takes the full amount back from you. The coordinator's email address stops working.

clinical-trial-scam.whyItWorks: Genuine trials do advertise for volunteers, do pay well and do ask intrusive health questions, so the early stages look exactly as they should. The only thing out of place is the direction of the money, and by then you have already been 'accepted'.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate paid trials do not charge volunteers to join, and the sponsor pays for the screening tests.
realVsFake.fake: A 'registration' or 'kit' fee is requested before you have met a single member of medical staff.

realVsFake.real: A real trial screens you in person at a named clinic and has you sign a consent form explaining the risks.
realVsFake.fake: Everything is done by email and chat app, with no clinic address, no named doctor and no consent paperwork.

realVsFake.real: Volunteers are paid after completed visits, for the amount agreed, usually by bank transfer or prepaid card from the clinic.
realVsFake.fake: Money arrives before you have done anything, as a paper cheque with an instruction to send part of it on.

steps.title: Copying a public profile
steps.detail: The scammer saves a real person's profile picture and cover photo, creates a new account under the same name, and works through that person's visible friends list.

steps.title: A request from a familiar face
steps.detail: You get a friend request from someone you thought you were already connected to. Accepting triggers a chatty message explaining the old account was locked or hacked.

steps.title: Small talk, then the ask
