steps.detail: After 'how are the kids', the tone shifts. Their banking app is down, a bill is due today, and could you lend a couple of hundred until Friday.

steps.title: Payment to a third name
steps.detail: The bank details belong to a stranger, explained as a landlord or cousin. Other versions push a 'government grant' link or ask you to read out a texted code.

cloned-account-friend-request-scam.whyItWorks: The face and name belong to someone you trust, and people really do open new accounts after being locked out. A modest loan to a friend in a tight spot is something most of us would send without a second look.

realVsFake.real: A friend who truly changed accounts tells people in person, by phone or in a group you already share.
realVsFake.fake: The new profile appears from nowhere, while the original is still live with all its old posts.

realVsFake.real: Your actual friend can answer a question only they would know, or pick up when you ring their usual number.
realVsFake.fake: The copy dodges calls, says the microphone is broken and steers back to the money.

realVsFake.real: Someone borrowing from a mate gives their own account details, which match the name you know.
realVsFake.fake: You are given a different payee, a gift card request or a payment-app handle that is not theirs.

steps.title: A genuine advert is copied
steps.detail: The scammer lifts photos and wording from a real agent's listing, then reposts it on a free classifieds site or social marketplace at a noticeably lower rent.

steps.title: The owner 'working away'
steps.detail: Your enquiry gets a long, friendly email. The owner says a job has taken them out of the country, and asks about your work, pets and move-in date.

steps.title: A form that feels like vetting
steps.detail: They email an application asking for ID, employer and current address. A day later they write that you have been chosen from several applicants.

steps.title: Deposit for couriered keys
steps.detail: You are told to transfer the deposit today, after which keys will come by courier with a tracking number. The number is invented and the home already has tenants.

cloned-rental-listing-scam.whyItWorks: The property is real, the address checks out on a map and the photos match the street view, so everything a careful renter might verify comes back clean. Only the person claiming to hold the keys is invented.

realVsFake.real: The original listing sits on the agent's own website at the full rent, with an office number that answers.
realVsFake.fake: The clone appears on a free site at a lower price with only a personal email or messaging number.

realVsFake.real: A real landlord or their agent opens the door and lets you look inside before taking a deposit.
realVsFake.fake: The owner is permanently abroad and offers to courier keys once the money clears.

realVsFake.real: A tenancy deposit is taken alongside a signed agreement and, where the law requires, lodged in a protection scheme.
realVsFake.fake: The deposit goes by bank transfer to a named individual, with paperwork promised for later.

steps.title: Mining without the machines
steps.detail: An advert, messaging group or friend's referral link promotes a site that rents out mining power, promising a fixed payout every day with no hardware or electricity bill.

steps.title: The starter contract
steps.detail: You buy a 300 starter contract in crypto. Photos of a server hall and a 'hash rate' figure appear in your new account.

steps.title: A counter that ticks up daily
steps.detail: The dashboard credits earnings each morning. A small first withdrawal is paid promptly, which encourages a bigger contract and invitations to friends for a referral bonus.

steps.title: Withdrawal needs an upgrade
steps.detail: A larger withdrawal is refused until you reach a higher membership tier or pay a 'network tax'. Paying brings a new condition, then the site goes offline.

cloud-mining-scam.whyItWorks: Mining is known to be profitable for those with warehouses of equipment, so renting a share sounds reasonable. That early small withdrawal is paid from other people's deposits and does the persuading: it looks like proof the machines exist.

realVsFake.real: Actual mining income rises and falls with coin price, network difficulty and power costs, and can be negative.
realVsFake.fake: The contract pays the same amount every day regardless of what the market does.

realVsFake.real: A genuine hosting company names its data centre, its legal entity and the mining pool where payouts can be seen.
realVsFake.fake: The site shows stock photos of server racks, an address that turns out to be a shared office, and no pool records.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate services take their charges out of what you have earned before paying you the rest.
realVsFake.fake: You must send fresh crypto from outside to cover a fee, even though the balance on screen is many times larger.

steps.title: Your address is on a list
steps.detail: Names and addresses come from leaked shopping data. Sometimes a text arrives the day before, saying an order is out for delivery and to keep cash ready.

steps.title: A genuine courier knocks
steps.detail: The driver works for a real delivery firm and knows nothing. The label carries a family member's name and a cash-on-delivery amount such as 35.

steps.title: Pay before you open
steps.detail: The driver says the box cannot be opened before payment. A parent or flatmate, assuming somebody in the house ordered it, hands over the cash or taps a card.

steps.title: Tissue paper in a box
steps.detail: Inside is a cheap trinket or crumpled packing. The sender's number is disconnected, and the delivery firm passes your payment to the seller as it would for any order.

cod-parcel-scam.whyItWorks: Households share one front door, so whoever answers assumes someone else placed the order. Turning a driver away feels ruder and riskier than paying a modest sum, and the courier on the step is entirely real.

realVsFake.real: With a genuine order, somebody in the house chose to pay on delivery at checkout and has a confirmation naming the seller.
realVsFake.fake: Nobody can find an order, and the label's sender is a mobile number or a vague trading name.

realVsFake.real: Delivery firms accept a refusal. An unpaid parcel simply travels back to whoever sent it, at no cost to you.
realVsFake.fake: The scheme depends on the driver's hurry and your worry that refusing causes trouble for a relative.

realVsFake.real: A real seller answers the phone number printed on the label and can quote what was bought.
realVsFake.fake: The return address is half complete and the number rings out or is switched off.

steps.title: A mention notification
steps.detail: Your phone shows that an unfamiliar account mentioned you in a comment. Opening it reveals your handle in a block of thirty or forty other tagged names.

steps.title: The bait line
steps.detail: Above the tags sits one line: a free phone for selected users, discounted sunglasses, or 'I can't believe this is you in the video', with a shortened link.

steps.title: Spin, survey or sign in
steps.detail: The link opens a prize wheel that always wins, a three-question survey, or a copy of the platform's login screen asking you to sign in to watch.

steps.title: Your account does the tagging
steps.detail: Prize pages take card details for 'postage'. Login pages take your password, and within hours your own profile is tagging your friends in the same comment.

comment-tagging-scam.whyItWorks: A tag produces the same notification you get when a friend mentions you, so curiosity is automatic. Seeing dozens of other names beside yours suggests a real promotion with many winners, when it is a script working through a list.

realVsFake.real: Brands announce promotions in their own posts, from an established page with years of history.
realVsFake.fake: The offer appears as a comment under an unrelated post, written by a profile created this week.

realVsFake.real: A friend who spots you in a video sends it to you privately, with a note that sounds like them.
realVsFake.fake: The 'is this you' line is pasted identically for every person in the tag list.

realVsFake.real: Clips shared on a platform play inside its app, where you are already signed in.
realVsFake.fake: The link leaves the app for a browser page that demands your username and password before anything plays.

steps.title: Money you never claimed
steps.detail: A text states 'our records show' you are entitled to a set figure, such as £2,750, for a recent accident, a mis-sold product or a data breach.

steps.title: The eligibility questionnaire
steps.detail: The link opens a 'claims checker' with three or four easy questions. Whatever you answer, the result says you qualify and the payout is reserved.

steps.title: Identity and bank form
steps.detail: To 'release the award' the form asks for full name, address, date of birth, National Insurance number and the sort code and account number for payment.

steps.title: Fee, or a claim in your name
steps.detail: Some versions add an 'admin fee' by card. Others sell your details to cold callers or file invented injury claims using your identity.

compensation-claim-text-scam.whyItWorks: Genuine payouts for mis-sold insurance and breached data have been widely advertised, so being owed something seems plausible. A precise amount with a closing deadline suggests the case is already settled and only your bank details are missing.

realVsFake.real: Compensation follows a claim you or your solicitor started, with a reference number and paperwork you have seen.
realVsFake.fake: The text announces an award for an incident it never describes and you never reported.

realVsFake.real: A regulated claims firm names itself, gives its authorisation number and sends a written agreement before acting.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is a mobile number or a vague 'Claims Team' with no company behind it.

realVsFake.real: No genuine payout figure is fixed before anyone has assessed your injury, loss or policy.
realVsFake.fake: An exact sum is quoted in the first message, purely to make stopping feel like throwing money away.

steps.title: Dear esteemed Doctor
steps.detail: A flattering email cites one of your papers or your LinkedIn profile and invites you to give a keynote at an 'international summit' in a famous city.

steps.title: A website full of borrowed logos
steps.detail: The event site lists a grand scientific committee, university and sponsor logos used without permission, and a hotel venue. The programme itself stays vague.

steps.title: Registration, visa letter, hotel block
steps.detail: Confirming your slot means a speaker registration fee, then a charge for a visa invitation letter and a hotel booking through their agent, plus a passport scan.

steps.title: No podium at the end
steps.detail: After payment by transfer the organiser goes silent, or the 'summit' is a hired room holding a few other paying speakers. The passport copy is kept for reuse.

conference-invite-email-scam.whyItWorks: Being asked to speak is a professional compliment people want to believe, and academics and founders are under real pressure to present abroad. Genuine conferences charge registration too, so the first invoice does not look strange.

realVsFake.real: Established conferences choose speakers through a call for papers or a committee member who knows your field.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger offers a keynote slot to anyone who replies, then sends a bill for it.

realVsFake.real: Real events have past editions, recorded talks and named organisers at a society or company you can telephone.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser runs dozens of near-identical 'world congress' sites, and listed committee members have never heard of it.

realVsFake.real: You apply for a visa yourself at the embassy or its official service, and book hotels directly.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser insists its 'travel desk' handles both, and needs a passport scan and bank transfer first.

steps.title: A card or phone disappears
steps.detail: It is lifted from a pocket in a crowd, left in a taxi, or snatched from a pub table. Sometimes only the card is slipped out of a wallet.

steps.title: A burst of small taps
steps.detail: The thief makes quick purchases under the contactless limit at vending machines, transport gates, self-checkouts and corner shops, where nobody looks at the name on the card.

steps.title: Buying things to resell
steps.detail: Tobacco, alcohol, travel top-ups and gift cards are favourites. They move between shops so that no single terminal asks for the PIN.

steps.title: Loading it onto a wallet
steps.detail: Some try to add the card to their own phone's wallet, which needs a code from your bank. A phishing text or call to you often follows.

contactless-card-theft-scam.whyItWorks: Tap payments under the limit need no PIN and no signature, a convenience the thief inherits the second the card changes hands. Each purchase is small enough to pass for normal spending until the owner checks.

realVsFake.real: Your own tap payments match where you were: your station, your supermarket, your lunch stop.
realVsFake.fake: A string of charges appears from shops you never visited, minutes apart, starting soon after you last saw the card.

realVsFake.real: A bank message about adding your card to a wallet arrives because you are setting up your own phone.
realVsFake.fake: A 'wallet activation' code arrives unprompted, sometimes followed by someone asking you to pass it on.

realVsFake.real: Freezing a card in the banking app takes seconds and can be undone if it turns up.
realVsFake.fake: The thief counts on you spending an hour retracing your steps before you think of blocking it.

steps.title: A trader's lifestyle feed
steps.detail: A social media account posts profit screenshots, hired sports cars and beach laptops. A link in the bio invites followers to 'copy my trades and earn while you sleep'.

steps.title: Sign up through his link
steps.detail: In a private chat the 'master trader' tells you to register on one particular platform using his code, which he says is the only place the mirroring works.

steps.title: Switch on auto-copy
steps.detail: You deposit and enable copying. The account shows a run of winning trades matching his posts, and he suggests adding funds to reach the 'pro tier' with bigger positions.

steps.title: One bad trade, or a profit share
steps.detail: Either a single 'liquidation' wipes the balance overnight, or a withdrawal is held until you pay the trader's performance cut in advance from your own pocket.

copy-trading-scam.whyItWorks: Copy trading is a real feature on regulated brokers, so the idea is familiar. It appeals to people who believe trading profits exist but doubt their own skill, and a leaderboard of someone else's wins seems to remove the need to learn anything.

realVsFake.real: On a regulated broker, a trader's full history is published, including losing months and the deepest drawdown.
realVsFake.fake: The record consists of cropped screenshots, and losing trades never appear in the feed or on the leaderboard.

realVsFake.real: Genuine copy features let you choose among many traders and stop copying with one click.
realVsFake.fake: You are steered to a single website nobody has reviewed, reachable only through the trader's personal invitation link.

realVsFake.real: Any performance fee on a real platform is deducted automatically from realised profit.
realVsFake.fake: The trader asks you to send his share directly, in crypto, before the platform will release your funds.

steps.title: A real advert is cloned
steps.detail: The fraudster saves the photos and description from a genuine seller's listing and reposts them under a new profile with a similar name and a lower price.

steps.title: They message you first
steps.detail: After you comment on or save the original, a private message arrives: 'Saw you were interested in my item, I can do it cheaper.'

steps.title: Moved to another app
steps.detail: They ask to continue on a different messenger 'because notifications are broken here', which takes the conversation away from the platform's reporting and payment tools.

steps.title: A transfer to hold it
steps.detail: You send a holding payment or the full amount by bank transfer. The duplicate profile is deleted, and the real seller has never heard of you.

copycat-listing-scam.whyItWorks: Everything you can check about the item is true, because the photos, measurements and wording belong to a real seller with a real product. The only false thing is the person holding the account, and that is the hardest part to see.

realVsFake.real: The original seller has an account with months of history, past sales and reviews that mention similar items.
realVsFake.fake: The copy was created this week, has no feedback, and its only listings are borrowed ones.

realVsFake.real: A genuine seller waits for you to message them through the listing's own contact button.
realVsFake.fake: You are approached privately by an account that watched who commented on the real advert.

realVsFake.real: Ask the true owner for a new photo with today's date on a slip of paper and they can take one.
realVsFake.fake: Asked for one, the copier resends the saved images or says the item is already boxed up.

steps.title: Before-and-after pictures
steps.detail: An Instagram page or advert shows dramatic before-and-after photos and offers a tummy tuck, veneers or a hair transplant abroad, flights and hotel included, at a striking price.

steps.title: Consultation by chat
steps.detail: A 'patient coordinator' on WhatsApp asks for photos of the area, approves you within the hour, and never puts you in front of the surgeon.

steps.title: The slot deposit
steps.detail: They say one discounted slot is left next month. A deposit of several hundred, or the whole package price, must be wired to hold it.

steps.title: Arrival, or no arrival
steps.detail: Some patients land to find no clinic at the address. Others are met, asked for extra cash for 'anaesthesia', and operated on by someone different in a rented room.

cosmetic-surgery-scam.whyItWorks: Private procedures at home cost far more, and many clinics abroad are perfectly good, so a low overseas price is believable. A coordinator who is warm and available at midnight feels like care, which stands in for credentials.

realVsFake.real: A reputable clinic names the surgeon, whose registration you can look up with that country's medical board.
realVsFake.fake: The chat mentions 'our team of European-trained doctors', and no individual name is ever given.

realVsFake.real: Proper surgeons hold a consultation themselves, ask about medical history and medication, and sometimes say no.
realVsFake.fake: A salesperson approves three procedures at once from two selfies and asks nothing about your health.

realVsFake.real: Genuine providers explain in writing who handles complications and aftercare once you have flown home.
realVsFake.fake: Aftercare is described as 'message us any time', on the same chat account that vanishes after payment.

steps.title: A refund to the penny
steps.detail: Claiming to be your local council, a text or email says you overpaid and are owed 167.40, or that your home has sat in the wrong band for years.

steps.title: A page with no council named
steps.detail: The link shows a generic civic crest and a 'claim your rebate' form. It asks for your name, postcode and date of birth without naming any actual authority.

steps.title: Card details for a refund
steps.detail: To 'return the overpayment' it wants the long card number, expiry and security code, or the login you use for online banking.

steps.title: Three working days of silence
steps.detail: The promised rebate window gives the thieves time. While you wait for 167.40 to arrive, the card is being spent or your bank login tried.

council-tax-scam.whyItWorks: Council tax bills are recalculated when people move, change discounts or overpay, so refunds of odd amounts do happen. A sum like 167.40 looks calculated, and the arrears version borrows a real fear, because councils can and do send enforcement agents.

realVsFake.real: A council usually refunds an overpayment to the account your Direct Debit comes from, or credits it against your next bill.
realVsFake.fake: The message needs a card number to send money back, which is not how a refund to a bank account works.

realVsFake.real: Genuine council letters quote your council tax account number and the name of the authority that bills you.
realVsFake.fake: The text says only 'your local council', because the same wording has gone to phones in every borough.

realVsFake.real: Unpaid council tax moves through a posted reminder, a final notice and a court summons before any enforcement agent is involved.
realVsFake.fake: The arrears message skips every stage and promises bailiffs at your door unless a payment link is used tonight.

steps.title: A buyer who agrees at once
steps.detail: Someone accepts your asking price for a phone, console or bike without questions and says they have the exact cash and can come tonight.

steps.title: The meeting spot shifts
steps.detail: Shortly before the meet they change the place to a dim car park or a side street, and arrive saying a taxi is waiting.

steps.title: A folded bundle of notes
steps.detail: They hand over a wad held by a rubber band or tucked in an envelope, with a real note on the outside, and talk constantly while you hold it.

steps.title: Gone before you count
steps.detail: They take the item and leave within seconds. Under proper light the inner notes are photocopies, film props or cut paper, and the buyer's profile has been deleted.

counterfeit-cash-pickup-scam.whyItWorks: Sellers think of cash as the one payment that cannot bounce, so they relax once they see it. Counting notes slowly while a stranger waits feels rude, and the buyer's hurry gives you a polite excuse not to.

realVsFake.real: A genuine buyer is happy to meet inside a bank branch, a supermarket foyer or a police station lobby.
realVsFake.fake: This one insists on the far corner of a car park after dark and will not come indoors.

realVsFake.real: Real banknotes have raised print, a clear window or watermark, and a metallic thread you can find by touch.
realVsFake.fake: The notes feel waxy or papery, share one serial number, or carry small print saying they are for film use.

realVsFake.real: An honest buyer expects you to count the money and check it with a detector pen.
realVsFake.fake: They keep one hand on your item and say there is no time to go through the notes.

steps.title: The handbag at 180
steps.detail: A post in a resale group or on a social shop shows a designer bag, 'brand new with tags', at 180 against a retail price of 1,200.

steps.title: 'DM me, serious buyers only'
steps.detail: In private messages the seller says it was an unwanted gift or a staff purchase. Asked for a receipt, they send a blurred photo or say it was thrown away.

steps.title: Friends-and-family payment
steps.detail: They ask you to pay as a personal transfer 'to avoid fees', which removes buyer cover, and repeat that there are no returns and the price ends tonight.

steps.title: The parcel from overseas
steps.detail: Weeks later a thin package arrives with a bag that smells of glue, has uneven stitching and a misspelt logo stamp. The account has blocked you.

counterfeit-designer-goods-scam.whyItWorks: Second-hand luxury is a real market where genuine bags do sell below retail, so a discount alone proves nothing. The copies now come with dust bags, tags and serial stickers, which are the very things buyers were once told to look for.

realVsFake.real: Authentic pre-owned bags hold their value, and resale platforms that authenticate them price close to the going rate.
realVsFake.fake: The price is a small fraction of retail for an unused item, with several colours 'available'.

realVsFake.real: A genuine owner can photograph the date code, interior stamp and hardware from any angle you ask for.
realVsFake.fake: Every image is a white-background catalogue shot, and new photos are refused as 'too much hassle'.

realVsFake.real: Reputable resellers offer a return window if an independent authenticator rejects the item.
realVsFake.fake: The listing says no returns, and payment must go by a method that offers no dispute route.

steps.title: Searching by part number
steps.detail: You look up a brake pad set, airbag module, phone battery or oven element and find it listed as 'genuine OEM' at half the dealer price.

steps.title: A listing light on detail
steps.detail: The advert shows the manufacturer's box but gives a part number missing its suffix, no batch code, and a seller name made of random letters.

steps.title: Transfer for fast dispatch
steps.detail: Card payment is 'temporarily unavailable', so you are offered next-day shipping in return for a direct bank transfer, with an invoice that names no company.

steps.title: Fitted, then it fails
steps.detail: The part arrives in near-perfect packaging with a slightly wrong font or hologram. It fits, then overheats, swells, wears out early or fails when it is needed.

counterfeit-parts-scam.whyItWorks: Main-dealer prices feel like a mark-up, and everyone knows identical parts are sold more cheaply elsewhere. A buyer cannot test a brake pad or battery cell by looking at it, so the box and the word 'genuine' carry the whole sale.

realVsFake.real: Manufacturers list their authorised distributors, and those sellers give a warranty that the maker will honour.
realVsFake.fake: The shop appears on no distributor list and offers a 'seller guarantee' with no address behind it.

realVsFake.real: A real component carries a full part number, batch or date code and safety markings that match the maker's catalogue.
realVsFake.fake: Codes are missing, repeated across every unit, or printed on a sticker placed over another label.

realVsFake.real: Genuine parts have weight to them: dense friction material, proper battery protection circuits, thick wiring.
realVsFake.fake: The copy is noticeably lighter, and the box seals have been re-glued or printed in duller ink.

steps.title: Sold out everywhere else
steps.detail: In the weeks before a holiday, the toy your child keeps asking for is out of stock in the big shops. A sponsored advert says one store has it.

steps.title: A pop-up shop with a countdown
steps.detail: The site copies the brand's pictures, shows the toy at half price and runs a stock counter that ticks down from seven while you look.

steps.title: Checkout by transfer
steps.detail: At the payment stage the only options are bank transfer or a payment app, with 'fast shipping' promised and delivery guaranteed before the big day.

steps.title: A lookalike in a plain bag
steps.detail: What arrives, often after the holiday, is an imitation with a misspelt name, loose small parts and a chemical smell. Other families receive no parcel at all.

counterfeit-toy-scam.whyItWorks: A parent who has promised a particular present and found empty shelves everywhere is short of time and options. The advert appears to solve that exact problem, and the fear of a disappointed child outweighs doubts about an unknown shop.

realVsFake.real: When a toy is scarce, real retailers sell at full price, limit purchases per customer or run a waiting list.
realVsFake.fake: The one shop with plenty in stock is also the one selling it at half price.

realVsFake.real: Genuine toys carry the required safety mark, an age warning and the importer's name and address on the box.
realVsFake.fake: Packaging is a plain polybag or a box with fuzzy printing and no manufacturer details.

realVsFake.real: Branded toys close their battery compartment with a screw and have parts too large to swallow.
realVsFake.fake: Button cells sit behind a clip-on cover, magnets pull out easily, and seams split in a child's hands.

steps.title: A landline call about cloning
steps.detail: The caller, often targeting older people at home, says he is from the bank's fraud unit or a police station and that your card was copied at a local shop.

steps.title: The fake call-back check
steps.detail: To prove it, he invites you to hang up and dial the bank. He keeps the line open, plays a dial tone, and an accomplice 'answers' as the bank.

steps.title: PIN typed into the handset
steps.detail: You are asked to key your PIN on the phone keypad 'so the system can cancel it', or to write it on a slip and seal it with the card.

steps.title: A knock at the door
steps.detail: A smartly dressed courier or taxi driver, sometimes hired innocently, arrives with a password you were given and takes the envelope. The card is used within the hour.

courier-card-collection-scam.whyItWorks: Offering a call-back check makes the caller seem scrupulous, and few people know that some landlines stay connected when only one side hangs up. A courier at the door with the agreed password then looks like the bank being thorough.

realVsFake.real: When a card is compromised, the bank cancels it remotely and posts a replacement. The old one can be cut up.
realVsFake.fake: The caller insists the 'cloned' card is evidence and must be collected intact.

realVsFake.real: No bank or police officer ever sends someone to your home for a card, cash or valuables.
realVsFake.fake: A collection is booked for the same afternoon, and you are given a secret word to exchange on the doorstep.

realVsFake.real: Your PIN is never needed to cancel a card, and bank staff will not ask for it.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to enter it on the telephone keypad or put it in the envelope for 'verification at the depot'.

steps.title: A close-contact text or a kit advert
steps.detail: A text says you were near someone who tested positive and should order a free kit, or an advert offers home tests while 'limited stock' lasts.

steps.title: The health-service lookalike
steps.detail: The order page borrows a health service's colours and asks for your name, address, date of birth and sometimes an insurance or Medicare number.

steps.title: Postage on a free kit
steps.detail: The kit itself is free, but a postage charge of 1.99 needs your card number, expiry date and security code.

steps.title: No box in the post
steps.detail: Nothing is delivered. The card is billed for larger sums over the following weeks, and insurance numbers are used to claim for tests never supplied.

covid-test-scam.whyItWorks: Governments really did post out free kits and send exposure alerts by text, so both formats are familiar. Someone who feels ill, or needs a negative result for travel or work, wants a test quickly and is not inclined to question a small postage charge.

realVsFake.real: Official free-kit schemes asked for a delivery address and took no payment of any kind.
realVsFake.fake: The 'free' order cannot be completed without a card, supposedly to cover delivery.

realVsFake.real: Results come from the lab, pharmacy or clinic that took your sample, through the account you set up with them.
realVsFake.fake: A message offers a result or certificate for a test you never took, behind a link asking who you are.

realVsFake.real: Authorised kits sold by pharmacies show the manufacturer, a lot number and an expiry date on the box.
realVsFake.fake: The shop page shows a stock photo, names no maker and runs a countdown of kits remaining.

steps.title: A recorded warning about your SIN
steps.detail: A robocall says legal action has been filed against your Social Insurance Number, or a text claims a CRA refund is waiting as an e-transfer deposit.

steps.title: An 'agent' with a badge number
steps.detail: Press 1 and a caller gives a name, badge number and file number, then says an audit found errors in several past returns and a balance is owing.

steps.title: The second call from 'police'
steps.detail: Hesitate, and a new call arrives showing a local police or RCMP number. That voice confirms a warrant and says only immediate payment will stop it.

steps.title: Cash into a Bitcoin machine
steps.detail: You are kept on the phone while you withdraw cash and feed it into a crypto ATM using their QR code, or send an Interac e-transfer to a personal email address.

cra-tax-scam.whyItWorks: Newcomers to Canada and first-time filers often have no picture of how the CRA collects a debt, so a badge number and a matching call from 'police' fill the gap. The refund text copies the e-transfer deposit notices Canadians receive from friends every week.

realVsFake.real: The CRA sets out what you owe in a notice of assessment, sent by mail or posted in My Account.
realVsFake.fake: The first you hear of any debt is a phone call, and the caller cannot tell you which tax return it relates to.

realVsFake.real: Tax is paid to the CRA through your bank's bill payment service or pre-authorised debit, never by e-transfer, crypto or gift cards.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agent' directs you to a convenience store machine or a gift card rack and asks for the receipt or the codes.

realVsFake.real: Refunds arrive by direct deposit or cheque with nothing to click. The CRA does not send refunds by e-transfer or text.
realVsFake.fake: A text invites you to 'deposit' the refund by picking your bank from a list of logos and signing in.

steps.title: A call after breach news
steps.detail: Days after a data breach makes the headlines, a caller or email claiming to be a credit bureau's 'fraud protection team' says your file is exposed and offers to freeze it for you.

steps.title: The 'identity check'
steps.detail: To 'locate your file' they ask for your full name, date of birth, current address and all nine digits of your Social Security number, read out or typed into a form.

steps.title: An activation fee by card
steps.detail: Next comes a one-off 'activation' or monthly 'lock maintenance' charge, often around 30 dollars, taken over the phone along with your card's expiry date and security code.

steps.title: No freeze, new credit applications
steps.detail: Nothing is ever placed on your file. The same details you handed over are enough to apply for cards and loans, and the first sign is a lender's letter weeks later.

credit-freeze-scam.whyItWorks: A freeze is the advice everyone repeats after a breach, so an offer to do it for you sounds like the responsible next step. Few people know each bureau lets you place one yourself at no cost, in a few minutes.

realVsFake.real: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion place a freeze free of charge when you ask through their own websites, phone lines or by post.
realVsFake.fake: A caller quotes an activation fee and says the freeze cannot start until your card is charged.

realVsFake.real: You start the request, and you deal with each bureau separately because a freeze at one does not cover the others.
realVsFake.fake: Someone contacts you first and promises a single call will lock your credit 'everywhere' in one go.

realVsFake.real: A bureau gives you a PIN or account login to lift the freeze later, and you can see its status online.
realVsFake.fake: You get a vague 'confirmation number' by text and no way to check that anything was actually frozen.

steps.title: The 'clean slate' pitch
steps.detail: A radio advert, flyer or social media post promises to erase defaults, late payments and court judgments from your credit file within thirty days.

steps.title: Payment before any work
steps.detail: A consultant takes a sign-up charge of several hundred plus a monthly retainer, and asks for your ID and full access to your credit reports.

steps.title: Disputing everything
steps.detail: They flood the credit reference agencies with template letters claiming accurate debts are not yours. Entries may vanish briefly while under review, then return.

steps.title: The 'new identity' trick
steps.detail: Some go further and sell you a fresh nine-digit number or tell you to apply using altered details, which is itself fraud committed in your name.

credit-repair-scam.whyItWorks: A poor score blocks mortgages, rentals and phone contracts, and the rules behind it feel opaque, so a specialist claiming inside knowledge sounds worth paying. A temporary dip in negative entries during disputes looks like early proof it is working.

realVsFake.real: Credit reference agencies let you dispute a genuine error yourself for free, and must investigate it.
realVsFake.fake: The firm says only its 'legal team' can talk to the agencies and tells you not to contact them.

realVsFake.real: A reputable adviser explains that correct negative information stays on file until it ages off.
realVsFake.fake: The salesperson guarantees a set points increase and removal of debts you really do owe.

realVsFake.real: Free debt charities and honest advisers charge nothing upfront, or bill only once a service has been delivered.
realVsFake.fake: Money is taken on day one by card or transfer, with a retainer that continues whether or not anything changes.

steps.title: The cut-price cabin advert
steps.detail: A social media advert or sponsored search result offers balcony cabins at a fraction of the usual fare, on a site whose name is one word away from a real agent's.

steps.title: The cruise specialist on chat
steps.detail: A chat window or callback connects you to a 'cruise specialist' who says only three cabins remain at this price and the sale closes tonight.

steps.title: Deposit by bank transfer
steps.detail: They say the card system is down, or that card payments lose the discount, then send bank details in a personal or unrelated company name for the deposit.

steps.title: A reference that leads nowhere
steps.detail: You receive a PDF invoice with a booking reference. The cruise line has no record of it, extra 'port taxes' are requested, and then the chat stops answering.

cruise-booking-scam.whyItWorks: Cruises cost a lot and unsold cabins really are discounted late, so a steep reduction is more believable here than for most holidays. Paying a deposit months before sailing is normal, which hands the thieves a long head start.

realVsFake.real: A real agent's booking can be found on the cruise line's own website using the reference and your surname.
realVsFake.fake: The reference on the invoice returns 'booking not found' when you try it with the cruise line.

realVsFake.real: Cruise lines and established agents take deposits by credit or debit card, which gives you a route to dispute.
realVsFake.fake: The seller pushes a bank transfer or gift cards and has an excuse ready for why cards cannot be used.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fares show port fees in the quoted price or list them before you pay.
realVsFake.fake: New charges for taxes, gratuities or 'cabin release' arrive after the deposit, each described as the last.

steps.title: Tokens or a tag out of nowhere
steps.detail: A direct message, a reply under a project's post, or an unknown token appearing in your wallet announces that your address qualifies for an airdrop.

steps.title: A claim page with a timer
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the project's site, with the right logo and a domain one character off. A clock shows hours remaining to claim.

steps.title: Connect, then sign
steps.detail: Pressing 'Claim' opens your wallet with a signature request. The text is a block of code, or an approval giving the site's contract spending rights over your tokens.

steps.title: A drainer script empties it
steps.detail: Seconds after you confirm, an automated script sweeps your most valuable coins and NFTs to another address. No free tokens ever arrive.

crypto-airdrop-scam.whyItWorks: Genuine airdrops have handed early users valuable tokens for nothing, and claiming those did involve connecting a wallet. Because no money is requested and a signature feels like a login, people confirm a request they cannot read.

realVsFake.real: A real project announces an airdrop on its long-standing official channels, with eligibility rules published in advance.
realVsFake.fake: News of the drop reaches you by private message from an account posing as a moderator or support helper.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate claim transaction sends tokens to you and costs only the network fee.
realVsFake.fake: The prompt requests permission over tokens you already hold, such as 'set approval for all' or an unlimited spend.

realVsFake.real: Surprise tokens from a genuine distribution can be ignored safely and need no website visit.
realVsFake.fake: The mystery token's name is itself a web address, telling you to visit it to swap or unlock the reward.

steps.title: Upload your photo
steps.detail: An advert shows a hand-painted pet portrait, engraved necklace or carved name sign. The shop asks you to upload a photo or type the names you want.

steps.title: Full price at checkout
steps.detail: Checkout takes the full price and states that personalised orders cannot be cancelled or refunded. Delivery is quoted at six to eight weeks.

steps.title: The long wait, with updates
steps.detail: Emails say your piece is 'with the artist' or 'in quality control'. Each reply buys another fortnight, pushing you towards the deadline for disputing the payment.

steps.title: A print in a tube
steps.detail: What finally arrives, if anything, is a cheap digital print or a stamped trinket with the name misspelt. Refund requests get the 'custom items are final' reply.

custom-product-scam.whyItWorks: Real makers do ask for payment up front and do take weeks, so both the prepayment and the delay look normal. By uploading a photo of a pet or a child's name, the buyer has also become emotionally invested before paying.

realVsFake.real: A genuine maker sends a sketch, proof or mock-up for your approval before starting the final piece.
realVsFake.fake: No proof is ever offered, and questions about progress get a generic reply with your order number pasted in.

realVsFake.real: Craftspeople show work-in-progress shots, a workshop and past commissions with the customers' own photos in reviews.
realVsFake.fake: The gallery is made of polished renders and images that also appear on wholesale sites selling the item by the hundred.

realVsFake.real: An honest seller refunds or remakes an item that arrives wrong, damaged or not as described, custom or not.
realVsFake.fake: The 'bespoke' label is used as a shield, quoted in every reply to refuse refunds even when nothing was delivered.

steps.title: 'You have been selected'
steps.detail: A text or email carrying a supermarket, courier or phone brand's name invites you to answer four questions about your last visit in exchange for a free gift.

steps.title: Four questions nobody reads
steps.detail: The questions are trivial, such as how often you shop and whether you would recommend the store. A progress bar and countdown timer hurry you along.

steps.title: Pick your prize
steps.detail: A grid of gift boxes or a list of 'remaining' items appears, with invented shopper comments underneath. You 'win' a phone, air fryer or voucher.

steps.title: Shipping fee with small print
steps.detail: Paying £1.95 for shipping needs full card details. Faint text below the button enrols you in a subscription that takes a far larger sum every few weeks.

customer-survey-scam.whyItWorks: Real shops print survey invitations on receipts and offer prize draws, so the request looks routine. After a minute spent answering and 'winning', paying under two pounds for postage feels like finishing something you already earned.

realVsFake.real: Genuine feedback surveys enter you into a draw or give a small discount code. They do not hand every respondent an expensive gadget.
realVsFake.fake: Everyone who completes the four questions is told they have won a high-value item.

realVsFake.real: A real retailer survey is reached from your receipt or its own website and never needs a payment card.
realVsFake.fake: The last screen is a checkout asking for card number, expiry and security code for 'shipping'.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate offers state any recurring charge clearly, beside the price, before you pay.
realVsFake.fake: The subscription terms sit in pale grey text under the pay button, or on a separate page.

steps.title: An email from 'customs clearance'
steps.detail: The message carries a postal or courier logo and a subject like 'Shipment on hold: duty unpaid', with a reference that resembles a tracking code.

steps.title: The itemised charge
steps.detail: A neat table lists import VAT, a handling fee and a total of 3.50, with a warning that daily storage costs begin after 48 hours.

steps.title: The 'Pay duty' button
steps.detail: The button leads to a payment form on an unrelated domain asking for your name, home address, phone number and full card details.

steps.title: A fake bank approval screen
steps.detail: A mock 3-D Secure page requests the code your bank just texted. That code actually approves a far larger purchase, or adds your card to a criminal's phone wallet.

customs-duty-email-scam.whyItWorks: Import charges on overseas orders are real, and most shoppers have no idea how much to expect or who collects them. A table of VAT lines totalling a few coins looks like routine bureaucracy.

realVsFake.real: Real duty is worked out from the declared value of a specific item, and the notice quotes a tracking number that works.
realVsFake.fake: The email names no sender, country or item, and the fee is a suspiciously tiny figure.

realVsFake.real: The carrier collects import charges through its own website or app, by letter, or at the door.
realVsFake.fake: An emailed button sends you to a card form hosted somewhere with no connection to the carrier.

realVsFake.real: Parcels awaiting duty are generally kept for many days, with a reminder sent before anything is returned.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the goods will be destroyed or returned within two days.

steps.title: An ordinary sale
steps.detail: The buyer pays through the platform without fuss, and you post the item well wrapped with tracking. Delivery is confirmed a day or two later.

steps.title: 'It arrived smashed'
steps.detail: A message says the item came broken. The photos show damage on a unit of another colour or model, cropped so no box or label is visible.

steps.title: Keep it and refund most
steps.detail: They ask for more than half the price back and say posting it back is not worth the bother, presenting this as the easy option for both of you.

steps.title: Reviews used as a threat
steps.detail: If you ask for a return, they threaten one-star feedback and a formal dispute. Many small sellers pay up, and the buyer keeps a working item.

damaged-item-refund-scam.whyItWorks: Parcels do get broken in transit, so the claim is plausible and a decent seller wants to put it right. A new shop with a handful of reviews fears one bad rating more than losing half a sale, and the buyer knows it.

realVsFake.real: A customer with a truly broken item sends clear photos of the damage, the box and the shipping label together.
realVsFake.fake: The pictures are close-ups with no packaging, and one shows a serial number that is not yours.

realVsFake.real: Marketplaces handle damage through a return request: the buyer sends it back with a label and is refunded on arrival.
realVsFake.fake: The buyer wants money sent directly and refuses a prepaid return label when you offer one.

realVsFake.real: Most honest customers ask for a replacement or a repair, since they wanted the product.
realVsFake.fake: Only cash will do, the figure is negotiable, and the tone hardens the moment you mention evidence.

steps.title: The exposure scan advert
steps.detail: An advert or email invites you to type in your name for a free scan, then shows a red counter claiming your address and phone number appear on dozens of sites.

steps.title: Blurred results behind a paywall
steps.detail: The listings are blurred out. To see them and 'begin removal' you must pick a plan, with a timer warning that identity thieves could find the records first.

steps.title: A profile form and ID upload
steps.detail: Sign-up asks for every previous address, old phone numbers, relatives' names and a photo of your driving licence, supposedly so brokers can match and delete the right person.

steps.title: Progress bars that never finish
steps.detail: A dashboard shows removals 'in progress' month after month while the subscription renews. Search your name and the listings are still there, and the service now holds a fuller file than any broker.

data-broker-removal-scam.whyItWorks: Seeing your own home address on a stranger's website is unsettling, and opting out of people-search sites one by one is tedious. A service that promises to erase all of it for one payment sounds like relief, so the ID upload feels like a formality.

realVsFake.real: People-search sites run their own opt-out forms, which usually need only the link to your listing and an email address to confirm.
realVsFake.fake: The removal service wants a passport or licence scan plus your full Social Security number before it will lift a finger.

realVsFake.real: An honest removal company names the brokers it covers and sends reports you can check by searching the sites yourself.
realVsFake.fake: You are shown a round number of 'exposures' with no site names, and a status page that only ever says 'pending'.

realVsFake.real: A genuine provider has a company address, a privacy policy saying what it does with your data, and a clear way to cancel.
realVsFake.fake: The site appeared recently, lists no owner, and the only cancellation route is an email address that never replies.

steps.title: A request you never made
steps.detail: An email says your account data download is ready, imitating the export notices sent by Google, Facebook or Instagram when someone asks for a copy of their data.

steps.title: Two buttons, one destination
steps.detail: It offers 'Download file' and 'Wasn't you? Secure your account'. Both lead to the same counterfeit page, so curiosity and caution end in the same place.

steps.title: Sign in to retrieve the archive
steps.detail: The page mimics the 're-enter your password to continue' step that genuine exports use, then asks for the code sent to your phone.

steps.title: The export becomes real
steps.detail: With your login, attackers can request the true archive holding every message, photo and contact, or change the password and lock you out.

data-download-email-scam.whyItWorks: The email works in two directions. Curious people want to see the file, while cautious people fear someone else has asked for their data, and both groups reach for a button leading to one password form.

realVsFake.real: A genuine export exists only because you asked for it in account settings, and the notice follows that request.
realVsFake.fake: The email turns up with no request behind it and a 24-hour expiry.

realVsFake.real: Real services list pending and completed exports on a settings page you can open yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The only way offered to see the file is the button in the email.

realVsFake.real: Genuine security notices give the device, rough location and time of the activity.
realVsFake.fake: It says 'a request was received' and gives no device, place or time at all.

steps.title: A newly listed company gets a letter
steps.detail: Soon after incorporation, a letter or email headed with a regulator-style logo says the business has not registered as a data controller.

steps.title: Fines quoted in bold
steps.detail: It cites data protection law, mentions penalties running to thousands, and gives a compliance reference so it reads like an enforcement notice.

steps.title: A fee several times too high
steps.detail: The registration charge shown is well above the regulator's real tier for a small firm, sometimes padded with a 'certificate' or 'compliance pack'.

steps.title: Paid to a look-alike 'registry'
steps.detail: Payment goes by card on a copycat site or by transfer to a limited company. At best the firm is registered at a mark-up, at worst nothing is filed.

data-protection-fee-scam.whyItWorks: Many small businesses do owe a data protection fee and have never heard of it, so the demand contains a grain of truth. A new director facing a letter about GDPR fines would sooner pay a modest sum than read the legislation.

realVsFake.real: The data protection regulator publishes its fee tiers and a free self-assessment showing whether you need to pay at all.
realVsFake.fake: The notice assumes every business must pay and quotes one flat price with no mention of exemptions.

realVsFake.real: Payment is made on the regulator's own website, and the business then appears on its public register of fee payers.
realVsFake.fake: The payee is a company with 'data', 'registration' or 'compliance' in its name and a mailbox address.

realVsFake.real: A regulator's reminder gives a reference you can check by ringing its published helpline.
realVsFake.fake: A caller follows up within days offering to take card details over the phone to 'stop the fine being issued'.

steps.title: A dead drive and a search
steps.detail: After a phone, laptop or external disk fails, you look online for help. Paid listings promise high success rates and a free assessment with collection by courier.

steps.title: They have the device
steps.detail: Once it is posted off, the low price disappears. An email says the damage is severe and needs clean-room work at several times the advertised cost.

steps.title: The advanced recovery fee
steps.detail: Payment is required before work begins. Later come extra charges for donor parts, a replacement drive to hold the files, or an 'attempt fee' owed whatever the outcome.

steps.title: Pay again to get it back
steps.detail: If you refuse, they charge a release or return shipping fee for your own disk. It may come back opened and in worse condition, with nothing recovered.

data-recovery-scam.whyItWorks: The files at stake are often wedding photos or years of work with no backup, and the owner cannot judge whether a drive needs a simple fix or a specialist lab. Once the device is in someone else's building, walking away feels impossible.

realVsFake.real: Established labs diagnose first, then send a fixed written quote and a list of the files they can retrieve.
realVsFake.fake: The firm quotes by phone, will not put a ceiling on the price, and bills before saying what is recoverable.

realVsFake.real: Many reputable recovery companies charge nothing when no data comes back, and return the device either way.
realVsFake.fake: Your drive is held until you settle an invoice for work that produced no files.

realVsFake.real: A real lab has a street address you can visit, named engineers and reviews that describe specific jobs.
realVsFake.fake: The address is a mailbox shop or a house, and each city page on the site shows the same stock photo.

steps.title: A match keen to meet
steps.detail: Someone attractive matches with you on a dating app and is quickly ready to meet. They suggest a bar near you, then add one condition.

steps.title: The catfish story
steps.detail: They explain a previous date turned out to be fake or frightening, so now they only meet people holding a 'safe dating ID' or verification badge.

steps.title: The badge website
steps.detail: Their link opens a site with padlock icons and a short form: name, email, date of birth. The last screen asks for a card, 'only to confirm you are an adult'.

steps.title: Unmatched and billed
steps.detail: Submitting the card starts 'trial' memberships at several unrelated sites that renew monthly. The match asks for a screenshot of the badge, then goes quiet or unmatches.

dating-safety-verification-scam.whyItWorks: Worry about meeting strangers is sensible, and you would look careless or creepy for arguing with it. The request also comes with a date already half arranged, so the form looks like the last small step before meeting.

realVsFake.real: Dating apps that offer verification run it inside the app, usually with a selfie, and it is free.
realVsFake.fake: A match sends you to an outside website that issues its own 'ID number' and wants a card first.

realVsFake.real: A cautious date asks for a video call or picks a busy public place, which costs you nothing.
realVsFake.fake: They turn down a call and say only the badge from their chosen site will reassure them.

realVsFake.real: A real person replies in their own words and reacts to what you actually said.
realVsFake.fake: The same paragraph about being catfished arrives whatever you ask, because a bot is pasting it to every match.

steps.title: A free sign-up
steps.detail: You join a dating site from an advert promising local singles. Creating a profile is free, and you have not even added a photo yet.

steps.title: The inbox fills within minutes
steps.detail: Before the hour is out, a string of attractive 'members' have messaged, winked or favourited you. The previews are blurred or cut off after a few words.

steps.title: Pay to read, pay to reply
steps.detail: Opening a message needs a subscription. Replying costs credits or coins, bought in bundles, and every reply you send burns through some.

steps.title: Chats that never leave the site
steps.detail: Replies are flirty but vague, ignore what you wrote and never agree to a call or date. When your credits run low, new admirers appear.

dating-site-bot-scam.whyItWorks: Attention from several people at once is flattering, and the paywall sits just in front of finding out what they said. The small print often admits to operator-run 'entertainment profiles', but nobody reads terms while the inbox is filling.

realVsFake.real: On mainstream dating apps a new profile with no photo gets little attention, and a match needs both people to opt in.
realVsFake.fake: Flirty messages pour in before you have written a word about yourself.

realVsFake.real: Genuine members swap numbers, video call and arrange to meet within days or weeks.
realVsFake.fake: Every 'match' keeps the conversation on the site, where each reply costs credits.

realVsFake.real: Reputable apps charge a flat subscription you can cancel from your app store settings.
realVsFake.fake: The site sells per-message credits and renews a 'trial' at a higher price buried in its terms.

steps.title: One lower monthly payment
steps.detail: A cold call, advert or official-looking letter offers a 'government-backed relief programme' that rolls credit cards and loans into a single reduced payment.

steps.title: Stop paying your creditors
steps.detail: The adviser tells you to cancel direct debits to lenders and not to answer their calls, saying the firm now speaks for you.

steps.title: Money goes into their account
steps.detail: You set up a monthly payment to the company. The first several instalments are kept as 'set-up' and 'administration' charges, and nothing is passed on.

steps.title: Arrears, defaults and court letters
steps.detail: Months later your lenders write about missed payments, added interest and legal action. The firm's line is disconnected, or it blames you for 'breaking the plan'.

debt-consolidation-scam.whyItWorks: Someone juggling several creditors badly wants the calls to stop, and 'we will deal with them for you' offers exactly that. Being told not to speak to lenders hides the damage until it is serious.

realVsFake.real: A genuine consolidation loan pays off your old lenders directly, and you can see those balances drop to zero.
realVsFake.fake: Your creditors hear nothing, receive nothing, and your statements with them keep growing.

realVsFake.real: Free debt advice charities set up managed plans without charging and send statements of what each creditor received.
realVsFake.fake: The company keeps your early payments as fees and never produces a breakdown.

realVsFake.real: Honest advisers tell you to keep talking to lenders and warn that reduced payments will affect your credit file.
realVsFake.fake: You are instructed to ignore creditor letters and promised that half the debt will simply be written off.

steps.title: A message from the top
steps.detail: A finance employee receives an email or WhatsApp in the chief executive's name about a confidential acquisition, saying a lawyer will be in touch and to tell nobody.

steps.title: The meeting invitation
steps.detail: A calendar invite follows for a video call. On screen are the executive and sometimes other familiar colleagues, all generated from public interviews and conference footage.

steps.title: Instructions, then a quick exit
steps.detail: The fake executive speaks briefly, gives the amount and beneficiary, blames a poor connection and leaves. Any questions are pushed to chat or email.

steps.title: Payments in several slices
steps.detail: Staff send the transfer, often split into smaller payments to stay under approval limits, to a newly opened company account abroad. It is emptied within hours.

deepfake-ceo-scam.whyItWorks: Employees are trained to distrust odd emails, but seeing and hearing the boss on a call feels like the verification itself. Being chosen for a secret deal is flattering, and nobody wants to be the person who delayed it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine executive expects large payments to pass the usual dual sign-off, even for a deal still under wraps.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says the normal approvers must not be told, citing confidentiality rules around the deal.

realVsFake.real: On a live call a real person can turn their head, hold up a hand, or answer an unexpected question about last week.
realVsFake.fake: The face stays front-on and still, speech is short and scripted, and the call ends before anyone can probe.

realVsFake.real: Proper payment instructions arrive through the company's finance system, for a beneficiary already on file.
realVsFake.fake: Account details are pasted into the meeting chat or sent from a personal email, for a payee nobody has paid before.

steps.title: A sponsored clip in your feed
steps.detail: A paid ad shows a familiar presenter, entrepreneur or politician in what looks like a news interview, explaining a new platform that made ordinary people rich.

steps.title: The copied news page
steps.detail: Tapping through opens an article dressed in a broadcaster's colours and logo, quoting the celebrity and showing bank screenshots, with a registration box at the bottom.

steps.title: A call from an account manager
steps.detail: Minutes after you enter a phone number, a polite 'adviser' rings and walks you through a first deposit, typically around 250, by card or crypto.

steps.title: Profits you cannot withdraw
steps.detail: A dashboard shows the balance climbing, which prompts larger top-ups. Withdrawal requests meet a 'tax' or 'release fee', and then the site stops loading.

deepfake-endorsement-scam.whyItWorks: People trust a face and voice they have watched for years, and video used to be hard to forge. The clip only needs to hold up for twenty seconds on a small phone screen, with the sound low, to earn a tap.

realVsFake.real: When a public figure backs a product, it appears on their verified channels and in ordinary press coverage.
realVsFake.fake: The endorsement exists only in one advert from a page with an unrelated name and no other posts.

realVsFake.real: Genuine footage has lips, breathing and blinking that fit the sound, even on a poor recording.
realVsFake.fake: The mouth drifts out of time, the voice is flat, and the head barely moves between cuts.

realVsFake.real: Authorised investment firms appear on the financial regulator's public register and never promise to double deposits.
realVsFake.fake: The platform has a name registered weeks ago, no licence number, and a guarantee of daily profit.

steps.title: An advert between ordinary posts
steps.detail: A sponsored video shows a familiar entrepreneur or news presenter, apparently mid-interview, describing an automated trading platform that ordinary people can join.

steps.title: A cloned news article
steps.detail: Clicking leads to a page dressed as a national newspaper or broadcaster, with a headline about banks trying to suppress the system and a registration box.

steps.title: The call centre rings back
steps.detail: Minutes after you enter a phone number, an 'investment adviser' calls. He takes a 250 starting deposit by card and sets up a trading account for you.

steps.title: Bigger deposits, then a locked account
steps.detail: The account shows quick gains, and the adviser pushes for thousands more, sometimes via screen sharing. Requests to withdraw are met with tax demands and silence.

deepfake-investment-scam.whyItWorks: People trust what they see and hear, and a cloned voice saying the words in the right accent beats any written testimonial. The setting helps too: the clip sits inside a familiar feed, styled like a news interview the viewer half remembers.

realVsFake.real: Well-known business figures promote their own companies through official channels and do not front retail trading schemes.
realVsFake.fake: The clip appears only as a paid advert from a page with a random name and a handful of followers.

realVsFake.real: A genuine interview can be found in full on the broadcaster's own site, with the same words in context.
realVsFake.fake: The mouth drifts out of time with the voice, the face blurs when the head turns, and the original footage is about something else.

realVsFake.real: News organisations report on investments without sign-up forms and do not collect phone numbers for brokers.
realVsFake.fake: Every link on the fake article, including the menu and the weather, leads to the same registration form.

steps.title: A new pool with a huge rate
steps.detail: A group chat post, sponsored tweet or 'alpha' message promotes a freshly launched liquidity pool paying a fixed daily reward, with an audit badge on the homepage.

steps.title: Approve the staking contract
steps.detail: To stake, your wallet asks you to approve the contract for your stablecoins. The allowance is preset to unlimited, far more than the amount you plan to put in.

steps.title: Rewards pile up on screen
steps.detail: The farm page shows your stake and a reward figure climbing by the hour. A notice says the pool is nearly full, nudging you to add more.

steps.title: The contract owner pulls the funds
steps.detail: Using the allowance, the developers move your staked tokens and anything else of that type left in your wallet. The 'harvest' button fails and the site vanishes.

defi-yield-scam.whyItWorks: Early yield farms really did pay startling rates for a short while, so a high figure does not look impossible to someone who missed out. Approval prompts are routine in DeFi, and experienced users click them many times a week without reading the allowance.

realVsFake.real: Established protocols publish audited, verified contract code, and their yields move with market conditions.
realVsFake.fake: The audit badge links nowhere or to a firm that has never heard of the project, and the daily rate never changes.

realVsFake.real: A sound staking contract lets you set an allowance equal to your deposit and withdraw the stake yourself.
realVsFake.fake: Lowering the allowance makes the page throw an error, and withdrawal depends on a function only the owner can call.

realVsFake.real: Reputable projects have named or long-known developers and a history visible on a block explorer.
realVsFake.fake: The contract was deployed days ago by an anonymous team, and questions in the group chat get the asker banned.

steps.title: Verify your delivery account
steps.detail: An email or text says new security rules mean your courier account must be verified, or your saved delivery preferences will be wiped.

steps.title: The cloned app login
steps.detail: The link opens a browser copy of the courier's sign-in page, asking for your email, your password and then the code sent to your phone.

steps.title: A look around your account
steps.detail: Logged in to the real account, the thief can see saved addresses, your phone number, parcels currently on their way and sometimes a stored payment card.

steps.title: Parcels quietly diverted
steps.detail: Incoming deliveries are redirected to a pickup shop. The notification email is changed so you hear nothing, and the same password is tried on your email and shopping accounts.

delivery-app-phishing-scam.whyItWorks: A courier account seems to have no money in it, so people guard it less carefully than a bank login. The threat of deliveries stopping is enough to make one more sign-in feel like housekeeping.

realVsFake.real: Courier apps keep you signed in, and any security check happens inside the app you already have installed.
realVsFake.fake: A message pushes you to a web page to sign in again from scratch.

realVsFake.real: A genuine diversion request triggers a notice to the email and phone already on file.
realVsFake.fake: After a takeover the contact details are changed first, so every warning goes to the thief.

realVsFake.real: Delivery preferences such as a safe place are optional extras that nobody is penalised for skipping.
realVsFake.fake: The message claims your account will be deactivated and parcels refused unless you verify today.

steps.title: The thank-you message
steps.detail: Soon after a delivery, or at random, a text thanks you for your recent order and offers a reward for a thirty-second survey.

steps.title: Three easy questions
steps.detail: Was the parcel on time, was the driver polite, how many stars. A progress bar fills and a counter shows only a few rewards left.

steps.title: Pick a gift box
steps.detail: A grid of nine boxes appears. Your first choice is empty, your second 'wins' a phone or air fryer, and glowing comments from winners scroll underneath.

steps.title: Only the postage to pay
steps.detail: Claiming costs 1.95 for shipping, by card. The small print enrols you in a monthly subscription from a merchant whose name you will not recognise.

delivery-survey-scam.whyItWorks: Companies do send feedback requests after deliveries, so the opening looks routine. By the time the prize appears you have answered questions, and that sliver of effort makes the reward feel earned instead of random.

realVsFake.real: A genuine feedback request comes from the shop or courier you used, asks for a rating and ends with thanks.
realVsFake.fake: This one ends with a prize game and a payment form, whatever answers you give.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate prize draws do not bill winners for postage before sending the prize.
realVsFake.fake: The 'free' phone needs a small shipping payment that turns into repeating charges on your statement.

realVsFake.real: Real questionnaires stay open for days and work the same whenever you answer.
realVsFake.fake: A timer gives you four minutes, and the stock counter drops each time the page reloads.

steps.title: A nudge after your order
steps.detail: A text arrives in the evening, when takeaway and grocery orders peak, saying your driver did a great job and inviting a tip.

steps.title: The driver's profile page
steps.detail: The page shows a first name, a smiling photo, a five-star rating and three buttons offering to send 2, 5 or 10.

steps.title: Card details for a gratuity
steps.detail: Picking an amount opens a form for the long card number, expiry date and security code, although the real app already holds your payment method.

steps.title: Thanks, and nothing sent
steps.detail: A cheerful confirmation appears. No driver gets a penny. The card is tested with a small charge, then used for bigger spending elsewhere.

delivery-tip-scam.whyItWorks: Tipping is a small kindness with a little guilt attached, especially if you forgot to do it at the door. A couple of coins for a named driver seems too minor to question, and the page is built around that.

realVsFake.real: Food and grocery apps take tips on the order screen inside the app, using the card you paid with.
realVsFake.fake: A texted link opens a browser page where the whole card must be typed in.

realVsFake.real: A real tip prompt names the restaurant or shop and shows the order you placed.
realVsFake.fake: The message says only 'your driver', because it was sent to thousands of numbers at once.

realVsFake.real: In genuine apps you can add a gratuity hours later, or not at all, without consequence.
realVsFake.fake: The page suggests the driver loses out unless you pay within minutes.

steps.title: Nine a month, any dentist
steps.detail: A social advert or recorded call offers full dental cover for $9 a month, accepted by any dentist, with no waiting period and no health questions.

steps.title: Instant enrolment
steps.detail: The sign-up page takes your name, date of birth and card in under a minute. Buried wording calls the product a 'discount membership', not insurance.

steps.title: A membership card by email
steps.detail: You receive a PDF card with a member number and a helpline. It looks like cover, and for months there is no reason to test it.

steps.title: The receptionist has never heard of it
steps.detail: When a filling or crown is needed, the practice cannot find the plan. You pay in full, the monthly charge continues and the helpline rings out.

dental-plan-scam.whyItWorks: Dental work is costly and often left out of ordinary health cover, so people go looking for a cheap plan and find this one. Because nobody tests a dental policy until a tooth hurts, the monthly payments can run for a long time before anyone notices.

realVsFake.real: Real dental insurance usually has waiting periods for major work, an annual limit and a named network of practices.
realVsFake.fake: The advert promises crowns and implants from day one, with no cap and no exclusions.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate discount plan lets your own dentist's front desk confirm, before you join, that they honour it.
realVsFake.fake: The seller says 'all dentists accept it' and discourages you from ringing your practice to ask.

realVsFake.real: An insurer's policy document names the underwriter and gives a policy number and a regulator registration.
realVsFake.fake: Your only paperwork is a welcome email and a card image, with no terms, underwriter or cancellation address.

steps.title: An ad aimed at stuck renters
steps.detail: A sponsored post or text reads 'No deposit? No problem!' and promises to cover your tenancy deposit instantly, whatever your credit history.

steps.title: A form that wants everything
steps.detail: The link opens a short application asking for your landlord's name, the monthly rent, your bank account number, a photo of your ID and a selfie.

steps.title: 'Approved' in minutes, fee due
steps.detail: Approval comes back almost at once. Before the cover is 'activated' you must pay an arrangement or insurance fee, usually by bank transfer.

steps.title: A certificate nobody honours
steps.detail: You receive a PDF certificate, or nothing. When the landlord or agent checks, the provider is unknown to them and the deposit is still owed in full.

deposit-loan-scam.whyItWorks: Deposit replacement products do exist and tenants hear about them from agents, so the idea is familiar. Someone days from losing a flat for want of five weeks' rent will accept instant approval without asking who stands behind it.

realVsFake.real: Genuine deposit alternatives are offered through the letting agent or landlord, who has to agree to accept that product.
realVsFake.fake: The scheme approaches you directly and never asks whether your landlord has signed up to it.

realVsFake.real: A real lender runs affordability and credit checks and shows the total cost of borrowing before you commit.
realVsFake.fake: Everyone is approved within minutes, and the only figure shown is the fee to pay now.

realVsFake.real: Regulated firms appear on the financial regulator's register under the name they trade as.
realVsFake.fake: The deposit scheme's name is missing from the register, or copies a listed firm with one letter changed.

steps.title: A quote that beats the rest
steps.detail: A trade-in site or comparison advert offers noticeably more for your handset or laptop than the well-known recyclers. You choose 'good condition' and lock in the price.

steps.title: Wiped and posted
steps.detail: You erase the device, remove it from your account and send it in their free postage bag. Tracking shows it reached their warehouse.

steps.title: The 'revised offer' email
steps.detail: Days later an email says testing found screen burn, a weak battery or scratches on the frame. The new figure is a small part of the quote.

steps.title: Paying to get it back
steps.detail: Declining triggers a return fee, a long wait, or silence. Some firms pay the reduced amount automatically after a few days, and others send nothing.

device-buyback-scam.whyItWorks: Trading in old tech by post is normal, and every recycler reserves the right to regrade on inspection. The seller cannot prove what state the device was in when it left, and has usually bought a replacement already.

realVsFake.real: Established recyclers publish grading criteria with example photos, so you can predict which band your device falls into.
realVsFake.fake: The grades are never defined, and a hairline mark moves a 'good' phone straight to 'faulty'.

realVsFake.real: A fair service sends evidence of any fault it finds and returns the device free if you say no.
realVsFake.fake: The email gives no photos, sets a 48-hour deadline, and charges postage for sending it home.

realVsFake.real: Manufacturer and network trade-in schemes credit your account or bill, with the terms shown before you post.
realVsFake.fake: Payment is promised 'on arrival' by an unknown company with only a web form for contact.

steps.title: A form to 'check your details'
steps.detail: A fax, letter or email asks someone at the business to confirm its name, address and phone number for a trade directory, and to sign and return it.

steps.title: The price hides in grey print
steps.detail: Near the bottom, in small type, the form states that signing places an order for a paid listing running two or three years.

steps.title: The renewal invoice lands
steps.detail: Weeks later an invoice headed 'renewal' arrives for several hundred a year, addressed to accounts payable and quoting the signed form as the contract.

steps.title: Reminders, then a 'collections' letter
steps.detail: Unpaid invoices are followed by late fees and letters from a debt collector with the same address as the directory. Many firms pay to make it stop.

directory-listing-scam.whyItWorks: The person who signs the form and the person who pays the invoice are rarely the same, so each assumes the other approved it. A directory listing is a dull, plausible expense that nobody in a busy office remembers ordering or cancelling.

realVsFake.real: A directory you actually advertise with has an order on file, a named sales contact and a listing that brings in enquiries.
realVsFake.fake: The 'directory' is a bare website few people visit, and nobody in your office recalls speaking to them.

realVsFake.real: Genuine publishers put the price and term at the top of an order form and call it an order.
realVsFake.fake: The document is styled as a free data update, with the cost and multi-year commitment tucked into a footnote.

realVsFake.real: A real renewal matches a supplier already in your accounts system, with past invoices at a similar amount.
realVsFake.fake: The word 'renewal' is used on the very first invoice, and the name echoes a well-known phone directory.

steps.title: Appeal within days of the news
