steps.detail: While flood, earthquake or wildfire footage is still leading bulletins, a text arrives describing families who have lost everything and asking for an urgent gift.

steps.title: A charity name that almost fits
steps.detail: The sender uses a title such as 'Flood Relief Fund' or a well-known charity's name with one word changed, so a quick search seems to confirm it.

steps.title: Donation page with victim photos
steps.detail: The linked page shows news photographs, a rising total and preset amounts. It asks for card details, home address and sometimes a tick box for monthly giving.

steps.title: Gift goes to the sender
steps.detail: The payment is taken under an unrelated merchant name. Nothing reaches the disaster zone, and the stored card may be charged again weeks later.

disaster-donation-text-scam.whyItWorks: In the first days after a disaster people want to help immediately and real charities are also asking loudly. With genuine appeals everywhere, one more message with a donate link does not stand out, and checking feels like delaying aid.

realVsFake.real: Established relief charities appear on the national charity register, where you can search the name and see a registration number.
realVsFake.fake: The name in the text is generic or slightly off, and no matching registered charity exists.

realVsFake.real: A real emergency appeal is announced on the charity's own website and by broadcasters, where you can donate directly.
realVsFake.fake: The only way to give is the link in the text, which leads to a recently created web address.

realVsFake.real: Text giving to a genuine charity uses a short code and adds a fixed sum to your phone bill.
realVsFake.fake: The page wants full card details and an address, far more than a text donation needs.

steps.title: A DM from a server friend
steps.detail: Someone you game with messages out of the blue: they have a spare year of Nitro expiring tonight and you can have it. Their account was hijacked earlier.

steps.title: The gift link
steps.detail: The link preview shows Nitro artwork and a web address one letter away from the real thing, such as a swapped 'i' or an added hyphen.

steps.title: Log in to redeem
steps.detail: A page in Discord's dark theme asks for your email and password, then your authenticator code. Some versions show a QR code to scan with the mobile app.

steps.title: Your token, their account
steps.detail: The attacker captures your login token, changes the email, and within minutes your account is sending the same Nitro message to every friend and server you belong to.

discord-nitro-scam.whyItWorks: Nitro gifts are a real feature that friends do hand around, and the message sits in a chat thread full of old jokes with that person. Being asked to sign in again feels routine to anyone who uses Discord in a browser.

realVsFake.real: A genuine Nitro gift shows as a card inside the Discord app with an accept button, and you are already signed in.
realVsFake.fake: The 'gift' opens an outside page where you must type your email, password and two-factor code from scratch.

realVsFake.real: Scanning a Discord QR code is only for logging yourself in on a computer you are sitting at.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to scan a code to 'claim' something, which signs the attacker's device in as you.

realVsFake.real: A friend giving something away will chat normally and answer if you ask about it in voice.
realVsFake.fake: The hijacked account pastes one identical message to its whole friends list and ignores every reply.

steps.title: Cards at 70 for 100
steps.detail: A post in a local group or a deals forum offers store or gaming gift cards below face value. The seller says they were unwanted presents or work rewards.

steps.title: A balance screenshot as proof
steps.detail: To reassure you they send a screenshot or screen recording of the retailer's balance checker showing the full 100 sitting on the card.

steps.title: E-transfer first, codes after
steps.detail: You pay by e-transfer or crypto. The code arrives as typed text or a photo, and may even show a balance when you check it that evening.

steps.title: Empty at the till
steps.detail: The seller, who kept a copy of the number, spends it online before you do. Other cards were bought with stolen bank details and get cancelled by the retailer.

discounted-gift-card-scam.whyItWorks: People do sell unwanted gift cards at a loss, so the discount has an honest explanation. A balance check feels like proof, but a code is only a string of digits, and whoever else knows it can empty the card at any time.

realVsFake.real: Retailers sell their gift cards at face value through their own tills, websites and named partner shops.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger has 'lots available' at thirty off each and offers a better price for buying five.

realVsFake.real: A card bought in a shop comes with an activation receipt and a sealed, unscratched PIN panel.
realVsFake.fake: You get a photo of the back of a card, already scratched, and no receipt.

realVsFake.real: A private seller acting in good faith will meet at the store and let staff check the balance before you pay.
realVsFake.fake: The seller will only send codes online and wants money that cannot be recalled.

steps.title: The 48-hour text
steps.detail: A text headed 'DMV Notice' says your driver's licence renewal is overdue and the licence will be suspended in 48 hours unless you update your record.

steps.title: A state seal and a form
steps.detail: The link opens a page with your state's seal and colours. It asks for the licence number, date of birth, home address and the last four digits of your SSN.

steps.title: Photos of the card itself
steps.detail: Some versions then ask you to upload pictures of the front and back of the licence, which gives a forger everything printed on it.

steps.title: A small renewal fee
steps.detail: The final screen charges a modest fee by card. The amount matters less than the card number, which is billed again later alongside accounts opened in your name.

dmv-license-renewal-scam.whyItWorks: Hardly anyone knows their licence expiry date without pulling the card out, and many states now offer online renewal, so the request sounds normal. Losing the right to drive means losing the commute, which is enough to make people tap before they check.

realVsFake.real: State licensing agencies usually send a renewal notice to the address on your record well before the expiry date.
realVsFake.fake: The text is the first reminder you have seen, and it already calls the renewal overdue.

realVsFake.real: An expired licence simply lapses until you renew it. Suspension follows specific events such as unpaid tickets, and comes by letter.
realVsFake.fake: The message threatens suspension for nothing more than failing to tap a link within two days.

realVsFake.real: The real renewal fee is fixed, published on the state's site, and the same for everyone in your licence class.
realVsFake.fake: The fee on the fake page is a round, low figure chosen so you will not think twice about entering a card.

steps.title: A free ancestry kit advert
steps.detail: A social media advert or email offers a DNA ancestry or health kit for nothing, as long as you cover a small postage charge today.

steps.title: The long sign-up form
steps.detail: The order page wants far more than an address: date of birth, ethnicity, family medical conditions, sometimes an insurance or national ID number 'to match your sample'.

steps.title: Card taken for postage
steps.detail: You enter card details for a shipping fee of a few pounds. The confirmation email has an order number but no laboratory name or tracking.

steps.title: No swab, new charges
steps.detail: The kit never turns up, or a plain cotton swab arrives with no return label. Meanwhile the card shows larger payments and your health answers are sold on.

dna-test-kit-scam.whyItWorks: Genuine ancestry companies do run steep promotions and really do ask personal questions, so a long form feels normal. Paying only postage seems like a tiny risk, which hides the fact that the form itself is the product being collected.

realVsFake.real: Established DNA testing firms name the laboratory that processes samples and publish a privacy policy saying who can see your genetic data.
realVsFake.fake: The site lists no lab, no company address, and a privacy page that is one vague paragraph or a dead link.

realVsFake.real: A real kit comes with a barcode you register in your own account, plus a prepaid return box for the sample.
realVsFake.fake: Nothing arrives, or a loose swab turns up with no barcode, no instructions and nowhere to send it.

realVsFake.real: Reputable providers put health questions after purchase, inside your account, and let you skip them.
realVsFake.fake: Medical history and ID numbers are demanded on the order form before you can even pay for postage.

steps.title: Harvesting expiry dates
steps.detail: Scammers pull domain names, owner emails and renewal dates from public registration records and from contact pages on small business websites.

steps.title: The 'final notice' invoice
steps.detail: An email or posted letter styled as an invoice shows your domain, an expiry date and a fee several times the usual, sent by 'Domain Registry Services' or similar.

steps.title: The pay-now page
steps.detail: The link opens a card form on the sender's own site, or a copy of your registrar's login that captures the account password.

steps.title: What you actually bought
steps.detail: You have paid for nothing, or for a worthless 'search engine listing'. With the registrar login, criminals repoint your website and email and demand money to return them.

domain-renewal-scam.whyItWorks: Domains are bought once and forgotten, often by whoever built the site years ago, so few owners remember the registrar or the date. The prospect of the website and all company email going dark is enough to pay first.

realVsFake.real: Your actual registrar writes from its own domain, names your account and normally renews automatically from the card on file.
realVsFake.fake: A company you have never dealt with sends a 'final notice' as its very first contact.

realVsFake.real: Genuine renewal prices match last year's and are visible in the registrar's control panel.
realVsFake.fake: The invoice is several times higher, bundles five years or adds a 'search submission' service.

realVsFake.real: Most registrars allow a grace period after expiry during which the owner can still renew.
realVsFake.fake: The notice threatens permanent loss of the name within 24 hours.

steps.title: A letter about forgotten money
steps.detail: An email or posted letter from an 'asset reunification office' says an old savings account, pension pot or a late relative's estate has been traced to you.

steps.title: Claim form and proof of identity
steps.detail: You are asked to complete a form with your date of birth, bank account and a passport copy so the 'claims officer' can match the records.

steps.title: The release fee
steps.detail: Before payout there is a modest charge, perhaps 45 for 'administration', a 'probate stamp' or an 'unclaimed assets tax', payable by transfer.

steps.title: More hurdles, then details sold
steps.detail: Each payment produces a new obstacle: a solicitor's certificate, an anti-fraud bond. When you stop paying, your documents are used or sold for identity fraud.

dormant-account-scam.whyItWorks: Lost accounts and unclaimed estates do exist, and most people have an old savings book or a distant relative they have lost track of. A specific, modest sum of a few thousand feels more believable than a lottery jackpot.

realVsFake.real: Official lost-account tracing services are free, and you start the search yourself through the bank or a national scheme.
realVsFake.fake: Somebody you have never heard of writes to say they have already found your money.

realVsFake.real: A bank returning dormant funds asks you to prove identity, then pays the balance without deductions in advance.
realVsFake.fake: A fee must reach them before anything is released, and it cannot be taken from the balance.

realVsFake.real: Genuine heir-hunting firms can name the deceased and the family connection, and work for a share agreed in a written contract.
realVsFake.fake: The letter is vague about whose money it was and carries no postal address or company number.

steps.title: Someone shared a file with you
steps.detail: An email with the blue box logo says a named person, sometimes a real contact whose mailbox was hacked, has shared 'Invoice_0387.pdf' or 'Scan'.

steps.title: The blurred preview
steps.detail: 'View file' opens a page showing a blurred document behind a sign-in box. Some versions start on a real Dropbox page holding a PDF with a second link.

steps.title: Choose your email provider
steps.detail: The box offers Google, Microsoft 365, Yahoo or 'Other mail' and asks for your email address and its password, not a Dropbox one.

steps.title: Wrong password, try again
steps.detail: An error makes you type the password twice, then a harmless PDF loads. The attackers now read your mailbox and send the same lure to your contacts.

dropbox-shared-file-scam.whyItWorks: Shared files are how offices work, and many of these emails come from a real colleague or supplier whose account was already taken over. A blurred invoice behind a sign-in box creates enough curiosity to type a password.

realVsFake.real: A real Dropbox share opens the file in the browser, often with no sign-in, and never needs your email password.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks you to pick a mail provider and enter that password to 'view' the document.

realVsFake.real: Genuine share emails come from Dropbox's own sending address and link to its own domain.
realVsFake.fake: The button points to a form builder, a file host or a domain registered last week.

realVsFake.real: A colleague sharing something usually mentions it first, and the file name relates to work you know about.
realVsFake.fake: There is no covering note, a generic file name and a line about access expiring.

steps.title: One gadget, everywhere in your feed
steps.detail: A slick video advert shows a single 'viral' product, a posture corrector or mini projector, with a today-only discount and a shop name you have never seen.

steps.title: A checkout built to hurry
steps.detail: The store has one or two products, a stock counter ticking down, and a delivery estimate that only appears in small text after you enter your card.

steps.title: Weeks of 'processing'
steps.detail: Your order is forwarded to an overseas marketplace supplier at a fraction of the price. Tracking shows a label created, then nothing for three or four weeks.

steps.title: The refund runaround
steps.detail: A flimsy version arrives in a plain grey bag. Support offers a small partial refund, or tells you to post it back to a foreign warehouse at your own cost.

dropshipping-scam.whyItWorks: The advert makes an ordinary cheap item look like a new invention, and few people think to search for the same photo elsewhere. Because something does eventually arrive, buyers blame slow post instead of the shop, and many never chase the refund.

realVsFake.real: An honest retailer shows the delivery time on the product page and gives a returns address in the country it sells to.
realVsFake.fake: Shipping time is hidden until checkout, and returns must go overseas at a cost higher than the item.

realVsFake.real: Established shops hold their own stock and can tell you where your parcel is.
realVsFake.fake: The 'store' never touches the goods. It passes your address to a third-party supplier and waits.

realVsFake.real: Real brands have a range, a history and reviews on sites they do not control.
realVsFake.fake: One hero product, a domain registered recently, and glowing reviews that exist only on its own page.

steps.title: 'DVLA' on the sender line
steps.detail: A message labelled DVLA says your latest vehicle tax payment failed, or that you overpaid and a refund is waiting, and warns of a penalty.

steps.title: A copy of the government page
steps.detail: The link leads to a page with the crown logo, black header and green button of an official service, asking for your registration number first.

steps.title: Keeper details requested
steps.detail: Next come name, address, date of birth and sometimes driving licence number, presented as checking you are the registered keeper.

steps.title: Bank details for the 'retry'
steps.detail: The final screen asks for card or account details to retake the tax payment or send the refund. Those are used for purchases or new direct debits.

dvla-text-scam.whyItWorks: Vehicle tax is paid once or twice a year, often by direct debit, so few drivers remember when the last payment went out. An untaxed car can be clamped, which makes a failed-payment warning feel too risky to ignore.

realVsFake.real: DVLA does not send texts or emails asking you to confirm payment details or claim a vehicle tax refund.
realVsFake.fake: The text offers a refund or 'failed payment' fix through a link and asks for bank information.

realVsFake.real: Vehicle tax refunds are issued automatically by cheque to the registered keeper's address after the tax is cancelled.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to enter a card number so the tax refund can be 'credited back'.

realVsFake.real: You can check whether a vehicle is taxed, free of charge, on the government's vehicle enquiry service using the registration.
realVsFake.fake: A penalty is threatened within hours, with no letter and no way to look up the tax status.

steps.title: You lose an auction
steps.detail: You bid on a camera, guitar or watch and are outbid in the final minutes. The ended listing and its bid activity are public, so losers are easy to target.

steps.title: The 'winner backed out' email
steps.detail: An email styled with eBay colours and the item's photo says the top bidder withdrew, and that you may buy at your last bid within 24 hours.

steps.title: Checkout is 'currently down'
steps.detail: You are told to reply to the email, not use the site, because checkout has a fault. The reply goes to a free mailbox the fraudster controls.

steps.title: Bank details for a 'payment agent'
steps.detail: A follow-up invoice gives a sort code and account number for a 'payment agent'. You transfer the money, a fake tracking number arrives, and nothing is ever dispatched.

ebay-second-chance-scam.whyItWorks: Second Chance Offers are a real eBay feature, and the email arrives while you are still annoyed at being outbid on that exact item. Getting it at your own last bid feels like luck, so the odd payment route gets less scrutiny.

realVsFake.real: A genuine Second Chance Offer shows up inside your eBay account, in your messages and offers, as well as by email.
realVsFake.fake: The offer exists only as an email, and nothing about it appears when you log in to eBay yourself.

realVsFake.real: Real offers are paid through eBay's own checkout with the usual card and wallet options.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent bank details and asked to wire the money, with a note that protection 'still applies'.

realVsFake.real: eBay sends its emails from its own domain, and its links open pages on that same domain.
realVsFake.fake: The sender address is a lookalike or a free webmail account, and the button opens an unrelated site.

steps.title: The console everyone wants
steps.detail: A games console, recent phone or laptop is posted locally at a price low enough to make you message within minutes of seeing it.

steps.title: 'Loads of people are interested'
steps.detail: The seller replies that their inbox is full of offers and they cannot keep it for anyone, but they like you and would prefer to sell to you.

steps.title: Fifty to hold it overnight
steps.detail: They ask for 50 by bank transfer or e-transfer to take the advert down, and agree to meet tomorrow at a place and time you suggest.

steps.title: Nobody at the meeting point
steps.detail: The next day your messages show as undelivered. The same advert is still live, collecting the same 50 from a dozen other buyers that week.

electronics-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: Fifty feels like a small risk against a saving of a few hundred, and holding deposits are common enough to sound fair. The seller's claim of a queue turns a cautious buyer into a competitor trying to get in first.

realVsFake.real: Most private sellers simply say first to turn up with the money gets it.
realVsFake.fake: This seller will not name a time to meet until a deposit has been sent.

realVsFake.real: Someone who owns the console can send a short video of it switched on with your name on a note beside it.
realVsFake.fake: You get the same three advert photos again, plus a reason why filming is not possible right now.

realVsFake.real: A local sale is settled in one go at collection, once you have seen the item working.
realVsFake.fake: Part of the price must travel ahead of you to an account in a name the seller never mentioned.

steps.title: The quota warning
steps.detail: An email from 'Mail Administrator' or 'IT Helpdesk' shows a red bar nearly at its limit and says incoming messages are being held back.

steps.title: Release pending messages
steps.detail: Buttons offer a free storage upgrade or the release of 'seven held messages', with a note that queued mail will be deleted after 48 hours.

steps.title: A login that already knows you
steps.detail: The page shows your email address pre-filled and your provider's or employer's logo pulled in automatically, leaving only the password box empty.

steps.title: The mailbox becomes a master key
steps.detail: With mailbox access, the criminals add a forwarding rule, search for invoices and bank messages, reset passwords on other accounts and send phishing from your address.

email-storage-full-scam.whyItWorks: Mailboxes do fill up and real providers do send quota warnings, so the message matches something people have seen before. Finding your own address already typed into the form feels like proof that the page knows you.

realVsFake.real: Your provider shows storage use inside mailbox settings, and a truly full mailbox bounces mail back to the sender.
realVsFake.fake: The email claims messages are queued somewhere and will be wiped unless you sign in.

realVsFake.real: A workplace IT team writes from an internal address, signs with a name and can be phoned.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is 'Admin Team' at an outside domain, with no name and no extension number.

realVsFake.real: Extra storage is bought or freed from your account's own subscription page.
realVsFake.fake: The 'upgrade' is free, instant and needs nothing except your password.

steps.title: A mailbox is broken into first
steps.detail: Long before you see anything, someone in the conversation loses their email password to an earlier phish. The intruder reads their sent folder and picks threads still in progress.

steps.title: A reply lands mid-conversation
steps.detail: A new message arrives under the subject line you know, 'Re: Project update', with every earlier email quoted below it. The only new part is one short line and a file.

steps.title: The document wants a login
steps.detail: The link opens a page styled like a shared-drive viewer and asks for your email password to show the 'revised document', or the attachment asks you to enable content.

steps.title: Your contacts get the next reply
steps.detail: With your password or a foothold on your machine, the intruder searches your own inbox for live threads and sends the same one-line reply to the people you were writing to.

email-thread-hijacking-scam.whyItWorks: You check a stranger's email carefully, but a reply sitting under your own words from last Tuesday gets none of that scrutiny. The quoted history is real, so the one invented line borrows all of its credibility.

realVsFake.real: A colleague sending a revised file usually says what changed and refers to something specific from the earlier discussion.
realVsFake.fake: The hijacked reply is one generic line, 'please see attached and let me know your thoughts', that would fit under any thread at all.

realVsFake.real: Files from a real contact open in the tool your team already uses, without asking for your mailbox password again.
realVsFake.fake: The link leads to an unfamiliar viewer page that wants your email address and password before it will show anything.

realVsFake.real: Your contact will confirm they sent it if you ring them or message them on a different app.
realVsFake.fake: A reply to the email itself reaches the intruder, who answers 'yes, that was me' and urges you to open it.

steps.title: 'GOV ENERGY REBATE' arrives
steps.detail: The message says you are eligible for a cost-of-living payment of about £150 from your supplier, without saying which supplier that is.

steps.title: 'Check eligibility' form
steps.detail: A linked page asks for your postcode and how you pay for gas and electricity, then confirms within seconds that you qualify for the full amount.

steps.title: Asking where to send it
steps.detail: To receive the rebate you are asked for the account holder's name, sort code, account number and often the card number 'for verification'.

steps.title: Direct debit in reverse
steps.detail: Nothing is paid in. The details are used to set up payments out of your account, or a caller posing as your bank rings soon after.

energy-rebate-scam.whyItWorks: Governments and suppliers have genuinely handed out bill support during price rises, and the amounts were close to the figure quoted. When heating costs are a worry, a message saying help is waiting sounds like news you were hoping for.

realVsFake.real: Genuine energy support has been applied automatically as a credit on the bill or paid to accounts already on file.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the money will be lost unless you apply through a link before an expiry date.

realVsFake.real: Your supplier already holds your payment details and names itself, with your account number, when it writes.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is a blend of 'government' and 'supplier' and never states which energy company you are with.

realVsFake.real: Receiving an energy bill credit never requires a card number or security code.
realVsFake.fake: The claim form asks for card details 'to verify the account' the rebate will go to.

steps.title: 'Your account is in credit'
steps.detail: A text or email in a supplier's colours says a billing review found you overpaid and a refund is waiting, with a precise sum such as 86.40 to look calculated.

steps.title: The refund portal
steps.detail: The link opens a claim page asking for name, address and date of birth. No account number is requested, because the senders do not know who supplies you.

steps.title: Bank details for the payout
steps.detail: The next screen asks for sort code and account number, then the card number, expiry and security code 'so the refund can be matched to your payment method'.

steps.title: The follow-up call from 'your bank'
steps.detail: A day or two later someone phones posing as your bank's fraud team, armed with everything you typed, and talks you into moving money or approving a payment.

energy-refund-scam.whyItWorks: Direct debit accounts really do build up credit, and talk of rebates and support schemes makes a payout feel overdue. Money coming towards you seems to carry no risk, so the form gets filled in without the usual suspicion.

realVsFake.real: A real supplier credits a refund to your energy account or back to the direct debit it already collects from.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks you to type bank and card details as though the supplier had never held them.

realVsFake.real: Genuine messages about your balance quote your account number and match what you see when you log in.
realVsFake.fake: There is no account number, and the greeting is 'Dear customer' or your email address.

realVsFake.real: Government help with energy bills has typically been applied to accounts automatically, with no claim form.
realVsFake.fake: A deadline is set, with the refund 'returned to the scheme' if it is not claimed within 48 hours.

steps.title: The bill-shock advert
steps.detail: An advert framed as a news story claims electricity firms are furious about a small plug-in box that 'stabilises voltage' and trims your bill.

steps.title: Fake science and a fake inventor
steps.detail: The sales page shows a meter reading falling, quotes an unnamed engineer, and offers three units at a bundle price so you can 'cover every room'.

steps.title: Paying on a stranger's checkout
steps.detail: You type your card into a page with no company name behind it. Extra units or a 'warranty' are often ticked in the basket already.

steps.title: A box with a green light
steps.detail: What arrives is a plastic shell holding a small capacitor and an LED. Your meter reads the same, and some units overheat in the socket.

energy-saving-device-scam.whyItWorks: Rising bills make people willing to try anything cheap, and the pitch uses real-sounding terms like power factor that few householders can check. The green light glowing in the socket then feels like evidence the thing is doing something.

realVsFake.real: Real savings come from using less: insulation, efficient appliances, a better tariff. Your supplier's bill shows the units you actually used.
realVsFake.fake: A gadget claims to cut the reading on your meter simply by sitting in a spare socket.

realVsFake.real: Electrical goods sold lawfully carry a named manufacturer, a model number and safety markings you can look up.
realVsFake.fake: The box has a made-up brand, no maker's address, and markings printed on without any testing behind them.

realVsFake.real: Genuine product tests are published by named consumer bodies you can find independently.
realVsFake.fake: The 'proof' is a video of a clamp meter and a quote from an engineer with no surname.

steps.title: The knock about your tariff
steps.detail: Someone with a lanyard and tablet says they are 'working with your supplier' or 'from the comparison service', and that your street is on the wrong rate.

steps.title: 'Can I see a recent bill'
steps.detail: They ask for a bill to 'check your rate'. It hands them your account number, meter numbers and tariff, which is all a company needs to start a transfer.

steps.title: A signature 'for the quote'
steps.detail: You are asked to sign the tablet 'just to show I called' or 'to receive the quote'. The signature is attached to a contract with a different company.

steps.title: A welcome letter from a stranger
steps.detail: Direct debit details are taken 'to lock in the saving'. Weeks later a welcome pack arrives from a supplier you never chose, on a dearer rate with exit fees.

energy-switch-scam.whyItWorks: Energy tariffs are confusing and most households suspect they are overpaying, so a person offering to sort it out on the spot sounds useful. Claiming to come from your existing supplier removes the feeling of dealing with a salesman.

realVsFake.real: Your own supplier already holds your account and meter details and has no need to see a bill.
realVsFake.fake: The agent claims to be from your supplier yet asks you to fetch a bill and read out the numbers.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate switch comes with written terms, the unit rates and standing charge, and a cooling-off period to cancel.
realVsFake.fake: You are shown a monthly saving on a screen and asked to sign before any paperwork is offered.

realVsFake.real: Accredited comparison services let you run the comparison yourself and choose in your own time.
realVsFake.fake: The seller says the price lasts only while they are standing at your door or holding on the line.

steps.title: A small ad with big numbers
steps.detail: A newspaper small ad, lamp-post flyer or email promises a dollar or two for every envelope you stuff at home, adding up to as much as 2,000 dollars a week.

steps.title: Send 39.95 for the kit
steps.detail: To get started you post or pay online a registration fee of 39.95, for which you are promised envelopes, inserts, postage and a list of companies needing mailers.

steps.title: One sheet of instructions arrives
steps.detail: What comes back is a single page. It tells you to place the very same advert under your own name and wait for people to send you their fee.

steps.title: The only envelopes are replies
steps.detail: The 'stuffing' is posting that same sheet to whoever answers your advert. You earn only if you take money from the next person, and you bear the advertising costs.

envelope-stuffing-scam.whyItWorks: Stuffing envelopes is work anyone can picture doing, so the offer needs no explaining and seems to suit people stuck at home. The fee is set low enough that few chase a refund once they see what they bought.

realVsFake.real: Businesses that send bulk mail use machines or mailing houses that fold and insert thousands of letters an hour.
realVsFake.fake: The advert claims a company will pay a stranger a dollar or more per envelope to do it by hand.

realVsFake.real: A genuine mailing job names the business whose letters you would be sending and supplies the stationery.
realVsFake.fake: No client is ever named, and you buy your own stamps to mail out the scheme's instruction sheet.

realVsFake.real: Real home-based work has an employer with a street address and someone who interviews you.
realVsFake.fake: The whole operation is a PO box and a payment page, with a new trading name every few months.

steps.title: The advert before your trip
steps.detail: An ad appears soon after you search for flights, promising unlimited data in every country for a few pounds, with a countdown showing the price ending today.

steps.title: A checkout with no company behind it
steps.detail: The site has a country picker and plan sizes like a real eSIM store, but no company address, no app and no way to reach anyone before paying.

steps.title: The QR code arrives
steps.detail: After payment an email brings a QR code or activation string. Scanning it gives 'unable to add eSIM', or it installs and never finds a network abroad.

steps.title: Silence at the other end
steps.detail: Support emails bounce while you stand in a foreign airport without data. In the following weeks, payments you do not recognise appear on the card you used.

esim-travel-scam.whyItWorks: Roaming bills are a familiar worry, and genuine travel eSIMs really are cheap and delivered by email, so the offer matches what buyers expect. The fault only shows after landing, when there is no connection to complain with.

realVsFake.real: Established eSIM providers have an app in the official stores showing your plan, data used and expiry date.
realVsFake.fake: The product is a single emailed image, with no account and nothing to log in to.

realVsFake.real: A genuine plan states the data allowance, the validity in days and the local networks it uses in each country.
realVsFake.fake: The listing says 'unlimited, worldwide' with no network names and no fair-use terms.

realVsFake.real: A real seller lets you install the eSIM before you fly, and it shows as ready in your phone's mobile settings.
realVsFake.fake: You are told not to scan the code until you arrive, which postpones the moment you find out it is dead.

steps.title: The 'final notice' robocall
steps.detail: A recorded voice or a pink postcard says your vehicle's factory cover is about to lapse and this is the last attempt to reach you.

steps.title: Press 1 for an agent
steps.detail: A live seller picks up and asks you for the make, model and mileage, details a real warranty holder would already have on file.

steps.title: The one-day price
steps.detail: They quote 'bumper to bumper' protection with a down payment due on this call, and say the offer cannot be held while you read the terms.

steps.title: Card read out, cover never used
steps.detail: You give card or bank details by phone. The paperwork, if it comes, is a service contract full of exclusions that refuses the first claim.

extended-warranty-scam.whyItWorks: Most drivers have no idea when their manufacturer cover ends, so 'about to expire' sounds plausible for almost any car. The fear of one enormous repair bill makes a monthly fee feel sensible before anyone has seen a page of terms.

realVsFake.real: Your manufacturer or dealer writes to you by name, quoting your registration or VIN and the exact end date of cover.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says only 'your vehicle' and has to ask you what you drive.

realVsFake.real: A genuine provider posts or emails the full contract and lets you take days to compare it.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the price dies when the call ends, and written terms come only after payment.

realVsFake.real: Real cover names the administrator and insurer backing it, which you can check before buying.
realVsFake.fake: The company name changes between the recording, the agent and the charge on your statement.

steps.title: A message in an old chat
steps.detail: The request arrives in your existing Messenger thread with a friend, under years of real conversation. Their account has already been taken over by the sender.

steps.title: You are my trusted contact
steps.detail: They say Facebook is making them confirm their identity through a friend, and ask for your mobile number or email 'so the system can send you my code'.

steps.title: The text on your phone
steps.detail: Using that number, the scammer clicks 'forgotten password' on your own profile. Facebook texts you a reset code, which looks exactly like the code your friend described.

steps.title: Six digits and it is gone
steps.detail: You send the digits back. They set a new password on your account, remove your email, and start messaging your friends with the identical trusted-contact story.

facebook-account-recovery-scam.whyItWorks: The code arrives exactly when your friend said it would, which seems to confirm their story. Few people realise that a password reset text for their own profile can be triggered by anyone who knows their phone number.

realVsFake.real: A code texted to your phone only ever unlocks the account tied to that phone, which is yours.
realVsFake.fake: The message claims the code on your handset belongs to your friend's locked profile and must be passed along.

realVsFake.real: Someone locked out of Facebook recovers it using their own email, phone or ID, through Facebook's forms.
realVsFake.fake: Your 'friend' needs your number first, then a code within the next minute, and gets pushy if you pause.

realVsFake.real: A friend genuinely locked out cannot be typing to you from the very account they say is locked.
realVsFake.fake: The plea to 'get back in' is sent from inside the profile that is supposedly inaccessible.

steps.title: A notice in the page inbox
steps.detail: A message reaches your page from a sender named something like 'Business Support Team', with a blue tick emoji in the name and a Meta logo as its picture.

steps.title: Unpublished by tomorrow
steps.detail: It says the page breached advertising or community standards and is scheduled to be unpublished, and that the admin must 'verify the business' to keep it.

steps.title: The verification form
steps.detail: The link opens a help-centre lookalike asking for the page name, business email and phone number, then your Facebook password, then the two-step code just texted to you.

steps.title: New admin, your ad budget
steps.detail: With a live session, the attacker adds their own profile as admin, removes yours, and runs adverts for their own schemes on the payment card saved to the ad account.

facebook-business-page-scam.whyItWorks: For a small business the page is the shop window, the booking system and the customer list in one, so the threat of losing it overnight hits hard. Owners also know Meta's rules are opaque, which makes an unexplained violation easy to believe.

realVsFake.real: Real restrictions show inside Facebook, in the page's own quality and support screens, with the rule named.
realVsFake.fake: The warning comes as a Messenger chat or a tagged post from another page dressed up as support.

realVsFake.real: An appeal is started from a button inside your own page settings while you are logged in.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent to a separate website that asks you to log in again and hand over a texted code.

realVsFake.real: Business verification with Meta involves company documents uploaded in its business settings, not your personal password.
realVsFake.fake: The fake form skips any paperwork and goes straight to the admin's login and security code.

steps.title: An email headed 'Copyright Infringement'
steps.detail: An email or tagged post claims a rights holder has reported a photo, song or video on your page. It carries a made-up case number to look official.

steps.title: The removal clock
steps.detail: The text says the page will be permanently deleted in 24 hours if no objection is filed, and offers a single button labelled 'Appeal' or 'Submit a counter-notice'.

steps.title: An appeal that wants your password
steps.detail: The form asks for your full name, login email, phone and date of birth. A final box requests your password 'to confirm you own the account'.

steps.title: 'Incorrect password, try again'
steps.detail: The page rejects your first attempt on purpose so you retype it, catching typos and older passwords. Then it thanks you while the thieves log in.

facebook-copyright-violation-scam.whyItWorks: Almost every page has shared a song clip or an image found online, so an accusation of copying is hard to rule out. The fear of being in legal trouble pushes owners to object first and read the sender's address later.

realVsFake.real: A real copyright removal names the exact post taken down and who reported it.
realVsFake.fake: The notice never says which content is at fault, only that 'your page' broke the policy.

realVsFake.real: Facebook removes the reported item and then lets you dispute that removal from your support inbox.
realVsFake.fake: Nothing has been removed, yet the whole page is said to be hours from permanent deletion.

realVsFake.real: Emails from Facebook can be checked against the list of recent security emails in your account settings.
realVsFake.fake: The sender's address is a free webmail account or a jumble of words containing 'meta' and 'support'.

steps.title: An order you never placed
steps.detail: An email styled like an Amazon confirmation thanks you for buying a laptop at 1,299.99, with a delivery address in another city and an order number that looks plausible.

steps.title: The cancel button and helpline
steps.detail: Underneath sit a 'Cancel order' button and a support phone number. Both occupy the spot where the genuine email would put 'View or manage order'.

steps.title: Sign in to stop the delivery
steps.detail: The button opens a copy of the Amazon sign-in screen. After your password it asks you to 'confirm the card on file', security code included, to process the cancellation.

steps.title: A refunds agent on the phone
steps.detail: People who ring the number reach a 'refunds agent' who asks for the one-time passcode Amazon just texted, or for gift cards to 'reverse' the charge.

fake-amazon-order-email.whyItWorks: Seeing a four-figure purchase headed to a stranger's address makes you think your account has already been broken into. Cancelling feels like the careful thing to do, and the email has put the button right there.

realVsFake.real: Every genuine order appears under Your Orders when you open the Amazon app or type the site address yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The laptop exists only in the email. Nothing matching it shows in your order history or on your card statement.

realVsFake.real: Amazon lets you cancel an unshipped item from the order page, with no need to re-enter a card number.
realVsFake.fake: The cancellation page asks for the full card number, expiry date and security code before it will 'stop the shipment'.

realVsFake.real: Amazon does not ask customers to pay for or verify anything with gift cards, and its staff never need your sign-in passcode.
realVsFake.fake: The agent on the support line says gift cards are how the refund is 'balanced', and wants the codes read aloud.

steps.title: An alert beside the clock
steps.detail: A notification styled like a well-known security brand says your subscription expired and five threats were found. It is a browser notification from a website you once allowed.

steps.title: The invoice version
steps.detail: Others get an email receipt saying a three-year protection plan has renewed for several hundred, with a phone number to ring if the charge is a mistake.

steps.title: A scan that runs in the browser
steps.detail: Clicking opens a web page with an animated progress bar 'scanning' your files and listing trojans by name. It is an animation, not a scan.

steps.title: Renew, download or call
steps.detail: The button leads to a card form for a bogus licence, or installs a program that is itself the infection. The phone line sells a 'cleaning' session.

fake-antivirus-scam.whyItWorks: Most people have had antivirus installed at some point and cannot remember when it runs out, so an expiry notice is plausible. The alert appears where real system messages do, and few users know a website can put it there.

realVsFake.real: Installed security software reports from its own window, opened from the icon near the clock or the applications list.
realVsFake.fake: The warning carries a website's name in small print and vanishes if you close the browser.

realVsFake.real: A genuine renewal shows in your account on the vendor's site, against the card you registered with them.
realVsFake.fake: The receipt has an order number but no trace on your bank statement, and it pushes a phone line, not a login.

realVsFake.real: Real protection removes what it finds as part of the product you already have.
realVsFake.fake: Scareware lists infections for free and then wants payment, or a new download, before it will remove one.

steps.title: Locked for your security
steps.detail: Under an Apple logo, the email says your Apple ID was locked after a sign-in attempt from another country. You have 24 hours to verify or the account is disabled.

steps.title: A sign-in page on another address
steps.detail: The 'Unlock account' button opens a white page with the Apple logo and two boxes. The address bar shows a long string with 'apple' buried somewhere in the middle.

steps.title: Identity questions pile up
steps.detail: After the password, further screens ask for your date of birth, the answers to your security questions and sometimes a card 'to confirm ownership of the account'.

steps.title: The six-digit code
steps.detail: As the criminal signs in with what you typed, your iPhone shows a real verification code. The fake page has a box waiting for it, and entering it hands over the account.

fake-apple-id-locked-email.whyItWorks: An Apple ID sits behind your photos, messages and every device you own, so the word 'locked' lands hard. Apple does lock accounts for security reasons, which makes the story plausible before you have looked at the link.

realVsFake.real: When an Apple ID really is locked, your own iPhone or Mac says so on screen the next time you use it.
realVsFake.fake: The only sign of a lock is the email. Your devices carry on working normally, and so does the App Store.

realVsFake.real: Apple unlocks accounts through its own recovery process, started from your device settings or by typing Apple's account address yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The email supplies its own button and says the unlock must happen through that link within the day.

realVsFake.real: Apple staff never ask you to share a verification code, and the prompt on your device shows roughly where the sign-in is coming from.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for the code that just appeared on your phone and calls it 'the final step to unlock'.

steps.title: An 'update required' text
steps.detail: A message or search advert says your bank's app is being retired, with a button to install the replacement. On Android it downloads a file ending in .apk.

steps.title: Switching off the phone's defences
steps.detail: The installer asks you to allow 'unknown sources', then to grant accessibility permission, which lets the app read the screen and press buttons by itself.

steps.title: A login screen that matches
steps.detail: It opens with the bank's logo and colours. You type customer number, password and card details, which are sent straight to the operator.

steps.title: Texts read silently
steps.detail: With permission to read messages, the malware forwards one-time codes unseen, or draws a fake 'updating' screen over the real app while money is moved.

fake-banking-app-scam.whyItWorks: Apps demand updates constantly, so one more prompt looks routine, and a warning that access is about to stop gives a practical reason to act now. On a small screen, a copied logo is all most people check.

realVsFake.real: A bank's app updates through the phone's official store, usually automatically, with no action needed.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent a download link by text or email and told the store version no longer works.

realVsFake.real: The genuine app is listed under the bank's registered name with a long history of reviews.
realVsFake.fake: The fake has a publisher name like 'Secure Mobile Ltd', a handful of five-star reviews and a release date last week.

realVsFake.real: Real banking apps ask for a passcode or fingerprint on opening, using details you set up before.
realVsFake.fake: The counterfeit asks for everything at once on first launch: full password, card number, CVV and telephone banking PIN.

steps.title: New number, familiar name
steps.detail: A text opens 'Hi, it's' followed by your manager's or chief executive's name, taken from the company website or a professional networking profile.

steps.title: 'I'm in a meeting'
steps.detail: They say they cannot take calls and ask if you are free for a quick favour. This rules out the one check that would expose them.

steps.title: The gift card errand
steps.detail: You are asked to buy several gift cards for a client or staff reward, pay on your own card, and expect reimbursement through expenses.

steps.title: Photos of the codes
steps.detail: They ask you to scratch the panels and send pictures of the codes. The balances are spent or resold within minutes and the number stops replying.

fake-boss-text-scam.whyItWorks: New starters and junior staff rarely question a direct request from someone senior, and wanting to look capable makes a quick errand attractive. 'Keep this between us' removes the colleague who would have said the boss never does this.

realVsFake.real: A real manager asks through work email, the company chat tool or a number already saved in your phone.
realVsFake.fake: The request comes from an unknown mobile with an explanation about a broken or personal phone.

realVsFake.real: Company purchases go through a purchasing card, an expense system or the finance team, with a record.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to pay from your own pocket and pass the gift card codes on by text.

realVsFake.real: A genuine senior colleague is fine with you ringing back or checking with their assistant.
realVsFake.fake: The sender insists on secrecy and becomes impatient when you suggest a call.

steps.title: An ordinary site, quietly altered
steps.detail: You visit a blog, recipe page or small shop whose code has been tampered with. Nothing looks wrong for a second, then the article is covered.

steps.title: 'Your Chrome is out of date'
steps.detail: A full-page overlay uses your browser's real logo and colours, chosen to match what you are running, and says the page cannot display until you update.

steps.title: The Update button downloads a file
steps.detail: Pressing it saves something like 'ChromeUpdate.zip' or an installer to your downloads folder, with on-screen instructions to open it and click Run.

steps.title: Nothing seems to happen
steps.detail: The file installs a password stealer or remote-access program in the background. The site then loads normally, so the 'update' appears to have worked.

fake-browser-update-scam.whyItWorks: People are told constantly to keep software updated, so a prompt to do exactly that feels like good practice. It appears on a site they chose to visit, in their own browser's branding, which hides the fact that the page is speaking.

realVsFake.real: Chrome, Edge and Firefox update themselves in the background or from their own menu, then ask for a restart. Safari updates with macOS.
realVsFake.fake: The prompt sits inside the web page, scrolls with it, and disappears when you open a different tab.

realVsFake.real: A real browser update never hands you a file to find in your downloads and open by hand.
realVsFake.fake: You are given a zip, an .exe or a script, plus step-by-step pictures showing how to bypass the security warning.

realVsFake.real: Flash Player was retired by its maker and modern browsers play video without any add-on.
realVsFake.fake: The page claims a Flash, codec or font pack is missing and must be installed to view the content.

steps.title: A link to something you wanted
steps.detail: You click a video description, a search ad or a social post promising a film, a game crack or a document. The page shows a familiar 'I'm not a robot' box.

steps.title: The tick that copies
steps.detail: Ticking the box silently places a line of code on your clipboard. A panel then appears with 'verification steps' numbered one to three.

steps.title: Windows key, paste, Enter
steps.detail: The steps tell you to press Windows and R together, then Ctrl and V, then Enter. In effect you open the Run box and launch the hidden command yourself.

steps.title: A silent download
steps.detail: The command fetches a password-stealing program that copies saved browser logins, session cookies and crypto wallet files, then sends them off. The page simply says 'verified'.

fake-captcha-scam.whyItWorks: Everyone clicks through robot checks many times a week without reading them, so one more set of instructions gets followed on autopilot. Because the victim types the keys personally, the browser's download warnings never appear.

realVsFake.real: A real CAPTCHA stays inside the web page: tick a box, pick the traffic lights, type some wobbly letters.
realVsFake.fake: This one sends you to the keyboard to open Run, PowerShell or Terminal, which no human test needs.

realVsFake.real: Proving you are a person never involves pasting anything, because the site checks your clicks, not your computer.
realVsFake.fake: The text you paste looks like a harmless 'I am not a robot' note, with the real command hidden before it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine check finishes and takes you to the content you came for.
realVsFake.fake: After the paste, the film or file never loads, and the tab redirects to an unrelated site.

steps.title: News breaks, appeals appear
steps.detail: Within hours of an earthquake, flood or wildfire, new pages and profiles spring up with names close to well-known relief organisations and photos lifted from news coverage.

steps.title: Pasted into your messages
steps.detail: The appeal reaches you as a DM or a copied post. It says every penny goes straight to survivors and begs you not to scroll past.

steps.title: Give by wallet or gift card
steps.detail: The donation link shows a crypto wallet address, a personal payment-app tag, or instructions to buy gift cards and send the codes 'because banks there are down'.

steps.title: The page moves on
steps.detail: No receipt arrives and no relief work is ever shown. When the story fades from the news, the page is renamed for the next disaster or deleted.

fake-charity-donation-scam.whyItWorks: In the first days after a catastrophe people want to act at once, while the pictures are still on every screen. A page already collecting, under a name that sounds nearly right, catches that impulse before anyone checks a register.

realVsFake.real: A registered charity has a number you can look up on the national charity register, with accounts and trustees listed.
realVsFake.fake: The name is one word off a famous charity, and no registration number appears anywhere on the page.

realVsFake.real: Relief organisations take donations by card or bank on their own website and email a receipt.
realVsFake.fake: You are steered to gift card codes, a wallet string or an individual's payment-app account.

realVsFake.real: Established appeals explain what the money buys, such as tents, water or medical teams, and report back later.
realVsFake.fake: The wording stays at 'helping families who lost everything', with no partner named on the ground.

steps.title: Searching for a help page
steps.detail: You have a problem with an airline booking, a crypto wallet or a streaming account and search the company's name plus 'support'. The top result is an advert.

steps.title: The chat bubble opens itself
steps.detail: The advert leads to a lookalike help centre. A chat window pops open with a named agent, a headshot and a typing indicator, greeting you in seconds.

steps.title: 'To verify you, please confirm'
steps.detail: The agent asks for your username and password, then the code just sent to you. For crypto wallets, they request the twelve-word recovery phrase.

steps.title: Signed in while you wait
steps.detail: As the chat says 'one moment while I check', the scammer logs in as you. Bookings are cancelled for refunds to their card, or balances are moved out.

fake-chat-support-scam.whyItWorks: The victim started the conversation, so there is none of the suspicion a cold call brings. Chat is how most companies now offer help, and a reply within seconds feels like good service after struggling to find a contact page.

realVsFake.real: Official chat is opened from inside the company's app or from its website after you have signed in yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The widget sits on a page reached from a sponsored search result, at an address with extra words around the brand.

realVsFake.real: Genuine agents identify you with details like an order number or part of your postcode, never a full password.
realVsFake.fake: The chat asks you to type your password and one-time code straight into the message box.

realVsFake.real: Real support will let you end the chat and return later with a ticket reference.
realVsFake.fake: If you hesitate, the agent says the session will time out and the account will stay frozen.

steps.title: A buyer, a job or a prize
steps.detail: Someone answers your online advert without haggling, hires you as a 'mystery shopper' or 'personal assistant', or announces a sweepstake win. Payment will come by cheque.

steps.title: The envelope arrives
steps.detail: A professional-looking cheque or banker's draft turns up by courier, drawn on a real company's account, for noticeably more than agreed.

steps.title: Funds 'available' the next day
steps.detail: You pay it in and the balance rises, because banks often release money before a cheque has been fully checked. The sender calls this proof it cleared.

steps.title: Send back the surplus
steps.detail: They ask you to forward the excess to a 'shipping agent' or 'supplier' by wire, payment app or gift cards. Later the cheque is returned as forged.

fake-cheque-scam.whyItWorks: Most people believe that once money shows in their balance, the cheque is good. In fact the bank has only advanced the funds, and discovering a forgery can take weeks, long after the difference has been sent on.

realVsFake.real: A genuine buyer pays the asking price, and one who overpays by mistake can cancel the cheque and write a correct one.
realVsFake.fake: The sender wants you to bank the oversized cheque and return the surplus yourself, today.

realVsFake.real: Employers pay wages after you have worked and do not route company money through a new starter's account.
realVsFake.fake: Your first 'task' is to deposit a cheque and buy gift cards or wire funds with it.

realVsFake.real: Lotteries and competitions pay winnings in full without asking for anything back.
realVsFake.fake: The 'prize' cheque comes with instructions to return part of it for taxes or handling.

steps.title: A voucher shared by a friend
steps.detail: A post or group chat message shows a big-name retailer's logo and a voucher worth hundreds, apparently to celebrate an anniversary.

steps.title: The wheel that always wins
steps.detail: You answer three easy questions or spin a wheel. It lands on the top prize every time, and a timer under ten minutes starts.

steps.title: Share to unlock
steps.detail: Before claiming, the page makes you forward the link to a set number of contacts or groups, which is how it reached you.

steps.title: Card for a 'free' prize
steps.detail: A final form asks for name, address and card number to cover a token fee. No voucher is issued; the card is billed again later.

fake-coupon-scam.whyItWorks: The link usually comes from someone you know, because they were made to forward it, so it carries their trust. Winning on the first spin gives a small thrill, and the timer leaves no room to wonder why a shop would give so much away.

realVsFake.real: Retailers publish genuine codes in their own app, emails you signed up to, or printed on receipts.
realVsFake.fake: The offer lives on an odd web address and arrives as a forwarded chat message.

realVsFake.real: A real discount code is typed in at the shop's checkout and simply lowers the total.
realVsFake.fake: You must hand over card details and pay a fee before any code is shown.

realVsFake.real: Shops do not make you recruit friends before a coupon will work.
realVsFake.fake: A progress bar insists you share to five groups, then says 'verification' needs a survey as well.

steps.title: The 'Court Enforcement Office' rings
steps.detail: A recorded voice or text says an unpaid parking or speeding fine has gone to enforcement and a warrant will be issued today. Press 1 for an officer.

steps.title: A reference number, no details
steps.detail: The 'officer' reads out a case reference and an amount, but cannot name the court, the road, the date or the vehicle registration involved.

steps.title: The one-hour settlement
steps.detail: You are offered a way out: settle within the hour and the hearing is cancelled. Hang up to check, they say, and the higher charge applies.

steps.title: Payment to a 'clerk'
steps.detail: Payment is taken as gift card codes read down the line, a transfer to a named individual described as the court clerk, or a card typed into a linked page.

fake-court-fine-scam.whyItWorks: Few drivers can swear they have no forgotten parking ticket or camera fine, especially after moving house, when a notice could easily have gone to the old address. That small doubt is enough for a confident voice quoting a case reference to sound real.

realVsFake.real: A genuine penalty notice states the vehicle registration, location, date and time, and tells you how to challenge it.
realVsFake.fake: Ask where and when the offence happened and the caller changes the subject back to the warrant.

realVsFake.real: An unpaid fine grows in written stages over weeks, with each increase and deadline set out in a posted letter.
realVsFake.fake: The scam compresses the whole process into a single phone call with sixty minutes on the clock.

realVsFake.real: Courts take card payments through their own payment line or site, against the notice number printed on your paperwork.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent to a supermarket for vouchers, or given the sort code of a personal account to pay 'the clerk'.

steps.title: A new friend mentions an exchange
steps.detail: Someone met on a dating app or through a 'wrong number' text chats for weeks, then mentions an uncle or analyst who gives them trading tips on a particular exchange.

steps.title: An app from outside the store
steps.detail: They send a link to the exchange's website or an app installed through a test-build link. It has live price charts and a customer service chat.

steps.title: Buy real coins, send them across
steps.detail: You buy crypto on a well-known exchange and transfer it to a deposit address on the fake one. Guided trades show profit, and one small withdrawal succeeds.

steps.title: The tax bill on 8,400
steps.detail: When you try to cash out the 8,400 shown, support demands a tax payment sent to a wallet first, then a security deposit, then freezes the account for 'money laundering'.

fake-crypto-exchange-scam.whyItWorks: The first purchase happens on a genuine exchange, so everything feels legitimate up to the moment coins are sent across. The balance on the fake site is only a number typed into a database, but it looks like winnings worth paying a fee to collect.

realVsFake.real: Established exchanges are installed from the official app stores and have years of public history under one name.
realVsFake.fake: The app comes through a direct download or beta-testing link, and the web address changes every few weeks.

realVsFake.real: An exchange takes trading and withdrawal fees out of your balance. Tax is a matter between you and your own tax authority.
realVsFake.fake: Support insists the tax cannot be deducted from the profit and must arrive as a separate deposit within 48 hours.

realVsFake.real: Regulated platforms verify your identity before you fund the account, during sign-up.
realVsFake.fake: Deposits are accepted with no checks at all, and 'verification' is raised for the first time when you ask for money out.

steps.title: An advert above the real result
steps.detail: Searching for a wallet by name brings up a sponsored link first, or an app store shows a clone with a near-identical icon and a slightly different developer.

steps.title: Installed and looking right
steps.detail: The app or browser extension opens with the familiar fox, shield or colour scheme. Its welcome screen offers 'Create new wallet' or 'Import existing wallet'.

steps.title: Twelve words typed in
steps.detail: Choosing import, you type your 12-word recovery phrase to restore the wallet. Some clones instead show an error and ask you to 'verify' the phrase again.

steps.title: Restored on the thief's device
steps.detail: The phrase is transmitted to the criminals, who restore your wallet on their own machine and send every coin out. With clones that generate a new wallet, they already hold its phrase.

fake-crypto-wallet-scam.whyItWorks: Entering a recovery phrase is exactly what a genuine wallet asks for when you move to a new phone, so the request raises no alarm. The fraud lies entirely in which program is asking, and adverts and store listings make that hard to judge.

realVsFake.real: Wallet makers link to their downloads from their own website, and the store listing shows the same developer name.
realVsFake.fake: The listing has a publisher name with an extra word or character, a recent release date and a handful of five-star reviews.

realVsFake.real: A genuine wallet asks for your phrase once, on your own decision to restore, and never through a pop-up or email.
realVsFake.fake: A warning says the wallet will be locked unless you re-enter the phrase to verify your account.

realVsFake.real: Hardware wallets show the phrase on the device's own screen at set-up and ask you to write it down.
realVsFake.fake: A companion app or a card in the box tells you to type the words into a phone or computer.

steps.title: A voicemail from 'legal processing'
steps.detail: A recorded or live message gives a 'case number' and says papers will be served at your home or workplace unless you ring back today.

steps.title: Details that sound right
steps.detail: The collector recites part of your national insurance or social security number, an old address, or the name of a payday lender you once used.

steps.title: The threat ladder
steps.detail: They say officers are on the way, your employer will be informed, your licence suspended. Then comes a 'one-time settlement' at half the balance, valid for this call.

steps.title: Payment over the phone
steps.detail: A debit card number is taken, or you are directed to a transfer, payment app or prepaid card. No receipt or settlement letter ever arrives, and the calls return.

fake-debt-collector-scam.whyItWorks: Plenty of people have an old overdraft, payday loan or phone bill they are not sure was ever settled, so the claim cannot be dismissed outright. Talk of arrest or a visit to the workplace adds shame, which stops people asking family for advice.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate collection agency sends a written notice naming the original creditor, the amount, and how to dispute it.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says there is no time for letters and that asking for proof is 'refusal to cooperate'.

realVsFake.real: Unpaid consumer debt is a civil matter. Collectors cannot have you arrested, and court papers come from a court.
realVsFake.fake: A 'warrant' or 'sheriff visit' is promised for this afternoon unless a card payment is made now.

realVsFake.real: Proper agencies accept traceable payment into a company account and confirm it in writing.
realVsFake.fake: You are given a personal account, a prepaid card reload or a payment-app handle to send the money to.

steps.title: A document awaits your signature
steps.detail: An email laid out like a DocuSign notice, yellow button included, says a company you have never dealt with sent 'Contract_Final.pdf' for signature and that the envelope expires soon.

steps.title: Review Document goes elsewhere
steps.detail: 'Review Document' does not open a signing screen. It lands on a page offering to 'continue with Outlook, Gmail or Office 365' so the file can be 'securely decrypted'.

steps.title: A password in place of a signature
steps.detail: You pick your provider and type your mailbox password into a copied login box. The page then shows an error or a blank PDF, with nothing to sign.

steps.title: The mailbox is the prize
steps.detail: With the password, the criminal reads your inbox for invoices and contracts in progress, sets a forwarding rule, and sends the same fake envelope to your contacts.

fake-docusign-email-scam.whyItWorks: Signing requests routinely arrive from senders you have never heard of: a letting agent's system, a new supplier, a solicitor's office. An unfamiliar name on a DocuSign notice does not feel odd, and 'expires soon' discourages asking around first.

realVsFake.real: A genuine DocuSign notice carries a security code you can enter on the DocuSign site yourself to open the envelope without clicking anything.
realVsFake.fake: The fake has no code, or one that leads nowhere. Its button is the only route offered to the document.

realVsFake.real: Signing a real envelope needs no password for your mailbox. You open the document and add your signature.
realVsFake.fake: Before any document appears, a box asks for your email account password 'to verify the recipient'.

realVsFake.real: Whoever sent a real contract can tell you what it is when you ask them directly.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is a vague 'Accounts Department' or a firm with no reason to send you paperwork.

steps.title: A call from 'immigration'
steps.detail: A caller or email says it is the embassy or immigration office and that there is a problem with your visa, such as a missing form or an unpaid charge.

steps.title: Details that sound official
steps.detail: They quote your name, nationality and sometimes your passport number, often lifted from a form you once filled in on an unofficial visa site, and give a badge and case number.

steps.title: The threat to your status
steps.detail: You are told the visa will be cancelled, or that detention and deportation will follow, unless the matter is settled today. Speaking to family is 'forbidden' during the case.

steps.title: Processing fee and passport scan
steps.detail: Payment is demanded by money transfer, gift cards or crypto, along with photos of your passport and visa. The scans are later used to open accounts in your name.

fake-embassy-scam.whyItWorks: Students, workers on visas and travellers mid-application have a great deal riding on their status and often little experience of how the host country's officials behave. A threat to that status crowds out the thought of checking.

realVsFake.real: Embassies and immigration offices write through the application portal or official email, and do not phone to collect money.
realVsFake.fake: A phone call or chat message is the first and only notice of the problem.

realVsFake.real: Visa fees are paid on the government's own site or at the visa centre, with an official receipt.
realVsFake.fake: The 'officer' wants a wire to a named individual, gift card codes or a crypto payment.

realVsFake.real: A genuine query about an application gives a written deadline and a way to respond or appeal.
realVsFake.fake: You are kept on the line, told arrest is imminent and warned against hanging up or asking a friend.

steps.title: A big-ticket deal agreed
steps.detail: You are buying or selling something expensive, such as a car, boat, watch or tractor, and the other party has agreed the price by message.

steps.title: 'For both our safety'
steps.detail: They suggest a neutral escrow company to hold the funds until collection, and send a link to one they say they have used before.

steps.title: Registering on the escrow site
steps.detail: The site has padlock icons, a live chat box and a transaction page already showing your deal. You create an account and enter card or bank details.

steps.title: Funds 'held', then gone
steps.detail: The dashboard shows your deposit as secured. If you are the seller it shows the buyer's money as received, so you release the goods. Then the site goes offline.

fake-escrow-scam.whyItWorks: Escrow is a real and sensible way to handle an expensive sale between strangers, so the suggestion makes the other party look careful. Because the idea is presented as protecting you, checking who runs the site feels unnecessary.

realVsFake.real: Licensed escrow firms are registered with a financial regulator, and you can confirm the licence on the regulator's own website.
realVsFake.fake: The 'licence' is a badge image on the homepage, and the web address was registered recently.

realVsFake.real: A trustworthy counterparty lets you pick the escrow provider, or agrees to the marketplace's built-in payment protection.
realVsFake.fake: Only their chosen site will do, and they lose interest when you propose a well-known alternative.

realVsFake.real: Real escrow services take funds by bank wire into a client account held in the company's registered name.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for your full card number and security code, or for a transfer to a private individual.

steps.title: A fare nobody else has
steps.detail: A search advert or social post lists a long-haul return at a price far under every airline, on a site styled like a comparison page.

steps.title: Handed to an 'agent'
steps.detail: Instead of a card checkout you are passed to a person on a messaging app who says the fare holds for thirty minutes.

steps.title: Transfer and passport photo
steps.detail: The agent sends personal bank details for the deposit and asks for a photo of your passport 'to issue the e-ticket'.

steps.title: The cancellation follow-up
steps.detail: A PDF itinerary arrives with a reference the airline cannot find. Days later a message says the flight is cancelled and to ring a number to rebook, where card details are taken.

fake-flight-booking-scam.whyItWorks: Air fares really do swing wildly and vanish within minutes, so a deadline on a cheap seat feels ordinary. Sending a passport photo also seems routine for travel, which lets the criminal collect identity documents alongside the payment.

realVsFake.real: An airline or accredited agent takes payment at a card checkout and emails a booking reference straight away.
realVsFake.fake: A named individual asks for a bank transfer and promises the ticket once it clears.

realVsFake.real: A genuine reference opens your trip under 'manage booking' on the airline's own site.
realVsFake.fake: The six-character code on the PDF returns 'booking not found', or shows a seat that was held and never paid for.

realVsFake.real: Airlines announce cancellations in their app and rebook you without asking for card details again.
realVsFake.fake: A text from an unknown number says to call a 'rebooking desk' that wants your card and passport.

steps.title: A child's photo is borrowed
steps.detail: The scammer lifts pictures of a sick child, an injured dog or a burnt-out house from a news story or someone else's campaign, and writes a new caption.

steps.title: Shared by kind people
steps.detail: The post names a first name only, a surgery date and a target such as 5,000 by Friday. It asks for shares as much as money, so friends spread it.

steps.title: The donate button
steps.detail: The link leads to a personal money-request page or a copy of a crowdfunding site. Comments are switched off, and the organiser's link to the family is never explained.

steps.title: Same story, new name
steps.detail: Gifts go to the scammer's own balance. When donors ask for an update the post disappears, and the same photos resurface under a different child's name.

fake-fundraiser-scam.whyItWorks: The appeal usually reaches you through a friend who shared it sincerely, so it borrows that friend's credibility. Asking whether a seriously ill child is real feels heartless, and a fiver seems too little to be worth checking.

realVsFake.real: Genuine crowdfunding pages name the organiser, state their relationship to the person helped and say who withdraws the funds.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser is a first name and an avatar, and questions about the family go unanswered or get deleted.

realVsFake.real: A real family appeal has roots you can trace: a local paper, a school, a named hospital ward, neighbours commenting.
realVsFake.fake: A reverse image search finds the photo attached to a different story in another country.

realVsFake.real: Honest organisers post updates as treatment goes on and explain what happens to anything left over.
realVsFake.fake: The deadline keeps sliding, the total is never shown, and each repost says time is nearly up.

steps.title: 'HMRC is filing a lawsuit'
steps.detail: An automated call says HMRC has started legal proceedings against you for tax fraud. Other versions arrive as a 'FINAL NOTICE' text about a rebate or unpaid bill.

steps.title: The caseworker and the shortfall
steps.detail: A 'caseworker' gives a staff ID, says a review of your Self Assessment or PAYE record found an underpayment, and asks you to confirm your National Insurance number.

steps.title: Officers 'on their way'
steps.detail: Question the figure and the tone hardens. A warrant is supposedly with local police, who will attend your address within the hour unless the balance is cleared.

steps.title: A transfer or a fake Gateway
steps.detail: Callers dictate account details for a bank transfer or ask for voucher codes. The rebate texts lead to a copied Government Gateway page that collects your login and card.

fake-hmrc-tax-scam.whyItWorks: Tax codes and Self Assessment are confusing enough that most people can believe they got something wrong.
