The messages cluster around the January filing deadline and when real tax calculation letters go out, so a demand or rebate arrives exactly when one is half expected.

realVsFake.real: HMRC explains underpaid tax in a posted calculation letter or inside your personal tax account, with time to query it.
realVsFake.fake: A recorded voice announces a lawsuit and tells you to press 1, with no letter ever having arrived.

realVsFake.real: A genuine rebate is claimed by signing in to your tax account yourself, or it arrives as a cheque.
realVsFake.fake: The text quotes a figure such as 276.48 and asks for card details so the rebate can be 'returned'.

realVsFake.real: People who cannot pay a tax bill are offered instalment plans. HMRC does not send police to collect over the phone.
realVsFake.fake: The caller rules out any payment plan and insists the full sum must leave your account during the call.

steps.title: 'Your policy lapses today'
steps.detail: A text or call headed as an insurance notice says your motor, home or health cover ends today, without naming the insurer or a policy number.

steps.title: Driving uninsured as the threat
steps.detail: The message stresses that you would be driving illegally or left unprotected from midnight, and gives a link or a callback number to renew.

steps.title: A quote lower than last year
steps.detail: The page or caller offers to renew at a discounted price if you pay now, and asks for the card details or your insurer login.

steps.title: Transfer to an 'agent'
steps.detail: Phone versions ask for a bank transfer to a named individual or payment in gift cards. A 'refund' variant asks for account details instead.

fake-insurance-renewal-scam.whyItWorks: Insurance is bought once a year and then forgotten, so most people could not say their exact renewal date. The prospect of an uncovered crash or burst pipe tomorrow is frightening enough that checking the policy feels slower than paying.

realVsFake.real: Insurers send a renewal notice weeks ahead, by post or email, showing the policy number, the new price and last year's price.
realVsFake.fake: The first you hear is a same-day warning with no policy number and no premium figure.

realVsFake.real: Many policies renew automatically on the card or direct debit already on file unless you opted out.
realVsFake.fake: You are told cover will vanish tonight unless you enter fresh payment details through the link.

realVsFake.real: Premiums are paid to the insurance company or a named broker by card or direct debit.
realVsFake.fake: The caller wants a transfer to a personal bank account, or codes from shop-bought gift cards.

steps.title: Shortlisted for a summer placement
steps.detail: A message reaches your student email or a course group chat saying you have been shortlisted for a paid summer internship at a recognisable firm, though you never applied.

steps.title: Pay 60 pounds to confirm
steps.detail: The 'programme coordinator' says only a few seats remain. To hold yours you must pay a 60 pound registration fee within 24 hours through a link or to a personal account.

steps.title: Student ID and bank details
steps.detail: A form asks for a scan of your passport or student card, your home address and bank details 'for the stipend', which is everything needed to impersonate you.

steps.title: A certificate, or nothing
steps.detail: Some victims hear nothing more. Others get unpaid 'tasks' such as promoting the programme to classmates, then a PDF certificate that no employer recognises, with an extra charge to download it.

fake-internship-scam.whyItWorks: Students are told constantly that they need experience on their CV, and real internships are scarce and competitive. A message saying a place is already theirs, for the price of a night out, arrives exactly when rejection emails are piling up.

realVsFake.real: Employers list internships on their own careers page and through university careers services, and you apply before anyone shortlists you.
realVsFake.fake: You are 'shortlisted' for a role you never applied to, by someone using a personal email or chat account.

realVsFake.real: A paid internship pays the intern. Nobody buys a seat, and there is an interview with the team you would join.
realVsFake.fake: The place is yours as soon as the registration fee clears, with no interview and no named supervisor.

realVsFake.real: Bank details are requested by payroll after you have signed an offer on company letterhead.
realVsFake.fake: ID and account numbers are demanded on day one, with a countdown to stop you asking a tutor.

steps.title: An agency that exists only online
steps.detail: The 'agent' has a logo, a template website and a string of adverts across property portals and social media, all posted within the last few weeks.

steps.title: Everyone gets the same reply
steps.detail: Each enquirer hears that the flat is very popular and viewings are fully booked or the agent is away, but that you can secure it ahead of the queue.

steps.title: Holding deposit plus referencing fee
steps.detail: They want a holding deposit and a referencing fee by bank transfer the same day, and send a tenancy 'pack' asking for payslips and a passport scan.

steps.title: The office address is a mailbox
steps.detail: Once several people have paid for the same flat, the phone goes unanswered. The office address turns out to be a mailbox shop or another firm's premises.

fake-letting-agent-scam.whyItWorks: Renters expect agents to ask for holding deposits and referencing, so the request raises no alarm. A branded email signature and a contract pack look like routine admin, and one advert can collect from many applicants.

realVsFake.real: Genuine letting agents can show membership of a redress or client money protection scheme, checkable on the scheme's own site.
realVsFake.fake: The agency names no scheme, or shows a badge with a membership number that matches nobody.

realVsFake.real: A real agency has a staffed office or a landline that someone answers, and a history of past lets.
realVsFake.fake: Contact is by mobile and email only, and the company was registered a few weeks ago.

realVsFake.real: A holding deposit follows a viewing and comes with written terms on when it is refunded.
realVsFake.fake: The 'property manager' wants holding deposit, referencing fee and sometimes rent together before you have stepped inside.

steps.title: One new message from a recruiter
steps.detail: The email uses LinkedIn's blue header and says a recruiter messaged you about a role, or that you 'appeared in 9 searches this week'. A button says 'View message'.

steps.title: A login screen on the wrong address
steps.detail: That button brings up a replica of the LinkedIn login screen hosted somewhere else. Typing your email and password there sends both to whoever runs the page.

steps.title: The recruiter moves to WhatsApp
steps.detail: In the job-offer version a friendly hiring manager replies, praises your profile, and asks to move to WhatsApp or Telegram for a 'quick text interview'.

steps.title: Fees, forms and a borrowed profile
steps.detail: You are offered the job within days, then asked for passport scans, bank details 'for payroll' or a fee for training or equipment. Meanwhile your stolen login messages your connections.

fake-linkedin-email-scam.whyItWorks: LinkedIn sends so many notification emails that clicking through is a habit, and a message from a recruiter is exactly what the site exists for. Anyone job hunting wants this particular email to be real.

realVsFake.real: Real LinkedIn messages are waiting in the Messaging tab when you open the app yourself.
realVsFake.fake: Open the app and no recruiter has written to you. The promised message is nowhere in your Messaging tab.

realVsFake.real: A real recruiter names the employer and the role, and is content to hold a proper interview by video or phone.
realVsFake.fake: The hiring manager avoids calls, interviews by text chat only, and offers the job after a handful of questions.

realVsFake.real: Employers pay you. Equipment and training are provided, or reimbursed through payroll once you have started.
realVsFake.fake: Before any start date you are asked to pay for a laptop, a background check or a training pack.

steps.title: 'We're having trouble with your billing'
steps.detail: A red-and-black email says Netflix could not take this month's payment and your account is on hold. It gives you 24 hours before the membership is cancelled.

steps.title: The red 'Update account' button
steps.detail: It leads to a dark sign-in screen identical to the real one, on an address that merely contains the brand's name. You type your email and password as usual.

steps.title: A billing form with extras
steps.detail: The next page asks for the card number, expiry, security code and billing postcode. Some versions add your date of birth, which a streaming service has no use for.

steps.title: A code from your bank
steps.detail: A final screen says your bank must verify the card and asks for the code it just texted. That code approves a purchase the criminal is making elsewhere.

fake-netflix-payment-email.whyItWorks: A Netflix login is often shared across a household, so whoever opens the email assumes someone else's card has expired and does not want to be the reason the television goes dark tonight. Failed payments are common enough that nothing sounds odd.

realVsFake.real: When a Netflix payment really fails, the app or the TV shows a notice the next time someone tries to watch.
realVsFake.fake: Netflix still plays normally on your television while the email insists the account is on hold.

realVsFake.real: Netflix does not ask for card numbers or passwords to be sent by email or text. Billing is changed under Account after you sign in yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The email takes you straight to a card form through its own link and never mentions the Account page.

realVsFake.real: A real billing hold simply pauses playback until a working card is added. There is no countdown.
realVsFake.fake: You get 24 hours, a ticking timer, and a threat that your profiles and viewing history will be erased.

steps.title: Your account has been limited
steps.detail: PayPal has supposedly noticed unusual activity and restricted sending and withdrawing until you confirm your information. The message opens with 'Dear Customer' and ends with a 'Resolve now' button.

steps.title: A cloned login screen
steps.detail: The button leads to a page with the PayPal logo and the familiar two-box login. The address is a lookalike, often 'paypal' followed by extra words and hyphens.

steps.title: The 'confirm your identity' form
steps.detail: Once the password is in, a second form asks for your full name, address, card number, and the bank account linked to your PayPal balance.

steps.title: Balance sent as friends and family
steps.detail: The criminal logs in, changes the email and phone on the account, and sends the balance to another account as a personal payment, which carries no buyer protection.

fake-paypal-email-scam.whyItWorks: PayPal really does limit accounts, and sellers in particular dread it because their money gets frozen. The scam borrows the genuine term 'limited', so anyone who has heard of a real limitation assumes this is one.

realVsFake.real: PayPal emails address you by the full name on your account, or by your business name.
realVsFake.fake: The greeting is 'Dear Customer', 'Dear User' or just your email address pasted in.

realVsFake.real: A real limitation is listed in the Resolution Centre when you log in by typing the address yourself, with the steps needed to lift it.
realVsFake.fake: Log in the normal way and no limitation is listed. The restriction lives only on the page behind the emailed button.

realVsFake.real: PayPal does not ask for your password, full card number or bank details by email.
realVsFake.fake: The form wants all three on one page and says access stays frozen until every box is filled.

steps.title: An outrage headline
steps.detail: A post with a distressing image, perhaps a caged animal or a threatened park, says a decision is days away and only signatures can stop it.

steps.title: The signing form
steps.detail: The page asks for far more than a signature needs: full name, email, mobile, home address and date of birth, with a counter ticking towards a goal.

steps.title: Confirm, share, chip in
steps.detail: After signing you are told to 'confirm' by logging in with a social account, share to ten friends, and add a small card payment to 'boost' the campaign.

steps.title: Your details change hands
steps.detail: Nothing is delivered to any council or parliament. The list of names, numbers and addresses is sold on, and nuisance calls and tailored phishing emails begin.

fake-petition-scam.whyItWorks: Signing feels free and virtuous, the opposite of a purchase, so nobody reads a petition form the way they would read a checkout. Anger at the cause also crowds out the question of who is collecting the signatures.

realVsFake.real: Established petition sites ask for a name, an email and perhaps a postcode, then send one confirmation email.
realVsFake.fake: The form insists on a mobile number, a birth date and a street address before it will count you.

realVsFake.real: A real petition says who started it and which minister, council or company will receive it.
realVsFake.fake: No author or recipient is given, just a slogan, a photo and a number that jumps on every refresh.

realVsFake.real: Campaign groups that also fundraise keep the donation separate, optional and on their own named site.
realVsFake.fake: Your signature is 'pending' until you pay or sign in through a login box on the petition page.

steps.title: A thank-you from your network
steps.detail: A text signed 'NETWORK NOTICE' or with a mobile brand's name says you have earned a loyalty reward, or that a billing error has put the account on hold.

steps.title: Sign in to your account
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the network's customer login. It asks for the mobile number, account password and sometimes the account security PIN.

steps.title: Payment details 'refreshed'
steps.detail: After login, a second screen says the stored payment method needs updating to release the reward or lift the hold, and takes your card.

steps.title: Upgrades ordered on your account
steps.detail: With the login, the fraudster signs in to the real site, orders a new handset on your contract to another address, or requests a replacement SIM.

fake-phone-carrier-text-scam.whyItWorks: Mobile networks text their customers constantly about bills, data allowances and offers, so one more notice blends in. The message arrives on the very device and service it is talking about, which makes it feel like it came from inside the network.

realVsFake.real: Your network knows your name and account number and can show any reward or billing issue inside its own app.
realVsFake.fake: The text greets nobody by name and the loyalty reward exists only behind the link.

realVsFake.real: A carrier with a billing problem retries your direct debit or adds the amount to the next bill.
realVsFake.fake: You are given 24 hours to type card details into a web form or lose service.

realVsFake.real: Genuine handset upgrades need security checks and are confirmed by email and text to you.
realVsFake.fake: The copied network login collects the password and PIN that those upgrade checks rely on.

steps.title: A quote request from 'procurement'
steps.detail: An email signed by a named purchasing officer at a university or large company asks for prices on laptops, hard drives, projectors or lab equipment.

steps.title: The purchase order PDF
steps.detail: Your quote is accepted without negotiation. A purchase order follows with the institution's logo, a PO number and a request for standard 30-day credit terms.

steps.title: Deliver to a different address
steps.detail: The ship-to line is a warehouse, self-storage unit or residential address described as an off-campus receiving site, where a freight forwarder re-ships the goods.

steps.title: The invoice reaches the real organisation
steps.detail: After thirty days you chase payment. The genuine accounts office has no record of the order, the officer never wrote to you, and the stock is long gone.

fake-purchase-order-scam.whyItWorks: Universities and public bodies are known to pay reliably on credit, and landing one as a customer feels like a break for a small supplier. The officer's name is real and can be found on the institution's website, which passes a quick check.

realVsFake.real: A genuine institution emails from its own domain and asks new suppliers to complete vendor registration before ordering.
realVsFake.fake: The address swaps a letter, adds a hyphen or ends in a different suffix, and no supplier onboarding is mentioned.

realVsFake.real: Real orders deliver to the organisation's own campus, depot or office, through its goods-in department.
realVsFake.fake: The delivery address is in another town, and the contact asks for the tracking number the moment the goods leave.

realVsFake.real: Purchasing staff can be reached through the main switchboard listed on the official website.
realVsFake.fake: The only phone number is the one on the purchase order, answered by a mobile or an internet voice line.

steps.title: An agency with roles to fill
steps.detail: A 'staffing agency' advertises warehouse, care or admin vacancies, or messages you after finding your CV online, and says a client is ready to take you on at once.

steps.title: Registration and induction fee
steps.detail: To go on the agency's books you must pay a one-off registration and training fee of about 95, described as refundable from your first pay packet.

steps.title: Onboarding pack by web form
steps.detail: An 'onboarding' form collects your passport or licence, proof of address, national insurance or tax number and bank account, supposedly so the client's payroll can be set up.

steps.title: The start date keeps slipping
steps.detail: The client 'postpones', then the consultant goes quiet. The fee is gone, and the identity pack you sent can be used to open accounts or sold to other fraudsters.

fake-recruitment-agency-scam.whyItWorks: Agencies are a normal route into work, and registering with one always involves handing over ID and bank details. Because that paperwork is expected, the only unusual part is the fee, and a promise to refund it from wages makes it feel harmless.

realVsFake.real: Agencies bill the client company an hourly margin on top of your wage, so they have no reason to charge you.
realVsFake.fake: The jobseeker is billed for joining the books, with a second 'induction' charge once the first has been paid.

realVsFake.real: A genuine consultant emails from the agency's own domain and can be reached on a landline at a registered office.
realVsFake.fake: Contact runs through a free webmail address and a mobile number that only accepts messages.

realVsFake.real: Agencies check your right to work face to face or by video, after telling you which client and role you are going to.
realVsFake.fake: Full document scans are requested through a link before you have been told the employer's name.

steps.title: Typing work at 30 an hour
steps.detail: A job-board post or direct message offers data entry from home at about 30 dollars an hour, flexible hours, no experience, with a 'hiring manager' to contact on a chat app.

steps.title: An interview typed in chat
steps.detail: The interview is a list of typed questions about your typing speed and availability. Minutes after you answer, you are told the panel has approved you.

steps.title: Software activation and deposit form
steps.detail: To receive your first assignment you must pay a one-time 49 dollar activation fee for the company's data portal and fill in a direct deposit form with your bank details and ID.

steps.title: The assignment turns into transfers
steps.detail: No spreadsheet ever arrives. Either the manager vanishes with the fee, or your first 'task' is to accept a payment into your account and send it on to a vendor.

fake-remote-data-entry-job-scam.whyItWorks: Data entry is the one remote job almost anyone feels qualified for, so the high hourly rate reads as luck. An activation fee for a work portal sounds like an IT formality, and 49 dollars is quickly weighed against a first day's pay.

realVsFake.real: Real data entry roles pay close to the going clerical wage and usually include a timed typing or accuracy test.
realVsFake.fake: The rate is double or triple the norm, and nobody tests whether you can type.

realVsFake.real: Employers give remote staff logins to their systems at no charge, and often send the laptop too.
realVsFake.fake: Access to the 'data portal' has to be bought by the worker before any task is released.

realVsFake.real: A data clerk keys records into a database. Nothing in the role involves their own bank account.
realVsFake.fake: Within a week the work has become 'payment reconciliation', meaning money arrives in your account for you to pass on.

steps.title: A wall of five stars
steps.detail: You find a product or shop with a near-perfect score. Dozens of short reviews landed in the same few days, all praising 'amazing quality' in similar words.

steps.title: The 'independent' comparison site
steps.detail: Searching the name brings up a 'top ten' or review blog that ranks this seller first. The same people run it, or are paid per click.

steps.title: Buying on borrowed trust
steps.detail: Reassured, you order. Some listings were hijacked from an older, unrelated product, so the star rating belongs to something else entirely.

steps.title: Complaints go missing
steps.detail: The item is poor, fake or never arrives. Your one-star review is rejected or buried, or the seller offers a refund only if you delete it.

fake-review-scam.whyItWorks: Shoppers treat a star rating as the voice of strangers with nothing to gain, and rarely open the individual reviews. A high score takes seconds to read, while spotting forty near-identical comments from new accounts takes effort almost nobody spends.

realVsFake.real: Genuine feedback builds up slowly and includes grumbles about sizing, delivery or battery life.
realVsFake.fake: Scores jump overnight, with bursts of five-star posts that never mention how the item was used.

realVsFake.real: Real reviewers have a history across different shops and write in their own uneven style.
realVsFake.fake: Accounts created this week have reviewed a phone case, a drill and a face cream on the same day.

realVsFake.real: An honest seller answers bad reviews in public and leaves them up.
realVsFake.fake: Inside the parcel is a card offering a gift voucher in exchange for a five-star rating.

steps.title: A buyer from out of town
steps.detail: Someone agrees to buy your listed item at full price without seeing it, says they live far away, and asks you to post it.

steps.title: Their own prepaid label
steps.detail: They email a label as a PDF, explaining that their courier account gets a discount. The delivery name and address on it differ from the buyer's details.

steps.title: The 80 they 'overpaid'
steps.detail: A payment notice shows the price plus 80 too much for postage. They ask you to send that 80 back by a separate app and post today.

steps.title: Parcel rerouted, payment reversed
steps.detail: The original payment is a forged email or a stolen card that gets charged back. Because the label was theirs, you hold no tracking that proves delivery to the paying address.

fake-shipping-label-scam.whyItWorks: A buyer covering postage looks like a favour that saves you a trip to price up the parcel. Seller protection usually depends on posting to the address on the order with your own tracked label, a rule most casual sellers have never read.

realVsFake.real: On mainstream marketplaces the seller buys or prints the label from the order page, addressed to the buyer on record.
realVsFake.fake: The label comes as an email attachment and sends the parcel to a name you have not seen before.

realVsFake.real: A real buyer pays the listed total. If postage was overcharged, the platform's own partial refund tool corrects it.
realVsFake.fake: The extra must go back through a different payment app, to an account that is not the buyer's.

realVsFake.real: A genuine payment appears in your account balance when you log in to the payment service directly.
realVsFake.fake: Proof of payment is a screenshot or an email saying funds are 'pending until you ship'.

steps.title: A wholesale price list
steps.detail: Your business finds a supplier through a trade directory, a search advert or a cold email, quoting 500 units at well under your current cost.

steps.title: Samples and a small first order
steps.detail: They send a product catalogue, a company certificate and sometimes a sample. A modest trial order may arrive on time and exactly as described.

steps.title: The pro forma invoice
steps.detail: For the main order a pro forma invoice lists bank details, sometimes in a different country or company name. Card and escrow 'incur extra fees'.

steps.title: Dispatch delayed indefinitely
steps.detail: After the transfer you get a made-up container number or a port delay story, perhaps a request for customs fees, and then the website and inbox go dead.

fake-supplier-scam.whyItWorks: Paying a deposit by bank transfer is how real wholesale trade works, so the request does not stand out. A small order that arrives perfectly is the strongest reference a buyer can get, and it is exactly what the fraudster pays for.

realVsFake.real: An established supplier's bank account is in its registered company name, in the country where it trades.
realVsFake.fake: The beneficiary is an individual or an unrelated firm, and the bank is somewhere the supplier has never mentioned.

realVsFake.real: Real manufacturers welcome a factory visit, a video tour of the production line or a third-party inspection before shipment.
realVsFake.fake: Requests to inspect are met with stock photos, excuses about confidentiality and a reminder that stock is limited.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate exporters accept letters of credit or trade assurance on large orders, and split payment around shipping documents.
realVsFake.fake: Full payment is wanted before dispatch, and any protected method is priced to put you off.

steps.title: Searching for a helpline
steps.detail: You have a real problem, a late refund or locked account, and search for the company's phone number. The top result is a paid advert.

steps.title: An agent who answers instantly
steps.detail: No queue, no menu. The person confirms they are from the company and asks for your order number and email to 'pull up the file'.

steps.title: The problem gets bigger
steps.detail: They say the account has been compromised or the refund is stuck, and the fix needs a screen-sharing app or a 'verification' payment.

steps.title: Gift cards or a reversed refund
steps.detail: You are told to buy gift cards to cancel a bogus charge, or to read out a full card number and code so the refund can be 'pushed through'.

fake-support-number-scam.whyItWorks: You made the call, so your guard is down: it feels like you chose the company, not the other way round. People who are already annoyed about an order will follow almost any instruction that promises to close the matter today.

realVsFake.real: The genuine contact route is inside the retailer's app or printed in your order confirmation email.
realVsFake.fake: The number appears in a sponsored result, a map listing anyone can edit, or a forum reply.

realVsFake.real: Real support staff can see your order already and refund to the original payment method.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agent' needs your card's long number, expiry and security code to send money back.

realVsFake.real: No retailer's helpdesk asks you to buy vouchers or install software to sort out a delivery.
realVsFake.fake: You are kept on the line while you drive to a shop for gift cards.

steps.title: You complain in public
steps.detail: You post about a delayed flight, a failed bank payment or a dead broadband line and tag the company. Bots watching those brand names pick it up in seconds.

steps.title: First to answer
steps.detail: An account with the company logo and a handle like 'Brand_HelpDesk' apologises before the real team has replied, and invites you to message it privately.

steps.title: Verification in the DMs
steps.detail: In private it asks for your booking reference or account number, then your online banking login or full card details 'to locate the transaction'.

steps.title: A refund that costs money
steps.detail: Some send a WhatsApp number or a form link. Others say a small 'verification payment' is needed to release your refund, then use the card for much more.

fake-support-reply-scam.whyItWorks: You asked for help, so a reply from 'support' is exactly what you expected to see. After an hour on hold or a cancelled flight you are frustrated and relieved that someone has finally answered, and you do not inspect the handle.

realVsFake.real: The company's genuine support handle is the one linked from its website, with a long posting history.
realVsFake.fake: The replying account joined recently, follows almost nobody, and its timeline is nothing but apologies to strangers.

realVsFake.real: Real agents may ask for a reference number, never a password, PIN or the three digits on your card.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor wants your login and complete card details typed into a direct message.

realVsFake.real: Refunds are returned to the original payment method without any charge to release them.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to send a small sum first, or to approve a payment request disguised as a refund.

steps.title: The screen that will not close
steps.detail: A browser tab goes full screen with a Microsoft logo, a count of 'viruses found', a looping alarm sound and a line saying 'Do not restart. Call support.'

steps.title: The diagnosis on the phone
steps.detail: The 'engineer' who answers gives a badge number, asks you to press Windows and R, and has you type a command that fills the screen with harmless listings he calls infections.

steps.title: A tool that hands over control
steps.detail: Next comes a legitimate remote-control program such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer. You install it and read out the number it displays, which lets him move your mouse and open your files.

steps.title: The lifetime protection plan
steps.detail: He quotes a one-off fee or a 'lifetime protection plan' of a few hundred, payable by card over the phone or by gift cards. Some then set a password that locks you out.

fake-tech-support-scam.whyItWorks: The page is built to look as if the computer itself is speaking: it hides the browser's edges and refuses to close. A frozen screen and a blaring alarm leave the printed phone number as the only obvious way out.

realVsFake.real: Microsoft says its error messages never include a phone number, and it does not ring customers about viruses.
realVsFake.fake: A toll-free number sits in the middle of the alert, sometimes read aloud by a recorded voice.

realVsFake.real: A genuine security warning comes from the antivirus program installed on your machine and can be dismissed like any other window.
realVsFake.fake: The alert lives in a browser tab, blocks the close button, and says restarting will destroy your data.

realVsFake.real: A repair shop quotes a price before starting work, on a job you brought to them.
realVsFake.fake: The price appears only after he controls the screen, and gift cards are suggested as the fastest way to pay.

steps.title: An update in the shop's colours
steps.detail: An email or text carrying a retailer's logo, fonts and order-status layout says your parcel hit a 'delivery exception' and is on hold.

steps.title: A copy of the tracking page
steps.detail: The link opens a page with a progress bar stuck at 'held at depot' and a button to release or reschedule the delivery.

steps.title: A fee under a pound
steps.detail: It asks for a handling charge of about ninety pence within 24 hours, or for your shop login, so the parcel is not sent back.

steps.title: The card is the real prize
steps.detail: The pennies never matter. The full card number, expiry and security code go to the criminal, and a saved login lets them order on your account.

fake-tracking-update-scam.whyItWorks: If you really are waiting for a delivery, the message lands as an answer to a question you already had. A charge of less than a pound seems too small to be worth stealing, so people pay it without checking the order in the shop's app.

realVsFake.real: A retailer shows delivery status inside your account, under the order you actually placed.
realVsFake.fake: The update quotes no item, no real order number, and greets you as 'customer'.

realVsFake.real: Postage is settled at checkout. Shops do not add release fees once an order has shipped.
realVsFake.fake: A tiny surcharge appears mid-delivery, payable only through the link in the message.

realVsFake.real: If a parcel cannot be delivered, the carrier leaves a card or offers free redelivery.
realVsFake.fake: You are warned the parcel will be returned to sender by tomorrow unless you pay.

steps.title: '1 new voicemail (0:38)'
steps.detail: A text or email reports a missed call and a recorded message with a believable length, and gives a link to listen instead of your usual voicemail number.

steps.title: A player that will not play
steps.detail: The page shows an audio bar or a play button. Pressing it does nothing except bring up a request to sign in or download a 'voicemail app'.

steps.title: Sign-in or sideloaded app
steps.detail: Email versions show a copy of a work email login. Android text versions offer an install file and tell you to allow apps from unknown sources.

steps.title: Passwords read, texts sent
steps.detail: A stolen login opens your mailbox. The installed app can read incoming codes, lay fake screens over banking apps and text the same lure to your contacts.

fake-voicemail-text-scam.whyItWorks: A missed call with a message suggests someone specific tried to reach you, perhaps a delivery driver, a clinic or family. Curiosity about a 38-second recording is hard to resist, and listening seems far less risky than paying or logging in to a bank.

realVsFake.real: Voicemail on a mobile is heard by calling your network's voicemail number or opening the phone app's voicemail tab.
realVsFake.fake: The recording can supposedly only be played through a web link sent by text.

realVsFake.real: Your phone already has everything needed to play a voicemail. No extra software is involved.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to install a separate 'player' from outside the official app store and grant it permissions.

realVsFake.real: A real work voicemail email arrives from your company's phone system with the audio attached or in the app you already use.
realVsFake.fake: The email shows a play button that leads to a password prompt on an unrelated address.

steps.title: A tour date is announced
steps.detail: When a concert or match is confirmed, pages calling themselves the official fan club or 'VIP team' appear and message people who commented on the announcement.

steps.title: Selected for backstage
steps.detail: The DM says you have been picked for a meet-and-greet with photo and signed merchandise, limited to twenty fans, and attaches a booking form or a mock pass.

steps.title: Deposit to hold the place
steps.detail: A deposit is due within hours by bank transfer or gift card. After that come a 'security clearance' charge and an insurance fee for entering the artist area.

steps.title: Not on the door list
steps.detail: You receive a PDF pass with a barcode that scans to nothing. At the venue, staff have no record of your name, and the page has blocked you.

fan-event-scam.whyItWorks: VIP packages do exist and sell out fast, so fans expect scarcity and a short window. Being 'chosen' flatters years of loyalty, and the fear of losing the place to the next fan outweighs the oddness of paying by transfer.

realVsFake.real: Meet-and-greet packages are sold through the official ticket seller or the artist's site, bundled with a seat.
realVsFake.fake: Access is offered by private message, with no ticket attached and no listing on the venue's page.

realVsFake.real: You pay the full advertised price once at checkout, and the order appears in your ticketing account.
realVsFake.fake: A deposit is followed by clearance, insurance and 'wristband' fees, each one supposedly refundable on the night.

realVsFake.real: Venues and promoters can confirm a VIP booking if you ring the box office with the order number.
realVsFake.fake: The 'fan club manager' tells you not to contact the venue because the session is unannounced.

steps.title: A twin of the creator's profile
steps.detail: An account reposts a creator's public photos under a handle with one extra character. It follows their fans and replies to comments on the genuine page.

steps.title: The secret link
steps.detail: It messages that the exclusive page 'can't be linked on my main', and sends a web address that copies the look of a well-known subscription platform.

steps.title: Unlock for a monthly price
steps.detail: The page asks for card details for a monthly tier, or tells you to pay a sign-up fee by payment app or gift card and send a screenshot.

steps.title: Old posts, repeat billing
steps.detail: You receive a folder of images already public on the creator's feed, or nothing. The card is charged again each month, with no account page to cancel from.

fan-subscription-scam.whyItWorks: Creators often do keep paid pages off their main profiles because some platforms restrict such links, so 'not on my main' sounds like inside knowledge. The fan already wants the content and recognises every photo.

realVsFake.real: A creator's paid page is reachable from their long-standing verified profile, usually through one link hub.
realVsFake.fake: The link comes only by DM from a newer account, with a warning not to ask about it publicly.

realVsFake.real: Subscription platforms bill inside your own account, where you can see renewals and switch them off.
realVsFake.fake: Payment goes to a personal tag or a bare card form, and there is nowhere to log in afterwards.

realVsFake.real: Paid tiers contain material that is new to subscribers, posted on a regular schedule.
realVsFake.fake: The 'exclusive' set is screenshots from the public feed, some still carrying another site's watermark.

steps.title: A recording about funeral bills
steps.detail: A recorded voice says funerals now cost more than most families can cover, and that a 'state-approved' final expense plan is open to people your age.

steps.title: Press 1 for a 'benefits adviser'
steps.detail: Pressing 1 connects a live seller who gives a first name and a made-up licence number, and says no medical exam is needed.

steps.title: Medications, then bank details
steps.detail: They run through your date of birth, prescriptions, Social Security or National Insurance number and next of kin, then ask for a bank account for the first premium.

steps.title: Premiums for cover that isn't there
steps.detail: Monthly debits begin. No policy document ever arrives, or the plan has a waiting period and exclusions that mean it would pay almost nothing.

final-expense-call-scam.whyItWorks: Nobody wants their children handed a funeral bill, and the recording says so out loud to someone who may live alone. Mentioning a government-sounding programme makes a sales pitch feel like a benefit being handed out.

realVsFake.real: Licensed insurers send a written quote and policy document, and give a cooling-off period in which you can cancel.
realVsFake.fake: The seller wants bank details before any paperwork exists and says the rate expires when the call ends.

realVsFake.real: A real insurance agent's licence can be looked up by name with the state or national regulator.
realVsFake.fake: The 'adviser' offers a first name only and hangs up when asked which insurer underwrites the plan.

realVsFake.real: Government agencies and Medicare do not phone people to sell burial or funeral insurance.
realVsFake.fake: The robocall implies the plan is a new state benefit that pensioners are entitled to claim.

steps.title: A simple app, heavily advertised
steps.detail: An advert pushes a QR scanner, wallpaper pack, horoscope or photo filter app. It sits in the official store with a high rating padded by fake reviews.

steps.title: The trial screen on first launch
steps.detail: Before any feature works, a full-screen panel offers a three-day trial. The big button says 'Continue'; the weekly price sits beneath in pale grey.

steps.title: One tap on the fingerprint sensor
steps.detail: Confirming with your thumb or face starts a subscription through the app store, billed weekly at a rate that adds up to hundreds a year.

steps.title: Deleting it changes nothing
steps.detail: You remove the app, assuming that ends it. Billing continues, because the subscription lives in your store account settings, not in the app.

fleeceware-app-scam.whyItWorks: Being inside the official app store makes the app feel vetted, and a free trial sounds harmless. Most people believe deleting an app cancels it, so the weekly charges run for months before anyone looks closely at a statement.

realVsFake.real: A fairly priced app shows the cost in the same size text as the trial offer, and works in a basic way without paying.
realVsFake.fake: The close button on the paywall is a faint cross that appears after several seconds.

realVsFake.real: Phones already scan QR codes, work as a torch and edit photos at no cost.
realVsFake.fake: A weekly fee is charged for something the handset does out of the box.

realVsFake.real: Honest developers send a reminder before a trial converts and link to the cancellation screen.
realVsFake.fake: Nothing is said until the first weekly payment has already gone, three days after install.

steps.title: 'Your flight has been cancelled'
steps.detail: A text naming an airline, or no airline at all, says your flight is cancelled and offers a link or a 'support line' to rebook or get a refund.

steps.title: A helpline that answers instantly
steps.detail: Calling reaches a polite agent with no queue. They ask for the booking reference, surname and passport details 'to pull up the reservation'.

steps.title: The rebooking fee
steps.detail: The agent finds a replacement flight and says a change fee or fare difference must be paid now by card to hold the seat.

steps.title: Refund form or a second charge
steps.detail: Link versions show a refund form that needs card number and security code. Either way the card is charged, and the original booking was never cancelled.

flight-cancellation-text-scam.whyItWorks: Flights really are cancelled at short notice and airlines do notify by text. A traveller with a connection, a hotel and a family depending on that seat feels they must sort it out within minutes, before the remaining seats are gone.

realVsFake.real: A genuine cancellation appears under your booking reference in the airline's app and in an email from the airline.
realVsFake.fake: The text is the only notice, and the airline app still shows the flight on time.

realVsFake.real: When the airline cancels, it offers another of its flights or a refund without charging a rebooking fee.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agent' says a seat can only be held if you pay a change fee during the call.

realVsFake.real: Airline phone numbers are listed on the airline's own website and on your booking confirmation.
realVsFake.fake: The number arrives inside the text, or appears as a sponsored result above the real airline.

steps.title: 'Our records show a delay'
steps.detail: An email, call or advert says your recent flight was delayed and you are owed several hundred in compensation. The flight number is missing or copied from public arrival boards.

steps.title: The passenger claim form
steps.detail: You fill in passenger names, booking reference and passport number, and upload a photo of your boarding pass, which together are enough to get into the booking.

steps.title: Approved, then a release fee
steps.detail: The payout is 'approved' within minutes, then held until you pay a claim-handling or legal fee by card or transfer.

steps.title: Card details 'to receive the money'
steps.detail: Last, they ask for your long card number and security code so the compensation can be 'credited'. The card is charged, and no claim ever reached the airline.

flight-compensation-scam.whyItWorks: Delay compensation is a real entitlement on many routes, and plenty of travellers suspect they were owed something they never claimed. A firm offering to handle the paperwork resembles the claims companies that do exist.

realVsFake.real: You can claim straight from the airline through its website at no cost, using your booking reference.
realVsFake.fake: The message implies only their firm can release the money and never mentions the airline's own form.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate claims companies work no-win, no-fee and take their share only after the airline has paid.
realVsFake.fake: A handling fee is charged first, before any payout exists.

realVsFake.real: Compensation is paid by bank transfer, which needs an account number and nothing more.
realVsFake.fake: They ask for the card's long number, expiry and security code, details that are only used for taking money.

steps.title: Selected for a paid panel
steps.detail: An email or text says you have been picked for a consumer research panel paying 300 dollars for an hour's opinions on a new product, with no screening questionnaire.

steps.title: A check 'for materials'
steps.detail: Before any session takes place, a check for about 1,200 dollars arrives. The covering note says it includes your fee plus money for product samples and testing materials.

steps.title: Send 900 to the coordinator
steps.detail: You are told to deposit it with your phone, keep 300, and send the other 900 to the 'panel coordinator' today, because the check supposedly expires in 48 hours.

steps.title: No session, deposit reversed
steps.detail: The samples never come and no meeting link is sent. When the check is returned unpaid, your bank claws back the full 1,200, including the 900 already gone.

focus-group-job-scam.whyItWorks: Market research firms really do pay people for their opinions, and a fee of a few hundred dollars is high but not absurd. The supposed expiry date on the check hurries the transfer through before the bank has had time to reject it.

realVsFake.real: Research companies screen you with questions about age, habits and purchases, and reject people who do not fit the brief.
realVsFake.fake: You are 'selected' by name from nowhere, and every reply you give is accepted without question.

realVsFake.real: Participants are paid after the session, typically by voucher, prepaid card or bank transfer for the agreed amount.
realVsFake.fake: Payment turns up first, four times the agreed fee, with orders to pass the surplus to someone else.

realVsFake.real: Any products to be tested are sent to you by the research firm or handed out in the room.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to fund the samples yourself by forwarding money, or to pay a joining fee for access to future panels.

steps.title: Invited to a VIP signals group
steps.detail: You are added to a messaging channel where an admin posts currency pair tips and members reply with screenshots of winning trades and thanks.

steps.title: Let me manage it for you
steps.detail: The admin messages privately, offering to trade your account for a share of profit. You are told to open one with a broker he names and fund it.

steps.title: Up sixty in a month
steps.detail: The broker's dashboard shows fast growth. He says a major trade on the pound or gold is coming and you need a bigger balance to qualify, perhaps with a deposit bonus.

steps.title: Margin call or missing manager
steps.detail: When you ask to withdraw, the bonus terms require impossible trading volume, or a sudden losing position needs topping up. Soon after, the manager and broker stop replying.

forex-trading-scam.whyItWorks: Currency trading is a real profession full of jargon about pips, lots and margin, so handing the decisions to a confident manager seems sensible. The group's daily stream of other members' wins makes staying out feel like the costly choice.

realVsFake.real: A licensed forex broker appears on the financial regulator's register and carries a prominent warning about the risk of losses.
realVsFake.fake: The broker is registered on a small island or nowhere, and its site talks only about winning months.

realVsFake.real: Anyone managing money for others needs authorisation and works under a written agreement with their firm's name on it.
realVsFake.fake: The 'account manager' is a first name and a profile photo, and asks for your trading password or remote access.

realVsFake.real: Withdrawals from a genuine broker return to the bank account or card that funded it, usually within days.
realVsFake.fake: Deposits are requested in crypto or to rotating personal accounts, and cashing out triggers a 'verification' charge.

steps.title: A turnkey business advert
steps.detail: An advert or expo stand offers a vending route, cleaning brand, coffee kiosk or online store 'in a box', described as proven and ready to run.

steps.title: The discovery call
steps.detail: A 'franchise consultant' walks you through earnings projections on a slide deck and says only one territory is left in your area.

steps.title: Fee before paperwork
steps.detail: You are asked to pay the franchise fee, plus setup and training charges, to lock the territory. The agreement is thin and the disclosure document never appears.

steps.title: A manual and little else
steps.detail: What you receive is a generic operations manual, a logo file and a list of suppliers. The promised leads, site and support line do not exist.

franchise-scam.whyItWorks: Franchising has a reputation as the safer route into self-employment, because somebody else has already worked out the model. People spending redundancy money or savings want that reassurance, and a polished brochure with a 'guarantee' supplies it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine franchisor hands over its disclosure documents and accounts, and gives you weeks to read them with an adviser.
realVsFake.fake: Documents are 'being updated', and the discount on the fee runs out on Friday.

realVsFake.real: Real franchises give you a full list of current owners and encourage you to phone any of them.
realVsFake.fake: You are offered two hand-picked 'success stories' on a call arranged by the salesperson.

realVsFake.real: Established brands turn applicants down, because a failing outlet damages the name.
realVsFake.fake: Anyone who can pay is approved the same day, with success described as guaranteed.

steps.title: The winning call
steps.detail: A phone call, text or scratch card handed out near a resort says you have won a week away or a cruise, in a draw you do not remember entering.

steps.title: Taxes and a booking fee
steps.detail: The trip is free, they say, but government taxes and a booking fee must be paid by card today to hold it, usually under a couple of hundred.

steps.title: The ninety-minute presentation
steps.detail: To collect the voucher you must sit through a talk that runs for hours, where salespeople push a holiday club or timeshare contract and keep dropping the price.

steps.title: A voucher you cannot use
steps.detail: The voucher covers only certain weeks, excludes flights, needs further payments or cannot be redeemed at all. The card you gave may be charged again.

free-holiday-scam.whyItWorks: A prize removes the usual question of whether you can afford the trip, and the fee looks tiny beside a week abroad. People approached on holiday are relaxed, have time to spare and are already in a mood to say yes.

realVsFake.real: A real prize draw is one you entered, run by a named company, and winners pay nothing to receive the prize.
realVsFake.fake: You are told you won without entering, and a fee stands between you and the tickets.

realVsFake.real: Genuine promoters put the terms in writing: dates, hotel, what is included and who the travel provider is.
realVsFake.fake: Details stay vague until after you pay, and the 'provider' cannot be found under the name it gives.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate membership contract comes with time to read it at home and a cooling-off period.
realVsFake.fake: The price is 'today only', and the paperwork must be signed in the room before you may leave with the voucher.

steps.title: Free to a loving home
steps.detail: An advert shows a pedigree puppy or kitten being given away because the owner has a new job, a new baby or has lost a relative.

steps.title: Questions about your home
steps.detail: The owner asks about your garden, your children and your experience with the breed, sends more photos, and tells you that you have been chosen.

steps.title: Only the flight to cover
steps.detail: The animal is in another region, so you pay a pet courier for shipping. An email from the 'airline' then needs a 250 refundable crate deposit by gift card.

steps.title: Stuck at the airport
steps.detail: New charges follow for travel insurance, vaccinations or a quarantine permit, each with a warning that the puppy is waiting in a cargo bay and you could be reported for abandonment.

free-pet-rehoming-scam.whyItWorks: The 'interview' about your home makes you feel selected, and by the first fee you have named the animal and told the family. Each charge is called refundable, and refusing it means picturing a frightened puppy alone in a crate.

realVsFake.real: Rescue centres want you to visit, meet the animal and often have your home checked before adoption.
realVsFake.fake: The owner is always away and cannot manage a live video call with the pet in the room.

realVsFake.real: Shelters charge one stated adoption fee that covers vaccinations and microchipping, paid to the charity itself.
realVsFake.fake: The pet is free, yet a string of courier, crate and insurance charges arrives one at a time.

realVsFake.real: Airlines and licensed animal transporters bill the person who books the flight and take cards.
realVsFake.fake: A 'pet courier' with a free email address demands gift card numbers before the crate can be loaded.

steps.title: A free jar of face cream
steps.detail: An advert, often dressed as a magazine article, offers a sample of anti-ageing cream or serum. You only cover postage of about 4.95.

steps.title: The pre-ticked small print
steps.detail: Below the card form, in tiny grey text or behind a 'terms' link, it says the trial lasts fourteen days from order, not from delivery.

steps.title: Full price on day fifteen
steps.detail: The jar arrives late, with most of the trial gone. Then a charge of eighty or ninety lands for the 'sample', and a second jar ships.

steps.title: A phone line nobody answers
steps.detail: Cancelling means ringing an overseas number in office hours. Emails bounce, and each month another parcel and another charge arrive.

free-trial-subscription-trap-scam.whyItWorks: Paying a few pounds for postage on a free sample feels like the safest purchase there is. The costly part is written down, technically, so the seller can claim you agreed, and the clock starts before the parcel has even left the warehouse.

realVsFake.real: A real sample offer from a known brand needs no card, or states any future price beside the pay button.
realVsFake.fake: The monthly price appears only on a separate terms page that few buyers open.

realVsFake.real: Honest subscriptions email a clear receipt naming the next billing date and amount.
realVsFake.fake: The confirmation mentions only the postage, with no word about what follows.

realVsFake.real: Reputable sellers let you cancel online in a couple of clicks.
realVsFake.fake: You must phone, quote a 'membership number' you were never sent, and return the product at your own cost.

steps.title: A client has hired you
steps.detail: The email copies the styling of a site such as Upwork or Fiverr and says a client accepted your proposal. A button reads 'Accept contract', above a brief of two vague lines.

steps.title: Log in, or message on WhatsApp
steps.detail: The button leads to a fake platform sign-in that takes your password. Alternatively the 'client' gives a WhatsApp number and says the site's own chat is 'too slow'.

steps.title: Payment outside the platform
steps.detail: Off-platform, they offer to pay by cheque or bank transfer 'to save you the service fee', then send more than agreed or ask for a refundable 'onboarding deposit' first.

steps.title: Send back the difference
steps.detail: You are asked to return the overpaid amount, or forward it to their 'designer', before the cheque bounces or the transfer is reversed. The work itself is never paid for.

freelance-platform-email-scam.whyItWorks: Freelancers send out dozens of proposals and wait, so an email saying one has landed is the best news of the week. Platform fees are a real irritation, which makes a client's offer to skip them sound generous.

realVsFake.real: Real offers and contracts sit in your dashboard on the platform, where you accept them after logging in the usual way.
realVsFake.fake: Your dashboard shows no new contract and no message from that client. The offer is nowhere but the inbox.

realVsFake.real: Platforms hold a client's money in escrow or charge it up front, then release it to you through the site.
realVsFake.fake: The client proposes a cheque, a direct transfer or a payment app, and wants your bank details in chat.

realVsFake.real: A genuine client pays what was agreed and has no reason to send extra.
realVsFake.fake: An overpayment arrives 'by mistake', followed by a polite, pressing request to wire the surplus to a third person.

steps.title: Cheaper fuel, guaranteed
steps.detail: An advert or text offers a discount card that takes a third off every fill-up at any forecourt, with only a handful of cards left.

steps.title: The activation fee
steps.detail: A sign-up page asks for name, address, vehicle registration and a one-off activation payment before the card can be posted.

steps.title: A card that will not swipe
steps.detail: Either nothing comes, or a plastic card arrives that pumps and tills reject. Support says it needs a 'top-up' or a second fee to go live.

steps.title: Monthly 'membership' appears
steps.detail: Your statement shows a recurring club fee you never noticed agreeing to, taken by a company with a different name from the card.

fuel-card-scam.whyItWorks: Fuel is a cost drivers feel every week, and real loyalty schemes and fleet cards do exist, so a discount card is easy to accept. An activation fee sounds like routine admin when it is set against months of promised savings.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fuel cards come from fuel brands or fleet providers and are aimed at businesses, with credit checks and invoices.
realVsFake.fake: Anyone with a debit card is approved on the spot through a social media link.

realVsFake.real: Supermarket and forecourt loyalty schemes are free to join and give a few pence off a litre.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger promises a huge cut at every pump in the country for an upfront payment.

realVsFake.real: A real card names the stations that accept it and has a working account you can log in to.
realVsFake.fake: The 'accepted everywhere' card has no network logo and no balance to check.

steps.title: Found through your own complaint
steps.detail: After you post about your loss on a forum or review site, or because your name is on a list sold by the original fraudsters, a 'recovery specialist' gets in touch.

steps.title: They have 'traced' your money
steps.detail: They claim blockchain analysis or an international task force has located the funds in a frozen wallet or overseas account, and email an impressive report with seals.

steps.title: The retainer
steps.detail: To begin, they need a legal retainer, a 'court filing cost' or a refundable deposit, usually requested in crypto or by wire to a foreign account.

steps.title: The wallet 'sync'
steps.detail: Next they ask for your exchange login or seed phrase to 'return the coins', or for banking details to 'receive the refund'. Whatever is left gets taken.

fund-recovery-scam.whyItWorks: After a loss, the hope of undoing it is stronger than caution, and the caller names the exact platform and amount involved. An official-sounding title such as 'asset recovery division' suggests that somebody in authority is finally on your side.

realVsFake.real: Police, regulators and your bank's fraud department do not charge victims to investigate or return money.
realVsFake.fake: A private 'agency' wants a fee, tax or deposit paid before it will lift a finger.

realVsFake.real: A genuine solicitor can be looked up on the professional regulator's register and will not promise a result.
realVsFake.fake: The 'lawyer' guarantees full recovery within days and has a website registered only recently.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate investigators never need the recovery phrase for your crypto wallet or your online banking password.
realVsFake.fake: They say the refund must be 'synchronised' with your wallet and ask for the twelve words.

steps.title: A 100k account for a small fee
steps.detail: An advert offers the chance to trade the firm's capital and keep most of the profit. All you pay is a challenge fee of a few hundred.

steps.title: The evaluation rules
steps.detail: You get a demo login with a profit target, a daily loss limit and a time limit. Extra rules about news events, lot sizes and 'consistency' sit deep in the terms.

steps.title: Breached, with a reset on offer
steps.detail: A widened spread or slipped stop-loss tips the account past the daily limit. An email declares the challenge failed and offers a discounted reset if bought within a day.

steps.title: Passing brings a payout review
steps.detail: Traders who do pass and request a payout are told a rule was broken in hindsight, and the account is closed. Others find the firm's site and chat server gone.

funded-trader-scam.whyItWorks: The offer flatters a trader's belief that only a lack of capital is holding them back. Each failure looks like their own mistake, so buying another attempt feels like persistence, and the firm earns from fees whether anyone is ever funded.

realVsFake.real: A credible prop firm publishes every rule before you pay and applies the same rules after you pass.
realVsFake.fake: New conditions surface at payout time, citing clauses such as 'abusive trading' that are never defined.

realVsFake.real: Firms that do pay can show a long record of withdrawals confirmed by traders on independent forums.
realVsFake.fake: Proof of payouts is a wall of certificate images on the firm's own site, and its company registration is weeks old.

realVsFake.real: An honest evaluation uses price feeds that match the wider market, so results can be checked against another platform.
realVsFake.fake: Prices on the firm's in-house platform spike in ways no other chart shows, always at the moment a limit is near.

steps.title: Sad news, no name given
steps.detail: A text says something like 'sad news about your friend' and offers funeral details and a live-stream, without saying who has died or who is writing.

steps.title: A memorial page with a blurred video
steps.detail: The link shows a candle image, a service time and a video window that stays locked until you 'register to watch'.

steps.title: Registration asks for a card
steps.detail: Signing up needs an email and password, then a card 'to confirm your identity, no charge'. Some pages copy a social network login instead.

steps.title: Donations to the 'family'
steps.detail: A collection box for flowers or funeral costs takes a card payment too. The money goes to the page's owner and the card details are kept.

funeral-notice-text-scam.whyItWorks: Not knowing who has died is exactly what makes people tap, because the mind runs through every friend who has been unwell. Grief and worry leave little room for inspecting a web address, and nobody wants to seem suspicious of a bereaved family.

realVsFake.real: News of a death comes from a relative or friend you know, who names the person and can be phoned.
realVsFake.fake: The text mentions 'your friend' with no name and comes from a number you have never seen.

realVsFake.real: Funeral directors share a free viewing link through the family. Watching a service does not need a payment card.
realVsFake.fake: The stream is locked behind a sign-up form that wants card details 'for verification'.

realVsFake.real: Genuine memorial collections are set up by the family on a known fundraising platform and name the charity or purpose.
realVsFake.fake: The donate button sits on the same anonymous memorial page, with no named organiser.

steps.title: A maxed account, priced to go
steps.detail: In a Discord server, marketplace group or forum, a seller posts screenshots of a high-level account with rare skins at well under the going rate: 'quitting the game, need it gone today'.

steps.title: Friends and family only
steps.detail: In direct messages the seller wants PayPal friends and family, crypto or a gift card code, and refuses the group's middleman 'because the last one robbed me'.

steps.title: The login arrives and works
steps.detail: After payment you receive an email and password that work. You log in, change the password, and for a few days the account appears to be yours.

steps.title: Pulled back by the original owner
steps.detail: The seller contacts the game's support with the original receipts and creation email, has the account 'recovered', and resells it. Support will not help you, because buying accounts breaks the terms.

game-account-trading-scam.whyItWorks: Hundreds of hours of grinding or a discontinued skin cannot be bought from the publisher at any price, so the grey market is the only source. Buyers already know they are breaking the rules, which makes them slower to ask questions or complain.

realVsFake.real: Where a game allows trading at all, it happens through an in-game trade window or official marketplace that swaps both sides at once.
realVsFake.fake: The deal runs on trust in a chat window: you send money first and wait for a login to appear.

realVsFake.real: Whoever created an account keeps the proof of ownership for good: the first email address and the earliest receipts.
realVsFake.fake: The seller promises 'full access, original email included' but can still reclaim everything through support months later.

realVsFake.real: A payment for goods carries some protection, and an honest seller accepts that.
realVsFake.fake: Only irreversible payment is accepted. As a buyer, the same scammer pays, takes your account, then files a chargeback.

steps.title: An invite from a 'developer'
steps.detail: A Discord message, often from a friend's hacked account, says 'we're testing our new game, want to try it and give feedback?' and links to a polished site with a trailer.

steps.title: The launcher download
steps.detail: The site offers a 'beta client' installer inside a password-protected archive, with the access key shown beside the button. The password also stops email and browser scanners looking inside.

steps.title: It crashes on launch
steps.detail: You run the installer and get an error such as 'missing DLL', or a window that closes. The 'developer' apologises and stops replying. The real work has already been done.

steps.title: Sessions and wallets drained
steps.detail: An info-stealer has copied your browser's saved logins, Discord and Steam session tokens and any crypto wallet files. Your Discord account then sends the same invite to your friends.

game-beta-scam.whyItWorks: Closed betas for anticipated games really are handed out through invites and keys, and getting one feels like luck. When the message comes from a friend's account, asking for a favour, the request is flattering and hard to refuse.

realVsFake.real: Real betas are distributed through Steam playtests, console stores or the publisher's own launcher, after you sign up on the official site.
realVsFake.fake: The 'client' comes from a file-sharing link or a brand-new website and is unknown to any store.

realVsFake.real: A real studio has a history: earlier games, named staff, store pages and a social account older than a few weeks.
realVsFake.fake: The studio's site was registered recently, the trailer is borrowed from another game, and the team cannot be found anywhere.

realVsFake.real: A game tester is never asked to switch off antivirus or connect a crypto wallet to start playing.
realVsFake.fake: The instructions say to 'disable your antivirus, it gives a false positive' and to link a wallet for 'tester rewards'.

steps.title: Guaranteed rank in three days
steps.detail: An advert in a game's Discord, a comment under a ranked video or a slick website promises a climb to the top tier, with a price list by division and 'pro players on standby'.

steps.title: Pay first, then share the login
steps.detail: You pay up front, usually by crypto or a friends-and-family transfer, and are told to send your username and password and switch off two-step login 'so the booster can get in'.

steps.title: A few wins for show
steps.detail: Some services play a handful of matches so the rank ticks up. Then comes a request for a top-up: the account is 'harder than quoted' or needs a 'priority slot'.

steps.title: Stripped or held hostage
steps.detail: The booster changes the email and password, trades away skins and currency, and sells the account. Others demand a ransom to return it, or simply stop logging in once paid.

game-boosting-scam.whyItWorks: Being stuck one division below your friends is a specific, nagging frustration, and boosting is an open secret in ranked games, so the service itself sounds normal. Handing over the password seems unavoidable because someone else has to play.

realVsFake.real: Most publishers treat account sharing and paid boosting as a breach of their rules, and punish the account owner with rank resets or bans.
realVsFake.fake: The site calls its boosting 'safe and undetectable' and offers a ban-proof guarantee it has no way to honour.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate coaching happens with you at the controls: a stronger player reviews your matches or plays alongside in a party.
realVsFake.fake: The service insists on your password, and on two-step protection being switched off, before work begins.

realVsFake.real: A real business has traceable reviews away from its own website and takes payment methods that allow a dispute.
realVsFake.fake: Testimonials exist only as screenshots on the seller's page, and payment must be crypto or a gift code.

steps.title: Unlimited coins, no download
steps.detail: A short video or search result shows someone typing a username into a site and watching the balance jump. The link in the description leads to the 'generator'.

steps.title: Username, platform, amount
steps.detail: The page asks for your in-game name, your platform and how much currency you want, then plays a fake console animation: 'Connecting to server... injecting 10,000 coins.'

steps.title: Human verification
steps.detail: At the last moment a box says you must prove you are not a bot by completing two 'offers': a quiz, a mobile game install, a prize draw needing a phone number.

steps.title: Paid per click, plus your details
steps.detail: Each offer earns the site owner a commission. Phone numbers get signed up to premium-rate texts, and some versions ask for the account password, which is then used to empty it.

game-currency-generator-scam.whyItWorks: The audience is mostly children and teenagers who cannot buy currency without asking a parent. The animation, with its scrolling code and rising counter, looks like hacking does in films, and the comments underneath are full of invented success stories.

realVsFake.real: In-game currency is stored on the publisher's servers and is added only by buying it in the official store or earning it in play.
realVsFake.fake: A third-party web page claims it can add coins to any account from outside with just a username.

realVsFake.real: Official giveaways are announced on the game's verified channels and delivered as redeemable codes.
realVsFake.fake: The offer comes from an anonymous video with comments switched off or filled with identical praise.

realVsFake.real: A real CAPTCHA is a quick puzzle on the same page that takes seconds.
realVsFake.fake: 'Verification' means installing apps and entering a mobile number on other sites, and it never completes however many you finish.

steps.title: The showcase video
steps.detail: A YouTube clip or Discord post shows an aimbot or coin generator working in a live match. The download link sits in the description, usually behind a link shortener.

steps.title: A locked archive
steps.detail: The file arrives as a zip or rar with a password printed in the post. Encrypting it stops your browser and antivirus scanning what is inside.

steps.title: 'Turn off your antivirus'
steps.detail: The readme says security software wrongly flags all cheats, so you should switch off real-time protection and run the loader as administrator.

steps.title: The loader empties your browser
steps.detail: Nothing changes in the game. In the background the program copies saved passwords, login cookies and Discord or Steam session tokens, and your accounts start messaging the same link to friends.

game-mod-scam.whyItWorks: Cheat tools really do trip antivirus alarms because they tamper with a running game, so players who have used mods before read 'disable it first' as routine. Wanting an edge that is against the rules also makes people less likely to ask anyone for a second opinion.

realVsFake.real: Established mod libraries such as Steam Workshop keep version history, author profiles and open comment threads under every upload.
realVsFake.fake: The cheat lives on a file-hosting page reached through a shortened link, with comments switched off on the video.

realVsFake.real: A normal mod is a set of files you drop into the game's mod folder. It needs no administrator rights.
realVsFake.fake: You get a single .exe 'injector' that demands admin access and refuses to start while protection is on.

realVsFake.real: Coins and premium currency are stored on the publisher's servers and sold only through the in-game shop.
realVsFake.fake: A 'generator' on your own PC claims it can add unlimited coins to a balance it has no way of reaching.

steps.title: 'Overdue and legally required'
steps.detail: A text says your annual gas safety inspection or boiler service has lapsed and that penalties apply, without naming an engineer, landlord or energy company.

steps.title: Book a slot online
steps.detail: The link opens a booking page with a calendar of visit times and a registration-style logo, and asks for your address and who is home during the day.

steps.title: Pay to secure the visit
steps.detail: An inspection fee is requested up front by card, often with a discount for booking today, plus a contact number for the 'engineer'.

steps.title: A caller without a card
steps.detail: Often nobody comes. Sometimes a person turns up with no Gas Safe ID, 'finds' a dangerous fault and demands cash for parts or to avoid cutting off the supply.

gas-safety-text-scam.whyItWorks: Gas carries a real fear of leaks and carbon monoxide, and tenants know checks happen yearly without knowing who arranges them. The word 'legally' makes a homeowner assume a rule they had not heard of, and paying seems safer than arguing.

realVsFake.real: The yearly gas safety check is a legal duty on landlords, who arrange and pay for it themselves.
realVsFake.fake: The text tells whoever receives it, tenant or owner, that they personally face penalties.

realVsFake.real: A genuine engineer carries a Gas Safe ID card with a licence number you can check on the register before they start.
realVsFake.fake: The booking page shows a yellow logo but gives no engineer name or licence number.

realVsFake.real: Boiler servicing is booked with a firm you chose, or your landlord's agent tells you the date.
realVsFake.fake: An unknown sender picks you, sets a deadline and takes payment before any boiler visit.

steps.title: A renewal you never agreed to
steps.detail: You are thanked for renewing 'Geek Squad Protection' for another year at 399.99. An invoice number is quoted, and the charge will supposedly reach your statement within a day.

steps.title: One way to cancel: the phone
steps.detail: There is no link, only a toll-free number. The message often comes from a free webmail address with the invoice as an image or PDF, which helps it slip past spam filters.

steps.title: The refund form
steps.detail: The agent agrees to refund you, has you install a remote-access tool 'to open the cancellation form', then asks you to log in to your bank and type the amount yourself.

steps.title: Too many zeros
steps.detail: The screen blanks briefly. He then shows a bank balance edited to suggest 3,999 was refunded instead of 399, pleads for his job, and asks for the difference back by wire or gift cards.

geek-squad-renewal-email-scam.whyItWorks: The email asks for nothing, which is what disarms people. You make the call yourself, to cancel a charge and get money back, so by the time the agent mentions remote access you believe you are talking to a billing department.

realVsFake.real: Geek Squad plans are sold through Best Buy, and any plan you hold can be checked in your Best Buy account or in store.
realVsFake.fake: The invoice names no card, no store and no account of yours. The 'customer ID' is a random string.

realVsFake.real: A real refund is sent back to the original payment card by the retailer. You take no part in processing it.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says you must enter the refund amount yourself while he watches your banking screen.

realVsFake.real: If a business refunds too much, it corrects the mistake through the card network or the bank.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to drive to a shop, buy gift cards for the 'extra' amount, and stay on the line throughout.

steps.title: A booth, a knock or a call
steps.detail: At a senior centre, health fair or your front door, someone offers a free DNA cancer-risk screening and says Medicare or your insurer covers it fully.

steps.title: Family history, then your card
steps.detail: They ask whether cancer or heart disease runs in the family, nod at the answer, then copy your insurance number and photograph your ID.

steps.title: The cheek swab
steps.detail: A cotton swab is rubbed inside your cheek on the spot, or a kit is posted. A doctor you never speak to signs the order.

steps.title: A large claim in your name
steps.detail: A laboratory bills your insurer a very large sum for a panel of tests. Results often never come, and you can be billed if the claim is refused.

genetic-test-scam.whyItWorks: Worry about an illness that took a parent or sibling is easy to stir, and people know genetic tests are expensive, so 'fully covered' sounds like a benefit they have earned. A painless swab at a community event does not feel like a financial transaction.
