realVsFake.real: A genetic test is ordered by a doctor who knows your history, and the results go back to that doctor to explain.
realVsFake.fake: The sample is taken by a sales representative at a folding table, and nobody ever discusses a result with you.

realVsFake.real: Insurers and Medicare pay for genetic testing only in limited cases where your own doctor shows it is medically needed.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch is that everyone over a certain age qualifies automatically and it costs nothing.

realVsFake.real: Consumer DNA companies charge you a set price and never ask for an insurance or Medicare number.
realVsFake.fake: This 'free' test cannot go ahead until the number on your insurance card has been written down.

steps.title: A stranger with a supercar
steps.detail: After you like a few finance or side-hustle videos, a 'mentor' DMs you. His feed is rented sports cars, beach laptops and screenshots of trading profits.

steps.title: The free strategy call
steps.detail: He asks about your income and debts on a short call or voice note, says you remind him of himself, and mentions three places left in his programme.

steps.title: Four ninety-seven to join
steps.detail: You pay for the mentorship and get a chat group and some videos covering what free tutorials already explain. Questions are answered with motivational quotes.

steps.title: The inner circle upsell
steps.detail: Real results, he says, need the premium tier at several times the price, plus an account with his chosen broker, where he earns commission on your deposits.

get-rich-coaching-scam.whyItWorks: The pitch finds people who are short of money and tired of their jobs, then offers a named person who claims to have escaped the same situation. Buying a course feels like investing in yourself, which is easier to justify than a gamble.

realVsFake.real: Qualified financial advisers are listed on a regulator's register and explain that losses are possible.
realVsFake.fake: The mentor's only credential is a profit screenshot, which takes a minute to fake on a demo account.

realVsFake.real: A reputable course publishes its syllabus, tutor background and refund terms before taking payment.
realVsFake.fake: Details are 'revealed inside', the price changes during the chat, and there are always three spots left.

realVsFake.real: Someone making a living from trading has no need to recruit beginners one message at a time.
realVsFake.fake: His income comes from course fees and broker referrals, so your results make no difference to him.

steps.title: Cheap cover in your DMs
steps.detail: A social media post or a message from a friend of a friend offers car insurance for young or convicted drivers at half the usual quote.

steps.title: 'Send me your licence'
steps.detail: The 'broker' asks for a photo of your driving licence and registration by chat, and comes back within minutes with a price.

steps.title: Transfer to a personal account
steps.detail: You pay the premium to an individual's bank account. A certificate arrives as a PDF with a real insurer's logo on it.

steps.title: Stopped at the roadside
steps.detail: The policy was forged, cancelled after purchase, or bought with a false address and age. Police or a claim reveal you were never insured.

ghost-broking-scam.whyItWorks: Young drivers face quotes they cannot afford, so someone who 'knows a way' to get it cheaper sounds like a favour. The certificate looks right, and nothing tests it until a crash or a police stop.

realVsFake.real: A regulated broker appears on the financial regulator's register and trades from a business address and website.
realVsFake.fake: The seller exists only as a profile, a first name and a mobile number.

realVsFake.real: Insurers send policy documents from their own systems and let you log in to see your cover.
realVsFake.fake: The only proof is a PDF forwarded in a chat, and the broker says not to ring the insurer.

realVsFake.real: Premiums are paid by card or direct debit to the insurer or broker firm.
realVsFake.fake: Money goes by transfer to a personal account, sometimes in a different name from the 'broker'.

steps.title: Looking up what is left
steps.detail: You search 'check gift card balance' with the shop's name. An advert above the real result leads to a page in the retailer's colours.

steps.title: Sixteen digits and a PIN
steps.detail: The form asks for the full card number and the scratch-off PIN, the same two things needed to spend the card online.

steps.title: 'Balance unavailable, try later'
steps.detail: After you submit, the page shows an error or a zero. Behind it, the numbers have been sent to the scammer in real time.

steps.title: Spent before you reach the till
steps.detail: Within minutes the balance is used for online orders or moved to another account. The shop's records show a normal purchase.

gift-card-balance-scam.whyItWorks: Checking a balance feels like looking, not paying, so entering the PIN does not register as handing over money. A gift card has no name or password on it, which means whoever holds both numbers is treated as the owner.

realVsFake.real: The retailer's own site or the number printed on the back of the card gives the balance.
realVsFake.fake: A third-party 'balance checker' covers dozens of brands from one unfamiliar domain.

realVsFake.real: A genuine balance page shows a figure and nothing else.
realVsFake.fake: The page throws an error, then dangles bonus credit if you enter a second card.

realVsFake.real: Store staff can read the balance at the till without you revealing the PIN to anyone online.
realVsFake.fake: A text claims your card credit is about to expire and links to a checker.

steps.title: A cheerful post in November
steps.detail: A friend shares a 'secret sister' or wine-swap post: buy one gift worth about ten pounds, and up to thirty-six will come back to you.

steps.title: The two-name list
steps.detail: Comment 'in' and you are messaged a list with two names and addresses. You post a present to the first name, then move the second to the top.

steps.title: Recruit six more
steps.detail: You add your own name and home address in second place and must persuade six friends to do the same, sending the list onward under your name.

steps.title: The chain runs out of people
steps.detail: Each layer needs six times as many newcomers as the last, so recruitment stalls within a few rounds. Late joiners have sent a gift and published their address for nothing.

gift-exchange-scam.whyItWorks: It looks like an office Secret Santa and arrives from a friend, with a stake so small that nobody does the arithmetic. The pyramid shape is hidden because each person only ever sees two names on the list.

realVsFake.real: In a proper Secret Santa a fixed group each buys one present and each receives one.
realVsFake.fake: Here one gift out is meant to bring dozens back, which can only happen if the group never stops growing.

realVsFake.real: A genuine swap among friends has an organiser who knows every participant and who is buying for whom.
realVsFake.fake: Nobody runs this one. Your present goes to a stranger several links up a chain you cannot see.

realVsFake.real: Friends exchanging gifts already have each other's addresses and do not need them posted in a thread.
realVsFake.fake: Your name and home address travel onward to people you will never meet, with every forward of the list.

steps.title: You enter a real giveaway
steps.detail: An influencer or brand runs a genuine prize draw: follow, like, tag a friend. Scammers copy the account's picture and bio and scrape the list of commenters.

steps.title: Congratulations from a near-twin
steps.detail: A profile whose handle adds 'winners', 'promo' or a stray full stop messages you with party emojis, saying your comment was drawn and the prize is reserved.

steps.title: Nine dollars for delivery
steps.detail: A claim page asks for your address and then a small shipping charge by card. The low figure is the point: it gets the full card number, expiry and security code.

steps.title: No parcel, larger charges
steps.detail: Nothing is ever dispatched. Days later the card shows purchases you did not make or a recurring 'membership', and the winner account has been deleted.

giveaway-winner-dm-scam.whyItWorks: You really did enter, so a win is possible and the timing fits. A delivery fee of a few dollars seems fair for a prize worth hundreds, and the copied logo and bio look right at thumbnail size.

realVsFake.real: Winners are announced by the same account that ran the draw, usually in the post, a story or its comments.
realVsFake.fake: The news comes from a second account with a slightly different handle and a few dozen followers.

realVsFake.real: A brand giving something away pays the postage and needs only a name and delivery address.
realVsFake.fake: The 'prize' cannot ship until a card is entered on a claim site for shipping or customs.

realVsFake.real: Genuine organisers give winners days to respond and will answer a comment asking if the message is theirs.
realVsFake.fake: You have two hours before the prize 'passes to the next entrant', and are told to keep the win quiet.

steps.title: The sponsored search result
steps.detail: You search for Global Entry renewal and the top result is an advert with a flag, an eagle-style seal and a name like 'application centre', on a commercial address.

steps.title: A form copied from the real one
steps.detail: The site asks the same questions as the official application: passport number, date of birth, address history, employment and driving licence details.

steps.title: The expedited processing charge
steps.detail: At checkout the total is well above the government fee, labelled 'expedited processing' or 'application assistance'. Nothing they do can move you up the interview queue.

steps.title: What the money bought
steps.detail: Some sites submit nothing. Others file a careless application and keep the mark-up. Either way a stranger now holds your passport details and card number.

global-entry-scam.whyItWorks: Government websites can be clunky, so a clean page sitting first in search results looks like the proper front door. Applicants expect to pay a fee and hand over passport details anyway, so nothing about the form feels out of place.

realVsFake.real: Global Entry applications and renewals go through the Trusted Traveler Programs site, which is on a .gov address.
realVsFake.fake: The lookalike sits on a .com or .org address and is reached through a paid advert.

realVsFake.real: The government charges one set application fee, paid inside your official account.
realVsFake.fake: A higher total appears at checkout, with a 'service' or 'concierge' line added.

realVsFake.real: Approval speed depends on the agency's background check and interview availability, which no third party controls.
realVsFake.fake: The site promises faster approval or a guaranteed interview slot in exchange for its fee.

steps.title: A call about protecting savings
steps.detail: A salesperson rings, or an advert follows your searches, warning that inflation and shaky banks are about to eat your savings and that physical gold is the shelter.

steps.title: The senior metals broker
steps.detail: A named account manager phones most days and posts a brochure. He quotes 'collector grade' coins and bars at a price far above the daily bullion rate.

steps.title: Vault storage instead of delivery
steps.detail: Home delivery is discouraged as unsafe. Your metal will sit in their 'allocated vault', and you receive a certificate with a bar number in place of anything you can hold.

steps.title: The bars you cannot collect
steps.detail: You wire savings or move a retirement account. Asking later to sell or collect brings storage arrears, a buy-back delay, and then a dead phone line.

gold-investment-scam.whyItWorks: Gold feels like the opposite of a gamble, a solid thing that grandparents trusted. A salesperson talking about fear of banks is repeating what the buyer already believes, so nobody asks to see the metal.

realVsFake.real: A reputable bullion dealer publishes buy and sell prices beside the live market rate, so you can compare before ordering.
realVsFake.fake: The price arrives only by phone, wrapped in a 'portfolio' of coins whose mark-up is never stated.

realVsFake.real: Genuine storage is with a named independent vault that issues its own bar list and lets you take delivery.
realVsFake.fake: Storage is 'in our secure facility', proven by a certificate the firm printed itself, and delivery requests trigger new fees.

realVsFake.real: Honest dealers say plainly that gold pays no income and its price can fall for years.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch promises a fixed yearly return on your gold and a deadline before prices 'jump next week'.

steps.title: Your listing is pending removal
steps.detail: Styled in Google's colours, the warning says your Business Profile failed a verification check and will disappear from Search and Maps in 48 hours unless you confirm ownership.

steps.title: The 'verify listing' page
steps.detail: The link opens a form showing your shop's name and address, copied from the public listing. It asks you to sign in with the Google account that manages the profile.

steps.title: A fee to stay visible
steps.detail: Some versions add a payment page: an annual 'listing maintenance' or 'verification' charge, often under a hundred, to be paid by card before the deadline.

steps.title: The profile changes hands
steps.detail: With the login, the criminal adds himself as an owner, removes you, and can swap the phone number on the listing for his own or demand money to hand it back.

google-business-email-scam.whyItWorks: For a café, plumber or salon, the map listing is where most new customers come from, so losing it sounds like losing the business. Owners also know Google does ask for verification, though few remember exactly how it was done.

realVsFake.real: Appearing on Google Search and Maps is free. Google does not charge to create, verify or keep a Business Profile.
realVsFake.fake: The email quotes a yearly fee to keep the listing live and warns that non-payment means removal.

realVsFake.real: A real suspension shows as a status on the profile itself when you sign in and search for your own business name.
realVsFake.fake: Your profile looks normal when you check it directly. Only the email claims anything is pending.

realVsFake.real: Google verifies a business through the profile's own dashboard, using a postcard, phone call, email or video.
realVsFake.fake: Verification is offered only through the emailed link, with a countdown and a form asking for the account password.

steps.title: Someone shared a document
steps.detail: An email in Google's sharing layout says a named person invited you to view 'Invoice_Q2_Final'. The blue 'Open' button and the small file icon look just as they should.

steps.title: Choose an account
steps.detail: Clicking Open shows a Google account picker, sometimes the genuine one. You select your address as you have done a hundred times before.

steps.title: The permission screen
steps.detail: Then a consent box appears: an app with a name like 'Docs' or 'Drive Viewer' wants to read, send and delete your email and see your contacts. One button says Allow.

steps.title: Access without a password
steps.detail: Pressing Allow gives the app a token that keeps working after you change your password. It reads your mail and forwards the same share invite to everyone in your address book.

google-docs-sharing-scam.whyItWorks: Shared documents are how offices run, and the account picker in the middle is often the real Google page, so every familiar check passes. The dangerous moment is a permissions box most people have learned to click through.

realVsFake.real: A document shared through Google opens directly if you are already signed in. Viewing it never requires granting an app access to your mail.
realVsFake.fake: An app you have never installed asks for permission to read and send email before any document appears.

realVsFake.real: Genuine shares also appear under 'Shared with me' in Drive, which you can check without touching the email.
realVsFake.fake: Nothing by that name is listed in 'Shared with me'. The file is just a button in the message.

realVsFake.real: A colleague sharing an invoice usually adds a note about what it is, and it relates to work you know about.
realVsFake.fake: The file name is generic, the note field is empty, and the sharer is someone you have had no dealings with.

steps.title: One-star reviews overnight
steps.detail: A café, salon or tradesperson wakes to several new one-star ratings on their Google listing, from reviewers with no photo and no other reviews, most with no text.

steps.title: The message claiming credit
steps.detail: An email, WhatsApp or contact-form message follows. The sender says the reviews are theirs and that hundreds more are queued to post through the week.

steps.title: A wallet address and a rate
steps.detail: They name a price in cryptocurrency or gift cards to delete the ratings and stop, and warn that the average will sink a little further each day.

steps.title: Pay once, pay again
steps.detail: Owners who pay may see a few ratings vanish, then receive a new demand weeks later. Their details are also passed around as a business that pays.

google-review-extortion-scam.whyItWorks: A local firm's star rating decides whether new customers ring or scroll past, and the owner can watch it drop in real time. Paying a modest sum tonight seems cheaper than a slow dispute with Google while bookings dry up.

realVsFake.real: Google removes reviews that break its policies when they are flagged through the business profile, and charges nothing.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger offers removal as a paid service for reviews that the same stranger wrote.

realVsFake.real: An unhappy customer describes a visit: the date, the dish, the member of staff, what went wrong.
realVsFake.fake: The ratings land minutes apart from blank profiles and say nothing, or repeat one vague sentence.

realVsFake.real: A real complaint comes with a request you can meet, such as a refund, a redo or an apology.
realVsFake.fake: The only remedy offered is a transfer to a crypto wallet, with a countdown attached.

steps.title: A sign-in you did not make
steps.detail: What arrives is a copy of Google's alert card: 'New sign-in on Windows', a city you have never visited, and two buttons, 'Yes, it was me' and 'No, secure account'.

steps.title: Securing the account
steps.detail: 'No, secure account' opens a page that looks like Google's sign-in. It asks you to 'confirm it's you' by typing your current password before you can change it.

steps.title: The relay
steps.detail: Software behind the page enters your password on the real Google site at the same moment. Google then sends a genuine code to your phone, or a tap-to-approve prompt.

steps.title: Code typed, account gone
steps.detail: The fake page asks for that code. Once you enter it or tap Yes, the criminal is signed in, replaces the recovery phone and email, and signs out your devices.

google-security-alert-scam.whyItWorks: Google does send sign-in alerts, and the correct response to a real one is to act quickly. The scam copies the one email you have been taught to take seriously, then uses your wish to protect the account as the way in.

realVsFake.real: Real alerts are also listed under Security in your Google Account, in the recent security activity panel.
realVsFake.fake: The supposed sign-in from a strange city is missing from your account's security activity. Only the email mentions it.

realVsFake.real: The safest route is Google's own Security Checkup, opened by typing the account address or through your phone's settings.
realVsFake.fake: The email says the account can be secured only through its button, and that the alert will expire.

realVsFake.real: A verification code arrives because someone is signing in at that moment. Google never needs it read back to 'cancel' anything.
realVsFake.fake: The page says entering the code will block the intruder, when in fact it completes the intruder's sign-in.

steps.title: Good news from a friend's profile
steps.detail: A Facebook message from a friend's hijacked account says they collected a federal grant and saw your name on the list. Or a caller says you were selected.

steps.title: Meet the 'grant agent'
steps.detail: You are passed to an agent from an agency with a plausible name. They ask your age, income and address, then send an approval certificate covered in seals.

steps.title: A $200 fee by gift card
steps.detail: Before the $9,000 can be released there is a one-time processing fee. You are told to buy a gift card and send photos of the back.

steps.title: More fees, bigger promises
steps.detail: After that come a delivery charge, a 'tax clearance' fee, or an offer to upgrade to a larger grant for more money. It continues until you stop paying.

government-grant-scam.whyItWorks: The offer usually comes through someone you know, with a story that they have already been paid, which does the persuading for the criminal. Set against $9,000 that never needs repaying, a $200 fee looks like a small formality.

realVsFake.real: Government grants fund organisations, research and public projects, and are awarded after a written application through an official portal.
realVsFake.fake: You are told you were picked for paying taxes on time, with the money free to spend on bills or a car.

realVsFake.real: Applying for a federal grant costs nothing, and no agency takes gift cards for anything.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agent' asks for the numbers on a store gift card and says the fee will be refunded with the grant.

realVsFake.real: Real grant programmes are listed publicly and staff do not recruit applicants through Messenger or WhatsApp chats.
realVsFake.fake: Everything happens in a private chat with one person, whose agency name returns no official listing when you search it.

steps.title: A permanent post, guaranteed
steps.detail: A text, social media post or 'consultant' offers a permanent clerk, postal or railway job in public service, with a pension, and says selection is already assured.

steps.title: The insider who fixes lists
steps.detail: You are introduced to someone who claims a contact inside the department, able to add your name to the merit list or let you skip the written exam altogether.

steps.title: Appointment letter with a crest
steps.detail: An 'approval' arrives bearing a government crest, a file number and a joining date. To confirm it you must pay a 95 processing fee and send a copy of your ID today.

steps.title: More charges before 'joining day'
steps.detail: Further non-refundable payments follow for document verification, a medical and a training deposit. On the joining date the office named in the letter has no record of you.

government-job-scam.whyItWorks: Public-sector jobs mean security for life, and the official route is slow and fiercely competitive. Many applicants half believe that posts are quietly arranged through contacts, so a fixer asking for a modest fee fits what they already suspect.

realVsFake.real: Government vacancies are published on the official recruitment portal, and applications go in through that portal alone.
realVsFake.fake: The 'vacancy' exists only in a forwarded message, and your application is a chat with a middleman.

realVsFake.real: Public posts are filled by open competition, so no official can promise a named person a job in advance.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the appointment is confirmed before sitting any exam or interview, provided the fee is paid.

realVsFake.real: Where an exam fee exists, it is a fixed amount paid on the official site, with a government receipt.
realVsFake.fake: Money goes to an individual's bank account or mobile wallet, and each payment is followed by a request for another.

steps.title: 'Your postcode has been selected'
steps.detail: A caller, leaflet or agent at the door says your postcode has been allocated government funding for loft insulation, solar panels or a heat pump, and the scheme closes this month.

steps.title: The free survey
steps.detail: A 'surveyor' spends twenty minutes in the loft or photographing the roof, then reports damp, thin insulation or a roof 'ideal for solar' and produces a savings chart.

steps.title: Your contribution to the scheme
steps.detail: You are told the funding pays the bulk and you owe only a 'contribution', payable today by transfer to reserve your place before the allocation runs out.

steps.title: Finance in the small print
steps.detail: The form signed on the tablet turns out to be a loan agreement for the full price. Work is botched or never starts, and no grant was ever applied for.

green-energy-grant-scam.whyItWorks: Governments do fund home energy upgrades and the rules change often, so few homeowners know what is on offer this year. Hearing that the money is already set aside for your street makes refusing feel like throwing it away.

realVsFake.real: Official schemes are listed on government websites, and you apply through an approved installer or your local council.
realVsFake.fake: The agent cannot name the scheme exactly, or uses an official-sounding title that no government site lists.

realVsFake.real: With genuine grants the funding is paid to the installer for completed work, and your share is set out in writing.
realVsFake.fake: A deposit is requested by bank transfer before any application has been made.

realVsFake.real: Certified installers hold accreditation, such as MCS for solar and heat pumps, that anyone can look up.
realVsFake.fake: The company was formed weeks ago, quotes no accreditation number and gives a mobile as its only contact.

steps.title: A supermarket voucher by text
steps.detail: A text or social post in a supermarket's branding says you have been picked for a ninety-pound grocery voucher as a loyal shopper.

steps.title: A short loyalty survey
steps.detail: The link opens a few questions about how often you shop. Every answer leads to 'Congratulations', with invented comments from happy winners below.

steps.title: One-pound delivery activation
steps.detail: To redeem, you enter address and card details for a one-pound 'delivery activation' charge on a page that is not the supermarket's.

steps.title: No shopping, repeat billing
steps.detail: No voucher or groceries come. The card is signed up to an unrelated monthly service, or a bogus delivery app asks for the card again.

grocery-delivery-scam.whyItWorks: Supermarkets do send real vouchers to loyalty members, and food prices make ninety pounds hard to ignore. Asking for one pound seems to prove the offer is real, since a thief would surely ask for more.

realVsFake.real: Supermarket vouchers show up in the loyalty app or at the till, tied to your account.
realVsFake.fake: The voucher arrives from an unknown mobile number with a shortened link.

realVsFake.real: A genuine money-off code is entered in the grocer's own basket and needs no separate fee.
realVsFake.fake: You pay an 'activation' charge on a different site before any code exists.

realVsFake.real: The real delivery app is listed under the supermarket's developer name in the official store.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to download an app file from a web page instead.

steps.title: Joining puts you on a list
steps.detail: You join a Telegram channel, Discord server or Facebook group. Scammers watch the member list and copy the admin's display name and avatar onto a fresh account.

steps.title: A private word from 'the admin'
steps.detail: Soon after you join or ask a question, the copy messages you directly. It welcomes you, or says your account was flagged by the group's anti-spam bot.

steps.title: Verify within the hour
steps.detail: The message says to complete member verification through a link or be removed. Crypto groups get a variant: connect your wallet to claim a members-only airdrop.

steps.title: What the link collects
steps.detail: The page takes your platform login and code, or a wallet approval that empties it. Some fake admins simply ask for a 'refundable membership deposit'.

group-admin-impersonation-scam.whyItWorks: New members do not yet know how the group runs, so a rule delivered by someone with the admin's name and picture is taken at face value. Nobody wants to be thrown out of a community they have only just found.

realVsFake.real: Real admins post rules and announcements in the group itself, where the platform shows an admin label beside their name.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor only ever appears in your private messages, where no role label or badge is displayed.

realVsFake.real: Groups that screen newcomers do it with questions on joining or a bot inside the server.
realVsFake.fake: The 'verification' happens on an outside page that wants your password, a login code or a wallet connection.

realVsFake.real: The true admin's username matches the one in the group's member list, character for character.
realVsFake.fake: The display name is identical, but the handle underneath swaps a letter for a digit or adds 'support'.

steps.title: A bulk deal for the group
steps.detail: In a hobby forum, parents' chat or collector server, a member announces a wholesale order: keyboards, trainers, concert merchandise or baby gear at well under shop price.

steps.title: The spreadsheet fills up
steps.detail: A shared sheet lists who wants what, and a counter shows how close the group is to the supplier's minimum. Watching neighbours sign up makes it feel safe.

steps.title: Shares sent as 'friends and family'
steps.detail: The organiser asks everyone to pay their share by bank transfer or as a personal payment 'to avoid fees', which also removes any buyer protection.

steps.title: Delays, then an empty seat
steps.detail: Weeks of updates follow: the factory is behind, the shipment is at the port. Then the organiser leaves the group, deletes the sheet and stops answering.

group-buy-scam.whyItWorks: Group buys are a normal, well-liked practice in many communities, and the organiser appears to be a fellow member, not a seller. Seeing familiar usernames already on the list persuades each new buyer that someone else must have checked.

realVsFake.real: A trusted organiser has run earlier orders in the same community, and past buyers can vouch for deliveries.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser joined a few weeks ago, was very active very quickly, and has no completed order to point to.

realVsFake.real: Honest pooled orders use an invoice or a goods-and-services payment, so each buyer keeps a claim.
realVsFake.fake: Every payment goes to one private account as a gift, and requests for an invoice are brushed aside.

realVsFake.real: Once the order is placed, a real organiser shares the supplier's confirmation and a tracking number.
realVsFake.fake: Proof is always coming tomorrow, and the supplier's name is withheld 'to protect the discount'.

steps.title: An offer to vouch for you
steps.detail: An advert or message aimed at students, new arrivals and the self-employed offers to stand as your rent guarantor today, with approval guaranteed.

steps.title: The 49 setup fee
steps.detail: Before any assessment you are asked for a setup fee of about 49 GBP, payable by card or transfer on a page reached from the message.

steps.title: Bank login for 'instant verification'
steps.detail: They ask for a photo of your ID and your online banking username and password, saying this lets them confirm your income instantly without payslips.

steps.title: A letter the landlord rejects
steps.detail: A guarantee letter arrives on headed paper. The landlord's agent cannot verify the company and refuses it, while your banking login sits with a stranger.

guarantor-service-scam.whyItWorks: Being told you need a guarantor when nobody in your family qualifies is a wall many renters hit days before signing. A service that promises to remove it in an afternoon for 49 sounds like the answer they were searching for.

realVsFake.real: Genuine guarantor companies assess your income and sometimes say no, and their fee is tied to the rent being guaranteed.
realVsFake.fake: Approval is promised to everyone before a single question is asked, provided the setup fee is paid.

realVsFake.real: Real providers check income through payslips or open banking, where you log in on your own bank's page.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to send your banking username and password to the guarantor service itself.

realVsFake.real: A real guarantee is a contract with the landlord, so the landlord or agent is contacted and signs it.
realVsFake.fake: Nobody from the guarantor service ever speaks to your landlord.

steps.title: An enrolment-season robocall
steps.detail: During open enrolment a recorded call or a search advert offers full health coverage for $50 a month and invites you to press 1 for an adviser.

steps.title: The 'licensed agent' takes notes
steps.detail: A fast-talking agent collects your ZIP code, age, income and Social Security number, then describes a plan with no deductible that every doctor accepts.

steps.title: Rushed through 'verification'
steps.detail: You are coached to answer yes to a recorded script read at speed, then asked for a card to cover the first premium and an enrolment fee.

steps.title: A card that covers almost nothing
steps.detail: What arrives is a discount card or a limited plan paying a small fixed sum per visit. You learn this when a hospital bill is refused.

health-insurance-scam.whyItWorks: Real premiums are high and the plan types are hard to compare, so a cheap offer sounds like the subsidised deal people have heard others get. Open enrolment has a real closing date, which lets the agent rush you with a deadline you already believe in.

realVsFake.real: The official marketplace does not cold call to sell plans and charges nothing to enrol or to get help applying.
realVsFake.fake: The call comes from a number you have never dealt with, and an 'enrolment fee' is added to the first payment.

realVsFake.real: A genuine insurer gives you a written summary of benefits, with deductibles and exclusions, before you pay anything.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says documents are 'sent after activation' and will not email a single page until your card is charged.

realVsFake.real: Licensed agents will give a licence number that your state insurance department can confirm.
realVsFake.fake: Request the licence number or the insurer's name and you get a first name and a callback extension.

steps.title: The $39 advert
steps.detail: A newspaper insert or social advert shows a tiny 'invisible' digital hearing aid for $39, with a free hearing test and stock said to be running low.

steps.title: A 'test' that always finds loss
steps.detail: The free test is a few beeps on a website or a salesperson's tablet at your kitchen table. The result is always a loss needing their device.

steps.title: Card first, trial second
steps.detail: A 'risk-free trial' needs your card. The trial clock starts on the order date, not delivery, and returns go overseas at your cost.

steps.title: An amplifier in a box
steps.detail: The parcel holds a plain amplifier that makes plates and traffic as loud as voices. The full price is charged, often with a monthly 'care club' added.

hearing-aid-scam.whyItWorks: Properly fitted hearing aids cost a great deal, and hearing loss creeps up with some embarrassment attached, so a cheap, discreet fix with no clinic visit is appealing. A buyer cannot judge the device until it is in the ear at home, after the card is charged.

realVsFake.real: An audiologist tests each ear with headphones in a quiet room and gives you the audiogram to keep.
realVsFake.fake: The seller's check takes two minutes, produces no chart, and ends with a 'today only' price.

realVsFake.real: A proper aid is programmed to boost the pitches you have lost, and is adjusted again at follow-up visits.
realVsFake.fake: The $39 gadget has one volume wheel and raises every sound equally, including the hiss of the device itself.

realVsFake.real: Reputable sellers put the trial length and refund terms in writing and have a local address for returns.
realVsFake.fake: Refund requests meet a restocking fee, an unanswered phone line and a return address on another continent.

steps.title: Adverts under worried posts
steps.detail: Comments and profiles advertise a 'certified ethical hacker' who can read a partner's messages, change a university grade, clear a credit record or reopen a banned account.

steps.title: A quote and a guarantee
steps.detail: On Telegram or email he asks for the target's phone number or username, promises results within hours, and quotes a fee payable in Bitcoin before work starts.

steps.title: The job hits a firewall
steps.detail: After payment he sends a doctored screenshot of a half-opened inbox and says finishing needs extra software, a 'decryption key' or a server upgrade, each costing more.

steps.title: Your request used against you
steps.detail: If you stop paying, he may threaten to show your messages to the partner, the university or the police, turning a failed purchase into blackmail.

hire-a-hacker-scam.whyItWorks: Buyers arrive suspicious of a partner or desperate about a grade, and they know the service they want is not above board. That leaves them with nobody to complain to when the money goes, which the seller understands perfectly.

realVsFake.real: Ethical hackers are security testers hired by a system's owner, under a signed contract, to probe that owner's systems.
realVsFake.fake: This one offers to break into a third person's phone or a university database for anyone who pays.

realVsFake.real: Professional security firms have a company registration, an office and invoices paid by bank or card.
realVsFake.fake: The 'hacker' is a webmail address and a Telegram handle, and takes only crypto or gift cards.

realVsFake.real: Nobody skilled enough to breach a major platform sells that ability for the price of a weekly shop.
realVsFake.fake: A guaranteed result is promised for a small flat fee, with five-star 'client' comments posted by the seller's own spare accounts.

steps.title: The half-price all-inclusive
steps.detail: A social media page or advert shows a seven-night resort stay with flights at half the going rate, using photos lifted from a real hotel.

steps.title: Dates held for a deposit
steps.detail: A 'travel consultant' messages to say two rooms remain for your week and a deposit by bank transfer will secure them today.

steps.title: A confirmation that looks official
steps.detail: You receive a booking PDF with logos, a reference and a balance due date. Neither the hotel nor the airline has any record of it.

steps.title: Balance paid, agent gone
steps.detail: The remaining balance is collected a few weeks before departure. Then the page is deleted, messages go unread, and there is no holiday.

holiday-package-scam.whyItWorks: Package deals and late offers are a normal part of travel, and paying a deposit first is how real agents work too. Families booking months ahead will not discover the gap until they contact the hotel, often days before flying.

realVsFake.real: A genuine tour operator shows its travel protection membership number, which you can check with the scheme itself.
realVsFake.fake: A protection logo is pasted on the page but the number belongs to nobody or to another firm.

realVsFake.real: Real agents take cards, which gives you a route to dispute the charge.
realVsFake.fake: Only transfer is accepted, with a story about card fees or a broken terminal.

realVsFake.real: The hotel can confirm your name against the reservation when you ring it directly.
realVsFake.fake: You are told not to contact the resort because it 'confuses the group booking'.

steps.title: A knock about local burglaries
steps.detail: A rep at your door, in a branded jacket, says several homes nearby were broken into this month and your house has been chosen for a free alarm.

steps.title: 'We are upgrading your system'
steps.detail: If you already have an alarm sign outside, they claim to be from that company, or say it went bust and they have taken over its accounts.

steps.title: Signing on a tablet
steps.detail: Installation is offered the same afternoon. You sign a screen without a paper copy, agreeing to monitoring fees for three to five years.

steps.title: Two contracts, one doorbell
steps.detail: Your old provider keeps billing, the new one starts, and cancelling means paying most of the remaining term. Any deposit paid is gone.

home-security-scam.whyItWorks: A stranger describing break-ins on your own street creates fear that feels local and urgent. 'Free equipment' draws attention away from the monthly figure, and signing on a tablet at the door leaves no document to read afterwards.

realVsFake.real: Your existing alarm company contacts you by letter or account email and books engineer visits ahead.
realVsFake.fake: Someone turns up unannounced saying they need to 'swap the panel' today.

realVsFake.real: A reputable installer leaves a written quote and lets you take several days to think it over.
realVsFake.fake: The offer is 'only for homes signed tonight', and the rep waits on the step while you decide.

realVsFake.real: Genuine reps carry ID you can verify by phoning the company's published number.
realVsFake.fake: The badge has a first name only, and they discourage you from calling head office.

steps.title: A swap request for your dates
steps.detail: Through a home-exchange site or travel group, someone with a beautiful house in exactly the city you want proposes a simultaneous swap.

steps.title: Warm messages, no live video
steps.detail: They write at length about their neighbourhood and family, yet a live walk-through never happens. The camera is broken, or the wifi is poor.

steps.title: Arranging it away from the site
steps.detail: They suggest finalising by email to skip the exchange site's rules, then mention a refundable security deposit and a 'membership' contribution to confirm.

steps.title: A stranger answers the door
steps.detail: You pay, book flights and travel. The address belongs to someone who has never heard of the exchange, and the partner now knows when your own home stands empty.

home-swap-scam.whyItWorks: Home exchange runs on trust between strangers and no rent changes hands, so guards sit lower than with a paid rental. A partner who wants your house in return appears to have as much at stake as you do.

realVsFake.real: Exchange platforms charge membership through your account on the platform, and members do not bill each other for it.
realVsFake.fake: Your swap partner asks you to pay a membership or confirmation fee to them personally.

realVsFake.real: Genuine swappers welcome a live video tour, since they want to see your home too.
realVsFake.fake: Every request for a video call meets a new excuse, and only still photos are sent.

realVsFake.real: Established exchangers have completed swaps and reviews from other households on their profile.
realVsFake.fake: The profile is new, shows no past exchanges, and its photos turn up on a property sales site.

steps.title: A schoolmaster at a low price
steps.detail: An advert on an equestrian site or social group offers a well-schooled horse or pony, or a small herd, for noticeably less than similar animals fetch.

steps.title: Videos, but no yard
steps.detail: The seller sends riding clips taken from someone else's page and says they have relocated abroad, so the animal is with a friend or at livery.

steps.title: Deposit and vetting fee
steps.detail: They ask for a deposit to stop other viewings and a fee for a vet check they will organise, promising to email the vet's report.

steps.title: The transporter's bill
steps.detail: A haulier is said to be booked. Before loading, more money is needed for transport, a health certificate or border paperwork, and no lorry ever arrives.

horse-sale-scam.whyItWorks: Horses are often sold in a hurry by people whose circumstances have changed, and good ones go fast, so paying to hold one is common. Buyers who have searched for months for the right temperament will bend their own rules when one appears.

realVsFake.real: A genuine seller expects you to come to the yard, watch the horse ridden and ride it yourself.
realVsFake.fake: There is always a reason the yard cannot be visited, and the address is never given.

realVsFake.real: The buyer chooses and pays the vet for a pre-purchase examination, so the vet works for the buyer.
realVsFake.fake: The seller arranges the vetting, collects the fee and forwards a report with no practice name on it.

realVsFake.real: A real horse has a passport and microchip number the seller can read out and you can check with the issuing body.
realVsFake.fake: Passport photos are refused, or show a different name, colour or age from the advert.

steps.title: A message inside your booking
steps.detail: After reserving a room, you get a note in the platform's own chat or by email, apparently from the hotel's reservations team.

steps.title: 'Your card could not be verified'
steps.detail: It says the card failed a check and the room will be released within the hour unless you reconfirm through a 'secure link'.

steps.title: A cloned payment page
steps.detail: The link shows your real dates, hotel name and price, taken from the hotel's hacked account, and asks for full card details again.

steps.title: Charged twice or cleaned out
steps.detail: The card is billed by the criminals, sometimes for more than the stay. The real hotel still expects payment when you arrive.

hotel-booking-scam.whyItWorks: The message quotes your actual booking and sits in the same thread as the genuine confirmation, because the hotel's login was stolen. Travellers fear arriving to no room far more than they fear typing a card number twice.

realVsFake.real: Payment for a platform booking is taken in the platform's own app or site, where you made the reservation.
realVsFake.fake: A link in chat leads to a page whose address is a jumble of the platform's name and extra words.

realVsFake.real: If a card truly fails, the platform emails you and asks you to update it under 'manage booking'.
realVsFake.fake: The hotel 'itself' chases you in chat with a one-hour deadline and a link.

realVsFake.real: A hotel can take a card at the front desk or by phone when you ring its listed number.
realVsFake.fake: You are steered to a messaging app and asked for a transfer or crypto deposit.

steps.title: 'You qualify' in your feed
steps.detail: A post, advert or direct message says housing vouchers or rental assistance are open, and that you are pre-approved or guaranteed a placement.

steps.title: A lookalike housing authority site
steps.detail: The link leads to a page with flags and seals imitating a housing authority. It offers places on waiting lists, including ones that are closed.

steps.title: The 75 application fee
steps.detail: You are asked for a 75 fee by card, cash app or prepaid card to 'process' the application, and told it secures your spot today.

steps.title: Social Security number and bank account
steps.detail: The form collects your Social Security number, date of birth, income and bank account. No voucher ever comes, and the identity details are used or sold.

housing-voucher-scam.whyItWorks: Real voucher waiting lists stay closed for long stretches and open briefly with little notice, so word that one is open spreads fast among people who need it. A fee seems a small price for jumping a queue that long.

realVsFake.real: Public housing authorities do not charge to apply for a voucher or to join a waiting list.
realVsFake.fake: A fee is required to apply, to be 'registered' or to move up the list.

realVsFake.real: Applications go through the local housing authority's office or government website, and places are given by lottery or waiting time.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger in a social media group guarantees a voucher and names a move-in date.

realVsFake.real: A housing authority writes to applicants by letter or through the portal they applied on.
realVsFake.fake: The offer arrives as a direct message from a personal profile using an agency seal as its picture.

steps.title: A notice from 'HR'
steps.detail: Mid-morning, a message lands with a subject like 'Updated benefits: acknowledgement required by Friday'. The display name is 'Human Resources', but the address behind it is outside the company.

steps.title: The staff portal, copied
steps.detail: The link opens a page with your employer's logo, lifted from the public website, and the same single sign-on box you use for payslips and holiday requests.

steps.title: Username, password, approval
steps.detail: You enter your work login. If your company uses an authenticator prompt, the page waits while the criminal triggers a real one and you tap Approve.

steps.title: Payday goes elsewhere
steps.detail: Inside the real portal, the criminal changes the bank account your salary is paid into. Nothing looks wrong until payday, when the money lands in an account you have never seen.

hr-portal-email-scam.whyItWorks: Staff are used to HR emails that demand a click by a set date, and ignoring them usually earns a reminder from a manager. Benefits and payslips also concern your own money, so the message feels personal and worth opening.

realVsFake.real: HR announcements normally come from an internal address and are echoed on the intranet or by your manager.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is external, nobody else mentions the update, and your email system may tag it as coming from outside.

realVsFake.real: Most staff reach the portal from a bookmark or the intranet, where single sign-on logs them in without retyping anything.
realVsFake.fake: The emailed link asks for your full username and password from scratch, on an address that is not your company's.

realVsFake.real: A change to salary bank details usually triggers a confirmation from payroll, and many employers require a form or a call.
realVsFake.fake: The criminal changes the account quietly and filters the confirmation email out of your inbox so you never see it.

steps.title: Your storage is full
steps.detail: An email or text signed 'Apple' says your iCloud is full and that photos, documents and backups will be deleted in 48 hours. A bar graphic shows the storage maxed out in red.

steps.title: A cheap upgrade offer
steps.detail: The link opens a page offering 50 GB extra for a token sum, less than a coffee, as a 'loyalty reward'. A timer counts down beside a 'Claim upgrade' button.

steps.title: Sign in, then pay
steps.detail: You are asked for your Apple Account email and password, then a card number, expiry and security code to cover the small monthly fee.

steps.title: A much bigger charge
steps.detail: The token fee is never taken. The card is used for larger purchases or enrolled in a subscription under an unrelated company name, and the Apple login is tried on your real account.

icloud-storage-scam.whyItWorks: Many iPhone owners really are close to the free storage limit and have seen Apple's genuine 'storage almost full' banner. The threat is aimed at the one thing people cannot replace, years of photographs.

realVsFake.real: Apple does not delete existing photos because storage is full. New photos and backups simply stop uploading until you free space or upgrade.
realVsFake.fake: The message says everything already stored will be wiped in two days unless you pay now.

realVsFake.real: Storage is checked and upgraded in Settings, under your name and then iCloud, and billed to the payment method already on your account.
realVsFake.fake: The upgrade happens on a web page that asks you to type in a card from scratch.

realVsFake.real: Apple's storage plans have fixed, published prices. Surprise loyalty discounts do not arrive by text.
realVsFake.fake: A one-off bargain is offered to you alone, valid until a timer on the page reaches zero.

steps.title: Hype before anything exists
steps.detail: Paid influencer posts and a Telegram channel point to a slick site with a whitepaper, a countdown clock and a bar showing the presale almost filled.

steps.title: Whitelist forms and bonus tiers
steps.detail: You apply for the whitelist, then learn that bigger contributions earn bonus tokens. An admin messages privately to 'help you secure your allocation' before the round closes.

steps.title: Coins sent to the presale address
steps.detail: You send ETH, BNB or USDT to a wallet address shown on the page. A dashboard displays your token balance, though your own wallet holds nothing yet.

steps.title: A launch that keeps slipping
steps.detail: Listing day is postponed for an 'audit' or an 'exchange partnership'. Then the chat is muted, the site goes offline, or tokens arrive that no exchange will trade.

ico-presale-scam.whyItWorks: Everyone has heard about somebody who bought a coin for pennies before it listed, and a presale sells that exact seat. Because honest start-ups also raise money before the product exists, paying first seems normal.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate token sale names its founders, publishes a contract audit from a known firm and sets out vesting terms.
realVsFake.fake: The team are cartoon avatars with first names, and the 'audit' is a badge image that links nowhere.

realVsFake.real: Established launchpads hold contributions in a contract with written refund rules if the raise fails.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to send coins straight to a personal wallet address pasted into a chat.

realVsFake.real: Serious projects warn that a new token can list below the sale price and stay there.
realVsFake.fake: Promoters name the multiple you will make on launch day and say the allocation closes within hours.

steps.title: A call that shows the agency's number
steps.detail: Your phone displays a real immigration helpline number. The caller knows your name and nationality and says a form in your file was completed incorrectly.

steps.title: The paperwork 'offence'
steps.detail: An 'officer' explains that the mistake counts as a breach of your visa conditions and that removal proceedings open today unless it is corrected.

steps.title: Do not call your sponsor
steps.detail: You are told not to contact your employer, university or a lawyer because the matter is confidential, and to read out your passport number and entry date.

steps.title: The fee that fixes everything
steps.detail: A 'processing fee' or penalty will close the file. It must be paid at once by gift cards, a wire to a 'government attorney', or cryptocurrency.

immigration-scam.whyItWorks: For someone on a visa, status holds up the job, the home and the right to stay with family, and the rules are complex enough that an unnoticed form error is easy to believe. Students and recent arrivals often cannot tell how the host country's officials really behave.

realVsFake.real: Immigration agencies raise problems in writing, by letter to your address on file or a message in your online case account.
realVsFake.fake: The only notice is a phone call, and the caller will not put anything in the post.

realVsFake.real: Official fees are paid through the agency's own payment system, using the methods listed in the form instructions.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent to buy store gift cards or wire money to an individual described as a government lawyer.

realVsFake.real: Removal is a legal process with written notice, a hearing and the chance to get advice. It does not start by phone.
realVsFake.fake: Deportation is described as hours away, and hanging up to ring an adviser is called 'refusing to cooperate'.

steps.title: Free coins in a video description
steps.detail: A video, advert or direct message from a 'giveaway' account promises thousands of coins or a rare skin to the first hundred players.

steps.title: A generator with a progress bar
steps.detail: The site asks for your username and platform, then shows fake console text 'injecting' currency before stopping for 'human verification'.

steps.title: Log in to receive
steps.detail: A login box styled like the game's own asks for your password and, straight after, the code emailed to you.

steps.title: Account stripped and resold
steps.detail: The email on the account is changed, skins are traded away, and any saved card buys currency. Paid 'discount' top-ups never arrive either.

in-game-currency-scam.whyItWorks: Younger players see friends with expensive skins and have no money of their own, so a free route is hard to resist. Games do run real giveaways and code drops, which makes a countdown for the 'first hundred' sound like just another event.

realVsFake.real: Currency is bought in the game's own store or the console's shop, and appears in your wallet at once.
realVsFake.fake: A third-party site sells it at a fraction of the price and wants a gift card code as payment.

realVsFake.real: Publishers hand out promo codes you redeem inside the game while already signed in.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to type your password into a web page reached from a chat link.

realVsFake.real: No genuine giveaway needs the security code sent to your email.
realVsFake.fake: The page says the code is needed to 'link the delivery' and gives you two minutes.

steps.title: Affection first, for weeks
steps.detail: The relationship starts on a dating app or social site and runs through weeks or months of daily messages before money is ever mentioned.

steps.title: News of a fortune
steps.detail: Your partner announces that a late father's estate, a consignment of gold or a frozen overseas account has come through, and talks of building a life together on it.

steps.title: A 'barrister' and a stamped certificate
steps.detail: A lawyer or bank official emails stamped documents. Release needs an inheritance tax, a transfer fee or an anti-money-laundering certificate, and your partner's funds are tied up.

steps.title: Each fee uncovers another
steps.detail: You pay, then a customs charge appears, then a payment for an official. The partner weeps, promises repayment from the estate and suggests you borrow.

inheritance-romance-scam.whyItWorks: The request is framed as an investment in a shared future, not a loan, and it comes from someone who has spent months earning affection. Once several fees are paid, stopping means admitting both the fortune and the romance were false.

realVsFake.real: A genuine estate is handled by executors and probate courts, and any tax is paid from the estate before heirs receive anything.
realVsFake.fake: A sweetheart you have never met in person must find cash first, and turns to you for it.

realVsFake.real: Real lawyers bill their own client, through a firm you can look up and telephone.
realVsFake.fake: The 'barrister' writes from a free email account and wants fees sent by wire or cryptocurrency.

realVsFake.real: A partner with a real windfall will meet you, on video at the very least, long before finances come up.
realVsFake.fake: Video calls fail every time, yet paperwork for the inheritance arrives promptly.

steps.title: A lawyer with your surname on file
steps.detail: An email from a 'barrister' abroad says his late client shared your surname, died without heirs and left a seven-figure estate. He proposes presenting you as next of kin.

steps.title: Paperwork covered in stamps
steps.detail: Reply, and he sends a death certificate, a 'certificate of deposit' and a bank letter. He asks for your passport copy, home address and bank details for the transfer.

steps.title: The first fee
steps.detail: Just before release, a cost appears: an affidavit, a probate stamp or an 'inheritance tax clearance' of a few hundred, payable by wire transfer to a named individual.

steps.title: Always one more charge
steps.detail: Once you pay, a new obstacle follows: an anti-money-laundering certificate, a courier bond, a bribe for an official. Each is larger, and each is described as the last.

inheritance-scam.whyItWorks: The email asks you to picture the money as already yours, so every fee looks tiny beside it. Once the first payment is sent, walking away means accepting that money is gone, which keeps people paying the next one.

realVsFake.real: Genuine heir-tracing firms identify you through family records and can explain exactly how you are related to the deceased.
realVsFake.fake: The only link is a shared surname, and the 'lawyer' openly suggests passing you off as a relative.

realVsFake.real: Genuine costs of administering an estate are paid out of the estate before the heirs receive their share.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to send fees from your own pocket, by wire or crypto, before a penny is released.

realVsFake.real: A real solicitor has a regulated firm, a listed office number and a professional email address you can look up independently.
realVsFake.fake: He writes from a free webmail account, gives only a mobile number, and insists the matter stay secret from your family.

steps.title: A flattering DM from a 'brand'
steps.detail: An account using a clothing or skincare brand's logo, with a handle one letter off, says it loves your feed and wants you as a paid ambassador.

steps.title: The partnership 'portal'
steps.detail: You are sent a link to 'activate' the deal. The page copies Instagram's sign-in screen, and whatever you type goes straight to the scammer.

steps.title: The starter kit charge
steps.detail: Next comes a small cost, often around $25, described as shipping for free products. The checkout exists to collect your card number, not to post a parcel.

steps.title: Your profile becomes the bait
steps.detail: With your password they lock you out, change the recovery email, and message your followers with the same ambassador offer under your name.

instagram-collab-scam.whyItWorks: Small creators hope to be noticed, and genuine brands do recruit through DMs. A fee the size of a postage charge feels like a fair trade for free products and a paid deal, so the request rarely sets off alarm.

realVsFake.real: A brand that wants you sends a brief and a contract, and it pays you or posts products at its own cost.
realVsFake.fake: The 'brand' asks you to cover shipping or buy the products with an ambassador discount code before any deal exists.

realVsFake.real: Paid partnerships are set up with Instagram's own branded content tools, inside the app you are already signed in to.
realVsFake.fake: A link opens a page outside Instagram that asks for your username and password to 'confirm' the collaboration.

realVsFake.real: Marketing teams write from the company's email domain or its main verified account and are happy to wait while you check.
realVsFake.fake: The message comes from a lookalike handle with few posts, and the offer expires in a day or two.

steps.title: Your cover lapses tomorrow
steps.detail: Carrying your insurer's logo, the notice says your motor or home policy renews tomorrow, but the payment on file was declined. Without action you are uninsured from midnight.

steps.title: A renewal quote with a saving
steps.detail: The linked page shows a renewal price slightly below what you would expect, labelled an 'early payment saving', beside a 'Confirm and pay' button.

steps.title: Policyholder details
steps.detail: The form collects your name, date of birth, address, vehicle registration or property details and driving licence number, on the grounds that the policy must be 'matched'.

steps.title: A premium that buys nothing
steps.detail: You pay the premium by card. No policy is issued, the card is reused elsewhere, and you may be driving, or living in a home, with no cover and no idea.

insurance-email-scam.whyItWorks: Few people remember their exact renewal date, and driving uninsured carries real penalties, so 'lapses tomorrow' is hard to shrug off. Insurers also email constantly around renewal, which makes one more message from them unremarkable.

realVsFake.real: Insurers send renewal notices weeks ahead, quoting your policy number, the old premium and the new one.
realVsFake.fake: The notice arrives the day before, with no policy number or an invented one, and no comparison with last year.

realVsFake.real: If you pay by direct debit or stored card, renewal is normally collected automatically, and a failure is reported by letter or in your online account.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the only way to keep cover is to type card details into the linked page tonight.

realVsFake.real: After a real renewal you receive policy documents and, for a car, a certificate of insurance.
realVsFake.fake: After paying you get a generic 'thank you' page and nothing you could show anyone as proof of cover.

steps.title: 'Cardholder services' on the line
steps.detail: A recording from 'cardholder services' or 'account services' says this is your final notice to lower your credit card rate. It never names your bank.

steps.title: Press 1, hear the guarantee
steps.detail: A live agent claims a special relationship with card issuers and guarantees your rate will fall to almost nothing, wiping out years of interest.

steps.title: Every card number you hold
steps.detail: They ask for each card number, the balances, the security codes and your Social Security number, saying they need them to negotiate with the lenders.

steps.title: The fee lands on your card
steps.detail: A one-time programme fee of several hundred is charged to the card you just read out. Later you might receive a booklet of budgeting tips.

interest-rate-call-scam.whyItWorks: Anyone carrying a balance feels the interest every month, and 'final notice' suggests an offer about to lapse. The vague name 'cardholder services' lets each listener assume the call is from their own card company.

realVsFake.real: Your card issuer already has your card number and discusses rates only after you pass security on its own line.
realVsFake.fake: The agent asks which cards you hold and wants each number read aloud.

realVsFake.real: You can ask your issuer for a lower rate yourself, free, by ringing the number on the card.
realVsFake.fake: A middleman charges up front to make that same request, or to do nothing at all.

realVsFake.real: Non-profit credit counselling agencies set out a written repayment plan before taking any payment.
realVsFake.fake: The rate-reduction 'programme' is sold in one call with a money-back guarantee nobody honours.

steps.title: Reading the mailbox first
steps.detail: Criminals break into a supplier's or customer's email account, or simply research who supplies whom, and note invoice formats, names and payment dates.

steps.title: The change-of-details letter
steps.detail: Shortly before a large invoice is due, accounts payable receives a polite email on the supplier's letterhead saying they have moved banks after an audit.

steps.title: A thread that looks continuous
steps.detail: The message sits inside a real email chain or comes from a domain one character off. A follow-up may ask you to confirm once records are updated.

steps.title: The scheduled payment run
steps.detail: The next payment leaves with the usual batch to the new account. Nobody notices until the real supplier chases an overdue invoice weeks later.

invoice-redirection-scam.whyItWorks: Suppliers do change banks, and updating a record is a routine clerical job that rarely gets a second look. The fraudulent email arrives in the middle of a real business relationship, quoting real invoice numbers, so it reads as ordinary admin.

realVsFake.real: A supplier changing bank is content for you to confirm by phoning the contact number you already hold.
realVsFake.fake: The email supplies a new phone number for 'verification', or says the usual contact is away.

realVsFake.real: Genuine new details normally stay in the supplier's own company name and home country.
realVsFake.fake: The replacement account is in a different name, at an online-only bank, or abroad.

realVsFake.real: Proper change requests go through a supplier onboarding form or portal, with sign-off from a second person.
realVsFake.fake: A single email with a PDF attachment asks for the amendment before Friday's payment run.

steps.title: Every channel for pocket money
steps.detail: A social media post, a flyer or a message offers every sports, film and pay-per-view channel for about fifteen pounds a year.

steps.title: A reseller on a chat app
steps.detail: You are passed to a seller on an encrypted messenger who offers a 24-hour test line and then asks for a year upfront.

steps.title: Card, transfer or a loaded stick
steps.detail: Payment goes by transfer or through a rough checkout page. Some sell a pre-loaded streaming stick that needs an app installed from outside the store.

steps.title: Buffering, then a dead link
steps.detail: Streams freeze during the big match and stop within weeks. The seller's account is gone, and the side-loaded app can read what is on your network.

iptv-subscription-scam.whyItWorks: Legitimate TV packages cost a great deal, so a cheap alternative sounds like beating the system, and buyers know it is unofficial. That is the trap: someone who paid for a pirate service is unlikely to complain when it disappears.

realVsFake.real: Licensed streaming services are in official app stores under the broadcaster's name and bill monthly by card.
realVsFake.fake: The app comes as a file link in a chat, with a warning to switch off device protection first.

realVsFake.real: A real provider has a company name, terms and customer service you can reach.
realVsFake.fake: Support is one anonymous username that stops replying once the year is paid.

realVsFake.real: Sports rights are split between broadcasters, so no lawful single package carries everything.
realVsFake.fake: One login promises every league, every film channel and every fight night worldwide.

steps.title: A friend's account, a strange question
steps.detail: A message arrives on Messenger or Instagram from someone you know. It reads 'is this you in this video??' with a link and perhaps a shocked emoji.

steps.title: A blurred preview with a play button
steps.detail: The link shows a thumbnail that looks like a video player. Tapping it does not play anything. It opens a page styled as a Facebook sign-in.

steps.title: 'Log in to continue watching'
steps.detail: The page says your session expired or that you must confirm your age. The email and password you enter are saved, then you land on an unrelated site.

steps.title: Your contacts get the same question
steps.detail: Within minutes the thief signs in as you and an automated script sends the video line to everyone in your inbox, each one now trusting your name.

is-this-you-video-scam.whyItWorks: The fear of an embarrassing clip circulating is hard to sit on, and the sender is a real friend, not a stranger. Being asked to sign in again is so routine on phones that few people look at the address bar.

realVsFake.real: A friend who has found a video of you says where they saw it and answers when you ask what it shows.
realVsFake.fake: The hijacked account sends one line and a link, then ignores your questions or repeats the same message.

realVsFake.real: A video shared inside Messenger plays in the chat window, with no extra sign-in while you are using the app.
realVsFake.fake: The link leaves the app and demands your Facebook email and password before the supposed clip will load.

realVsFake.real: Facebook's sign-in page sits on its own domain, and your password manager offers to fill it in.
realVsFake.fake: The copy sits on a random address full of hyphens and numbers, and no saved password is offered.

steps.title: A sale that goes smoothly
steps.detail: Payment comes by card through the platform. The buyer sometimes picks the cheapest postage with no signature and gives an address at a flat block or shared house.

steps.title: Tracking says delivered
steps.detail: The courier scans the parcel as delivered. Within hours the buyer writes that nothing came, the tracking is wrong, or the box was empty.

steps.title: Straight to a dispute
steps.detail: They decline to ask neighbours or the depot and open an 'item not received' case, or contact their card issuer and request a chargeback.

steps.title: Funds frozen and clawed back
steps.detail: Your payout is put on hold while you gather evidence. Without a signature or delivery photo the case can go against you, taking the money plus a chargeback fee.

item-not-received-scam.whyItWorks: Dispute systems are built to protect buyers from sellers who never post, so the buyer's word starts with an advantage. The cheat knows a 'delivered' scan without a signature proves little, and that a small seller may refund to avoid the paperwork.

realVsFake.real: A buyer whose parcel has really gone astray will check with housemates, look at the delivery photo and wait a day.
realVsFake.fake: The complaint lands within the hour, and every suggestion to look for the parcel is rejected.

realVsFake.real: Genuine cases stay on the platform, where the tracking record and messages are visible to the staff deciding them.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to refund privately to a different account 'to sort it quicker', while the dispute stays open.

realVsFake.real: Couriers investigate lost parcels using GPS scan data and the driver's photo of the doorstep.
realVsFake.fake: The buyer will not let you raise a courier claim and says the box weighed nothing when opened.

steps.title: A ring with a valuation
steps.detail: The listing shows a ring or chain with a printed valuation, often quoting a retail figure of 3,000 and an asking price of 400 because of a divorce or inheritance.

steps.title: Stamps shown in close-up
steps.detail: Asked about hallmarks, the seller sends a blurry photo of '18K' or '750' stamped inside the band. Those marks are easy to punch into plated brass.

steps.title: A meeting away from any jeweller
steps.detail: They suggest a car park or café, and decline to step into a jeweller or pawnbroker for a quick acid or electronic test, saying they are short of time.

steps.title: Cash for brass and glass
steps.detail: You hand over cash or send a transfer. Days later a jeweller tells you the gold is plating over base metal and the stone is cubic zirconia or moissanite.

jewellery-sale-scam.whyItWorks: Few buyers can tell plated brass from solid gold, or a lab-made stone from a diamond, by eye. A stamp inside the band and a typed valuation look like proof, and the seller's sad backstory explains the low price.

realVsFake.real: A diamond of real value normally comes with a grading report from an independent laboratory, and the report number can be checked on that laboratory's site.
realVsFake.fake: The 'certificate' is a home-printed valuation card naming a shop that cannot be found, with no report number at all.

realVsFake.real: An honest private seller is happy to walk into a jeweller with you and have the metal tested before any money changes hands.
realVsFake.fake: The scammer finds a reason the test cannot happen today, then mentions another buyer coming at four o'clock.

realVsFake.real: Solid gold sells close to its scrap weight value at the very least, because any dealer would pay that on the spot.
realVsFake.fake: The asking price sits below what the gold alone would fetch melted down, which no real owner would accept.

steps.title: A guarantee in thirty days
steps.detail: A 'career placement service' advertises to people who have been job hunting for months, promising a job within 30 days through its private network of employers who never advertise.

steps.title: The consultation that closes a sale
steps.detail: A friendly 'career adviser' phones to review your CV, praises it, and says three partner employers want someone like you. Slots on the programme are limited this month.

steps.title: Pay 250 to join
steps.detail: The placement fee, about 250 dollars, is taken by card during the call. You are emailed a welcome letter and a money-back guarantee with conditions nobody mentions aloud.

steps.title: Recycled listings, voided refund
steps.detail: What you receive is a CV template and a weekly list of vacancies copied from public job boards. Refund requests fail because you did not log enough applications in their portal.

job-placement-service-scam.whyItWorks: After months of unanswered applications, the idea that the good jobs are hidden and someone can open the door explains the silence and offers a way out. A guarantee with a deadline sounds like the service carries the risk, when the small print hands it straight back.

realVsFake.real: Honest career coaches sell their time, such as CV rewrites and interview practice, and say plainly that they cannot promise a job.
realVsFake.fake: The service sells the outcome itself, a job by a set date, which no outsider controls.

realVsFake.real: Headhunters who do have unadvertised roles are retained by the employer and approach candidates at no cost to them.
realVsFake.fake: Access to the 'exclusive employer network' is sold to anyone with a card, whatever their field or experience.

realVsFake.real: A genuine provider will name past clients' employers or put you in touch with people it has helped.
realVsFake.fake: Testimonials are first names beside stock photos, and partner companies are 'confidential until you enrol'.

steps.title: A salary headline, then a course
steps.detail: The advert leads with 4,000 dollars a month from home in a field such as digital marketing, transcription or customer support, open to anyone who completes the company's certified training.

steps.title: Enrol now for 299
steps.detail: An 'admissions adviser' explains that the position is guaranteed on completion, but the course costs 299 dollars and this intake closes on Friday. Payment is by card or instalments.

steps.title: Videos, a quiz, a certificate
steps.detail: The training is a few hours of generic videos and a multiple-choice quiz that nobody fails. You download a certificate carrying the seal of an accrediting body that cannot be traced.

steps.title: The job needs 'level two'
steps.detail: When you ask about the guaranteed position, you learn that employers want the advanced module at a higher price, or you are handed a list of ordinary job sites.

job-training-course-scam.whyItWorks: Paying for a qualification to get a better job is how education normally works, so the fee looks like an investment. Tying it to a guaranteed position removes the usual doubt about whether a course will lead anywhere.

realVsFake.real: An employer that needs you trained hires you first and pays you during the training.
realVsFake.fake: The 'employer' and the course seller are the same outfit, and the course is the only thing on offer.

realVsFake.real: Recognised certificates come from awarding bodies you can look up, and hiring managers in the field know their names.
realVsFake.fake: The certificate cites an 'international accreditation council' whose only trace online is the seller's own site.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate colleges publish a syllabus, tutor names and a refund policy before taking any money.
realVsFake.fake: You see the course content only after paying, and the guaranteed role is never named or put in writing.

steps.title: A deputy leaves a voicemail
steps.detail: A man calling himself a sergeant in the sheriff's warrants division says you ignored a jury summons that was signed for at your address.

steps.title: A real judge's name
