steps.detail: He names an actual local judge, gives a badge and case number, and cites 'failure to appear' and 'contempt of court'. Caller ID shows the sheriff's office.

steps.title: Jail tonight or a bond
steps.detail: Two choices are offered: surrender and be held until a hearing, or post a $500 bond now, refundable once your signature is checked at the courthouse.

steps.title: Stay on the line to the shop
steps.detail: He keeps you on the phone while you drive to buy prepaid cards, then asks you to read the numbers aloud or scan them into a 'bonding kiosk'.

jury-duty-scam.whyItWorks: A jury summons comes by ordinary post and looks like any other official envelope, so almost nobody can be certain one never arrived. Add the name of a judge who really sits in the county courthouse and the story has just enough local truth.

realVsFake.real: Courts deal with jury service by mail. Miss a date and the usual result is a second letter with a new one.
realVsFake.fake: A 'deputy' phones your mobile about a summons you never saw and says the warrant is already active.

realVsFake.real: Any penalty for skipping jury duty is decided by a judge in court, after you have had a chance to explain.
realVsFake.fake: The amount is fixed by the caller, and must be paid before you could possibly reach the courthouse to ask.

realVsFake.real: Sheriff's offices do not phone people to collect money and cannot cancel a warrant in exchange for card numbers.
realVsFake.fake: The 'bond' is paid in prepaid card numbers or through a crypto machine the caller calls a federal kiosk.

steps.title: An 'official outlet' advert
steps.detail: An advert or search result uses a famous brand's logo and campaign photos, with a domain that adds 'outlet', 'clearance' or a country to the name.

steps.title: The whole range at one discount
steps.detail: Every trainer, bag or jacket is marked down by the same deep amount, in every size, including new-season lines the brand itself sells at full price.

steps.title: Checkout with odd options
steps.detail: The basket shows prices in a different currency or accepts only transfer or crypto. The card payment, if offered, bills a company with an unrelated name.

steps.title: A fake in a plain bag
steps.detail: Weeks later a counterfeit arrives from overseas with crooked stitching and the wrong box, or nothing comes and the site has changed its name.

knockoff-brand-store-scam.whyItWorks: Real brands do run outlet shops with heavy markdowns, so the idea is familiar. The site borrows genuine photography and layout, and most shoppers look at the logo and the price long before they look at the address bar.

realVsFake.real: A brand links to its outlet from its main website, on the same or a clearly related domain.
realVsFake.fake: The address strings the brand name together with hyphens and words like 'sale' or 'store'.

realVsFake.real: Genuine outlets sell past-season stock in patchy sizes and colours.
realVsFake.fake: Every current style is available in every size at the same slashed price.

realVsFake.real: Authentic goods arrive with proper tags, a branded box and a returns label for the brand's own warehouse.
realVsFake.fake: The parcel has customs stickers, chemical-smelling glue and no paperwork.

steps.title: A pitch about 'strategic land'
steps.detail: A sales agent phones, or you answer an advert, about plots on the edge of a growing town that are supposedly earmarked for new housing.

steps.title: The aerial photo and artist's impression
steps.detail: A glossy pack arrives showing a field divided into numbered plots, drawings of finished houses, and a 'planning consultant' predicting approval within two years.

steps.title: Reserving plot 47
steps.detail: A reservation fee holds your plot and the balance follows by bank transfer. You do receive a title document, because the field exists and your strip of it is registered.

steps.title: Planning consent never arrives
steps.detail: Years pass. The field is protected countryside or has no road access, the sales firm has dissolved, and no builder wants a patchwork of tiny plots with hundreds of owners.

land-banking-scam.whyItWorks: The title document is genuine and the field can be visited, which feels safer than shares. Buyers who have watched house prices climb nearby see a field beside a town as the same story at an earlier chapter.

realVsFake.real: Housebuilders acquire whole sites through land agents and option agreements after discussions with the planning authority.
realVsFake.fake: A sales office cuts one field into hundreds of garden-sized plots and sells them to the public by telephone.

realVsFake.real: The council's local plan and planning register are public, so anyone can see how a field is designated.
realVsFake.fake: The firm quotes its own consultant and discourages a call to the council, saying talks are 'at a confidential stage'.

realVsFake.real: A solicitor you choose checks access rights, restrictions on the title and what nearby farmland sells for.
realVsFake.fake: They supply a 'panel solicitor' and charge many times the agricultural value for each small strip.

steps.title: A plot priced to move
steps.detail: An advert shows a field or building plot with photos lifted from an old agent listing, priced well under nearby land because the owner has 'relocated overseas'.

steps.title: Paperwork by email only
steps.detail: The seller emails a scanned deed and a passport photo. The name may even match the true owner, whose identity was copied from public land records.

steps.title: Their escrow, their agent
steps.detail: You are told a particular escrow company or 'land agent' will handle everything. Its website was built for this sale and its phone number reaches the same person.

steps.title: The holding deposit
steps.detail: A reservation deposit is requested by bank transfer to stop the plot going to another bidder. After it lands, the seller asks for survey or legal fees, then vanishes.

land-sale-scam.whyItWorks: Vacant land has no tenant, no keys and often no neighbour who knows the owner, so nobody on site can contradict the advert. An absent seller sounds normal for an empty plot, and a deposit feels small beside the saving.

realVsFake.real: A genuine land sale runs through a solicitor, conveyancer or title company that you choose and whose registration you can confirm yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The seller names the only escrow firm they will accept and sends you its link, saying their lawyer insists on it.

realVsFake.real: Ownership is confirmed from the official land registry or county recorder, a record you order directly for a small fee.
realVsFake.fake: You get a scanned deed by email, and questions about the parcel number or boundaries are brushed aside.

realVsFake.real: A real owner expects you to walk the plot, speak to the planning office and take weeks over searches.
realVsFake.fake: The deposit is wanted today, before any search, because three other people have supposedly asked about the land this week.

steps.title: A lease 'up for transfer'
steps.detail: A post in a housing group says the tenant must relocate for work within days and wants someone to take over the remaining months at the current rent.

steps.title: A lease document as proof
steps.detail: They send a photo or PDF of a lease bearing their name. The names and dates may be edited, or it relates to a flat they left long ago.

steps.title: 'The landlord is fine with it'
steps.detail: Asked about the landlord, they say consent was given verbally or the building manager need not know. No contact details for either are offered.

steps.title: Paying back 'their' deposit
steps.detail: You are asked to reimburse the deposit they supposedly paid, plus the first month, by wire or gift card. On move-in day the locks do not open for you.

lease-takeover-scam.whyItWorks: People do leave leases early and look for someone to take them on, and the outgoing tenant seems like a peer in a bind, not a landlord chasing money. Reimbursing their deposit sounds fair between equals.

realVsFake.real: A genuine lease assignment needs the landlord's written consent, and the landlord normally screens the incoming tenant.
realVsFake.fake: The landlord is kept out of the conversation and consent is described as a formality.

realVsFake.real: In a real transfer the newcomer signs paperwork with the landlord or managing agent, who also handles the deposit.
realVsFake.fake: The deposit goes to the departing tenant's personal account before you have signed anything.

realVsFake.real: Someone truly leaving can show you round before they go, or ask a neighbour or the agent to.
realVsFake.fake: They have already relocated, and nobody local is able to open the door.

steps.title: A polished profile connects
steps.detail: A recruiter or fund manager with a stock headshot and a well-known employer in the headline sends a connection request, then praises your experience.

steps.title: 'Let's continue on WhatsApp'
steps.detail: After two or three messages they say LinkedIn is slow for them and ask for your number, which takes the conversation away from the site's reporting tools.

steps.title: The onboarding portal
steps.detail: A link leads to a candidate or investor portal. It asks for a passport scan, date of birth and bank details 'for payroll', or a first deposit.

steps.title: The role never starts
steps.detail: You are told to buy equipment from a named supplier, pay for a background check, or add funds to a trading dashboard. Then the profile disappears.

linkedin-dm-scam.whyItWorks: LinkedIn is where strangers are supposed to approach you about work, so a cold message from a recruiter is normal there. A job title and a company logo on a profile look like vetting, although anyone can type them in.

realVsFake.real: In-house recruiters follow up from a company email address and point you to the vacancy on the employer's careers page.
realVsFake.fake: The contact avoids email, uses a personal chat number, and the role cannot be found anywhere on the employer's site.

realVsFake.real: Employers collect bank and identity details after a written offer, through their HR system, once you have met real staff.
realVsFake.fake: A portal wants your passport and account number before any interview has taken place.

realVsFake.real: A genuine investor or business contact talks about their firm and is content to keep messaging on LinkedIn.
realVsFake.fake: Within days the chat turns to a private trading platform that only they can introduce you to.

steps.title: The unboxing video advert
steps.detail: A social media advert shows someone cutting open a shrink-wrapped pallet and pulling out tablets, headphones and game consoles, with a caption about returns sold by the truckload.

steps.title: A warehouse site with a countdown
steps.detail: The link opens a shop named after a big retailer's returns, listing 'electronics pallets' at 150 each with a stock counter ticking down and a spreadsheet-style manifest.

steps.title: Checkout, then a surprise fee
steps.detail: You pay by card, payment app or crypto and get an order number. A day later an email says the carrier needs an extra 'liftgate' or residential delivery fee.

steps.title: Nothing, or a box of junk
steps.detail: Tracking never updates and emails bounce. In some cases a small parcel arrives holding phone cases and broken chargers, which lets the seller argue the order was delivered.

liquidation-pallet-scam.whyItWorks: Return pallets are a real trade, and reseller videos make mystery boxes look like a lottery that pays. Because genuine liquidation stock is sold unseen and as-is, buying blind from an unknown warehouse site does not feel unusual.

realVsFake.real: Established liquidators sell through registered business accounts, often ask for a resale certificate, and list a warehouse where you can collect.
realVsFake.fake: The site sells to anyone from an Instagram advert, with no address beyond a contact form and a chat bubble.

realVsFake.real: A genuine manifest lists each item with model numbers and condition codes, and the lot price reflects that most of it is damaged.
realVsFake.fake: Every pallet is described as laptops and consoles worth thousands, with the same photo used for each listing.

realVsFake.real: Real pallets weigh hundreds of kilos, so freight is quoted separately by a named haulage firm and often costs more than the goods.
realVsFake.fake: Shipping shows as free at checkout, a sign nobody has priced moving a full pallet across the country.

steps.title: Bad news about a loved shop
steps.detail: An advert says a well-known high-street chain is closing for good after decades, sometimes with a photo of a boarded shopfront or tearful staff.

steps.title: The 'everything must go' site
steps.detail: The link opens a store with the chain's logo and a banner announcing the last days of trading, with a clock running down.

steps.title: A basket that fills fast
steps.detail: Coats, cookware and bedding all cost a few pounds, so buyers add several items. Checkout takes card details or steers you to a transfer.

steps.title: Silence after the closing date
steps.detail: No dispatch email comes. Complaints go unanswered because the shop has 'closed', and the real retailer says it was never involved.

liquidation-sale-scam.whyItWorks: Well-known chains really do collapse and hold closing-down sales, and the news often breaks on social media first. A shop that is shutting has an obvious reason to sell at silly prices, which removes the usual suspicion about a deep discount.

realVsFake.real: A retailer in administration sells off stock through its existing shops and usual website.
realVsFake.fake: The 'final sale' runs on a brand-new domain the chain has never used.

realVsFake.real: Real closing sales start with modest reductions that deepen over weeks.
realVsFake.fake: Everything is nine-tenths off from the very first day, with no line ever running out.

realVsFake.real: News of a genuine closure is reported by established outlets and on the company's own channels.
realVsFake.fake: The only source is the advert, with comments switched off or filled with identical praise.

steps.title: The stream pops up
steps.detail: A seller goes live holding up trainers, handbags or phones at a fraction of shop prices, with a viewer counter climbing and a host talking without pause.

steps.title: 'Comment SOLD to claim it'
steps.detail: Each item is offered for under a minute. The host reads out the names of people who commented, so it sounds as though stock is vanishing.

steps.title: Payment details by private message
steps.detail: A moderator messages you an account number or payment-app tag and asks for a screenshot of the transfer. There is no basket and no order number.

steps.title: A fake parcel, or none
steps.detail: Weeks later a cheap copy turns up, or nothing does. By then the stream is deleted, the account has a new name, and you are blocked.

live-shopping-scam.whyItWorks: Seeing the goods held up to the camera in real time feels like proof they exist. The pace of a live auction, with other viewers apparently buying, leaves no gap to ask why the seller will not use the checkout button.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate live sellers pin the product to the stream, and you pay through the platform's basket with an order confirmation.
realVsFake.fake: The host says the checkout is 'broken today' and takes payment by transfer to a personal account.

realVsFake.real: An established shop has past streams, reviews from buyers who received goods, and a returns address.
realVsFake.fake: The account appeared this month, has no earlier broadcasts, and comments asking about delivery are deleted on air.

realVsFake.real: A real retailer still has the item tomorrow and will answer sizing or warranty questions after the broadcast ends.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the price dies with the stream and that unpaid claims go to the next commenter in seconds.

steps.title: A stolen channel goes live
steps.detail: Criminals take over an existing channel with real subscribers, rename it after a famous founder or charity, and start a broadcast using old interview footage on a loop.

steps.title: The banner and the QR code
steps.detail: A frame around the video promises that any crypto sent to the wallet shown will come back doubled. A QR code points to a giveaway site.

steps.title: A feed of invented winners
steps.detail: The site shows a scrolling table of transactions arriving and larger ones leaving. Chat is restricted so only scripted accounts can post thanks.

steps.title: One-way transfer
steps.detail: You send coins or read out gift card numbers. Nothing returns, and the page may then suggest your amount was too small and invite a bigger attempt.

live-stream-donation-scam.whyItWorks: The face and voice on screen are genuine, taken from a real talk, and the channel may carry a large subscriber count from its original owner. Viewers assume a platform would not let an impostor broadcast live to a big audience.

realVsFake.real: Charity appeals on a live stream use the platform's built-in donate button or send you to the charity's registered site.
realVsFake.fake: The only way to give is a wallet address on screen or gift card codes typed into chat.

realVsFake.real: A company running a real prize draw never needs you to send money first in order to receive some.
realVsFake.fake: The stream says every deposit is matched twice over, with a bonus for the first hundred senders.

realVsFake.real: A public figure's own channel has years of uploads under one name, and the live event appears on their other official accounts.
realVsFake.fake: The channel's older videos are about gaming or cooking, or have been hidden, and nobody official mentions the event.

steps.title: Cash in five minutes
steps.detail: An advert on social media or a text promotes an app lending small sums, with nothing needed except a selfie and an ID card.

steps.title: Handing over the phone book
steps.detail: Before any offer appears, the app requires permission for contacts, photos, location and SMS, and uploads the lot to its servers.

steps.title: A short loan with a slice missing
steps.detail: You request 100 and receive 65 after a 'service fee', with the full 100 plus interest due in seven days instead of the advertised three months.

steps.title: Shaming the borrower
steps.detail: On or before the due date, collectors message your family, colleagues and friends calling you a thief, and send edited obscene images made from your photos.

loan-app-scam.whyItWorks: People borrowing a small amount for an emergency tap 'Allow' on every permission box to reach the money. Nobody expects a lender to want their contact list, and by the time its purpose is clear the data is already copied.

realVsFake.real: A licensed lender states the total repayable, the interest rate and the term before you accept.
realVsFake.fake: The app shows one figure when you apply, then a shorter term and smaller payout after approval.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate lending apps check income and credit history, and have no use for your photo gallery or contacts.
realVsFake.fake: The loan cannot proceed until you grant access to everyone in your phone book.

realVsFake.real: A real lender chases arrears by letter, phone and formal notice, addressed to you alone.
realVsFake.fake: Collectors threaten to send your ID and doctored pictures to your employer and relatives within hours.

steps.title: 'PRE-APPROVED' in capitals
steps.detail: A text congratulates you on being pre-approved for a set amount, such as £5,000, with guaranteed acceptance and no credit check, from a lender you never contacted.

steps.title: The two-minute application
steps.detail: A simple form asks for income, employer, address and bank account, sometimes with photos of ID and a bank statement. Approval comes back at once.

steps.title: A loan agreement arrives
steps.detail: You receive a document with a company logo and repayment table. It looks official, and a 'loan officer' follows up on a messaging app.

steps.title: The release fee
steps.detail: Before funds can be sent, a fee for insurance, processing or a first repayment is required by transfer or voucher. Paying brings another fee, never the loan.

loan-offer-text-scam.whyItWorks: The offer reaches people who have been refused credit or are short before payday, when 'no credit check' sounds like relief instead of a warning. A fee of a hundred or so seems reasonable set against thousands about to arrive.

realVsFake.real: A regulated lender checks your credit file and affordability before making any offer. Acceptance is never guaranteed.
realVsFake.fake: Approval is promised to everyone, with the loan amount fixed before you supplied a single detail.

realVsFake.real: Genuine lenders take their fees from the loan itself or add them to the repayments.
realVsFake.fake: You must send money first, by bank transfer, gift voucher or an app, to 'release' the funds.

realVsFake.real: An authorised lender appears on the financial regulator's register under the same name, address and phone number it gives you.
realVsFake.fake: The name is borrowed from a real firm, but the contact details are a mobile and a free email account.

steps.title: A prize post with a celebrity face
steps.detail: An influencer or a new 'giveaway' account posts a car, a designer bag or cash, and says entry is as easy as following a list.

steps.title: Following sixty strangers
steps.detail: You must follow every account the host follows. Each of those accounts has paid the organiser for a slot, buying your follow, not sponsoring a prize.

steps.title: The entry fee or 'bonus entries'
steps.detail: Some loops add a charge sent by payment app to 'qualify', or sell extra entries. The money goes to a personal account with no ticket or receipt.

steps.title: A winner nobody can find
steps.detail: The draw is announced in a story that disappears after a day. The winner is a private or empty profile, or you get a DM asking for delivery costs.

loop-giveaway-scam.whyItWorks: Following accounts costs nothing, so entering feels free of risk, and the well-known face fronting the post makes the prize seem funded. Few entrants realise the business model is selling their follows to the listed accounts.

realVsFake.real: A brand's own giveaway runs on its main page, asks you to follow one or two accounts, and publishes terms.
realVsFake.fake: A loop sends you through dozens of unrelated profiles and has no rules, closing date or named promoter.

realVsFake.real: Properly run prize draws are free to enter or sold as licensed raffle tickets with a numbered receipt.
realVsFake.fake: The organiser wants a 'qualifying' payment to a private payment-app handle and sends nothing back to show you entered.

realVsFake.real: Genuine winners are tagged publicly, post about the prize themselves, and pay nothing to receive it.
realVsFake.fake: 'Winners' are told by DM to cover insurance or shipping on the car before it can be released.

steps.title: Your poster gives them everything
steps.detail: You share a missing notice with your pet's name, breed, markings, the area and your mobile number. Scammers search local groups for exactly these posts.

steps.title: 'I think I have your dog'
steps.detail: A text or call repeats the description back to you as if they are looking at the animal. They say it is safe and well fed.

steps.title: The reason they cannot meet
steps.detail: They are a lorry driver who picked it up and is now hours away, or they left it with a vet. A current photo is always impossible.

steps.title: Pay before the handover
steps.detail: A courier charge, vet bill or crate deposit must be sent by transfer or gift card first. After you pay, a second cost appears or the number goes dead.

lost-pet-scam.whyItWorks: After days of searching, an owner will take almost any call seriously, and the caller recites details that seem like proof but came from the owner's own poster. Questioning a possible rescuer feels like risking the animal.

realVsFake.real: Someone who has your pet can send a new photo or video within minutes, or describe a detail you left off the poster.
realVsFake.fake: The 'finder' sends your own picture back, says their camera is broken, or gets angry when asked for proof.

realVsFake.real: A genuine finder suggests meeting nearby, or takes the animal to a local vet or shelter to have its microchip scanned.
realVsFake.fake: The caller is always in another town and proposes a paid delivery service you have never heard of.

realVsFake.real: If a reward was offered, it changes hands when you have the pet in your arms.
realVsFake.fake: Money is demanded up front, in gift cards or a transfer, with hints the animal may be sold or abandoned otherwise.

steps.title: Winning a draw you skipped
steps.detail: A text, email or letter announces that your number or email address was picked in an international draw, with a prize such as £850,000.

steps.title: Meet your claims agent
steps.detail: You are told to contact a named 'claims agent' at a free email address or on a messaging app, quoting a reference and keeping the win confidential.

steps.title: Forms and a certificate
steps.detail: The agent sends a winner's certificate and a claim form asking for passport copy, address, occupation and bank account, which makes the process feel administrative.

steps.title: Fees before the payout
steps.detail: A processing fee of about £25 is requested, then tax, then courier insurance, then bank clearance. Each payment unlocks the next charge and never the prize.

lottery-winner-scam.whyItWorks: The sum is life-changing, so a small fee looks trivial beside it, and each new charge is easier to pay because of the money already sent. The request for confidentiality keeps away the relative who would point out you never bought a ticket.

realVsFake.real: You can only win a lottery you bought a ticket for, and the operator pays out without charging a fee first.
realVsFake.fake: A draw you never entered demands a processing charge before it will release the jackpot.

realVsFake.real: Real lottery tax, where it exists, is deducted from the prize or settled with the tax office afterwards.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to send the tax up front to the agent by transfer.

realVsFake.real: Official lotteries ask big winners to phone a published claims line and check the ticket itself.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agent' writes from a free webmail address and asks you to tell nobody about the win.

steps.title: A balance about to vanish
steps.detail: A text says a specific number of points, such as 4,500, will expire in 24 hours. It may name a supermarket, airline, phone network or card scheme.

steps.title: The rewards catalogue
steps.detail: The link opens a page of headphones, kitchen gadgets and vouchers 'available with your points', each with a redeem button.

steps.title: Log in to redeem
steps.detail: Choosing a reward asks for your loyalty account email and password, or card details to cover a small delivery charge on the 'free' item.

steps.title: Real points drained
steps.detail: With the login, the thief empties your genuine balance into gift cards or flights within minutes. Entered card details are used separately.

loyalty-points-scam.whyItWorks: Points feel like savings built up over many shops or flights, yet hardly anyone knows their balance or expiry rules. A precise figure with a one-day deadline turns a vague asset into something you are about to lose.

realVsFake.real: Loyalty schemes show your true balance and any expiry date when you open their app or sign in the usual way.
realVsFake.fake: The points total in the text is invented and identical for every recipient.

realVsFake.real: Schemes that expire points usually give notice well ahead, by email to the address on the account.
realVsFake.fake: You get one day, by text, from a sender that never names your membership number.

realVsFake.real: Redeeming genuine points takes them off your balance. It does not need a bank card.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for card details to post a reward you supposedly already paid for with points.

steps.title: Envelopes lifted or mail diverted
steps.detail: A thief fishes letters from an unlocked or communal mailbox, or fills in a change-of-address request in your name so everything is forwarded to a drop address.

steps.title: A quiet gap in your post
steps.detail: The monthly statement does not turn up. Nor does the replacement card your bank said was on its way. A single 'redirection confirmed' letter may be the only clue.

steps.title: Paperwork becomes a profile
steps.detail: Statements give them account numbers and recent transactions. A utility bill proves 'your' address. Pre-approved credit offers and a posted PIN fill in whatever is missing.

steps.title: Cards activated, security reset
steps.detail: They activate the intercepted card, answer the bank's security questions using your own statements, and request new online-banking codes by letter, which arrive at their address instead of yours.

mail-theft-scam.whyItWorks: Nobody notices a letter that fails to arrive, so the thief gets weeks of head start. Banks and lenders still treat a posted statement or a code sent to the address on file as proof that they are dealing with you.

realVsFake.real: When you move home, you request the redirection yourself and the confirmation letter matches a form you remember completing.
realVsFake.fake: A confirmation arrives for a redirection nobody in the household asked for, naming a forwarding address you have never seen.

realVsFake.real: Ordinary postal delays hit one item at random, and the next statement lands on its usual day.
realVsFake.fake: Everything from your bank and card provider dries up together, often while junk mail and parcels keep coming.

realVsFake.real: A new card is posted because yours is about to expire, and the order shows in your banking app.
realVsFake.fake: Your bank says a card and PIN were delivered last week, yet neither reached your letterbox and the card is already in use.

steps.title: An invoice from nobody in particular
steps.detail: Invoice INV-4821 is overdue and attached, the sender writes. It is short, businesslike and addressed to 'Accounts' or to no one, with a file named something like Invoice_4821.docm.

steps.title: A blurred page and a yellow bar
steps.detail: Opening the file shows a blurred document and a notice: 'This document is protected. Click Enable Editing, then Enable Content to view.' Word's yellow security bar sits above it.

steps.title: The click that runs the code
steps.detail: Enabling content runs a macro hidden in the file. It downloads a second program in the background, and the document either stays blurred or shows a bland invoice.

steps.title: Quiet collection
steps.detail: The installed program copies saved browser passwords and session cookies, watches for banking logins, and in an office can clear the way for ransomware across the network.

malware-attachment-scam.whyItWorks: People who handle invoices, CVs or delivery notes open attachments from strangers as part of the job, so refusing feels like not doing it. The yellow warning bar looks like a routine nuisance, and the document itself tells you to dismiss it.

realVsFake.real: A supplier's invoice is usually a plain PDF that displays straight away and names a purchase order or contact you recognise.
realVsFake.fake: The file is a macro-enabled document, a zip or an HTML page, and shows nothing readable until you click a button.

realVsFake.real: Ordinary documents never need macros switched on to be read. Macros automate spreadsheets. They are not needed to display text.
realVsFake.fake: The page claims it was 'created in an earlier version of Office' and can only be viewed once content is enabled.

realVsFake.real: A business chasing payment will have contacted you before and can be reached on a number from earlier dealings.
realVsFake.fake: The email is the first you have heard from them, and the phone number in the signature goes nowhere.

steps.title: The bargain with one condition
steps.detail: You message about a cheap console or sofa. The seller replies warmly, then says their bank or payment app is 'under review', so they can only take gift cards.

steps.title: A trip to the supermarket
steps.detail: They name the brand and amount, usually a 100 or 200 card from a supermarket rack, and tell you to keep the till receipt as your 'proof of purchase'.

steps.title: Scratch and photograph
steps.detail: Next comes the request to scratch the silver panel and send a clear photo of the back. The balance is spent or resold within minutes of that picture arriving.

steps.title: The code 'did not work'
steps.detail: The seller claims the card failed or was already used and asks for a second one. When you refuse, the listing disappears and your messages go unread.

marketplace-gift-card-payment-scam.whyItWorks: A gift card feels like a small, ordinary purchase from a shop you trust, and you still hold the plastic afterwards. The value lives entirely in the digits under the scratch panel, which the other person can spend from anywhere.

realVsFake.real: Genuine marketplace sellers take cash on collection or the platform's own checkout, where a dispute can be opened.
realVsFake.fake: The scammer says cash and the app are both impossible this week, and a store card is the only option left.

realVsFake.real: A gift card is designed to be spent with the retailer that issued it, and many now carry a printed warning about sharing codes.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the code is a 'verification' or a refundable hold, and that reading it out is safe because you keep the card.

realVsFake.real: A real buyer who cannot pay yet simply waits, or loses the item to someone who can.
realVsFake.fake: A fake buyer of your item asks you to purchase a card yourself for a courier or 'insurance' charge they promise to repay.

steps.title: A glossy introduction site
steps.detail: The agency's website shows hundreds of striking profiles and lets you join free. Within hours, several women have written long, affectionate letters to you.

steps.title: Credits for every letter
steps.detail: Reading or answering each letter costs credits. So does live chat by the minute, and a 'translation fee' is added because she supposedly speaks no English.

steps.title: Flowers, perfume and a photo
steps.detail: The agency suggests gifts from its own catalogue at inflated prices. A staged photo of her holding the bouquet arrives, and swapping phone numbers is forbidden or costs extra.

steps.title: The visa that ends it
steps.detail: When you push to meet, the agency bills you for her visa, travel insurance and an escorted trip. Once that is paid she falls ill, or her account closes.

marriage-agency-scam.whyItWorks: Paying a company feels safer than sending money to a stranger, and each charge is small enough to seem like the normal cost of courting across a language barrier. The letters are often written by paid staff, so the affection never runs dry while credits keep selling.

realVsFake.real: A reputable introduction service charges a stated membership fee and lets matched couples swap contact details freely.
realVsFake.fake: Every letter, chat minute and translated line is billed separately, and direct email or phone contact is blocked.

realVsFake.real: Someone genuinely interested will video call you on an ordinary free app, even with clumsy English.
realVsFake.fake: Calls only happen through the agency's paid video room, with an interpreter present and the clock running.

realVsFake.real: A visa applicant pays the embassy herself and can show you the appointment confirmation.
realVsFake.fake: The agency collects visa and travel money on her behalf, then reports a refusal or a sudden family emergency.

steps.title: A proposal before meeting
steps.detail: After weeks of daily messages, your partner abroad says they want to marry you and move to your country. They start calling you husband or wife.

steps.title: The paperwork list
steps.detail: They send a list of costs: passport renewal, a fiancé visa application, a medical exam, a police certificate. Each one is a few hundred, sent by money transfer.

steps.title: An agent takes over
steps.detail: A 'visa agent' or 'immigration lawyer' emails you scanned forms with stamps, then says the embassy needs proof of funds deposited in your partner's name.

steps.title: Approved, then delayed again
steps.detail: The visa is 'approved' but the flight is missed over an exit tax or a document error. New fees follow until you stop paying, and then the replies stop.

marriage-visa-scam.whyItWorks: Immigration really is slow and full of forms most people have never seen, so a stamped PDF and a named fee sound plausible. Each payment also feels like the last obstacle between you and a wedding you have already pictured.

realVsFake.real: Visa fees are published on the government's own website and paid directly to the embassy or its visa centre.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to wire the fee to your partner, a cousin or an 'agent' with a personal account.

realVsFake.real: Countries that grant fiancé visas generally expect the couple to have met face to face first.
realVsFake.fake: The application is supposedly going ahead although you have never met, and every video call falls through.

realVsFake.real: A genuine applicant has receipts and appointment emails from the embassy that they can forward without hesitation.
realVsFake.fake: You get blurry scans with mismatched fonts, and questions about them are met with hurt feelings.

steps.title: 'Someone who cares about you'
steps.detail: A recorded call says a family member or your doctor has ordered you a free medical alert pendant, and to press 1 to arrange delivery.

steps.title: Already paid for
steps.detail: A live agent says the device is paid for and boxed. They only need to confirm your address, your age and whether you live alone.

steps.title: Activating the monitoring
steps.detail: Before it ships, a card or bank account is needed to 'activate the monitoring service', described as a formality your relative did not get round to.

steps.title: The monthly debit begins
steps.detail: From then on a monthly charge of thirty-odd pounds or dollars leaves your account. A cheap pendant may turn up with an invoice, or nothing arrives and the number is dead.

medical-alert-scam.whyItWorks: Grown-up children do buy these pendants for a parent, often without mentioning it first, so the story is believable. Turning down a present from family feels ungrateful, and someone who lives alone may already have been worrying about a fall.

realVsFake.real: A relative who bought you an alarm would say so, and would have chosen the company and arranged the bill.
realVsFake.fake: The agent cannot name the family member who ordered it and says that information is 'confidential'.

realVsFake.real: Genuine alarm providers show the monthly price and cancellation terms in a written agreement before taking payment.
realVsFake.fake: The price of monitoring is mentioned once, quickly, after you have already read out the card number.

realVsFake.real: Established firms sell through their own website, a pharmacy or a referral from your doctor or local council.
realVsFake.fake: The offer exists only as a recorded voice on your landline, from a company whose name changes between calls.

steps.title: Be your own billing business
steps.detail: An advert or webinar says doctors are desperate to outsource insurance claims, and that anyone with a computer can run a medical billing business from a spare room.

steps.title: The sales call with income figures
steps.detail: A representative walks you through what you would earn per claim, mentions local practices 'already waiting', and offers the software and certification bundle for 399 dollars if you enrol today.

steps.title: Software and a list of names
steps.detail: You receive a download of basic claims software, a short manual and a 'client lead list', which is a directory of clinics that have never heard of the company.

steps.title: Clinics say no, refunds denied
steps.detail: Each clinic you ring already has in-house staff or an established billing firm. The refund terms require proof that you contacted hundreds of practices, and support stops replying.

medical-billing-job-scam.whyItWorks: Healthcare paperwork is known to be vast and complicated, so a shortage of people to process it sounds believable. Selling it as a business, not a job, shifts the blame: when no clients appear, buyers conclude they failed at marketing.

realVsFake.real: Medical practices hand billing to trained in-house staff or to established billing companies with contracts and privacy obligations.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch says doctors will give patient records and claims to a newcomer working alone with a mail-order certificate.

realVsFake.real: Billing and coding credentials that employers accept are issued by professional associations after months of coursework and a proctored exam.
realVsFake.fake: The 'certification' is a printable page you receive after a weekend of reading the manual.

realVsFake.real: A company with real client demand would hire billers on wages and keep the profit itself.
realVsFake.fake: The seller's only revenue is the bundle, and its promise of clients ends the moment your card is charged.

steps.title: The 'new plastic card' call
steps.detail: A caller says Medicare is replacing paper cards with plastic or chip versions and yours cannot be posted until the account is verified.

steps.title: They read your details back
steps.detail: To sound official they recite your name, address and perhaps your doctor's name, details that are easy to buy or look up, then ask you to 'confirm' the rest.

steps.title: Reading out the card number
steps.detail: The rest is the Medicare number printed on your card and your date of birth. Refund versions add a bank account 'for the deposit'.

steps.title: Claims you never made
steps.detail: No card comes. Your number is used to bill Medicare for braces, tests or equipment you never received, and the charges surface months later on your summary notice.

medicare-scam.whyItWorks: Medicare has replaced everyone's card before, so a call about new cards sounds like a repeat of something that really happened. A stranger who already knows your address and doctor seems to have your file open, and confirming one more number feels harmless.

realVsFake.real: Medicare posts cards automatically and free of charge. You never have to ring, confirm or pay for one.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says your card is on hold and will be cancelled unless you read the number out today.

realVsFake.real: Medicare writes to you. It phones only when you have called first or asked for a call back.
realVsFake.fake: The call comes from nowhere, often with a caller ID reading 'Medicare' or a Washington area code.

realVsFake.real: Braces, monitors and other equipment are covered when your own doctor prescribes them after seeing you.
realVsFake.fake: A telemarketer offers a 'free' back brace and says they will handle the doctor's paperwork for you.

steps.title: A signed shirt at half price
steps.detail: A listing offers a jersey, guitar scratchplate or photo signed by a famous name, with a 'certificate of authenticity' and a price well under what dealers charge.

steps.title: The stage-door story
steps.detail: Asked where it was signed, the seller mentions a stage door, a charity dinner or a hotel lobby, with no photo of the signing and no ticket stub.

steps.title: A certificate from nobody
steps.detail: The certificate arrives as a glossy card with a hologram sticker. The company named on it has no searchable database, or is the seller under another name.

steps.title: Paid, posted, worthless
steps.detail: You pay by bank transfer for the 'today only' discount. The item does arrive, but the autograph was added with a marker pen or printed onto the fabric.

memorabilia-scam.whyItWorks: An autograph is a few strokes of marker that almost nobody can judge by eye, so buyers lean on the certificate. Anyone can print one, and a hologram sticker makes a home-made card look like an official verdict.

realVsFake.real: Recognised authenticators give each item a serial number that you can type into their public database to see the same item.
realVsFake.fake: The certificate carries a signature and a shiny sticker but no number, or a number that brings up nothing anywhere.

realVsFake.real: Reputable dealers photograph the exact piece from several angles and will send a new picture with today's date beside it.
realVsFake.fake: The same signed jersey image appears in several adverts from different accounts, sometimes with the watermark cropped off.

realVsFake.real: Genuine signatures vary slightly each time, with pen pressure and the odd skipped stroke where the fabric creased.
realVsFake.fake: Forged batches look identical from item to item, slow and shaky in the line, or perfectly flat because they were printed.

steps.title: A rep arrives with a savings sheet
steps.detail: A salesperson visits the shop or phones, glances at one card statement and announces they can cut your processing costs by a large margin.

steps.title: The headline rate
steps.detail: They quote one low debit rate and call the terminal 'free'. Monthly minimums, compliance charges and higher rates for credit and business cards go unmentioned.

steps.title: Two signatures on a tablet
steps.detail: You sign on a tablet at the counter. One signature is for processing, the other a separate equipment lease with a finance company, often for four or five years.

steps.title: Statements that don't match the pitch
steps.detail: Fees appear that were never discussed. Cancelling the processing leaves the lease running, and ending that means paying every remaining month at once.

merchant-services-scam.whyItWorks: Card statements are hard to read, so an owner cannot easily tell what they pay now, let alone test a rep's comparison. A promise of lower fees from someone standing at the counter during trading hours gets a signature before the paperwork gets read.

realVsFake.real: A fair provider gives a full written schedule of every rate and monthly charge, and leaves it with you to compare.
realVsFake.fake: The rep shows a one-page savings estimate, keeps the contract on their own tablet and wants it signed before they leave.

realVsFake.real: Card readers can be bought outright for a modest one-off price or rented on a short rolling term.
realVsFake.fake: A basic terminal is leased for years at a total many times its shop price, under a contract that cannot be cancelled.

realVsFake.real: Reputable processors state the exit terms plainly, and the same company handles both the reader and the processing.
realVsFake.fake: The seller is an independent agent, and complaints bounce between the processor, the leasing firm and a rep who has moved on.

steps.title: A violation notice in your inbox
steps.detail: A profile named something like 'Meta Business Support', using the blue infinity logo as its picture, messages you or tags your page in a post about a breach.

steps.title: Twenty-four hours to appeal
steps.detail: The text cites community standards or a copyright complaint and says the page will be permanently removed unless you file an appeal through the link today.

steps.title: The appeal form
steps.detail: Styled in Meta colours, the page asks for your page name, email, phone and date of birth, then says you must 'confirm ownership' by entering your password.

steps.title: The code that finishes it
steps.detail: Last comes a box for the six-digit login code just texted to you. The scammers are signing in live, and that code lets them past two-factor protection.

meta-support-dm-scam.whyItWorks: For anyone who runs a business page, losing it means losing customers and ad accounts overnight. Real removals do happen with little explanation, so an appeal deadline sounds plausible and filling in a form feels like the responsible reaction.

realVsFake.real: Meta does not open conversations by DM about violations. Notices show up in your account's own status and support sections.
realVsFake.fake: An ordinary profile or page with a support-sounding name sends the warning as a chat message or a tagged post.

realVsFake.real: A real appeal is filed with a button inside Facebook or Instagram while you are already logged in.
realVsFake.fake: The 'appeal' lives on an outside website and cannot be submitted until you type your password again.

realVsFake.real: Meta's staff never need the login code sent to your phone, because that code is meant only for you.
realVsFake.fake: The form's last step asks for the texted code and warns the appeal will fail without it.

steps.title: 'Here to read the meter'
steps.detail: A person in a hi-vis vest with a handheld device says a reading is overdue because your bills have been estimated, and asks where the meter is kept.

steps.title: The lanyard flash
steps.detail: An ID card is held up for a second. It carries a logo and a photo but no number you could check, and they step forward as they show it.

steps.title: A fault is discovered
steps.detail: After a glance at the dials they announce a broken seal, signs of tampering or dangerous wiring, and say the supply must be isolated unless it is dealt with today.

steps.title: Payment in the hallway
steps.detail: They ask for cash or a card payment for a 'recalibration', or copy your account number and bank details from a bill 'to update the records'.

meter-reading-scam.whyItWorks: Meter readers really do turn up without a fixed appointment, and most people have let one in before without a second thought. The meter lives in a cupboard few householders understand, so a claimed fault is hard to argue with.

realVsFake.real: Many suppliers let you register a doorstep password that a genuine reader must quote before stepping inside.
realVsFake.fake: The caller has never heard of the password and says the system is 'being updated'.

realVsFake.real: A real reader notes the figures and is gone within a couple of minutes, without asking for money.
realVsFake.fake: A problem is 'found' that must be paid for immediately, in cash or on a handheld card reader.

realVsFake.real: If a meter is faulty, the supplier writes to you, books an engineer and puts any cost on your account.
realVsFake.fake: The visitor diagnoses, prices and offers to fix the fault within a single visit.

steps.title: Your password is already out
steps.detail: The attacker starts with a working password, usually from an old data breach or a phishing page. The only thing in their way is the approval on your phone.

steps.title: The prompts start arriving
steps.detail: They try to sign in again and again, so your authenticator app buzzes with 'Approve sign-in?' requests, sometimes dozens in a row and often late at night.

steps.title: A helpful voice from 'IT'
steps.detail: A call or chat message claims to be the help desk. They say a system fault is causing the alerts and that tapping Approve once will clear it.

steps.title: One tap lets them in
steps.detail: You approve to make the buzzing stop. The attacker is now signed in, registers their own phone as a trusted device, and may change your recovery details.

mfa-fatigue-scam.whyItWorks: An approval prompt looks the same whether you or a stranger caused it, and people dismiss notifications on reflex. After the twentieth buzz at one in the morning, tapping Approve feels like silencing an alarm, not opening a door.

realVsFake.real: A genuine prompt appears seconds after you type your own password, on a device you are holding.
realVsFake.fake: Requests turn up while you are asleep, driving or nowhere near a login screen, and keep repeating.

realVsFake.real: Help desks and account providers do not ask you to accept a sign-in that you did not begin.
realVsFake.fake: Someone claiming to be support says approving is the fix, or asks you to read out the number shown.

realVsFake.real: Denying a prompt has no side effects. Your account stays as it was and you can change the password calmly.
realVsFake.fake: The attacker suggests that refusing will lock the account or that the alerts will continue all night.

steps.title: Your account number is already known
steps.detail: A fraudster holding your sort code and account number, from a cheque, an invoice or a leak, adds your account as a funding source on a payment app or brokerage.

steps.title: Two tiny credits appear
steps.detail: That service sends two deposits of a few pence or cents to prove ownership. You see odd small credits with a reference you do not recognise.

steps.title: A message asks for the amounts
steps.detail: A text, email or caller posing as your bank or the service says the deposits were a 'security test' and asks you to confirm both figures.

steps.title: The link goes live
steps.detail: Once the amounts are entered, the service treats the account as theirs to use and pulls money out by bank debit, in sums that grow.

micro-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: Receiving money feels harmless, and two amounts of a few pennies do not seem like a secret worth protecting. Hardly anyone realises that those figures work as a password proving control of the account.

realVsFake.real: Micro-deposits appear only after you have added your bank account to a service yourself, and you type the amounts into that service.
realVsFake.fake: The credits arrive when you have signed up for nothing, and a stranger wants the figures.

realVsFake.real: A company running the check never rings to ask what it sent, since it already knows.
realVsFake.fake: A caller says they need you to read out both amounts to 'cancel' or 'verify' the link.

realVsFake.real: Your bank can tell you which company sent a credit and can block future debits from it.
realVsFake.fake: The message warns you not to contact the bank because the 'test' will fail.

steps.title: Unusual sign-in activity
steps.detail: Microsoft's plain layout is copied closely: 'Sign-in details', a country, an IP address, a browser. Below, the fake adds something the real one never says: your account closes in 24 hours.

steps.title: The 'Review recent activity' button
steps.detail: The blue button opens a page with the four-colour logo and the 'Enter password' box used by Outlook and Hotmail. Your email address is already filled in.

steps.title: Password, then 'incorrect'
steps.detail: You type the password and the page says it was wrong, so you type it again. Both attempts are saved, then you are bounced to the genuine Microsoft site.

steps.title: The mailbox opens every other door
steps.detail: The criminal signs in to your Outlook, creates a rule hiding security emails, then uses 'forgot password' on shopping, banking and social accounts tied to that address.

microsoft-account-email-scam.whyItWorks: An old Hotmail or Outlook address is often the recovery email for everything else, so a threat to close it is alarming. The technical details, an IP address and a country, give the message an air of forensic accuracy.

realVsFake.real: A real unusual sign-in is listed on the Recent activity page of your Microsoft account, with the same time and location.
realVsFake.fake: Recent activity shows only your own sign-ins. The foreign login described in the email is nowhere to be found.

realVsFake.real: Microsoft closes accounts after long inactivity or at the owner's request. Missing a verification email is not a reason.
realVsFake.fake: The message threatens closure within a day unless you 'verify', a deadline with no basis in how accounts work.

realVsFake.real: The real sign-in page accepts a correct password the first time.
realVsFake.fake: The page rejects your password once whatever you type, so that it captures the same entry twice.

steps.title: A landline call about your computer
steps.detail: A caller with a call-centre hum behind them gives a name and an employee number, and says Windows has been sending error reports from your address.

steps.title: The 'unique licence ID'
steps.detail: They have you open the command prompt, type 'assoc', and read a long code aloud. They recite it too, though the same code appears on every Windows PC.

steps.title: Event Viewer as evidence
steps.detail: Next you are guided to Event Viewer, where yellow and red entries are normal. The caller counts them as infections and says the licence is about to lapse.

steps.title: A support plan, paid on the spot
steps.detail: After connecting through a remote tool, they offer one-year or lifetime cover and take card details by phone. Some set a startup password and charge to remove it.

microsoft-support-scam.whyItWorks: Nearly every household with a PC runs Windows, so the caller is right about that without knowing anything. Reading back a code that matches the one on your own screen feels like proof of identity to anyone unfamiliar with the command prompt.

realVsFake.real: Microsoft says it does not phone people to report problems with their computers. Any contact starts with you.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger rings a number found in a directory and claims your PC has been flagged at a 'security centre'.

realVsFake.real: A Windows licence bought with the computer does not run out and needs no yearly renewal.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says your licence key ends today and the machine will be switched off remotely.

realVsFake.real: Windows security updates arrive through Windows Update at no charge.
realVsFake.fake: The 'engineer' sells firewall or network protection as a multi-year plan and prefers payment by card over the phone or gift cards.

steps.title: Listings near the base
steps.detail: Adverts for houses close to an installation appear on classifieds and in spouse groups around transfer season, priced just under the local housing allowance.

steps.title: A fellow service member
steps.detail: The 'landlord' says they are active duty too, currently deployed or on orders overseas, and offers a military discount as thanks for your service.

steps.title: Timed to your report date
steps.detail: They ask when you report and stress that homes vanish before PCS season. With a cross-country move pending, visiting in person is difficult for you anyway.

steps.title: Wire the deposit, keys to follow
steps.detail: You wire the deposit and first month. Keys are supposedly left with a neighbour or mailed. The family arrives to an occupied house and no landlord.

military-housing-scam.whyItWorks: Orders set a fixed report date and often leave no chance to visit beforehand, so renting unseen is normal for military families. A landlord who claims to be deployed explains the absence and borrows the trust service members extend to each other.

realVsFake.real: The installation's housing office keeps lists of local rentals and will look over a listing or lease for you.
realVsFake.fake: The landlord discourages contacting the housing office and says it only slows things down.

realVsFake.real: A genuinely deployed owner appoints a property manager or someone holding power of attorney to show and let the home.
realVsFake.fake: The 'deployed' owner has nobody local, and everything hinges on a wire sent to them.

realVsFake.real: Landlords near bases are used to the military clause and send a full lease before any money moves.
realVsFake.fake: You get a two-line email agreement and a request for gift cards or an e-transfer before your PCS date.

steps.title: A celebrity 'secret' story
steps.detail: An article styled like a news site claims a TV doctor or actor lost weight with one capsule, and that the industry wants it hidden.

steps.title: Before-and-after proof
steps.detail: Scrolling down shows stolen transformation photos and comments from 'readers'. Every link on the page leads to the same order form.

steps.title: A trial bottle for postage
steps.detail: You pay a few pounds for shipping. The terms, far below the button, enrol you in monthly bottles at full price after a short trial.

steps.title: Pills, charges and no reply
steps.detail: Unlabelled capsules arrive with no ingredient list worth trusting. Large monthly payments start, and the 'customer care' address returns nothing.

miracle-supplement-scam.whyItWorks: People who have tried diets for years want to believe one thing will finally work, and a familiar face seems to vouch for it. The fake article format borrows the authority of journalism, so the claims read as reporting instead of advertising.

realVsFake.real: Licensed medicines for weight or illness are prescribed and dispensed by pharmacists, with a patient leaflet inside.
realVsFake.fake: A capsule sold through an advert claims to melt fat or reverse a disease without diet or doctor.

realVsFake.real: Celebrities who endorse a product do so on their own verified channels.
realVsFake.fake: The famous face appears only on the sales page, in a doctored photo or invented interview.

realVsFake.real: A real supplement lists every ingredient and dose, plus a maker you can contact.
realVsFake.fake: The label says 'proprietary blend', and the bottle carries no batch number or address.

steps.title: A card on the doormat
steps.detail: A printed 'Sorry we missed you' card comes through the letterbox, often along a whole street, carrying a generic parcel logo instead of a known courier's name.

steps.title: Blank boxes where details belong
steps.detail: The spaces for sender, tracking number and time of visit are empty or scribbled. The only instruction is to phone a number or scan a QR code.

steps.title: A long wait on hold
steps.detail: The number is premium rate. Recorded messages, menu options and hold music keep you on the line while the per-minute charge builds on your phone bill.

steps.title: The redelivery website
steps.detail: Scanning the code opens a page that charges a rebooking fee by card and collects your address, for a parcel that was never on any van.

missed-delivery-card-scam.whyItWorks: A piece of card on the mat suggests that somebody physically came to the house, which feels more official than a text. People expect fraud on a screen, so paper gets less scrutiny.

realVsFake.real: A courier's card names the company, gives a reference number and says where the parcel is now, such as a neighbour or depot.
realVsFake.fake: The card says 'Parcel Delivery Service', quotes no reference and never mentions where the item is waiting.

realVsFake.real: Genuine couriers rearrange delivery through a free website or a standard-rate helpline.
realVsFake.fake: The contact number begins with a premium prefix such as 09 and is billed by the minute.

realVsFake.real: The real card usually has handwriting or a printed label added by the driver at your door.
realVsFake.fake: Every house on the road receives the identical pre-printed card on the same morning.

steps.title: The side-hustle offer
steps.detail: On social media or a student group, someone offers quick money to anyone with a bank account and a phone, calling it 'payment processing' or a 'flip'.

steps.title: Photos of cheques arrive
steps.detail: They send images of cheques made out to you, or ask for your banking login so they can deposit them through the app themselves.

steps.title: The balance jumps
steps.detail: The deposits show as available within a day. You are told to keep a couple of hundred and move the remainder by payment app, crypto or cash withdrawal.

steps.title: The account is closed
steps.detail: The cheques come back as counterfeit or stolen. The bank removes the money, pursues you for the shortfall, and may shut the account and report you.

mobile-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: Snapping a photo in a banking app hardly feels like handling a cheque at all, and the recruiter presents it as a harmless loophole. Young people short of cash see money appear overnight and take that as confirmation it is real.

realVsFake.real: Cheques you deposit by phone should be made out to you, for something you sold or were owed.
realVsFake.fake: The cheques come from a business you have never dealt with, sent as photos by a stranger.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate employer pays you through payroll and has no need to use your personal account.
realVsFake.fake: The 'job' consists only of receiving deposits and passing most of the money on.

realVsFake.real: Nobody with an honest reason asks for your online banking username and password.
realVsFake.fake: The recruiter says it is quicker if they log in as you and make the deposits themselves.

steps.title: A cheap lot in a named park
steps.detail: An online advert offers a lot or a ready trailer in a named mobile home park, at a rent well under the neighbours', utilities included.

steps.title: The out-of-state 'owner'
steps.detail: The poster says they inherited the home or run the park from another state. They give the lot number and suggest you drive past.

steps.title: Drive by, but do not knock
steps.detail: You are asked not to disturb the 'current tenant' or the park office, which they say is being restructured or does not deal with their lot.

steps.title: Deposit to hold the lot
steps.detail: A deposit and first month go by wire or gift card. When you finally ask at the park office, the lot is occupied or was never for rent.

mobile-home-rental-scam.whyItWorks: Driving past feels like a viewing, and the trailer really is there with a lot number on it. Lot rents are low to begin with, so a bargain price does not stand out the way it would for a house.

realVsFake.real: Mobile home parks take an application through the park office, which approves every resident before move-in.
realVsFake.fake: The owner says the office need not be involved and warns you against calling it.

realVsFake.real: Park managers work on site or keep posted office hours, and can show you the lot and the park rules.
realVsFake.fake: The 'manager' lives in another state and can be reached only on a mobile.

realVsFake.real: A real owner renting out a trailer can produce the title and a current lot lease in their name.
realVsFake.fake: Ownership rests on a story about an inheritance, with no document behind it.

steps.title: A nearly new scooter, cheap
steps.detail: The advert shows a mobility scooter or powered wheelchair described as barely used, often said to belong to a parent who has died or moved into care.

steps.title: Delivery offered, viewing declined
steps.detail: When you ask to try it, the seller says they live far away but can have it delivered to your door, which sounds helpful if travelling is hard.

steps.title: A deposit to book the van
steps.detail: They ask for a holding deposit by bank transfer or voucher code to cover the van, promising the balance can be paid to the driver on arrival.

steps.title: The delivery day that slips
steps.detail: The van is delayed, then the battery 'needs replacing' for an extra sum. Eventually the phone goes dead, or a worn-out chair with a failed motor turns up.

mobility-equipment-scam.whyItWorks: New scooters and powered chairs cost a great deal, so a second-hand one is often the only affordable route. A buyer who cannot easily travel to inspect it welcomes the offer of home delivery, and that removes the one check that would expose the advert.

realVsFake.real: A mobility shop or honest private seller lets you sit on the scooter, drive it and check the battery charge indicator.
realVsFake.fake: You only ever see three photos, and a request for a short video of it moving is ignored.

realVsFake.real: Dealers supply the charger, the manual and a written warranty, and can tell you the age of the batteries.
realVsFake.fake: The seller does not know the model name, the weight limit or whether a charger is included.

realVsFake.real: With a genuine home delivery, payment is taken when the equipment is in front of you and working.
realVsFake.fake: Money has to move first to 'secure the driver', and a relative who offers to collect in person is turned away.

steps.title: A scout slides into your messages
steps.detail: A direct message on a photo-sharing app says a scout spotted your pictures and you have 'the look' for international campaigns. The profile shows glossy shoots lifted from real models.

steps.title: Compliments and a casting call
steps.detail: A booker follows up with praise and names a fashion client casting next week. You are invited to a 'test shoot' or told to reply YES to reserve one of a few places.

steps.title: The portfolio package
steps.detail: Nothing can go to clients, they say, without professional images. The agency's own photographer will produce your portfolio and comp cards for 350 dollars, payable before the shoot.

steps.title: Classes, listing fees, no bookings
steps.detail: After the photos come runway classes and a monthly fee to stay on the agency's website. Castings are always 'coming soon', and the campaign you were scouted for is never mentioned again.

modeling-agency-scam.whyItWorks: Being told by a stranger that you have a rare look is flattering in a way a job advert never is, and stories of models discovered by chance are part of fashion folklore. Paying for photos then feels like backing yourself.

realVsFake.real: A scout from a real agency gives a full name, and the agency's front desk will confirm that person works there.
realVsFake.fake: The scout's account is weeks old, uses a first name only, and the agency it names has no record of them.

realVsFake.real: To assess a new face, a real agency asks for plain snapshots in natural light, taken on a phone.
realVsFake.fake: You are told that nothing can happen until you have paid for studio pictures from their photographer.

realVsFake.real: When an agency does arrange test shots for a signed model, the cost is usually recouped from later earnings, not demanded upfront.
realVsFake.fake: Everyone who pays for the package is 'signed', because selling shoots is the whole business.

steps.title: An invitation from someone you trust
steps.detail: A relative, colleague or church friend shares a colourful wheel graphic with names in rings. They say they have already been paid and it really works.

steps.title: Buying an outer-ring seat
steps.detail: You send $100 by payment app to the person at the centre, labelled as a gift. Eight people on the outer ring fund one $800 payout.

steps.title: The board splits
steps.detail: Once the centre is paid, the wheel divides in two and everyone moves inward. Each new wheel needs eight fresh payers, and you are urged to bring friends.

steps.title: Recruits run out
steps.detail: The number of new people needed doubles at every split. The group chat goes quiet, the organisers leave, and those on the outer rings never reach the middle.

money-circle-scam.whyItWorks: It borrows the name and warmth of savings clubs that many communities have run honestly for generations, and it arrives from a friend who truly was paid. Early payouts are real, funded by the people who joined after them.

realVsFake.real: A traditional sou-sou has a fixed group who each pay in every round and take turns receiving the pot.
realVsFake.fake: A blessing loom only pays if strangers keep joining underneath you, and it has no end date.

realVsFake.real: In a real savings club you get back what you contributed, no more, because no money is created.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch promises eight times your stake for a single payment and a few invitations.

realVsFake.real: Members of a genuine club know each other and can say who holds the money this month.
realVsFake.fake: Participants appear as first names or emojis on a chart, and you are coached to describe payments as gifts.

steps.title: A job title that sounds official
steps.detail: A message on a chat app or social feed offers work as a 'payment processing agent' or 'transfer assistant', a few minutes a day, paid as a cut of each transaction.

steps.title: Questions about your bank
steps.detail: The recruiter's main interest is your bank. They ask which one you use, your daily transfer limit, and sometimes tell you to open a fresh account with a particular app.

steps.title: A deposit from a stranger
steps.detail: Money lands in your account from a name you do not know. It came from a victim of another fraud, perhaps a romance or invoice scam, who believes they paid a real business.

steps.title: Out again within the hour
steps.detail: Instructions follow fast: take your cut, then push everything else out by international transfer, cryptocurrency or cash withdrawal. When the victim reports the loss, the trail stops at your name.

money-mule-job-scam.whyItWorks: The task is so simple, and the first payment so prompt, that it feels like found money with nothing to lose. Recruits are told the firm just needs local accounts to avoid bank delays, which hides the fact that their account is the product being bought.

realVsFake.real: Companies that process payments are licensed firms using merchant accounts in the business's name.
realVsFake.fake: The 'company' has no account of its own and needs a new private individual's account every few weeks.

realVsFake.real: A wage is paid for work done, into your account, and stays there.
realVsFake.fake: Your 'pay' is whatever is left after you forward most of a stranger's deposit, and speed matters more than anything.

realVsFake.real: An employer never needs to know your transfer limits or ask you to lie to your bank about a payment.
realVsFake.fake: You are given a script: if the bank calls, say the money is a gift from a relative.

steps.title: A buyer who prefers paper
steps.detail: Someone answers your listing, agrees the price without haggling, and says they will post a money order because they are travelling or buying for a relative.

steps.title: The envelope holds too much
steps.detail: The money order arrives made out for 1,200 against an 800 item. A note explains the surplus covers the courier, and asks you to pass 400 on to their agent.

steps.title: Your bank shows the deposit
steps.detail: You pay it in at the counter and the balance goes up within a day or two. That is the bank advancing the funds, not confirming the paper is genuine.

steps.title: Counterfeit found, debit follows
steps.detail: Weeks later the issuer rejects the money order as a forgery. Your bank takes the full amount back, and the goods plus the 400 you forwarded are gone.

money-order-scam.whyItWorks: A money order feels like cash because someone supposedly paid for it up front at a post office or shop counter. When the bank credits it, sellers assume it has been checked, but the check against the issuer comes much later.

realVsFake.real: A genuine buyer sends a money order for the exact price and is happy for you to wait until the issuer confirms it.
realVsFake.fake: The amount is hundreds over, and the buyer wants the item posted and the change wired before you can check anything.

realVsFake.real: Money order issuers let you verify the serial number and amount with them directly before you release anything.
realVsFake.fake: The forgery has blurred print, a missing watermark or an amount that looks altered, and the buyer says there is no time to ring the issuer.

realVsFake.real: Someone who overpays by accident asks for the money order back so they can send a correct one.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to keep the paper and send the difference to a third person described as a shipper or agent.

steps.title: Good news with a catch
steps.detail: A message or call says a prize, parcel or approved loan is waiting, and only a small release fee stands between you and it.

steps.title: Only one way to pay
steps.detail: Card and bank transfer are refused with an excuse about tax or processing delays. You are sent to a Western Union or MoneyGram counter instead.

steps.title: A stranger's name on the form
steps.detail: The receiver is a private individual, often in another city or country, described as the company's cashier or agent. You may be coached on what to tell the clerk.

steps.title: The reference number is the key
steps.detail: Once you text over the tracking number from your receipt, the cash is collected within minutes using fake identification. A second fee is then invented.

money-transfer-service-scam.whyItWorks: Walking into a branded transfer counter feels official, and staff accept the cash without question. People assume a payment that needs a form and a receipt can be traced or cancelled later, when in practice a collected cash transfer is finished.

realVsFake.real: Transfer services are built for sending money to relatives and friends you know in person, and they say so on their forms.
realVsFake.fake: A business, lottery or lender asks you to wire a fee to a named individual you have never met.

realVsFake.real: The tracking number on your receipt is for you and the person collecting, nobody else.
realVsFake.fake: The caller stays on the line until you photograph the receipt and send it, then stops answering.

realVsFake.real: A real lender takes its charges out of the loan, and a real courier bills customs through its own checkout.
realVsFake.fake: Every fee must travel as cash to a different receiver name each time, and you are told to say it is a gift for family.

steps.title: An advert that ignores your credit
steps.detail: A social media ad or cold message promises mortgage approval whatever your credit file says, at a rate well below anything high street lenders quote.

steps.title: Approval in a single phone call
steps.detail: The 'broker' takes your income and address, asks for no payslips or bank statements, and rings back the same day to say a lender has agreed in principle.

steps.title: The rate lock fee
steps.detail: To hold the rate you must pay a 500 arrangement fee by bank transfer today. It is described as fully refundable when the mortgage completes.

steps.title: Insurance, valuation, then silence
steps.detail: More charges follow for a valuation or indemnity insurance. No offer letter from a lender ever arrives, and the phone number and website go dead.

mortgage-broker-scam.whyItWorks: People who have been turned down elsewhere badly want to hear yes, and real mortgages do involve arrangement and valuation fees. A refundable charge sounds like a small price for a rate that might vanish tomorrow.

realVsFake.real: A real broker appears on the financial regulator's public register under the same firm name and phone number they gave you.
realVsFake.fake: The firm name is close to a known lender's, but the register entry is missing or lists different contact details.

realVsFake.real: Lenders check payslips, bank statements and your credit file before saying yes, and some applicants are declined.
realVsFake.fake: Approval is guaranteed before anyone has seen a document, with the fee request arriving in the same call.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fees are itemised in a written mortgage illustration, and many can be added to the loan or paid at completion.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to transfer the fee to a personal account, with nothing in writing beyond a chat message promising a refund.

steps.title: 'Your MOT is overdue'
steps.detail: A text says the vehicle's MOT or service date has passed and that a penalty applies unless you book and pay online today.

steps.title: Registration plate lookup
steps.detail: The page asks for the number plate and shows a make and model, which anyone can look up, to suggest it holds your records.

steps.title: Choose a test centre
