steps.detail: A list of garages 'near you' with time slots appears. Selecting one requires name, address, phone number and an advance payment for the test.

steps.title: Payment with no garage attached
steps.detail: Card details are taken for the test fee or a 'late penalty'. No garage has the booking, and the car is no closer to a valid certificate.

mot-reminder-text-scam.whyItWorks: The MOT date comes round once a year and is easy to miss, and drivers know an expired certificate can mean a fine and void insurance. A reminder that happens to arrive near the right month looks like a helpful service.

realVsFake.real: The government's MOT reminder is free, something you sign up for yourself, and it only tells you the due date.
realVsFake.fake: A reminder you never subscribed to arrives with a payment link attached.

realVsFake.real: You book an MOT directly with a garage or test centre and pay that garage for the test.
realVsFake.fake: The page takes money in advance for an unnamed 'approved centre' and sends no booking confirmation.

realVsFake.real: You can see a vehicle's MOT expiry date free on the government's MOT history service by entering the registration.
realVsFake.fake: The text adds a 'late penalty' to the test price and says it rises tomorrow.

steps.title: A quote without a survey
steps.detail: You request prices online and one firm comes back far cheaper, quoting over the phone by number of rooms without visiting or asking for an inventory.

steps.title: Half up front
steps.detail: A booking email asks for a large deposit to 'secure the truck'. The estimate attached is non-binding, with weight or cubic footage left as an approximate figure.

steps.title: Loaded, then repriced
steps.detail: On moving day an unmarked rental van arrives. Once everything is aboard, the foreman announces the load is bigger than quoted and adds charges for stairs, packing tape and long carry.

steps.title: Furniture held for cash
steps.detail: At the other end the crew refuse to open the doors until the new total is paid in cash, or they drive your belongings to a storage yard.

moving-company-scam.whyItWorks: Moving has a fixed date, a lease ending and a household packed into boxes, so there is no room to start again. Once the furniture is locked in someone else's truck, paying the inflated bill looks like the only way to see it again.

realVsFake.real: A reputable remover walks through your home or does a video survey, then puts a written, itemised price in your hands.
realVsFake.fake: The rogue firm quotes in two minutes by phone and avoids committing the final figure to paper.

realVsFake.real: Established movers take a small booking fee or nothing, with the balance due on delivery by card or bank payment.
realVsFake.fake: Half the price is demanded weeks ahead, and the remainder must be banknotes handed over before a single box comes off.

realVsFake.real: A real company has its name on the lorry, a depot address, and insurance and licence numbers you can look up.
realVsFake.fake: The crew turn up in a hired van, the paperwork shows a different trading name, and the office line goes to voicemail.

steps.title: Unclaimed parcels for sale
steps.detail: An advert shows a pallet of 'undelivered packages' or returned electronics, sold blind at 9.99 a box, with phones and earbuds poking out.

steps.title: Unboxing videos as bait
steps.detail: Clips show buyers pulling out a tablet or a designer watch. The wording says 'worth up to' a large sum, which promises nothing at all.

steps.title: A box, plus a membership
steps.detail: At checkout a pre-ticked line adds a 'VIP club' with a monthly fee. Only a few boxes are said to remain.

steps.title: A phone case and a keyring
steps.detail: The box holds pound-shop trinkets, or never comes. The club fee keeps leaving your account under a name you do not recognise.

mystery-box-scam.whyItWorks: It is a gamble dressed as shopping: the low price makes losing feel affordable and the unboxing clips make winning feel likely. Since the contents are secret by design, a buyer cannot prove what should have been inside.

realVsFake.real: Genuine lost-parcel auctions are run by carriers or licensed auction houses, in person or on their own named sites.
realVsFake.fake: A pop-up shop on social media claims to be clearing a courier's warehouse.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate surprise bundle from a known retailer states a minimum value and what category of goods to expect.
realVsFake.fake: The only figure given is a ceiling, 'up to five hundred', with no floor.

realVsFake.real: One-off purchases stay one-off unless you choose a subscription on a clearly labelled page.
realVsFake.fake: A recurring club charge is tucked into a ticked box under the order total.

steps.title: Recruited as a secret shopper
steps.detail: A letter or email, sometimes using a real research firm's name, says you have been accepted as a secret shopper who will rate local stores and services for a fee.

steps.title: Assignment pack with a cheque
steps.detail: The first assignment arrives by post: a cheque for 1,950 dollars, an instruction sheet and an evaluation form asking about queue times and how polite the counter staff were.

steps.title: 'Test' the money-transfer counter
steps.detail: You are to pay the cheque in, keep 300 as your fee, and wire 1,650 to a named 'test recipient' at a money-transfer desk, noting how long the clerk takes.

steps.title: A second task: gift cards
steps.detail: Before the cheque is returned as forged, a follow-up assignment may send you to buy gift cards and photograph the codes for 'audit'. Both amounts end up owed by you.

mystery-shopper-scam.whyItWorks: Mystery shopping is a real industry, and evaluating a transfer counter sounds like evaluating any other shop. Framing the wire as the thing being tested turns the dangerous step into the job itself, so sending money feels like doing the assignment properly.

realVsFake.real: Real mystery shopping firms have you apply on their site, then offer small jobs paying a modest fee per visit.
realVsFake.fake: An acceptance letter arrives for a role you never applied for, with a first assignment worth hundreds.

realVsFake.real: Shoppers spend a little of their own money and are reimbursed after submitting a report and receipt.
realVsFake.fake: A large cheque comes before any work, and the report matters less than how quickly the wire is sent.

realVsFake.real: Genuine assignments assess service: cleanliness, greetings, whether the till receipt was offered.
realVsFake.fake: The assignment is itself a payment to a stranger, or a purchase of gift cards whose codes you hand over.

steps.title: A relocating family replies
steps.detail: A parent answers your profile on a childcare site, explaining that the family is moving to your area next month and needs a nanny for a toddler at well above the usual rate.

steps.title: Hired by email, sight unseen
steps.detail: There is no call and no meeting. Emails describe the child's routine and allergies in detail, and you are told the job is yours because your profile 'felt right'.

steps.title: First week's pay plus 'supplies'
steps.detail: A cheque arrives covering your first week and a much larger sum for a cot, pushchair or special equipment the family wants delivered to the new house before they land.

steps.title: E-transfer to the equipment supplier
steps.detail: You are asked to send 400 dollars or more to the supplier by e-transfer as soon as the cheque shows in your balance. It is later returned as fake and the family's emails stop.

nanny-job-scam.whyItWorks: Helping a family settle in is part of what a good nanny does, so buying the baby's things feels like the first act of the job. The parent's detailed, affectionate emails about the child make it hard to imagine there is no child.

realVsFake.real: Parents hiring someone to mind their child want to meet in person, see references and usually run a trial day.
realVsFake.fake: The family commits to you from another city or country without hearing your voice once.

realVsFake.real: A family that needs a pushchair orders it themselves and has it delivered to their own door.
realVsFake.fake: A brand-new nanny is made the go-between for a supplier who takes payment only by e-transfer.

realVsFake.real: Nannies are paid after the week is worked, for the hours agreed.
realVsFake.fake: Wages come before your first day, bundled into a cheque several times larger than a week's pay.

steps.title: The robot voice
steps.detail: A recorded message, often from a mobile number, says your National Insurance number has been suspended after suspicious activity and tells you to press 1.

steps.title: An 'officer' explains the fraud
steps.detail: A live voice says the number was used to open bank accounts tied to money laundering, and asks for your full name, address and the number itself.

steps.title: Your accounts will be frozen
steps.detail: You are warned that every account linked to the old number is about to be frozen, and that a replacement number must be issued today.

steps.title: Paying for a new number
steps.detail: The replacement carries an admin fee by card, or you are told to shift your savings into a 'protected' account while the old number is cancelled.

national-insurance-scam.whyItWorks: People know the number matters for wages, tax and the state pension, yet few could say who administers it or what can happen to it. With that gap, 'suspended' sounds possible, and a recorded menu feels like the phone system of a big department.

realVsFake.real: A National Insurance number is issued once and stays with you for life. It is never suspended or replaced.
realVsFake.fake: The whole call depends on the idea that the number has been switched off and a fresh one is needed.

realVsFake.real: HMRC and the DWP raise National Insurance matters by letter or through your online tax account.
realVsFake.fake: A machine dials numbers in bulk and connects an 'officer' only to people who press a key.

realVsFake.real: If someone misuses your number, you report it and carry on using the same one. There is nothing to buy.
realVsFake.fake: The 'officer' quotes a fee for reissue, or asks you to empty your account into one they control.

steps.title: Your details change hands
steps.detail: A name, date of birth, address and ID number, taken from a breached database, a phishing form or a stolen letter, are sold on as a ready-made applicant profile.

steps.title: Applications in your name
steps.detail: The buyer applies online for a store card, a phone contract with a handset, or a current account with an overdraft, using your identity but their own mobile number and email.

steps.title: Spending before the first bill
steps.detail: The handset is collected and resold, the card is taken to its limit, the overdraft is emptied. All of it happens inside the first billing cycle, before any statement exists.

steps.title: The debt comes looking for you
steps.detail: Missed-payment letters, a default notice and then a collection agency arrive at your door, because your name and address are the only real things on the application.

new-account-fraud-scam.whyItWorks: Online applications are approved by matching a few data points against a credit file, with no one meeting the applicant. If the name, birth date and address agree, the lender's system sees you, and you only hear about it once payments are missed.

realVsFake.real: A welcome pack follows an application you made, from a provider you chose, and quotes details you gave them.
realVsFake.fake: A card or SIM turns up from a company you have never dealt with, sometimes showing an email address that is not yours.

realVsFake.real: Hard searches on your credit report line up with the dates you applied for something.
realVsFake.fake: Several lenders you never approached have searched your file within the same few days.

realVsFake.real: A collector chasing a real debt names a creditor you recognise and an account you once used.
realVsFake.fake: The collector's letter cites an account opened a few months ago with a phone number and email you do not own.

steps.title: A sign-in from another city
steps.detail: A message styled as a security alert says a new device signed in to your email, social or shopping account, naming a far-off location and a browser.

steps.title: 'If this was not you'
steps.detail: A button marked 'secure your account' opens a login page that matches the real service, apart from the address in the browser bar.

steps.title: Password, then the code
steps.detail: You enter your current password. The page then asks for the verification code just sent to your phone, which the real service issued because the thief is logging in.

steps.title: Recovery details swapped
steps.detail: Inside the account, they change the recovery email and phone number, sign out your devices, and use the mailbox to reset other accounts.

new-login-alert-scam.whyItWorks: Real services send near-identical alerts, and the advice everyone has heard is to act fast when a strange login appears. The scam borrows that good habit: the victim believes they are locking an intruder out while letting one in.

realVsFake.real: A genuine alert can be confirmed by opening the service yourself and viewing the list of devices signed in to your account.
realVsFake.fake: The alert gives a city and device, but nothing matching it shows in your real security settings.

realVsFake.real: Real services let you review activity after you sign in at the address you always use.
realVsFake.fake: The button takes you to a look-alike address with extra words or a different ending.

realVsFake.real: A verification code is only for the device you are personally signing in on.
realVsFake.fake: The fake page requests the code right after your password and passes both to someone else.

steps.title: 'A new payee was added'
steps.detail: A text gives an exact time, such as 14:02, and says a new recipient was set up on your account, with a phone number or link to cancel.

steps.title: The 'fraud team' picks up
steps.detail: Whoever answers says they are your bank's fraud department, confirms a payment is pending to that payee, and offers to block it immediately.

steps.title: Codes read down the line
steps.detail: They say cancelling needs you to read out the passcode arriving by text, or approve a prompt in your app. Those approve their payment, not a cancellation.

steps.title: The safe account move
steps.detail: Last, they claim the account is compromised and tell you to transfer your balance to a new 'secure' account they have opened for you.

new-payee-text-scam.whyItWorks: Adding a payee is the step that comes right before money leaves, so the alert implies a theft is minutes away. A calm voice offering to stop it is welcome, and the timestamp makes it sound as though the bank is watching live.

realVsFake.real: Your banking app lists every saved payee, so a real addition can be seen there within seconds.
realVsFake.fake: The text reports a payee you cannot find anywhere when you open the app.

realVsFake.real: Your bank will never ask you to move money to a 'safe account', whatever the reason given.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says your savings are at risk and must be transferred to a new account today.

realVsFake.real: One-time passcodes are for you alone, and bank staff never need you to read one out.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to recite each code 'to cancel the payee' while the caller stays on the line.

steps.title: A stealth drop is announced
steps.detail: A post in the project's Discord, often from a hijacked moderator account, or a reply under its X posts, says a surprise mint is live for fifteen minutes.

steps.title: The cloned mint page
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the collection's site with the same artwork and a counter ticking down '312 left', hosted on a domain with one extra letter.

steps.title: Connect wallet, press Mint
steps.detail: Your wallet shows a request. Instead of a mint it is 'Set approval for all' or an unreadable signature that gives another address control of tokens you already hold.

steps.title: Drained in seconds
steps.detail: A script uses that permission to move your most valuable NFTs and tokens out at once. No new NFT arrives, and the announcement is deleted soon after.

nft-mint-scam.whyItWorks: Real collections do sell out in minutes, so collectors have learned that hesitating means missing the mint. A wallet pop-up looks much the same for a harmless mint and a drain, and speed beats reading.

realVsFake.real: Genuine projects announce mint dates days ahead on their verified accounts and repeat the contract address in several places.
realVsFake.fake: The mint is a 'surprise', announced once, in a DM or a channel locked so nobody can question it.

realVsFake.real: A true mint transaction calls a mint function and costs the stated price plus gas.
realVsFake.fake: The pop-up asks for blanket approval over your collections, which hands over what you already own.

realVsFake.real: Project moderators do not open private chats with members to hand out mint links.
realVsFake.fake: A 'mod' messages you first, says you made the whitelist and gives you ten minutes to claim.

steps.title: Loan signing agent income pitch
steps.detail: An advert or email claims loan signing agents earn 100 dollars or more per appointment witnessing mortgage paperwork, and that the company has more signings than agents to cover them.

steps.title: A 199 certification and supply bundle
steps.detail: To join the roster you pay 199 dollars for the company's own certification, a stamp, a journal and a background check, with assignments guaranteed once the bundle is paid for.

steps.title: Or a check for a printer
steps.detail: Some recruits are instead mailed a check to buy a dual-tray laser printer and scanner from the firm's 'approved vendor', and told to send the vendor's share by payment app.

steps.title: An empty assignment board
steps.detail: The certificate means nothing to title companies, the login shows no signings in your area, and any equipment check is rejected by the bank after your payment has gone.

notary-signing-job-scam.whyItWorks: Notary work does have real start-up costs, such as a commission, stamp and journal, so a bundle price looks like the normal cost of entry. Few newcomers know that the commission comes only from their state, or that title companies pick agents on experience, which no private certificate can guarantee.

realVsFake.real: A notary commission is granted by your state government, through its own application and fee.
realVsFake.fake: A private website implies its paid certificate is what authorises you to notarise loan documents.

realVsFake.real: Title and signing companies offer one appointment at a time and pay the agreed fee after the documents are returned.
realVsFake.fake: A steady flow of assignments is guaranteed in advance to anyone who buys the bundle.

realVsFake.real: Agents choose and buy their own printer from any shop, since the hiring company only cares that documents print correctly.
realVsFake.fake: The equipment must come from one vendor, funded by a check that is larger than the printer's price.

steps.title: An autodialler works through a block
steps.detail: A machine dials long runs of numbers in sequence, many of them guesses. It is not looking for you, only for lines that pick up.

steps.title: Dead air, then a click
steps.detail: You answer to silence. The system is listening for a human voice, and once you say hello it logs your number as live and drops the call.

steps.title: 'Can you hear me?'
steps.detail: Other versions play a cheerful recorded voice asking whether you can hear them, or whether you are the homeowner, to draw out a clear 'yes'.

steps.title: Your number goes on a list
steps.detail: The confirmed number, tagged with the time of day you answered, is sold to other call centres. Warranty, energy and prize calls follow over the coming weeks.

number-harvesting-call-scam.whyItWorks: Saying hello to a ringing phone is automatic, and a silent call feels like a fault on the line, so nobody thinks of it as giving anything away. The cost arrives later, from different callers, which hides the connection.

realVsFake.real: A caller with a genuine reason to ring says who they are within seconds, or leaves a voicemail.
realVsFake.fake: The line stays silent, or a recording asks something that needs only a yes.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate call centres using diallers display a number that reaches the company when you ring it back.
realVsFake.fake: Ring the number back and it is disconnected, or belongs to a puzzled stranger whose number was borrowed.

realVsFake.real: A business that dials a wrong number apologises, and you never hear from it again.
realVsFake.fake: After one answered silent call, the phone starts ringing daily with recorded sales pitches.

steps.title: Nurses wanted overseas
steps.detail: A post in a nurses' social media group or a direct email advertises hospital and care-home vacancies abroad with free accommodation, naming a well-known hospital or health service as the employer.

steps.title: Approved from a CV alone
steps.detail: You email your CV and nursing certificate. Within days an 'international recruitment officer' replies that the hospital has approved you, attaching an offer letter with a ward and salary.

steps.title: Registration and credential fees
steps.detail: The officer explains that the agency must register you with the nursing council and verify your credentials on your behalf, and asks for a fee to be sent to its accounts department.

steps.title: Visa processing, then a new delay
steps.detail: A visa processing charge follows, then a 'sponsorship certificate' or language-test waiver fee. Each payment produces a fresh document and another cost, until you stop paying.

nursing-recruitment-scam.whyItWorks: Nurses know that hospitals abroad recruit internationally and that the real process involves regulators, exams and visas. A recruiter who offers to handle that bureaucracy for a fee sounds like a shortcut through a system applicants already find daunting.

realVsFake.real: A nurse moving abroad registers personally with that country's nursing regulator, which checks qualifications and usually sets an exam.
realVsFake.fake: The recruiter says registration can be bought on your behalf and the exam or language test skipped.

realVsFake.real: Hospitals interview nurses by video with clinical scenario questions and take up references from past managers.
realVsFake.fake: An offer naming a ward and a salary appears after nothing more than an emailed CV.

realVsFake.real: Regulator and visa fees are paid by you or the employer straight to the regulator and the government.
realVsFake.fake: Every fee goes to the agency's 'accounts department', which turns out to be one person's bank account.

steps.title: Offshore pay, no experience needed
steps.detail: An email or job-site listing offers roustabout, catering or engineering work on an offshore platform at about 9,000 dollars a month, tax free, on a four-weeks-on rotation.

steps.title: A contract on an oil major's letterhead
steps.detail: With no interview beyond a short questionnaire, you receive a multi-page contract carrying an oil company's logo, a rig name and a helicopter mobilisation date.

steps.title: Travel and equipment processing
steps.detail: The 'crewing coordinator' asks for 600 dollars to process your flights, protective gear and contract, promising it will be refunded with your first salary once you are on the rig.

steps.title: Medical and survival-course fees
steps.detail: After that come charges for an offshore medical, a survival certificate and a work permit. In the romance version, an 'engineer' stuck on a rig asks you to cover the same costs for him.

oil-rig-job-scam.whyItWorks: Offshore work is known for high wages and for being remote and hard to check, so a huge salary does not seem strange. The long rotations and poor signal also give a ready excuse for why nobody can meet or call.

realVsFake.real: Operators and drilling contractors hire through their own careers pages or known crewing agencies, and expect trade experience.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger offers a senior offshore wage to someone with no rig history, from a webmail address.

realVsFake.real: Offshore medicals and survival training are booked with approved clinics and training centres, which you can contact and pay yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The coordinator collects the medical and certificate fees himself and sends back a scanned 'pass' without you attending anything.

realVsFake.real: Crew travel to the heliport is arranged by the employer's logistics team as part of the rotation.
realVsFake.fake: You are billed a 'processing fee' for flights and overalls, payable by wire before a ticket is issued.

steps.title: One ring, then nothing
steps.detail: An automatic dialler calls thousands of mobiles and hangs up after a single ring, often late at night so the call is missed instead of answered.

steps.title: A number that looks half familiar
steps.detail: The missed call shows an international code that can resemble a domestic area code at a glance, and it may repeat from slightly different numbers.

steps.title: You ring back
steps.detail: Returning the call connects to a premium-rate line abroad. You hear a ringing tone, hold music or a recorded voice saying 'please wait' to keep you connected.

steps.title: Charged by the minute
steps.detail: Every minute on the line is billed at a high international or premium rate. The number's owner receives a share of that charge from the carrier chain.

one-ring-call-scam.whyItWorks: A missed call with no message leaves an open question, and people worry it was a relative abroad, a hospital or a job. Calling back is something we do without thinking, and nothing about dialling a number feels like spending money.

realVsFake.real: Someone who genuinely needs you lets the phone ring, leaves a voicemail or follows up with a text.
realVsFake.fake: The call cuts off after one ring and no message of any kind follows.

realVsFake.real: A real caller's number connects to a person or a company greeting within a few seconds.
realVsFake.fake: The line plays a fake ringing tone or endless hold music so the minutes keep adding up.

realVsFake.real: Calls from abroad that matter usually come from a country where you actually know somebody.
realVsFake.fake: The dialling code belongs to a small island nation or distant country you have no link to.

steps.title: A tidy car, oddly cheap
steps.detail: A classifieds advert shows a clean, low-mileage car for much less than similar ones. Replies come by email only, never by phone.

steps.title: Deployed, divorced or bereaved
steps.detail: The seller explains they have been posted overseas with the military, or are selling after a divorce, and the car is already crated at a shipping depot.

steps.title: An invoice from the 'transport firm'
steps.detail: An official-looking invoice arrives from a shipping or escrow company, sometimes borrowing a known marketplace's logo, promising a five-day inspection period and door delivery.

steps.title: Wire the 'protected' payment
steps.detail: The instruction is to wire the full price, or pay in prepaid cards, to an agent's personal account. A delivery date is given, then quietly passes.

online-car-shipping-scam.whyItWorks: The promise of a third party holding the money until you approve the car removes the obvious worry about paying a stranger. The deployment story explains the low price, the hurry and why nobody can show you the vehicle.

realVsFake.real: Most classified sites are noticeboards. They do not hold buyers' money, store cars in depots or send invoices on a seller's behalf.
realVsFake.fake: The invoice claims a marketplace 'buyer protection programme' is running the sale, with a support chat that only appears through the seller's link.

realVsFake.real: A genuine owner, even one working abroad, can have a friend or relative show you the car and the registration document.
realVsFake.fake: Nobody at all can open the car for you, because it is 'sealed in a container ready to ship'.

realVsFake.real: A vehicle transporter is paid for haulage, usually on collection or delivery, and has no part in the purchase price.
realVsFake.fake: Here the 'shipping company' takes the entire cost of the car in advance, through a wire to a named individual.

steps.title: A bonus bigger than the deposit
steps.detail: An advert, streamer clip or message promotes a new casino that triples your first deposit, often accepting crypto and asking for no ID to join.

steps.title: Winning streak on screen
steps.detail: The slots and tables pay out generously at first. Your balance climbs to several times what you put in, which encourages a larger top-up.

steps.title: Withdrawal 'pending review'
steps.detail: When you try to cash out, support cites a wagering rule: the bonus must be played through many times, or a verification deposit is needed.

steps.title: Pay to unlock, then locked out
steps.detail: You pay a 'tax', a fee or a matching deposit. A new condition follows each time, until the account is closed for 'bonus abuse'.

online-casino-scam.whyItWorks: The balance on the screen looks like money you already own, so paying a fee to release it feels like protecting winnings instead of spending more. Real casinos do have wagering terms, which gives every new obstacle a plausible name.

realVsFake.real: A licensed operator shows its licence number in the footer, and the regulator's public register lists that exact domain.
realVsFake.fake: A badge image links nowhere, or names a regulator that does not exist.

realVsFake.real: Regulated sites verify identity early, and never ask for a fresh deposit before paying out.
realVsFake.fake: ID is 'not needed' until withdrawal, when checks and fees suddenly multiply.

realVsFake.real: Bonus terms are fixed and readable before you opt in.
realVsFake.fake: Rules are invented in live chat after you win, and change with each request.

steps.title: A small favour from a friend
steps.detail: A contact's taken-over account messages you about a cutest baby, pet or dance contest. Their child is 'so close to winning' and needs one more vote.

steps.title: The contest page
steps.detail: The link shows a gallery of children's photos with vote counts and a ticking deadline. Pressing Vote brings up 'sign in to confirm you are a real person'.

steps.title: Sign in, or enter your number
steps.detail: One version copies a Facebook or Google login box. Another asks for your mobile number, then for the code that arrives, which is really the key to your WhatsApp account.

steps.title: Your account asks for votes
steps.detail: The page says 'thank you for voting'. Meanwhile your contacts and group chats receive the baby contest plea from you, and some are later asked for a loan.

online-contest-vote-scam.whyItWorks: Helping a friend's child win a photo competition costs nothing and refusing feels mean. Many sites do offer sign-in with a social account, so being asked to log in before voting seems like a normal check against cheating.

realVsFake.real: Real competitions are hosted by a named organiser, such as a local paper or a brand, on its own website.
realVsFake.fake: The voting page names no organiser, lists no prize rules, and sits on an address unrelated to any contest.

realVsFake.real: A genuine poll counts a tap or a like and may ask for an email address at most.
realVsFake.fake: Casting a vote requires your social media password or a verification code sent to your phone.

realVsFake.real: A parent who is really asking can tell you by phone which contest it is and who is running it.
realVsFake.fake: The sender dodges a call, sends the same wording to everyone, and may not even have a child that age.

steps.title: Spam for pills without a script
steps.detail: A spam email, forum post or search result offers branded prescription tablets, slimming injections or sedatives with 'no prescription needed' and discreet packaging.

steps.title: A two-minute 'consultation'
steps.detail: The site may show a short tick-box health form to look proper. Whatever you answer, the order is approved instantly.

steps.title: Crypto discount at checkout
steps.detail: Card payments 'fail' or carry a surcharge, while crypto or a wire gets a reduction. You also enter your address and medical reasons.

steps.title: Customs letter or mystery tablets
steps.detail: Nothing arrives, or blister packs with foreign labels do. Some buyers then get a call from a bogus 'customs agent' demanding a fine.

online-pharmacy-scam.whyItWorks: People buy this way when they are embarrassed, cannot get an appointment, or cannot afford the usual price, so they do not want to ask anyone for a second opinion. Discreet shipping is sold as a kindness and doubles as a reason for no paper trail.

realVsFake.real: A registered online pharmacy displays its registration number and is listed on the national pharmacy regulator's register.
realVsFake.fake: There is no pharmacist named, no registration, and the address is a mailbox abroad.

realVsFake.real: Prescription medicine is supplied only after a prescriber reviews your details, and can be refused.
realVsFake.fake: Any quantity of any drug is approved the moment you click.

realVsFake.real: Dispensed medicine comes in sealed, labelled packs with a leaflet in your language.
realVsFake.fake: Loose strips arrive wrapped in newspaper or foil inside an unmarked envelope.

steps.title: Approved to teach online
steps.detail: After you post a tutoring profile or answer an advert, a 'platform coordinator' or a parent recruiting for several students says you are approved, without asking to see a degree certificate.

steps.title: A timetable full of pupils
steps.detail: You are sent a timetable of lessons starting next week, with pupils' first names, subjects and an hourly rate above what tutoring sites normally pay.

steps.title: Required teaching software, 120
steps.detail: To open the virtual classroom you must buy the platform's teaching software licence for 120 dollars. Free video tools you already have are 'not compatible with our student records'.

steps.title: Or an 'equipment' check to split
steps.detail: The other route is a check for a webcam, tablet and headset. You are told to deposit it and send 400 dollars to the supplier, and the pupils never log in.

online-tutoring-job-scam.whyItWorks: Tutors are used to platforms with their own classroom tools and sign-up steps, so one more piece of required software seems routine. A ready-made timetable of named pupils makes the income feel booked, and the fee looks small beside a month of lessons.

realVsFake.real: Tutoring platforms check your degree and identity, and many ask for a sample lesson before listing you.
realVsFake.fake: You are 'approved' on the strength of one message, for subjects nobody asked whether you can teach.

realVsFake.real: Real platforms make their money by keeping a share of each lesson fee, and the classroom runs in a browser at no charge.
realVsFake.fake: Teaching cannot begin until you have bought a licence from the platform's own checkout page.

realVsFake.real: A parent who books lessons pays the agreed rate, lesson by lesson or a month ahead at most.
realVsFake.fake: A check for far more than the lessons arrives, with a request to send the surplus to an equipment supplier.

steps.title: A refund or loan check appears
steps.detail: A text, advert or caller offers a tax refund, a loan eligibility check or a free budgeting tool, and says the quickest route is to connect your bank.

steps.title: Pick your bank from a list
steps.detail: The page shows a grid of bank logos, just as real open banking services do. Tapping yours hands you over to your own banking app to log in.

steps.title: The consent screen nobody reads
steps.detail: Your bank displays what is being granted: balances and past transactions, or a single payment to a named payee. People press 'Allow' expecting money to arrive.

steps.title: Consent becomes a withdrawal
steps.detail: The approval turns out to be a payment out of your account, or a data feed showing balances and salary dates that is used for a targeted follow-up call.

open-banking-scam.whyItWorks: The login happens inside your genuine banking app, with your real fingerprint or face check, so nothing looks fake. Because you never typed a password into a strange site, approving feels safe, and the wording on the consent screen goes unread.

realVsFake.real: Regulated open banking providers are listed on the financial regulator's register, and your bank names them on the consent screen.
realVsFake.fake: The name on the consent screen is one you have never heard of and does not match the app that sent you there.

realVsFake.real: Receiving a refund needs only your sort code and account number, or the original card. No connection to your bank is required.
realVsFake.fake: You are told money can only be paid in after you link your account and approve a prompt in your banking app.

realVsFake.real: A budgeting app asks for read-only access and explains how to switch it off in your bank's connected services menu.
realVsFake.fake: The request includes permission to make payments, which a refund or eligibility check has no use for.

steps.title: 'Your order was cancelled'
steps.detail: An email or text with a retailer's logo gives an order number such as #48217 and says payment did not go through.

steps.title: Curiosity does the work
steps.detail: Whether or not you bought anything, you want to know what the order was. The only way offered is a 'view order' or 're-confirm' button.

steps.title: A sign-in page, then a card page
steps.detail: First it asks for the email and password for your shopping account. Next it requests the card number again 'to restore the order'.

steps.title: The code that finishes it
steps.detail: A one-time passcode arrives from your bank. The page asks for it, and the criminal uses it to approve their own purchase.

order-cancellation-scam.whyItWorks: It works both ways: if you did order something, you fear losing it, and if you did not, you fear someone is using your account. Either reaction sends you to the same button without opening the retailer's app to check.

realVsFake.real: A genuine cancellation email names the item, and the order shows as cancelled in your account history.
realVsFake.fake: The message has a number but no product, price or delivery address.

realVsFake.real: When a payment fails, the shop asks you to update the card from inside your account.
realVsFake.fake: A link demands your password, card and bank code on three screens in a row.

realVsFake.real: A real retailer does not need the passcode your bank texts you.
realVsFake.fake: The page waits for the code and shows a spinning 'verifying' wheel while your card is used.

steps.title: A blue 'not genuine' screen
steps.detail: A full-screen page appears in the browser with a Windows logo, a product key field and the message that this copy is not genuine. A support number sits beneath.

steps.title: Any key you type fails
steps.detail: Entering the key from your sticker or email returns 'invalid'. The page is built to reject everything so that phoning the number looks like the only option.

steps.title: The activation desk
steps.detail: The person who answers says your key was blacklisted or the activation server is blocked, and quotes a price for a new licence or an unlock.

steps.title: The bargain key route
steps.detail: Others find a site selling keys for the price of a sandwich. The key is a leaked volume licence that later deactivates, or the 'activator' download carries malware.

os-activation-scam.whyItWorks: Few people know whether the Windows that came with their computer is properly licensed, especially on a second-hand or repaired machine. That doubt makes 'not genuine' believable, and a screen that seems to block the desktop makes it feel urgent.

realVsFake.real: Unactivated Windows shows a faint 'Activate Windows' watermark and keeps working. You can still open your files.
realVsFake.fake: The scam page covers everything, plays a warning tone and says the device will be locked within minutes.

realVsFake.real: Activation status lives in the Settings app under Activation, where a valid licence simply reads as active.
realVsFake.fake: The demand shows up in a browser tab, where closing the window makes the whole 'lock' go away.

realVsFake.real: Genuine licences are sold by Microsoft and authorised retailers at a broadly similar retail price.
realVsFake.fake: Grey-market sellers email a key or a 'phone activation' trick for a tiny sum, with no receipt naming Microsoft.

steps.title: Sold at the asking price
steps.detail: A buyer, new client or remote employer agrees terms quickly and says their assistant or accounts department will handle the payment.

steps.title: An apology for sending extra
steps.detail: A cheque, card payment or transfer screenshot arrives showing 1,200 for a 900 sale. Minutes later comes an embarrassed message blaming a typing error.

steps.title: Send the 300 back today
steps.detail: They ask you to keep what you are owed and return the surplus straight away, to a different account from the one that paid, or as gift cards.

steps.title: The original payment unwinds
steps.detail: The cheque bounces, the stolen card is charged back, or the 'pending' transfer never lands. Your refund was real money and stays with them.

overpayment-scam.whyItWorks: Returning money that is not yours feels like plain honesty, and the buyer's apology makes refusing seem rude. The scam depends on the gap between a payment appearing in your account and that payment being final.

realVsFake.real: A person who pays too much by mistake asks their own bank or the payment app to reverse the original transaction.
realVsFake.fake: The 'buyer' wants a fresh payment from you, sent somewhere other than where the money came from.

realVsFake.real: An honest customer will wait the days it takes for a cheque to clear fully before expecting anything back.
realVsFake.fake: You hear about a flight, a sick child or an angry boss, all reasons the 300 cannot wait until tomorrow.

realVsFake.real: Real payment confirmations show in your own banking app or account history, where you can see whether funds are available.
realVsFake.fake: Proof arrives as a screenshot or a forwarded email with a payment company's logo, sent by the buyer themselves.

steps.title: A job abroad, visa included
steps.detail: An agent, advert or social media page offers hotel, factory, farm or driving work in a wealthier country, with a salary, lodging and a work visa all 'arranged for you'.

steps.title: Passport copy and an offer letter
steps.detail: You send a scan of your passport and a photo. An offer letter comes back quickly with an employer's name, a start date and a note that visa processing has begun.

steps.title: The 850 placement fee
steps.detail: The agent asks for 850 dollars to cover the work permit, flights and his placement service, sent by wire transfer to a personal name, with the visa slot lapsing if you delay.

steps.title: A forged visa or a wasted flight
steps.detail: You may receive a fake approval letter followed by fresh charges for an 'embassy bond'. Some victims are told to fly out on a tourist visa and find nobody waiting at arrivals.

overseas-job-visa-scam.whyItWorks: Visa rules are confusing and differ by country, so applicants expect to need an agent who knows the system. The fee is far smaller than the wages on offer, and families often pool savings to pay it because one job abroad can support a household.

realVsFake.real: A work visa is applied for through the destination government's own system, usually with a sponsoring employer named on the application.
realVsFake.fake: The agent says he will 'process' the visa privately and that you need not deal with the embassy at all.

realVsFake.real: Visa fees are published in advance and paid to the government or its official visa centre, which issues a receipt.
realVsFake.fake: One lump sum covering visa, permit and flights is wired to an individual, and no itemised receipt ever appears.

realVsFake.real: A genuine foreign employer interviews you, issues a signed contract, and can be reached through contact details found independently.
realVsFake.fake: You never speak to the employer, only the agent, who advises entering as a tourist and 'converting' the visa later.

steps.title: A buyer takes your advert
steps.detail: You list coins on an exchange's P2P board. A buyer with a newly created account opens an order and starts messaging you in the trade chat straight away.

steps.title: A receipt picture arrives
steps.detail: They mark the order as paid and send an image of a banking app showing the transfer 'completed', sometimes with a forged email saying the exchange is holding your funds.

steps.title: Pressure in the chat
steps.detail: Your bank balance has not changed. They say transfers take hours, that another seller is waiting, and that they will open a dispute and wreck your rating.

steps.title: Release, and the coins go
steps.detail: You tap release and escrow hands the crypto over for good. The money never lands, or it comes from a stolen account and your bank later takes it back.

p2p-crypto-trade-scam.whyItWorks: In a P2P sale the release button is the seller's only brake. A receipt image looks like evidence, bank delays do happen, and nobody wants a dispute on their trading record, so releasing early feels like fairness.

realVsFake.real: An honest buyer pays from a bank account in the same name as their verified exchange profile, then waits while you check.
realVsFake.fake: Money comes from a different name, or exists only as an image, alongside pleas to release immediately.

realVsFake.real: Exchange staff speak only inside the official dispute screen, and escrow keeps the coins locked until you confirm receipt.
realVsFake.fake: A 'support agent' turns up on Telegram or by email telling you payment is verified and to release.

realVsFake.real: A genuine seller is content for coins to sit in escrow before you pay a penny.
realVsFake.fake: A fake seller offers a better rate if you pay him directly off the platform, then stops answering.

steps.title: An offer above market value
steps.detail: A stranger says they represent a media company buying pages in your niche and names a price well above what your follower count would normally fetch.

steps.title: Proof of funds
steps.detail: To look serious they send a screenshot of a pending bank transfer or a made-up escrow receipt, and say payment releases once the handover is verified.

steps.title: The verification step
steps.detail: They ask you to add their email to the account, make them full admin, or forward a code they 'sent to check you are the owner'.

steps.title: You are removed from your page
steps.detail: That code was a password reset. Within minutes your email, phone and admin rights are stripped out, the buyer blocks you, and no payment ever lands.

page-purchase-scam.whyItWorks: Pages and usernames do get bought and sold informally, so the approach is not absurd, and there is no familiar procedure to compare it with. The seller, thinking about the money, treats handing over access as the delivery.

realVsFake.real: A serious buyer pays into an established escrow service you choose and log in to yourself, before any access changes.
realVsFake.fake: The buyer picks the escrow site, emails you its 'confirmation', and wants admin rights before funds clear.

realVsFake.real: Nobody needs a code sent to your phone to check ownership. Your name on the admin list already shows it.
realVsFake.fake: They trigger a reset code and ask you to read it back as part of 'due diligence'.

realVsFake.real: Genuine acquirers ask about audience data, revenue and content rights, and expect a signed agreement.
realVsFake.fake: This buyer asks nothing about the audience and only wants to know how quickly you can hand over the login.

steps.title: A pitch in your business inbox
steps.detail: Shortly after you open a shop page or post a new product, an account calling itself a marketing agency or feature page offers to promote you.

steps.title: Packages and screenshots
steps.detail: They send a price list of bronze, silver and gold bundles, plus cropped images of other accounts' growth charts that cannot be traced to any client.

steps.title: The promo fee
steps.detail: An $80 payment is requested by gift card or friends-and-family transfer so work can 'start today'. An invoice or contract is never offered.

steps.title: Bots, then an upsell
steps.detail: Either nothing happens or a few hundred empty accounts follow you overnight. Then comes a message saying the algorithm needs a larger package to deliver sales.

paid-promotion-scam.whyItWorks: New sellers know they need visibility and have little idea what marketing ought to cost, so $80 for a promised audience seems cheap. A burst of fake followers the next morning even looks like the service working.

realVsFake.real: Advertising bought through a platform's own ads tool is billed by the platform and reports reach and clicks in your dashboard.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agency' takes money privately and reports results as screenshots it could have made in an image editor.

realVsFake.real: An honest marketer talks about targeting and budget and will not guarantee a number of sales.
realVsFake.fake: The DM guarantees a set follower total and 'real buyers' without asking what you sell.

realVsFake.real: Established shoutout pages have a visible history of paid features, and past clients you can message yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The promoter's own followers are mostly blank profiles, and its 'client' testimonials come from accounts with no posts.

steps.title: Bad news with a payout
steps.detail: A message says your parcel was damaged at a sorting hub and that, as the recipient, you are owed 80 in compensation.

steps.title: A claim portal, already filled in
steps.detail: The link opens a claims page with a claim number pre-entered. It asks for your name, address and date of birth to 'match the policy'.

steps.title: Where to send the money
steps.detail: Next come sort code and account number, then card details 'to verify the account', and in some versions your online banking username and password.

steps.title: The claims team calls
steps.detail: Days later a caller who knows all of it says the payout needs a code approving. That code authorises a payment leaving your account.

parcel-insurance-claim-scam.whyItWorks: Being owed money lowers the guard that a demand for money raises. Supplying bank details to receive a payment seems logical, since that is how anyone gets paid, and the sum is modest enough to believe.

realVsFake.real: Compensation for a damaged parcel is claimed by the sender, or by you through the retailer after reporting the problem.
realVsFake.fake: The offer arrives before you knew anything was wrong, for an item it cannot name.

realVsFake.real: A genuine refund returns to the payment method used for the order, or the shop sends a replacement.
realVsFake.fake: The page wants a security code and banking password in order to pay you.

realVsFake.real: Real claims ask for evidence: photographs of the damage, the order number and the item's value.
realVsFake.fake: The form asks nothing about the goods and everything about your identity and accounts.

steps.title: A parcel waiting in a locker
steps.detail: A text says an item has been placed in a locker near you and will be removed in three days if not collected.

steps.title: Identify yourself for the code
steps.detail: Instead of showing a pickup code, the link asks for your name, mobile number, email and a card 'for identification' before it will reveal one.

steps.title: A request for your real code
steps.detail: If you do have something waiting, a follow-up message or call from the 'locker team' asks you to reply with the pickup code to confirm collection.

steps.title: Someone else opens the door
steps.detail: The code is all the machine checks. Whoever types it walks off with your parcel, the system logs a normal pickup, and the card from the form is abused separately.

parcel-locker-scam.whyItWorks: A locker code works like a key that anyone can use, with no signature and no handover in person. People think of it as a notification, so reading it out to 'the courier' seems harmless.

realVsFake.real: The locker operator sends the pickup code or QR automatically, together with the locker's street location.
realVsFake.fake: The text withholds the code until you complete a web form about yourself.

realVsFake.real: Courier staff have their own access to the compartments and never need the customer's code.
realVsFake.fake: A caller or texter asks you to read the digits out or forward the QR image.

realVsFake.real: A genuine notice names the retailer and which locker bank holds the item.
realVsFake.fake: It says only 'a locker near you' and gives no address, shop name or compartment number.

steps.title: A charge of a few pounds
steps.detail: A text headed 'PARKING NOTICE' says you have an unpaid charge of about £3.50 and 48 hours before it rises, with no car park, date or vehicle named.

steps.title: Enter your registration
steps.detail: The page asks for the number plate, then displays a 'notice found' screen whatever is typed, with a countdown to the higher penalty.

steps.title: Pay the small sum
steps.detail: A checkout requests card number, expiry, security code and billing address for the £3.50. Some then say the card was declined and ask for another.

steps.title: Bigger charges follow
steps.detail: The £3.50 parking payment may go through as shown, which delays suspicion. The same card is then used for far larger purchases over the following days.

parking-fine-text-scam.whyItWorks: Almost every driver has parked somewhere in the last month and cannot be certain a ticket machine or app registered properly. The amount is so low that paying seems quicker than digging out where and when it supposedly happened.

realVsFake.real: Parking operators and councils get an address from the vehicle keeper record. That record holds no mobile number.
realVsFake.fake: The demand arrives by text to your phone, which no parking firm could have matched to your car.

realVsFake.real: A real penalty notice is fixed to the windscreen or posted, and states the location, time, vehicle and how to appeal.
realVsFake.fake: The text names no street or car park and offers payment as the only option.

realVsFake.real: Genuine penalty charges give weeks to pay or challenge, with a reduced rate for paying early.
realVsFake.fake: You are given two days and a 'reduced' amount that would not cover an hour's parking.

steps.title: The advert above the real result
steps.detail: You search 'renew passport online'. The top listing, marked 'Sponsored' in small type, carries a name like 'Passport Renewal Portal' and a crest-style logo.

steps.title: A form that feels official
steps.detail: The site walks you through numbered steps asking for your name, date of birth and old passport number, the same questions the government form asks.

steps.title: The charge at checkout
steps.detail: Only on the payment screen does a 'service fee' appear. A grey line in the footer admits the company is not connected to any government.

steps.title: A PDF and a second bill
steps.detail: After paying you receive a pre-filled form to print and post yourself, with the official fee still owed. Some sites send nothing and keep the card details.

passport-renewal-scam.whyItWorks: A passport is renewed about once every ten years, so nobody remembers what the real site looks like or what it charges. Renewals are usually done with a trip already booked, and the first search result gets trusted because it is first.

realVsFake.real: The government passport office charges one published fee, paid at the end of its own application.
realVsFake.fake: The copycat takes its own payment first and leaves you to pay the government separately when you post the form.

realVsFake.real: After a real application you get a reference you can track on the government's site and instructions for returning the old passport.
realVsFake.fake: The only email is a card receipt from a company name that appears nowhere on the site you used.

realVsFake.real: Urgent passports are handled by the passport office itself, through its own appointment or expedited service.
realVsFake.fake: The site sells 'fast-track processing' but only emails a form, so your application joins the same queue as everyone else's.

steps.title: New test results are ready
steps.detail: Results have been posted to your patient portal, the email announces, naming no clinic, doctor or test. Sometimes it is a statement instead: 'You have a balance due of 84.20.'

steps.title: A portal with a familiar look
steps.detail: The link opens a login page imitating a common portal system, with a stock photo of a nurse and boxes for username, password and date of birth.

steps.title: Verify your identity to continue
steps.detail: After logging in, a 'verification' form asks for your national insurance or Social Security number, insurer and member ID, and a card to settle the outstanding balance.

steps.title: Sold as a medical identity
steps.detail: No results ever appear. The details are bundled and used to bill insurers for treatment you never had, to order prescriptions, or to open credit in your name.

patient-portal-email-scam.whyItWorks: Anyone waiting on a biopsy, a scan or a blood test will open this email at once, and worry about the answer crowds out any thought about the sender. Real portals also send deliberately vague notices, for privacy reasons.

realVsFake.real: A real notice comes from the clinic or hospital you actually attended, after a test you remember having.
realVsFake.fake: The email names no provider, or one you have never visited, and you have had no tests recently.

realVsFake.real: You reach the genuine portal through the address on your appointment letter or the provider's app, with a login you set up yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The emailed link asks you to 'create or confirm' your login by supplying identity numbers the portal would already hold.

realVsFake.real: Medical bills arrive as itemised statements showing the date of service and what insurance has already paid.
realVsFake.fake: A round 'balance due' appears with no date or description, payable only through the card box on that page.

steps.title: A receipt for 499.99
steps.detail: A receipt arrives for a payment to a merchant you have never heard of, perhaps an antivirus firm or a crypto exchange, complete with a long transaction ID and today's date.

steps.title: 'Not you? Cancel here'
steps.detail: A line at the bottom says the purchase can be reversed within 24 hours, with a 'Dispute transaction' link and a helpline number for the 'billing desk'.

steps.title: The dispute form
steps.detail: The link opens a form asking for the card 'that was charged': the long number, expiry, security code, plus your online banking username 'so the refund can be matched'.

steps.title: A real charge follows the fake one
steps.detail: On the phone version, an agent says he must send a code to verify you. It is your bank's approval code for a payment he is making with your card as you speak.

payment-confirmation-email-scam.whyItWorks: The email never says which card was charged, so you cannot rule it out by glancing at one account. Disputing a payment feels like exercising a consumer right, and the form asks for what a dispute form would plausibly need.

realVsFake.real: A real charge appears in your banking app, usually as a pending transaction within minutes of the purchase.
realVsFake.fake: No pending payment of that amount shows on any card you own, however firmly the email insists.

realVsFake.real: You dispute a card payment with your own bank, using the number printed on the back of the card.
realVsFake.fake: The receipt tells you to dispute it with the 'merchant's billing desk', using contact details supplied in the same email.

realVsFake.real: A merchant refunding you already has the card on record and needs nothing more than the order reference.
realVsFake.fake: The form asks for the full card number and security code afresh, which is everything needed to spend on it.

steps.title: A refund is promised
steps.detail: Someone claiming to be a marketplace buyer, a utility agent or an old flatmate says they owe you money and will send it through your banking or payment app.

steps.title: A notification lands on your phone
steps.detail: The alert carries a friendly note such as 'Refund 85, tap to accept'. The note is free text written by the requester, not by the app.

steps.title: Approve to receive, they say
steps.detail: On the phone or in chat they talk you past the small print, where the button actually reads 'Pay' or 'Approve request' with your account as the source.

steps.title: Your PIN completes their request
steps.detail: You confirm with a PIN or fingerprint and 85 leaves your balance. When you query it, they send a second request to 'correct the error'.

payment-request-scam.whyItWorks: Request and payment screens look almost alike, and the scammer controls the one line of text people actually read. Anyone expecting money sees the word refund and a familiar app, then taps through from habit.

realVsFake.real: Incoming money needs nothing from you. It appears in your balance without a PIN, a tap or an approval.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the refund is 'waiting' and will expire unless you authorise it within a few minutes.

realVsFake.real: A genuine request-to-pay screen states the amount leaving your account and names who will receive it.
realVsFake.fake: The requester's display name is set to 'Refunds Dept' or a shop name, with the misleading instruction typed in the message field.

realVsFake.real: A shop refunding you sends the money to the card or account you originally paid from.
realVsFake.fake: The 'refund' comes through a person-to-person request from an individual profile created that week.

steps.title: A genuine email from PayPal
steps.detail: The criminal opens a PayPal business account, creates an invoice addressed to your email, and lets PayPal's own system send it. It passes spam filters and every sender check.

steps.title: The note from the 'seller'
steps.detail: The amount is 399.00 for an 'antivirus renewal' or 'Bitcoin purchase'. The seller's note field carries the real payload: 'If you did not authorise this, call our billing team', then a number.

steps.title: A fake PayPal agent
steps.detail: The person who answers says your account has been hacked, and that to block the charge you must install a 'security app', which is a remote-control tool, or confirm your login aloud.

steps.title: Paying to cancel
steps.detail: He directs you to send a 'reversal payment', buy gift cards, or log in to your bank while he watches. Others simply click 'Pay invoice' in a panic, which sends the money.

paypal-invoice-scam.whyItWorks: Every check people are taught passes: the sender is really PayPal, the links go to the real site, and the invoice shows in your account. The only false part is the phone number, typed into a free-text note that PayPal did not write.

realVsFake.real: An invoice is only a request. Nothing leaves your account unless you press Pay, and unwanted ones can be ignored or reported inside PayPal.
realVsFake.fake: The note claims the amount 'will be auto-debited within 24 hours' unless you ring to stop it.

realVsFake.real: PayPal's contact details are found in the Help section after you log in. They are never written in a seller's note.
realVsFake.fake: The only phone number offered sits inside the invoice text, supplied by the stranger who sent the bill.

realVsFake.real: PayPal staff do not ask you to install software, share your screen or move money to protect an account.
realVsFake.fake: Within minutes the 'agent' wants a remote-access app on your phone and your banking open in front of him.

steps.title: Staff names gathered from public profiles
steps.detail: The fraudster picks an employee from the company website or a professional networking profile, and notes who handles payroll and when staff are paid.

steps.title: A short note to HR
steps.detail: An email in the employee's name says they have switched banks and asks what is needed to update their direct deposit before the next pay run.

steps.title: The form comes back filled in
steps.detail: Payroll replies with a change form. It is returned within the hour carrying new routing and account numbers, often for a prepaid card or online-only bank.

steps.title: Payday goes to the wrong account
steps.detail: Salary is sent to the new account and withdrawn the same day. The loss surfaces only when the real employee asks where their wages are.

payroll-direct-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: Changing bank is an ordinary life event, and payroll teams process such requests every month without fuss. The email is brief, polite and names a real colleague, so nothing about it invites a second look near a busy payday.

realVsFake.real: Employees usually change their pay details themselves in the HR self-service portal, behind their own login.
realVsFake.fake: The sender says they are locked out of the portal or travelling, and asks payroll to key the change in for them.

realVsFake.real: A real colleague writes from their work address and will happily confirm on an internal call or at their desk.
realVsFake.fake: The display name is right but the address behind it is a free webmail account or a domain one letter off.

realVsFake.real: Genuine changes often come with a voided cheque or bank letter and can wait a pay cycle if needed.
realVsFake.fake: The request stresses that it must take effect this cycle and goes quiet when asked to ring the number on file.

steps.title: A free speed-up download
steps.detail: An ad promising to make a slow computer faster, or a tick-box hidden in another program's installer, puts a cleaner or 'driver updater' on your machine.

steps.title: The scan with a big red number
steps.detail: It runs automatically and reports hundreds of 'critical issues'. Most are leftover registry entries, browser cookies and temporary files that do no harm at all.

steps.title: 'Fix all' is locked
steps.detail: The repair button opens a payment page. The free version fixes a token handful, and a gauge marked 'PC health: poor' stays in the red.

steps.title: Pop-ups until you pay
steps.detail: The program starts with Windows and nags every few minutes. Buying it enrols you in an annual auto-renewal, and uninstalling leaves pieces that keep prompting.

pc-optimizer-scam.whyItWorks: Older computers really do slow down, and the owner has no way to know what a registry entry is or whether 437 of them matter. A precise count in red looks like measurement, and paying a modest sum seems easier than buying a new PC.

realVsFake.real: Windows includes its own disk clean-up and startup manager at no cost, and they describe plainly what will be removed.
realVsFake.fake: The optimizer labels routine clutter 'severe' and will not show details until you have bought a licence.

realVsFake.real: Honest utilities give the same result on a brand-new computer as you would expect: very little to fix.
realVsFake.fake: A rogue cleaner finds hundreds of faults even on a machine set up that morning.

realVsFake.real: Reputable software is removed from the normal apps list in one step and stops billing when cancelled.
realVsFake.fake: The uninstaller is buried or missing, and cancelling the subscription means ringing a number that upsells you.

steps.title: A laptop for five pounds
steps.detail: An advert shows a new laptop or phone 'sold' for under five pounds, with a ticking clock and a list of recent winners and their tiny final prices.

steps.title: Buying the bid pack
steps.detail: Before you can bid, you buy a pack, perhaps 100 bids at 50p each. The pack is charged to your card in full, long before the first auction you enter has finished.

steps.title: The clock that never reaches zero
steps.detail: Each click adds a penny to the price and ten or twenty seconds to the clock. With two seconds left, another username always appears and outbids you.

steps.title: Chasing what you have spent
steps.detail: Having used forty bids on one item, stopping feels like throwing them away, so you buy another pack. The auction ends with a stranger winning at 3.12.

penny-auction-scam.whyItWorks: The price on screen stays tiny, so each bid feels like pennies even though it cost fifty. After spending on bids, people keep going to avoid wasting them, and a site that runs its own bidders can stretch that for hours.

realVsFake.real: In an ordinary online auction, bidding is free and only the winner pays, at the amount of the final bid.
realVsFake.fake: Here every participant pays for every click, so a laptop that 'sold' for 4.80 took 480 paid bids to get there.

realVsFake.real: A genuine auction has a fixed closing time, or a short extension rule that is stated clearly in advance.
realVsFake.fake: The countdown is decoration. It jumps back up with each bid, and house accounts step in whenever it nears zero.

realVsFake.real: A trustworthy seller shows the total you will pay before you commit, and you can walk away having spent nothing.
realVsFake.fake: Winner lists show first names and stock photos, unused bids expire, and the 'buy it now' option costs more than a shop.

steps.title: The free pension review
steps.detail: A cold call, text or web advert offers a no-cost review, claiming your old workplace pension is 'frozen' or performing badly in an outdated fund.

steps.title: Forms brought to your door
steps.detail: A smartly dressed consultant or a courier brings paperwork: a letter of authority to obtain your pension details and transfer forms, sometimes with talk of a loophole for early cash.

steps.title: The pot moves to a new scheme
steps.detail: Your savings transfer into an obscure scheme and from there into overseas hotel rooms, forestry or storage units. A cash 'bonus' may be paid to you as a sweetener.

steps.title: Statements stop coming
steps.detail: Intermediaries take large fees on the way through. Later the statements dry up, the investment cannot be sold, and the tax office may bill you for money released early.

pension-scam.whyItWorks: A pension is often the largest sum a person owns, yet few have looked at theirs in years or know how it is invested. A free check-up from someone who names your old employer sounds like help.

realVsFake.real: Regulated advisers appear on the financial regulator's register, and you can ring the firm on the number listed there.
realVsFake.fake: The firm says it 'only introduces' so needs no authorisation, or borrows the name of a genuine adviser.

realVsFake.real: Your existing provider lets a transfer take weeks, sends risk warnings and will answer questions before anything moves.
realVsFake.fake: A courier waits on the doorstep while you sign, because the offer 'closes on Friday'.

realVsFake.real: A proper adviser charges a stated fee and usually recommends mainstream, regulated funds you can sell.
realVsFake.fake: The review costs nothing, yet the return is guaranteed and comes from one unusual asset abroad.

steps.title: A wealthy boss needs a chauffeur
steps.detail: A text or email from a businessman, surgeon or diplomat's assistant says he is relocating soon and needs a personal driver a few hours a day at a generous weekly wage.

steps.title: Always abroad, never on the phone
steps.detail: He cannot interview you because he is travelling, at sea or in meetings across time zones. A copy of your driving licence and your home address are enough to be hired.

steps.title: A cheque for the car
steps.detail: His cheque is meant to cover your first wages plus the vehicle he wants waiting for him: a deposit, insurance and registration, all to be settled through his preferred dealer.

steps.title: Pay the dealer in gift cards
steps.detail: You keep your pay and get the balance to the dealer by bank transfer, or by buying gift cards and sending the numbers. The car, the dealer and the cheque are all invented.

personal-driver-job-scam.whyItWorks: Rich people do employ drivers and do delegate errands, so being trusted to sort out the boss's car feels like a compliment and a test of reliability. His constant travel explains the lack of a meeting and the need for someone local.

realVsFake.real: Anyone hiring a chauffeur checks the driving record, meets the candidate and usually asks for a test drive.
realVsFake.fake: You are trusted with a job and a large cheque by a man who has never seen you behind a wheel.

realVsFake.real: Someone buying a car pays the dealership directly and puts the insurance in their own name.
realVsFake.fake: The purchase money passes through a new employee's account on its way to a 'dealer' with no showroom.

realVsFake.real: Car dealers take cards, bank transfers and finance agreements. None accepts gift card numbers.
realVsFake.fake: The 'dealer' wants store gift cards, with photos of the backs sent by text the same afternoon.

steps.title: A cosy kennel listing
steps.detail: A listing on a classifieds site or local group shows dogs on sofas and a fenced garden, with rates well under nearby kennels.

steps.title: Fully booked, except your dates
steps.detail: The sitter replies warmly, asks about your pet's routine, and says one space is left for the holiday week you need.

steps.title: Deposit before a meet-and-greet
steps.detail: They cannot manage a visit this week, a relative is ill or they are away, but a deposit by transfer or gift card will hold the place.

steps.title: No one at the address
steps.detail: Close to drop-off day the phone is off and the profile deleted. The address given is a stranger's house or does not exist.

pet-boarding-scam.whyItWorks: Owners book boarding just before school holidays, when good kennels are full and a free space feels lucky. A sitter who asks caring questions about feeding and walks seems to love animals, and that warmth stands in for any proof.

realVsFake.real: A genuine boarder invites you to see where your pet will sleep before taking any money.
realVsFake.fake: Every attempt to visit meets a fresh excuse, while the deposit request stays firm.

realVsFake.real: Licensed kennels and home boarders can show a licence, insurance and references from named clients.
realVsFake.fake: The photos are lifted from another business, and reviews come from profiles with no history.

realVsFake.real: Established sitters take payment through a booking platform or by invoice.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to send vouchers or a transfer to a personal account 'to avoid fees'.

steps.title: 'Registration has expired'
steps.detail: A text tells you your pet's microchip registration has lapsed and must be renewed for about $4.99, without naming the animal, the chip number or the database.

steps.title: A registry you never chose
steps.detail: The link opens a 'national pet registry' page with paw-print branding. It asks for owner name, address, phone, and the pet's name and breed.

steps.title: Renewal fee at checkout
steps.detail: A payment screen takes card details for the renewal. Some add a pre-ticked 'premium protection' option that turns the fee into a monthly charge.

steps.title: Record unchanged, card exposed
steps.detail: Your pet's entry on the real database is untouched. The scammer keeps the card details and a profile of your household for later use.

pet-microchip-text-scam.whyItWorks: Owners remember the chip being fitted at the vet but not which company holds the record or what was paid. The idea that a lost pet could not be traced back home is upsetting, and five dollars seems a tiny price to prevent it.

realVsFake.real: The chip itself has no expiry. It keeps the same number for the animal's whole life.
realVsFake.fake: The text implies the chip stops working or the record is deleted unless a fee is paid.

realVsFake.real: Your pet is registered with one specific database, named on the paperwork from the vet, breeder or rescue.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is a generic 'pet registry' that cannot tell you the chip number it claims to hold.

realVsFake.real: You can look up which database holds a chip by entering its number on a chip-checking site, then contact that company.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent straight to a payment page with no way to see the existing record first.

steps.title: A dog owner moving to town
steps.detail: Someone replies to your pet-sitting profile or a community group post, saying they are moving to your area and need daily walks for a named dog, described down to its breed and age.

steps.title: Off the app, onto text
steps.detail: They ask to continue by text or email 'because the app is glitchy', skip the usual meet-and-greet, and confirm you for the job after two or three messages.

steps.title: An 1,800 check for week one
steps.detail: A check for 1,800 dollars arrives, said to cover the first week plus food, a crate and the cost of transporting the dog to you ahead of the owner.

steps.title: Pay the pet courier
steps.detail: You are asked to keep 300 and e-transfer 1,500 to the pet courier so the dog can be collected. No animal ever arrives, and the check is refused days later.

pet-sitting-job-scam.whyItWorks: Sitters on these apps are used to strangers booking them at short notice, and a named dog with a personality makes the owner seem real. Refusing to pay the courier feels like leaving an animal stranded, which is the pressure the scammer wants.

realVsFake.real: Owners want you to meet the animal first, show you its lead and food, and watch how it reacts to you.
realVsFake.fake: The owner hires you unseen and the dog is always somewhere else, due to arrive by courier.

realVsFake.real: Bookings made on a sitting app are paid through the app, after the visit or walk is completed.
realVsFake.fake: Payment comes as a paper check posted to your home, weeks' worth at once, before you have met anyone.

realVsFake.real: An owner shipping a pet pays the transport company themselves and gives you a delivery time.
realVsFake.fake: The sitter is asked to pay the courier from the check, by e-transfer to a personal email address.

steps.title: An overdue balance by text
steps.detail: A message says your mobile account is overdue and the line will be suspended within 24 hours unless the balance is cleared through a link.

steps.title: Bill summary on a fake portal
steps.detail: The page shows an 'amount due', usually a modest figure, under a logo picker or a generic 'mobile billing' banner, with a pay-now button.

steps.title: Card and account PIN entered
steps.detail: The form takes the mobile number, card number, expiry, security code and sometimes the bill-payer's date of birth or account PIN.

steps.title: Thanks page, then card use
steps.detail: A 'payment received' screen appears and may forward you to the real network's homepage. The card is used elsewhere before the next genuine bill arrives.

phone-bill-text-scam.whyItWorks: Losing mobile service means losing calls, maps, banking codes and work messages at once, so a suspension threat lands hard. Many people pay by direct debit and never look at the bill, so they cannot say for sure that nothing is owed.
