realVsFake.real: A network chasing a missed payment sends the bill, retries the direct debit and writes more than once before restricting service.
realVsFake.fake: A single text jumps straight to suspension tomorrow with no earlier reminder.

realVsFake.real: A genuine billing text names the amount and the bill date, and matches what the network's app shows.
realVsFake.fake: The message gives no figure, and the sum on the linked page is the same for everyone.

realVsFake.real: You can pay a real bill by dialling the short customer service number from the handset itself.
realVsFake.fake: Payment is only accepted on a web page that is not your network's address.

steps.title: A detective with your name
steps.detail: A caller introduces himself as an officer with a collar number and says a bank account or parcel in your name has surfaced in a fraud investigation.

steps.title: The warrant on screen
steps.detail: To prove it he sends a warrant bearing your name and a force crest, or switches to video in uniform with a station noticeboard behind him.

steps.title: Sworn to secrecy
steps.detail: He says the case is sealed, that telling family or bank staff would be obstruction, and that you must keep the line open while 'enquiries continue'.

steps.title: Buying your way to 'cleared'
steps.detail: You can clear your name by paying a bond, or by moving your savings to an account the 'investigators' hold so the money can be checked and returned.

police-impersonation-scam.whyItWorks: Being accused of a crime you know nothing about is disorienting, and most people have never dealt with detectives, so they cannot tell what is normal. The instruction to keep quiet sounds like procedure, and it removes the very people who would recognise the trick.

realVsFake.real: Officers who need to speak to a suspect visit, or invite them to a station, and expect their identity to be checked.
realVsFake.fake: The entire 'investigation' runs over a phone or video call, and you are told not to ring the station yourself.

realVsFake.real: Bail is set by a court or custody officer after an arrest and is never collected by an officer over the phone.
realVsFake.fake: A 'bond' is demanded before any arrest, payable by bank transfer or gift card to stop one happening.

realVsFake.real: Police never ask a member of the public to move money, withdraw cash or hand over cards to help a case.
realVsFake.fake: Your savings are to be 'verified' in an account they supply, with a promise of return once you are cleared.

steps.title: 'Deadline is midnight'
steps.detail: A text in capitals says a fundraising deadline is hours away and that any gift will be triple-matched, using a candidate's or cause's name.

steps.title: A second and third text
steps.detail: If you ignore it, follow-ups arrive: 'we asked once', 'your record shows no donation', each more insistent and each with the same shortened link.

steps.title: Donation page with a pre-ticked box
steps.detail: The page shows the candidate's photo and suggested amounts. A small ticked box makes the gift weekly or monthly, and the form wants card, address and employer.

steps.title: Money to an unrelated group
steps.detail: The payment goes to a look-alike committee or an individual with no tie to the campaign, and the card keeps being charged until you cancel it.

political-donation-text-scam.whyItWorks: Real campaigns send breathless deadline texts too, so the tone alone proves nothing. Supporters who care about the outcome see a match offer as a way to make a small gift count for more, and midnight leaves no time to check who is asking.

realVsFake.real: An official campaign page carries a 'Paid for by' line naming the registered committee, and is linked from the candidate's own site.
realVsFake.fake: The page has the candidate's face but no committee name, or one you cannot find on the election regulator's records.

realVsFake.real: Genuine campaigns are happy for you to donate later through their website instead of the text.
realVsFake.fake: The messages insist the link is the only way and that the matching chance ends tonight.

realVsFake.real: A real donation form asks clearly whether you want a one-off or a repeating gift.
realVsFake.fake: Recurring payments are switched on by default in small print beside the donate button.

steps.title: A tip from someone you trust
steps.detail: A friend, relative or fellow member of your church or club mentions a fund that has paid them on the same date every month without fail.

steps.title: The test deposit pays
steps.detail: You put in a little. Payments arrive on the exact day with a tidy statement, and the explanation is a trading bot or currency arbitrage nobody can describe.

steps.title: Roll it over, bring a friend
steps.detail: The promoter suggests leaving payouts in to compound and offers commission for each person you introduce. You add your savings and tell your family about it.

steps.title: Withdrawals hit a 'system upgrade'
steps.detail: When fresh deposits slow, cash-out requests meet an audit, a lock-in period or a platform migration. Then the dashboard and the promoter both go quiet.

ponzi-scheme-scam.whyItWorks: The first payouts are real money in your bank, introduced by a person you already trust. Having watched the scheme pay, people stop asking where the profit comes from and become its most convincing recruiters.

realVsFake.real: Genuine funds have bad months, and their statements show losses alongside gains with assets held by an independent custodian.
realVsFake.fake: The return is identical every month whatever markets do, and the method is a 'proprietary' secret.

realVsFake.real: A regulated fund appears on the regulator's register, issues audited accounts and takes money through a client account.
realVsFake.fake: Deposits go to a personal bank account or crypto wallet, and your balance exists only on their dashboard.

realVsFake.real: Investment firms do not pay clients a commission for signing up relatives.
realVsFake.fake: Referral bonuses and 'ranks' reward you for bringing in workmates, because new deposits fund old payouts.

steps.title: In stock when nobody else is
steps.detail: A new console, graphics card or limited trainer is sold out everywhere. A small site or social account says it has an allocation arriving soon.

steps.title: Pay in full to reserve
steps.detail: The page takes the whole price now, by transfer or a payment marked as 'friends and family', with 'no refunds on pre-orders' in the terms.

steps.title: The date keeps moving
steps.detail: Launch day passes. Emails blame the supplier, a customs hold, then a warehouse fire. Each one asks for two more weeks.

steps.title: Past the dispute window
steps.detail: The delays are timed to outlast the period for a card or payment-app claim. Then the site goes offline.

pre-order-scam.whyItWorks: Scarcity is real for these products, so a shop claiming stock looks like a lucky find instead of a warning. Waiting is built into a pre-order, which means weeks pass before a buyer even begins to wonder.

realVsFake.real: Major retailers take a small deposit or charge your card only when the item ships.
realVsFake.fake: The entire amount leaves your account on day one, months before any release.

realVsFake.real: A real pre-order can be cancelled for a refund at any time before dispatch.
realVsFake.fake: The terms forbid refunds, and cancelling triggers a 'restocking fee'.

realVsFake.real: Authorised sellers are listed on the manufacturer's site as stockists.
realVsFake.fake: The seller has no trading history and explains its supply as 'a contact at the distributor'.

steps.title: A quiz that wants your number
steps.detail: A pop-up quiz, prize draw or free app asks for your mobile number 'to send your result', with pricing in tiny text at the foot of the page.

steps.title: A PIN to 'confirm'
steps.detail: A text delivers a short PIN to type into the page. Entering it is treated as agreeing to a paid subscription billed through your phone account.

steps.title: Texts that cost to receive
steps.detail: Messages from a five- or six-digit short code begin arriving, such as a daily quiz question. Each one received adds a charge, whether opened or not.

steps.title: Charges buried in the bill
steps.detail: The cost shows on your mobile bill under a vague service name, or drains prepaid credit. It continues weekly until the subscription is properly stopped.

premium-sms-text-scam.whyItWorks: Nobody hands over a card, so it never feels like buying anything. A phone number seems harmless to share, and the weekly amount is small enough to go unnoticed on a bill that most people only glance at.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate text service states the price and billing frequency clearly before you agree, and confirms them in its first message.
realVsFake.fake: The cost appears only in faint small print, or in a message weeks after charges began.

realVsFake.real: Replying STOP to the short code ends a properly run subscription, and the company confirms it.
realVsFake.fake: STOP is ignored or answered with an error, and the texts carry on from a different code.

realVsFake.real: Your mobile network can identify who runs a short code and can bar premium-rate services on your line.
realVsFake.fake: The service name on the bill is vague and the helpline number, if any, goes unanswered.

steps.title: Half-price credit at the door
steps.detail: Someone knocks, or posts in a local selling group, offering 50 of electricity credit for 25 in cash. They say they work for the supplier or get a staff discount.

steps.title: The key is loaded
steps.detail: They plug your top-up key into a device of their own, or tap a long code into the keypad. The display jumps by the promised amount, so it appears to work.

steps.title: Cash and no receipt
steps.detail: You pay in notes or by transfer to a personal bank account. Nothing is printed or emailed, and the seller offers to come back every week.

steps.title: The supplier claws it back
steps.detail: The supplier's records show energy used that it was never paid for. It recovers the amount through your meter or bill, so you have paid for that energy twice.

prepaid-meter-scam.whyItWorks: The credit really does show on the meter, which is all the proof most buyers ask for. Households on prepayment are often counting every pound, so half-price energy from a friendly face on the estate is hard to turn down.

realVsFake.real: Suppliers sell top-ups at face value only, through their app, by phone or at shops showing PayPoint, Payzone or Post Office signs.
realVsFake.fake: The seller is a person on your doorstep or a social media account offering credit at half its value.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate top-up produces a printed or emailed receipt showing your meter or key number.
realVsFake.fake: There is no receipt, and payment goes in cash or to an individual's bank account.

realVsFake.real: Energy company staff do not sell credit door to door.
realVsFake.fake: The caller wears a jacket with a supplier-style badge and calls the discount a 'loyalty offer' for your estate.

steps.title: A refill text with a problem
steps.detail: A text naming a large pharmacy chain says your prescription is ready but the payment did not go through, so it cannot be released.

steps.title: The pharmacy login copy
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the chain's sign-in page. It takes your account email and password, or your date of birth and home address.

steps.title: Settling the 'co-pay'
steps.detail: A payment screen asks for a few pounds or dollars as a co-pay, with full card details and sometimes your insurance member number.

steps.title: Into your medication record
steps.detail: The card is used elsewhere. With the pharmacy login, criminals can read your medication history, change the delivery address and order refills to themselves.

prescription-refill-scam.whyItWorks: Anyone on regular medication gets genuine 'ready to collect' texts every month, so one more raises no eyebrows. The thought of running out of insulin or blood pressure tablets over a weekend makes a failed payment feel like something to fix this minute.

realVsFake.real: A genuine refill text tells you the order is ready to collect or asks you to reply with a set keyword.
realVsFake.fake: This one cannot say which medicine is waiting and sends you to a web page to enter a card.

realVsFake.real: Pharmacies take payment at the counter or inside their own app, where your saved card already sits.
realVsFake.fake: A 'failed payment' is reported for a prescription you had not ordered or been charged for.

realVsFake.real: Ring the number printed on your medicine label and staff can see your order, your prescriber and what is due.
realVsFake.fake: A caller 'from the pharmacy' asks you to supply your date of birth and card, details the real one holds.

steps.title: 'Ready for delivery'
steps.detail: A text says your prescription has been prepared and is waiting to be sent out, without naming the pharmacy, the medicine or the prescriber.

steps.title: A delivery fee of £2.50
steps.detail: It adds that a small delivery or dispensing fee must be paid first, and that the medication will be returned to stock if you do not confirm.

steps.title: Address and health details
steps.detail: The form asks for full name, home address, date of birth and sometimes your GP surgery or the medicines you take, described as a safety check.

steps.title: Card taken, nothing dispensed
steps.detail: A card form collects the fee. No pharmacy is involved, and the thief now holds payment details plus health information useful for a convincing follow-up call.

prescription-text-scam.whyItWorks: People on repeat medication expect a message roughly every month, so one arriving at about the right time raises no eyebrows. Running out of tablets is a real worry, and a delivery charge is a normal thing for a pharmacy to mention.

realVsFake.real: Your pharmacy texts from the name or number it has always used, after you or your surgery ordered the item.
realVsFake.fake: The text arrives when nothing was ordered, from a number or name you have not seen before.

realVsFake.real: Prescription charges are paid at the counter or inside the pharmacy account you set up yourself.
realVsFake.fake: A link asks for card details on a page with no pharmacy name or registration number.

realVsFake.real: A real pharmacy already has your address and date of birth from the prescription.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to type in everything from scratch, including which medicines you are on.

steps.title: A printer that says 'offline'
steps.detail: Your new printer will not connect to Wi-Fi, so you search the brand name with 'setup' or 'driver download'. Sponsored results sit above the manufacturer.

steps.title: The driver install that fails
steps.detail: The site asks for your model number and shows a progress bar that always stops with a fatal error. A chat box or freephone number offers a technician.

steps.title: 'Your network is blocking it'
steps.detail: The technician connects to your computer, opens a few folders and announces that malware or a faulty network is stopping the printer from installing.

steps.title: A fee for a free driver
steps.detail: You are quoted a one-off setup charge or a device protection plan covering 'all your gadgets'. Card details are taken while they still control the screen.

printer-support-scam.whyItWorks: Setting up a printer or router is frustrating enough that people expect to need help, and they went looking for the number themselves. A site in the brand's colours with a model lookup box seems like the manufacturer's own support desk.

realVsFake.real: Printer and router makers publish drivers and setup apps free on their own sites, linked from the box or manual.
realVsFake.fake: The lookalike site never delivers a working driver. Every model number ends in the same error and a number to ring.

realVsFake.real: Manufacturer helplines deal with the device itself, and warranty support for a new product costs nothing.
realVsFake.fake: The 'technician' loses interest in the printer and starts selling a cure for problems on your computer.

realVsFake.real: The official support address is printed on the quick-start sheet and matches the brand's main website.
realVsFake.fake: The site's small print admits it is an 'independent service provider', usually at the very bottom of the page.

steps.title: 'Congratulations' from a recording
steps.detail: A bright recorded voice says your number was drawn for a holiday, a cruise or cash, and tells you to press 1 for the claims desk.

steps.title: A winner reference to write down
steps.detail: A live 'claims agent' reads out a winner reference, asks you to note it, and describes the resort or the cheque in loving detail.

steps.title: The release fee or 'prize tax'
steps.detail: Before the prize can be sent, they say, a release fee, port charge or tax must be paid today by card, wire or gift card.

steps.title: One fee turns into several
steps.detail: After the first payment comes customs, then insurance, then a courier bond. Each is described as the last, and the card is charged for things you never approved.

prize-call-scam.whyItWorks: Being told to write down a winner reference makes the prize feel filed and official. A fee that looks small beside a cruise or a cash cheque seems like a fair toll, and each payment makes walking away harder.

realVsFake.real: Genuine prize draws notify people who entered, usually in writing, and can say which entry or purchase put you in.
realVsFake.fake: The agent cannot name the promoter of the competition or say when you entered.

realVsFake.real: Real winnings are never held back for a fee, and any tax is settled with the tax authority afterwards.
realVsFake.fake: Payment has to come before the prize, and gift card numbers are accepted.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate holiday promotion sends written terms you can read before agreeing to anything.
realVsFake.fake: The 'free' cruise needs your card now for port fees, and the win expires when you hang up.

steps.title: An urgent safety notice
steps.detail: An email or text with a manufacturer's logo, or a regulator's crest, says an air fryer, charger or heater you bought has been recalled as a fire risk.

steps.title: Stop using it now
steps.detail: You are told to unplug the product at once and register within 48 hours, or lose the right to a refund or replacement.

steps.title: The registration form
steps.detail: The page asks for name, address, date of birth and where you bought it, never for a model or serial number.

steps.title: Bank details for the 'refund'
steps.detail: The last screen wants sort code, account number and card details so the refund can be paid. Those are used to take money instead.

product-recall-scam.whyItWorks: A fire warning about something plugged in at home demands action, and replying feels responsible. Recalls are real and people rarely remember exact models, so a vague 'kitchen appliance you purchased' fits nearly every household.

realVsFake.real: A real recall identifies the product by model and batch code and tells you where to find it on the item.
realVsFake.fake: The notice says only 'the appliance you purchased', with no model at all.

realVsFake.real: Manufacturers list recalls on their own site and on the official product safety database.
realVsFake.fake: The only place the recall exists is the page behind the link.

realVsFake.real: Refunds go back through the shop where you bought it, or a replacement is posted.
realVsFake.fake: A form demands online banking details and warns of a two-day cut-off.

steps.title: An invitation to test products
steps.detail: An email, text or social advert says a big retailer or a research panel needs home testers, with free gadgets to keep and a payment for each written review.

steps.title: The sign-up form
steps.detail: A short form asks for your address, date of birth and bank details 'for payroll'. Nobody interviews you, and a welcome pack is promised by courier within days.

steps.title: A starter cheque arrives
steps.detail: The envelope holds a cheque for around 1,950 and a task sheet: pay it in, keep 250 as your wage, and spend the rest on listed items or gift cards.

steps.title: Receipts, codes and a bounce
steps.detail: You photograph the receipts and card codes, or wire the leftover to a 'product supplier'. Days later the bank returns the cheque unpaid and takes the full amount back from you.

product-tester-scam.whyItWorks: Brands really do send out samples for review, so a testing role sounds ordinary. When the cheque shows in your balance the next morning, the job looks proven, even though the bank has only advanced the money and can reverse it later.

realVsFake.real: Genuine testing panels post you the product itself. You never handle company money to go and buy it.
realVsFake.fake: A cheque for far more than your pay arrives first, with instructions to shop and send the difference on.

realVsFake.real: Real review schemes pay small amounts, or simply let you keep the item, after your feedback is in.
realVsFake.fake: You are promised 250 before testing anything, as long as the cheque is banked the same day.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate panel collects your opinions through its own survey page and pays by voucher or bank credit after each test.
realVsFake.fake: Your 'reviews' are never read. The only thing chased is a photo of receipts or gift card numbers.

steps.title: The hotel-ballroom seminar
steps.detail: A free evening seminar or social media advert promotes 'hands-off' units: student pods, hotel rooms or off-plan flats abroad, each with rent 'assured' for five years.

steps.title: Renderings and a yield table
steps.detail: You are shown computer-generated images, a table of projected income and a rental guarantee issued by a management company the developer quietly owns.

steps.title: Reserve tonight for the discount
steps.detail: A reservation fee paid on the night secures a 'launch price'. Within weeks, staged payments of half the price or more go directly to the developer's account.

steps.title: A hoarding and a hole
steps.detail: Progress photos show the same fenced site for months. The developer enters administration, and the promised rent turns out to have been backed by nothing.

property-investment-scam.whyItWorks: Bricks and mortar feel dependable, and a contract with assured rent removes the one worry a first-time landlord has. A seminar room where other buyers are reaching for reservation forms supplies the rest of the push.

realVsFake.real: An established developer has finished buildings you can visit, with planning consent and land ownership on public record.
realVsFake.fake: There are only renderings, and the site still belongs to someone else or lacks permission to build.

realVsFake.real: Stage payments normally sit with a solicitor or in a protected account until building milestones are certified.
realVsFake.fake: Money goes straight to the developer or an overseas sales agent, with a discount for paying more upfront.

realVsFake.real: Honest agents say rent depends on finding tenants, and suggest you use your own independent lawyer.
realVsFake.fake: The 'assured' rent is paid out of buyers' own deposits for a while, and the recommended lawyer works for the seller.

steps.title: An advert with a queue
steps.detail: A flat is advertised at an attractive rent. Your enquiry gets an instant reply saying dozens of people have asked and viewing slots are limited.

steps.title: The £40 'slot' charge
steps.detail: To keep time-wasters away, they say, each viewer pays a £40 viewing fee, refundable on attendance or taken off the first month's rent.

steps.title: A booking link or bank details
steps.detail: You are sent an account number or a payment link styled as a booking system, then a confirmation showing a date, a time and sometimes an address.

steps.title: Nobody turns up
steps.detail: On the day the 'agent' postpones, wants a second fee to rebook, or cannot be reached. The same £40 was collected from everyone who enquired.

property-viewing-fee-scam.whyItWorks: The fee is small, and the excuse about filtering out time-wasters sounds like something a busy landlord might do. Where viewings fill within hours, paying to guarantee a slot seems a reasonable trade.

realVsFake.real: Landlords and letting agents show properties free, because viewings are how they find a tenant.
realVsFake.fake: Payment is demanded before anyone will give you the exact address or an appointment.

realVsFake.real: A genuine agent books viewings by phone or the portal's request form, with no card details involved.
realVsFake.fake: The viewing 'booking system' is a payment page or a personal bank account.

realVsFake.real: Real costs such as a holding deposit come after you have seen the place and chosen to apply.
realVsFake.fake: Money is the first thing requested, and the 'refund on attendance' never has to be honoured.

steps.title: 'Your energy called to me'
steps.detail: A tarot or healer account, sometimes a copy of a well-known reader's profile, messages to say spirit guided them to you and offers a free reading.

steps.title: A reading that fits anyone
steps.detail: They ask for your birth date and a photo, then describe a recent loss, money worries or a jealous person nearby. Most people recognise something.

steps.title: The curse appears
steps.detail: The tone darkens. A hex or blocked aura is said to hang over your family, and $200 is needed for candles, herbs and a ritual tonight.

steps.title: The ritual 'fails'
steps.detail: After payment, the curse turns out to be older or stronger than expected. Each new ceremony costs more, and stopping midway is described as dangerous.

psychic-scam.whyItWorks: The messages reach people during grief, illness or a break-up, when a stranger who seems to know their troubles is comforting. Once a threat to loved ones is named, paying for a ritual feels cheaper than the risk of ignoring it.

realVsFake.real: Readers with a real following take bookings through their own site and say publicly that they never message people first.
realVsFake.fake: A duplicate account with an extra underscore in the name slides into your DMs offering a reading.

realVsFake.real: A paid reading is a fixed session at a stated price, sold as entertainment or reflection.
realVsFake.fake: The price is open-ended, tied to removing a danger that only this person can see.

realVsFake.real: An ethical practitioner does not diagnose curses or tell you a relative will be harmed unless you pay.
realVsFake.fake: You are warned not to tell family about the work because 'doubt weakens the cleansing'.

steps.title: Invited to a 'signals' group
steps.detail: An ad, a reply under a finance post or a stranger's DM leads you into a Telegram or Discord channel showing screenshots of huge past gains.

steps.title: Organisers load up quietly
steps.detail: Before naming anything, the admins buy a thinly traded coin or penny share at the bottom. Paying 'VIP' members are promised the ticker a few seconds early.

steps.title: The 3pm call
steps.detail: A countdown ends and the ticker is posted with rocket emojis. Members pile in together, and the chart climbs steeply on their own buying.

steps.title: Sold into your order
steps.detail: The admins sell their holdings to the incoming buyers. Minutes later the price falls below where it started, and the chat urges everyone to 'hold'.

pump-dump-scam.whyItWorks: Members watch the price jump the moment the call goes out, which looks like proof the group can move markets. Each person believes they will sell before the crowd, not seeing that the organisers bought first and are the ones selling.

realVsFake.real: Regulated advisers explain risks, say prices can fall, and never promise that an asset will rise.
realVsFake.fake: The channel calls the coin 'guaranteed to moon' and mutes anyone who asks who is selling.

realVsFake.real: Sound research gives reasons to own something, such as earnings or products, and does not depend on a clock.
realVsFake.fake: The only instruction is to buy at an exact minute and to spread the name on other platforms.

realVsFake.real: Large listed companies trade in such volume that a chat group's purchases barely register.
realVsFake.fake: The pick is always an obscure token or tiny share where a few orders swing the price.

steps.title: A friend's 'be your own boss' post
steps.detail: Someone you know posts about quitting the nine to five, or messages you directly about a team they have joined that 'changed everything' in a few weeks.

steps.title: The presentation call
steps.detail: A group video call or hotel-room meeting shows income charts and photos of cars. The product gets two minutes. The 'compensation plan' and its ranks get forty.

steps.title: Paying for the starter pack
steps.detail: You pay the one-time 299 for a starter pack. Most of it flows upward as commission to the person who recruited you and the people above them.

steps.title: Now recruit your own
steps.detail: To earn anything back you must sign up others. You are handed a script, told to list everyone you know, and nudged to buy more stock to 'stay active'.

pyramid-scheme-scam.whyItWorks: The pitch comes from a friend or relative, not a stranger, and they honestly believe it because they still need recruits to recover their own joining fee. Early payouts to a few people at the top are shown as proof the plan pays.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate direct-selling company earns from customers outside the network who buy the product because they want it.
realVsFake.fake: Nearly all the money is joining fees and stock bought by members themselves, passed up the chain.

realVsFake.real: A real business can show you published figures for what a typical seller earns, including those who earn nothing.
realVsFake.fake: You see screenshots of one leader's bank balance and are told results depend on your 'mindset'.

realVsFake.real: Reputable direct-selling firms buy back unsold stock for most of what you paid.
realVsFake.fake: The starter pack is non-refundable, and questions about refunds are brushed off as negativity.

steps.title: A sticker over the real code
steps.detail: Someone places a printed QR sticker on a parking meter, charging point, restaurant table or poster, covering or sitting beside the genuine code.

steps.title: Your camera opens a web page
steps.detail: Scanning shows a short preview of the address, which few people read. The page that loads is headed 'pay for parking' with the right colours.

steps.title: Plate, duration, card
steps.detail: It asks for registration, how long you are staying, then full card details and home address, far more than the real parking app needs.

steps.title: No session, and a real ticket
steps.detail: The card is charged or sold on. Because no parking was actually paid for, a genuine penalty notice can turn up on the windscreen too.

qr-code-scam.whyItWorks: A code stuck on official equipment borrows the trust of the object it is attached to, and a QR pattern cannot be read by eye. Drivers in a hurry to pay before walking away have no reason to peel at a sticker.

realVsFake.real: Parking operators print the payment app's name and a location number on the sign, so you can open the app yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The sticker offers only a code to scan, sometimes slightly raised or misaligned over the original panel.

realVsFake.real: A genuine pay-to-park service works through a named app or a phone line listed on the meter.
realVsFake.fake: The scanned page is a plain website with no app, asking you to type card details into a browser.

realVsFake.real: Real venues and councils do not ask you to install unknown software or grant phone permissions to pay.
realVsFake.fake: Some codes open a download prompt or a login page for your email before any payment screen.

steps.title: Three messages on hold
steps.detail: Laid out like a system report, the message shows a small table of three held emails, with senders such as 'Accounts Payable' and subjects like 'Remittance advice', each beside a 'Release' link.

steps.title: Signed by your own domain
steps.detail: The notice is signed 'Mail Administrator' for your own email domain, inserted automatically from your address, and says the items will be purged in 24 hours.

steps.title: Release to inbox
steps.detail: Clicking Release opens a webmail login with your address pre-filled and your company's logo pulled in automatically. It asks for the password to 'authenticate the release'.

steps.title: No messages, one lost mailbox
steps.detail: The page reports 'messages released' or redirects to your real webmail. No held emails ever arrive, and the criminal now signs in to read your mail and reset other accounts.

quarantined-email-scam.whyItWorks: The held subject lines hint at money or a client waiting, so you want to see them. Spam filters do hold genuine mail by mistake, and most staff have no idea what their company's real quarantine notice looks like.

realVsFake.real: Real quarantine digests come from the filtering service your IT team set up, at the same time each day, listing mail you can recognise as spam.
realVsFake.fake: This one arrives once, without warning, and every held message sounds like something you would want.

realVsFake.real: Releasing a message from a real quarantine usually takes one click, or a visit to a portal where you are already signed in.
realVsFake.fake: The release link demands your mailbox password on a page hosted somewhere unrelated to your provider.

realVsFake.real: Personal accounts with Gmail or Outlook put suspect mail in a Spam or Junk folder. They do not email you about held messages.
realVsFake.fake: A 'security filter' claims to be holding mail for a free webmail address that has no quarantine at all.

steps.title: A 'limited mintage' pitch
steps.detail: A cold call or magazine advert offers a 'limited mintage' or 'key date' coin, described as a safe store of wealth while savings rates are poor.

steps.title: A slab and a certificate
steps.detail: The coin comes sealed in a plastic holder with a grade such as 'MS70' printed on the label, issued by a grading company nobody in the hobby uses.

steps.title: The Friday price rise
steps.detail: The salesperson says the price goes up on Friday, or that only a few remain from the allocation, and takes a card payment or bank transfer by phone.

steps.title: Completing the set
steps.detail: After the first purchase, calls continue about matching coins to 'complete the set'. When you try to sell, a dealer offers a fraction, or identifies a cast copy.

rare-coin-scam.whyItWorks: Coin values depend on grades and mintage figures that outsiders cannot check on the spot, so a sealed holder with a high grade reads like a bank statement. Gold and silver also carry a reputation for safety that the seller borrows.

realVsFake.real: Established coin dealers quote a buy price as well as a sell price, so you can see the gap before purchasing.
realVsFake.fake: The seller talks only about future value and changes the subject when asked what they would pay to take it back.

realVsFake.real: The main grading services print a certification number on the holder, and you can confirm the coin and grade on their websites.
realVsFake.fake: The holder looks similar but the grader is unknown, and its 'verification page' is hosted on the seller's own site.

realVsFake.real: Honest dealers describe coins as collectibles whose prices move both ways, and are content for you to compare auction records.
realVsFake.fake: You hear the word 'guaranteed', a deadline three days away, and a suggestion to move pension money into coins.

steps.title: Reading a hacked inbox
steps.detail: Criminals get into the email account of a solicitor, estate agent or title company and quietly read the threads to learn who is buying what and when.

steps.title: Waiting for completion week
steps.detail: They hold back until the deposit or closing funds are about to be requested, so their message will land exactly when you expect bank details.

steps.title: The 'updated client account' email
steps.detail: A reply in the genuine thread, with the firm's signature and your property address, says the client account has changed and earlier instructions should be disregarded.

steps.title: House money sent abroad
steps.detail: You wire the funds and confirm by email. The money is split across other accounts within hours, and the real firm rings days later asking where it is.

real-estate-wire-fraud-scam.whyItWorks: The message quotes your real case reference, purchase price and completion date, taken from the hacked mailbox. Buyers are anxious about losing the house over a late payment, so an instruction marked time-sensitive gets obeyed without a phone call.

realVsFake.real: Conveyancers give client account details at the start, often on paper, and warn that they will not change them by email.
realVsFake.fake: New account details appear the day before completion, with a line telling you to ignore everything sent before.

realVsFake.real: The firm's account is held in the firm's name, at a bank in the country where the property is.
realVsFake.fake: The payee is an individual or an unrelated trading company, sometimes at a bank in another region entirely.

realVsFake.real: Staff welcome a call to their office switchboard to read the account number back before you send anything.
realVsFake.fake: The email says the office phones are down or the solicitor is in meetings, and offers a new mobile number instead.

steps.title: A recruiter finds your CV
steps.detail: Someone from an agency you have not heard of messages on a job board or chat app, saying your profile suits a role with good pay and an immediate start.

steps.title: A ten-minute interview
steps.detail: A short text chat or call covers little beyond your availability. The same day you are told you are a great fit and an offer letter is attached.

steps.title: Fees before a start date
steps.detail: Before the start date can be confirmed you must cover registration and a background check, payable to the agency by bank transfer or gift card.

steps.title: Training, uniform, then no reply
steps.detail: Further charges follow for a training course, a uniform or a work laptop. The start date keeps moving until the recruiter's profile disappears.

recruitment-fee-scam.whyItWorks: Background checks and training are normal parts of starting work, so the fees sound like routine onboarding. Someone who has been job hunting for months is told the post is already theirs, and paying feels like the last formality.

realVsFake.real: Recruitment agencies are paid by the employer who hires you. Finding you a job costs you nothing.
realVsFake.fake: The agency's income is the candidate, charged for registration, vetting and equipment before any work exists.

realVsFake.real: A real recruiter names the hiring company and arranges an interview with someone who works there.
realVsFake.fake: The employer is 'a confidential client', and every conversation stays with one person on a messaging app.

realVsFake.real: Where a criminal record check is needed, the employer arranges it through the official checking service.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent a link to a private payment page and told the check must be bought through the agency's own provider.

steps.title: A refund 'could not be processed'
steps.detail: A text quotes an exact sum, such as $64.20, and says the refund bounced because your payment details are out of date.

steps.title: Which retailer is left vague
steps.detail: No shop is named, so you fill in the gap yourself with a recent return, a cancelled order or a utility bill you overpaid.

steps.title: Re-enter your details
steps.detail: The page shows the amount 'pending' and asks for card number, expiry and security code, or online banking login, so the money can be 'sent again'.

steps.title: Money goes out, not in
steps.detail: A code from your bank arrives and the page asks for it. That code approves a purchase by the thief, and no refund ever appears.

refund-failed-text-scam.whyItWorks: Being told money is coming to you lowers the guard that a demand for payment would raise. Most households have some return or overpayment in progress, and an odd amount down to the pence looks like something pulled from a real ledger.

realVsFake.real: A refund goes back automatically to the card or account you paid with. The seller does not need the details again.
realVsFake.fake: The page says the refund failed and wants the full card number and security code typed in.

realVsFake.real: A real retailer names itself and quotes the order number the refund relates to.
realVsFake.fake: The text gives an amount but no shop, order or date, leaving you to guess.

realVsFake.real: If a refund truly bounces, the retailer contacts you through your order account and you sort it out there.
realVsFake.fake: You are told the refund will 'expire' unless you act through the link today.

steps.title: A subscription refund call
steps.detail: A caller says an antivirus or streaming renewal was cancelled and you are due 500 back. They only need to guide you through the refund form.

steps.title: Screen sharing to 'help'
steps.detail: You are walked through installing a remote support tool such as AnyDesk, then asked to open online banking so the refund can be 'verified'.

steps.title: An extra zero on the form
steps.detail: They blank your screen, shift 5,000 from your savings into your current account, then show you the balance and cry out that they typed too much.

steps.title: Begging for 4,500 back
steps.detail: The caller pleads that they will be sacked, and asks you to return the difference by bank transfer, gift cards or cash in a parcel.

refund-recovery-scam.whyItWorks: You watch your own balance jump, so the overpayment looks proven. The money was yours all along, moved from another of your accounts, but the caller's panic about losing their job pushes you to fix their mistake before checking where it came from.

realVsFake.real: Companies refund the card that paid, automatically, and tell you by email. No call or software is involved.
realVsFake.fake: A refund agent phones you and says the money cannot be sent until you install a program.

realVsFake.real: If a business overpays you, its finance team recalls the payment through the bank. Staff do not phone to plead.
realVsFake.fake: The caller sobs about their children and their manager, then gets angry when you suggest ringing your bank first.

realVsFake.real: A true incoming credit shows a sender name in your statement, and your other accounts are untouched.
realVsFake.fake: The 'refund' has no outside sender, and your savings balance has dropped by exactly the same amount.

steps.title: 'Grade A' in the headline
steps.detail: A listing or small web shop offers a 'certified refurbished' laptop, phone or console, described as Grade A with a new battery, at a price well below established refurbishers.

steps.title: A warranty in words only
steps.detail: The seller mentions a twelve-month warranty in chat but nothing is written down, and offers a further discount if you pay by bank transfer instead of card.

steps.title: What comes out of the box
steps.detail: It turns up in a plain box with a third-party charger. It may be locked to a previous owner's account, blocked by a network, or fitted with a cheap replacement screen.

steps.title: 'Sold as seen'
steps.detail: When you complain, the reply points to the 'no returns' line in the listing, blames courier damage, or asks you to post it back at your cost to an address that does not exist.

refurbished-electronics-scam.whyItWorks: 'Refurbished' is a loose word that anyone can put in a listing, yet big brands have taught shoppers it means tested and guaranteed. A used device that powers on looks fine for the first hour, long enough for the seller to be paid.

realVsFake.real: Manufacturer and retailer refurbished programmes state the warranty length in writing and handle claims through their own support.
realVsFake.fake: The warranty is a sentence in a chat message from someone whose account was opened last month.

realVsFake.real: A reputable refurbisher will give you the serial or IMEI number so you can check for locks and blocks before buying.
realVsFake.fake: Requests for the serial number are refused 'for security', and photos show the lock screen but never the settings page.

realVsFake.real: Proper grading explains what Grade A or B means, with battery health figures and notes on any marks.
realVsFake.fake: The description says 'like new' and 'fully tested' and stops there, with one catalogue image standing in for the device.

steps.title: Hired from a job board
steps.detail: You apply for a remote support role on a jobs site. Within hours a 'recruiter' moves you to a chat app for a text-only interview with typed questions.

steps.title: An offer letter the same day
steps.detail: A PDF offer on borrowed company letterhead arrives with an hourly rate and start date. Onboarding, they say, begins once your home office is set up.

steps.title: The equipment cheque
steps.detail: A cheque for about 1,900 is emailed or couriered. You are told to pay it in by mobile deposit and send a screenshot of the receipt.

steps.title: Ordering from the 'approved vendor'
steps.detail: The vendor's page takes payment only by instant transfer or payment app for a laptop, headset and software licence. No parcel comes, and the cheque is returned unpaid.

remote-customer-service-job-scam.whyItWorks: Call-centre work from home really does need a laptop and headset, so being asked to get kitted out seems routine. The employer appears to be paying for it, which hides the fact that the vendor and the employer are the same person.

realVsFake.real: Companies that supply kit ship a configured laptop from their own IT department, with a returns label for when you leave.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent money and told to place the order yourself with one named vendor before your first shift.

realVsFake.real: A genuine support employer interviews by phone or video and checks your right to work before any offer.
realVsFake.fake: The whole hiring process is typed messages in a chat app and finishes inside an afternoon.

realVsFake.real: Real payroll starts after you have worked hours, paid by direct deposit on a set payday.
realVsFake.fake: Money lands before day one, and the vendor must be paid before the bank has finished clearing it.

steps.title: An email a few days before rent
steps.detail: Shortly before rent is due, tenants get an email or text in the landlord's or agent's name announcing that the payment system has changed.

steps.title: A near-miss sender address
steps.detail: The address differs from the real one by a letter, or uses a free mail service with the agency's name in front. Signature and logo are copied exactly.

steps.title: New portal or new account
steps.detail: The message links to a portal asking for card or bank login details, or attaches a letter giving a new sort code and account number for this month.

steps.title: Paid on time, chased for arrears
steps.detail: You pay punctually, to the wrong place. Weeks later the genuine landlord chases the missing rent, and the diverted money has long since been withdrawn.

rent-payment-portal-scam.whyItWorks: Rent is a large sum paid on a fixed day to someone tenants rarely speak to, and agencies do change systems now and then. The message arrives just as you were about to pay, so it reads as an instruction.

realVsFake.real: A landlord or agent changing bank details tells tenants formally, by letter or the existing portal, well before the due date.
realVsFake.fake: The switch is announced in a single email days before rent is due.

realVsFake.real: Genuine agents expect you to phone the office number on your tenancy agreement to confirm new account details.
realVsFake.fake: The message says to reply to that email or ring the number in its signature.

realVsFake.real: Your bank's payee name check comes back matching the agency or landlord you rent from.
realVsFake.fake: The new rent account is in a personal name or an unrelated business, excused as 'our accounts department'.

steps.title: 'Own this home, no bank needed'
steps.detail: Yard signs, flyers and online adverts offer a house on rent-to-own terms with no credit check, aimed at people who have been refused a mortgage.

steps.title: The option fee
steps.detail: The seller asks for an option fee, perhaps 4,000, for the right to buy later, and says you can move in this weekend once it is paid.

steps.title: Rent above the going rate
steps.detail: Monthly rent is set high on the promise that part is credited toward the purchase. The contract is thin, leaving out the price and the deadline.

steps.title: The purchase never happens
steps.detail: The 'seller' turns out to be a tenant, or the house is in foreclosure. Or you are evicted over one late payment and every credit is forfeited.

rent-to-own-scam.whyItWorks: For someone shut out of mortgages, rent-to-own sounds like the one door left open, and honest versions do exist. Paying extra each month feels like saving toward a house, which keeps people paying long after doubts begin.

realVsFake.real: A genuine seller appears as owner on the public deed or land records, and a title search shows no foreclosure or liens.
realVsFake.fake: The person offering the deal steers you away from checking who holds the title.

realVsFake.real: A proper lease-option contract fixes the purchase price, the option period and exactly how much rent is credited.
realVsFake.fake: The agreement is a page or two mentioning 'credits' but no price and no date.

realVsFake.real: Honest sellers expect you to bring a solicitor or attorney and arrange an inspection before paying an option fee.
realVsFake.fake: You are told lawyers only complicate things and the option fee must be paid in cash this week.

steps.title: A listing built to collect fees
steps.detail: The advert offers a well-priced flat and steers every enquirer to 'apply first'. The aim is volume, many small fees in place of one big deposit.

steps.title: 'We screen before we show'
steps.detail: The reply says that because of demand, viewings are only scheduled for approved applicants, so a 150 application and background-check fee comes first.

steps.title: E-transfer to a personal email
steps.detail: The fee is to go by e-transfer to an email address, or as a gift card code. Some send a 'credit report' link that also captures card details.

steps.title: Approved, then silence
steps.detail: You may get a cheerful 'approved' email and a viewing date that keeps slipping. Soon the listing vanishes, then reappears under another name.

rental-application-fee-scam.whyItWorks: Application and screening fees are a normal part of renting in many places, so being asked for one does not seem odd. The scam changes only the order, taking the fee before the viewing, and few renters know which comes first.

realVsFake.real: Genuine landlords show the property first and charge a screening fee only once you decide to apply.
realVsFake.fake: Paying the application fee is the condition for being allowed to see the place at all.

realVsFake.real: A real background check needs your written consent and runs through a named screening company that issues a receipt.
realVsFake.fake: The 'check' is an e-transfer to a personal email address with no screening company named.

realVsFake.real: A proper application fee is paid once, to the landlord or management company, against a receipt.
realVsFake.fake: A second 'holding' charge is requested as soon as the first 150 has gone through.

steps.title: A forty-pound screen fix
steps.detail: A website or advert quotes a price for a phone screen or laptop repair that undercuts every local shop, with free postage in.

steps.title: Post it and unlock it
steps.detail: You send the device in a prepaid bag. The form also asks for your passcode 'for testing', which opens your photos, email and banking apps.

steps.title: The 'diagnosis' call
steps.detail: A few days later they report water damage or a failed motherboard. The new price is several times the quote, plus a fee to decline.

steps.title: Held until you pay
steps.detail: Refuse, and the device stays put while 'storage charges' build. Pay, and it may return with a dim copy screen or parts missing.

repair-service-scam.whyItWorks: Once the phone is in their hands the bargaining power flips, because your photos, contacts and work are locked in a building you cannot visit. Most people will pay an inflated bill to get their own data back.

realVsFake.real: A reputable repairer gives a written quote and asks before doing work that costs more.
realVsFake.fake: The price multiplies after 'inspection', and declining carries its own charge.

realVsFake.real: Manufacturer-approved repair centres are listed on the maker's support pages, and state up front what a declined repair costs.
realVsFake.fake: Your handset is kept until an invented storage or diagnostic fee is settled.

realVsFake.real: Good shops suggest backing up and wiping the device, and rarely need your passcode.
realVsFake.fake: The booking form will not submit until you type in your unlock code.

steps.title: A table for four at 7pm
steps.detail: A text confirms a restaurant table or hotel room for a specific day and party size, under a venue name that is generic or slightly off.

steps.title: 'Pay or cancel here'
steps.detail: It says a deposit of about $20 is required to hold the booking and gives one link for both paying and cancelling.

steps.title: The cancel button
steps.detail: Since you never booked, you tap cancel. The page says a no-show fee will apply unless you 'verify the card on file' by entering it.

steps.title: Deposit charged anyway
steps.detail: The card details go to the scammer, who takes the 'deposit' and often more. There was no table, no venue and nothing to cancel.

reservation-confirmation-text-scam.whyItWorks: The natural reaction to a booking you did not make is to cancel it before you get charged, and the scam is built around that reflex. Others assume a partner or friend booked a surprise and pay the deposit to avoid spoiling it.

realVsFake.real: A real restaurant or hotel confirmation states its full name, address and phone number, and you can ring to check.
realVsFake.fake: The venue is called something like 'The Grill House' with no town, street or number.

realVsFake.real: Cancelling a genuine booking never needs your card number. You reply, phone, or use the booking platform.
realVsFake.fake: The cancel page asks for full card details to 'waive the no-show fee'.

realVsFake.real: Venues that take deposits do so at the moment you book, through their own site or a known reservation app.
realVsFake.fake: The deposit request appears afterwards, by text, for a booking nobody in your household made.

steps.title: The 'quality control' advert
steps.detail: A listing for a parcel inspector, shipping coordinator or logistics assistant promises a monthly salary for work done from your kitchen table, no experience required.

steps.title: A dashboard and a contract
steps.detail: After you upload ID and sign an online contract, you get a login to a tidy dashboard that lists incoming parcels and the tasks attached to each.

steps.title: Boxes at your door
steps.detail: Phones, laptops and trainers arrive addressed to you or to strangers. You open them, photograph the contents, strip the original labels and repack everything.

steps.title: Forwarded abroad, never paid
steps.detail: Prepaid labels from the dashboard send each box overseas. When the 30-day probation ends the login stops working, and your address is the one police trace.

reshipping-package-scam.whyItWorks: Nobody asks you for money, so it does not feel like a scam. The parcels are real, the dashboard looks like a courier system, and a month of unpaid 'probation' sounds like ordinary employment terms until the wages never come.

realVsFake.real: Freight forwarders and couriers run warehouses with staff on site. They do not route stock through private homes.
realVsFake.fake: Your spare room is the 'regional hub', and goods arrive there in other people's names.

realVsFake.real: A real logistics job leaves the sender's label and paperwork intact so the shipment can be traced.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to peel off every original label and invoice before the box goes back out.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate employers pay weekly or monthly from the first pay period, whatever trial period applies.
realVsFake.fake: Salary is held until a 30-day probation ends, and contact stops a day or two before.

steps.title: Looking up how to return
steps.detail: You search for a shop's returns page and click a sponsored result, or an email arrives after a purchase inviting you to 'start your return'.

steps.title: A lookalike returns centre
steps.detail: The page copies the retailer's colours and asks for your order number, email and account password so it can 'locate the order'.

steps.title: Paying for the label
steps.detail: A return shipping fee of 4.95 is requested by card before a printable label will be generated, with a note that the return window closes soon.

steps.title: A label to nowhere
steps.detail: The PDF carries a barcode no drop-off shop can scan, or a private address. The parcel vanishes, no refund comes, and the card is charged again.

return-label-scam.whyItWorks: Returns are a chore with a deadline, and every shop handles them differently, so an unfamiliar portal does not stand out. Plenty of real retailers charge for postage back, which makes the fee look ordinary.

realVsFake.real: Genuine returns start from the order history in your account, which then issues a label or QR code.
realVsFake.fake: An advert or email leads to a standalone 'returns centre' that makes you sign in a second time.

realVsFake.real: Where a real shop charges for sending goods back, it usually deducts the cost from the refund.
realVsFake.fake: Card details are taken upfront on the page, before any label exists.

realVsFake.real: A real label shows the retailer's warehouse and a tracking number that works on the carrier's site.
realVsFake.fake: The label names an unrelated address, and the tracking reference returns no result anywhere.

steps.title: A text as the plane lands
steps.detail: Minutes after you switch your phone on abroad, a message says 'Welcome abroad' and that roaming is not active on your line.

steps.title: Hidden among real welcome texts
steps.detail: It arrives beside genuine messages from the local network about call rates, so it looks like part of the same batch.

steps.title: Buy a travel data pass
steps.detail: The link offers a daily or weekly data plan for a small fee and asks for your mobile number, home network login and card details.

steps.title: Paid over airport Wi-Fi
steps.detail: You complete the form on public Wi-Fi with no way to phone home cheaply and check. The card and account login are both captured.

roaming-charge-text-scam.whyItWorks: Arriving in another country, you need maps, a taxi app and a way to tell family you landed. With no data and no easy way to ring the network, a message offering to switch roaming on looks like the obvious fix.

realVsFake.real: Roaming is switched on in your phone's settings and covered by your existing plan or billed to your usual account.
realVsFake.fake: The text says roaming must be 'activated' by paying through a web page.

realVsFake.real: Your home network's welcome text lists rates for calls and data and asks for nothing.
realVsFake.fake: The message has no prices, only a warning that you will be cut off and a link.

realVsFake.real: Travel add-ons are bought in the network's own app or by texting a keyword, charged to your bill.
realVsFake.fake: A browser form wants a card number even though your network already bills you every month.

steps.title: The knock about leftover tarmac
steps.detail: Men in hi-vis knock and say they are resurfacing nearby and have tarmac left over, or that they spotted loose tiles on your roof from the road.

steps.title: A price agreed on the step
steps.detail: A low figure is agreed verbally. They ask for cash to 'get materials', and may offer to drive you to the bank or a cash machine.

steps.title: Something worse underneath
steps.detail: Once the drive is dug up or tiles are off, they show you a piece of 'rotten' timber or crumbling base and say the job now costs several times more.

steps.title: Pay up or live with the mess
steps.detail: With your driveway in rubble or the roof open to rain, they demand the higher sum in cash. The finish is thin, cracks within weeks, and the van never returns.

rogue-trader-scam.whyItWorks: Most homeowners have never seen their own roof up close or what lies under the driveway, so a confident man holding a damp piece of wood is hard to argue with. Once the house is half dismantled, refusing to pay feels more dangerous than paying.

realVsFake.real: Reputable roofers and pavers are booked weeks ahead and rarely need to find work by walking the street.
realVsFake.fake: The rogue crew can start within the hour, and the special price ends when their lorry leaves your road.

realVsFake.real: A proper tradesperson leaves a written quote showing a business name and address, and is happy for you to ring back next week.
realVsFake.fake: You get a mobile number on a flyer, a first name, and a van with no signwriting or with magnetic signs.

realVsFake.real: If a genuine builder finds a hidden fault, work stops, you are shown it properly, and a revised quote follows in writing.
realVsFake.fake: The extra problem is announced when the damage is already done, with a demand for cash in hand before they will carry on.

steps.title: A surprise in the post
steps.detail: Your online partner, often working abroad on a ship, oil rig or army base, says a box of jewellery, a phone and cash is on its way.

steps.title: Tracking that looks real
steps.detail: They send a tracking number for a courier you have never heard of. Its website shows the box leaving, changing planes, then stopping with the status 'held by customs'.

steps.title: The courier agent's email
steps.detail: A 'clearance agent' writes or phones asking for a release fee, paid to a named individual's bank account or by money transfer, not to any customs office.

steps.title: Scanned cash and bigger demands
steps.detail: After you pay, the agent says a scanner found the cash, so an 'anti-money-laundering certificate' is needed. Refuse, and they hint you could be prosecuted.

romance-gift-customs-scam.whyItWorks: The fee is small beside the value supposedly sitting in the box, and your partner has promised to repay it. A second voice, the courier, makes the story feel confirmed by someone independent, when it is the same person or gang.

realVsFake.real: Import duty is collected by a known carrier through its own site or on the doorstep, with a proper receipt.
realVsFake.fake: The charge must go to a private person's account, a gift card or a crypto wallet before anything moves.

realVsFake.real: Customs officers who find undeclared cash seize it and issue formal written notices. They do not sell certificates.
realVsFake.fake: A friendly agent offers to make the problem vanish for a further payment, and warns you not to tell the police.

realVsFake.real: A tracking number from a genuine courier works when you type it into that courier's main website yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The number only works on the one site your partner linked, a company with no depot, phone line or history.

steps.title: Savings come up early
steps.detail: Weeks into the relationship, your partner hits a crisis: a frozen business account, a hospital bill, a deposit on 'our' home. You explain you have no spare cash.

steps.title: Borrowing is suggested for you
steps.detail: They propose a personal loan, a new credit card or a bigger overdraft in your name, and promise to cover the repayments once their money is released.

steps.title: Coached through the application
steps.detail: Your partner tells you what to put as the loan purpose, usually home improvements or a car, and to say nobody asked you to borrow if the bank checks.

steps.title: The debt stays behind
steps.detail: The funds land in your account and you send them on by transfer or crypto. One or two repayments may arrive, then nothing, and the lender chases you.

romance-loan-scam.whyItWorks: Borrowed money does not feel like your own money leaving, especially when someone you love has promised to make the repayments. Saying no is framed as proof you doubt the relationship, so the application becomes a test of loyalty.

realVsFake.real: A partner in real trouble borrows in their own name, from their own bank, family or employer.
realVsFake.fake: Someone you have never met in person wants the credit agreement signed by you and the cash sent to them.

realVsFake.real: Lenders ask what a loan is for because the answer matters, and an honest answer protects you.
realVsFake.fake: You are handed a script for the bank and told that mentioning your partner would 'complicate things'.

realVsFake.real: Shared finances between couples are built slowly, with joint paperwork both people can see and sign.
realVsFake.fake: The 'joint future' exists only in messages, while every agreement, card and missed payment carries your name alone.

steps.title: A favour for the business
steps.detail: Your online partner says a supplier will not ship to their country, or their warehouse has closed. They ask to use your home address for a few deliveries.

steps.title: Boxes start arriving
steps.detail: Phones, laptops, trainers and designer bags turn up from well-known retailers. Some are addressed to you, others to names you do not recognise.

steps.title: Relabel and send on
steps.detail: They email prepaid shipping labels and ask you to remove the invoices, repack the goods, mark them as gifts and post them to an overseas address.

steps.title: The trail leads to you
steps.detail: The orders were placed with stolen card details. When cardholders dispute the charges, retailers and police look at the delivery address, and the promised payment for helping never comes.

romance-package-scam.whyItWorks: No one asks you for money, so it does not look like the romance fraud people are warned about. Forwarding a parcel feels like the kind of small practical help couples give each other, and the goods arriving are real.

realVsFake.real: Companies that export goods use freight forwarders and commercial warehouses under contract, with customs paperwork in the firm's name.
realVsFake.fake: A 'businessman' routes stock through the spare room of a girlfriend or boyfriend he has never visited.

realVsFake.real: Honest shipments keep their invoices and declare the true contents and value on the customs form.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to strip out receipts, write 'gift' or 'used clothes' on the label and understate the value.

realVsFake.real: A retailer delivers what you ordered, in your name, paid for with your own card.
realVsFake.fake: Expensive electronics arrive that you never ordered, sometimes under a stranger's name at your address.

steps.title: Two ways in
steps.detail: If you are hunting for a room, the scammer advertises one. If you have a room to fill, they answer your advert as the keen new housemate.

steps.title: Happy to take it unseen
steps.detail: As 'tenant' they accept the room without a visit, being abroad, at sea or about to start a placement. As 'lister' they cannot show it this week.

steps.title: A cheque for too much
steps.detail: The incoming roommate sends a cheque or transfer for more than the deposit, says it covers utilities or a mover, and asks you to return the difference.

steps.title: The cheque bounces after your refund
steps.detail: Your refund leaves as real money. Days later the bank reverses the forged cheque. Room seekers, meanwhile, learn their deposit bought a room with no vacancy.

roommate-deposit-scam.whyItWorks: A cheque shows in your balance before the bank has finished checking it, so the money looks cleared when it is not. Sending back an overpayment feels like plain honesty towards a future housemate.

realVsFake.real: Someone who will live with you wants to see the room and meet the household, at least on a video call.
realVsFake.fake: The new housemate commits without a viewing and never has time for a call.

realVsFake.real: A real incoming roommate pays the agreed deposit and no more, by a method both of you can confirm.
realVsFake.fake: The payment is larger than asked, with a request to forward the excess to a 'mover' or back to them.

realVsFake.real: A person who truly holds the room can show a tenancy in their name and introduce the other housemates.
realVsFake.fake: The lister wants money to 'hold your spot' before you have seen the flat share or met anyone.

steps.title: 'This is your broadband provider'
steps.detail: A caller names a large internet company, often guessing correctly, and says its engineers have spotted foreign devices connected to your home Wi-Fi.

steps.title: The slow-internet hook
steps.detail: They ask whether your connection has been slow or dropping lately. Almost everyone says yes, and that answer is presented as confirmation of the hack.

steps.title: A list of 'intruders'
steps.detail: Once connected to your screen, they run a speed test or show the router's device list, pointing at your own television and phones as strangers.

steps.title: Compensation that needs your bank
steps.detail: They ask for the router's admin password, then offer a refund for the poor service or a new 'secure line', which requires logging in to your bank.

router-hacked-scam.whyItWorks: The router is a box of blinking lights that most households never log in to, so nobody can say what normal looks like. Everyone has had a bad connection recently, and a provider phoning to fix it sounds like overdue service.

realVsFake.real: A genuine provider can quote your account number and the name on the bill before discussing anything.
realVsFake.fake: The caller knows only your phone number and asks you to say which company supplies your broadband.

realVsFake.real: Providers test the line from their end and, if hardware is faulty, post a replacement or book an engineer visit.
realVsFake.fake: The fix supposedly requires software on your laptop and your eyes on the screen for an hour.

realVsFake.real: Credit for a service fault appears on your next bill without you doing anything.
realVsFake.fake: The 'refund' has to be collected by opening online banking while the caller watches.

steps.title: A token appears overnight
steps.detail: A new coin with a meme name launches on a decentralised exchange. Paid 'callers', X accounts and a busy Telegram post rocket emojis and a rising chart.

steps.title: Reassuring buzzwords
steps.detail: The pitch lists 'liquidity locked', 'contract renounced' and 'devs doxxed', perhaps with a face on video. The lock runs for days, or covers a sliver of the pool.

steps.title: The chart climbs
steps.detail: Buys from the team's own wallets push the price up. You swap ETH or SOL for the token and watch your holding multiply on screen.

steps.title: The pool is emptied
steps.detail: In one transaction the developers withdraw the pooled funds or dump a hidden supply. The price hits near zero within a minute, and some contracts block selling altogether.

rug-pull-scam.whyItWorks: The chart is the advert. A price that has already tripled looks like proof, and phrases such as 'liquidity locked' sound like safeguards to anyone who cannot read the contract code behind them.

realVsFake.real: Established tokens have a long trading history, thousands of holders and liquidity that no single wallet can remove.
realVsFake.fake: A handful of linked wallets hold most of the supply, and the deployer can withdraw the pool.

realVsFake.real: Teams with reputations at stake publish their code, pass outside audits and build something before selling.
realVsFake.fake: The product is a logo and a roadmap ending in 'moon', and the chat bans anyone asking about selling.

realVsFake.real: With a sound token, a small test sale goes through at roughly the quoted price.
realVsFake.fake: Test sales fail or lose most of their value to a hidden 'tax' written into the contract.

steps.title: The fraud team rings you
steps.detail: The call displays your bank's real number. A calm voice gives a name and staff ID, then asks whether you just tried to pay 900 to an electronics shop.

steps.title: Your account is 'under attack'
steps.detail: When you say no, they explain that criminals, possibly helped by branch staff, have access to your account and every pound in it is at risk.

steps.title: A new account, already opened
steps.detail: They read out a sort code and account number said to be freshly created in your name, and tell you to transfer your balance there.

steps.title: Coached past the bank's warnings
steps.detail: You are told to ignore the app's fraud warning and the name mismatch alert, and to say 'paying a friend' if asked. Savings follow in several transfers.

safe-account-scam.whyItWorks: The caller already knows your name, address and part of your card number, usually from an earlier phishing text, so they sound like the bank. Hearing that staff are involved explains in advance why you must not hang up and call the branch.

realVsFake.real: A bank that suspects fraud freezes the card or blocks the payment itself. Your money stays where it is.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to do the moving, by making a transfer from your own app to an account number read over the phone.

realVsFake.real: No bank or police force asks a customer to lie to branch staff or click past a fraud warning.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says the warnings are part of the attack and that telling anyone could tip off the insider.

realVsFake.real: Genuine fraud staff are content for you to hang up and ring the number printed on your card.
realVsFake.fake: They keep you on the line for an hour or more and warn that your money will be gone if the call drops.

steps.title: A note from 'the school office'
steps.detail: A text or email headed 'SCHOOL OFFICE' says the school, nursery or club has moved to a new online payment system this term.

steps.title: The trip place at stake
steps.detail: It ties the change to something specific, such as a residential trip, lunch account or club fees, and says your child's place depends on confirming.

steps.title: 'Confirm your card' page
steps.detail: The link opens a form using the school's crest, copied from its website. It asks for parent name, child's name and class, then card details.

steps.title: A small charge, then larger ones
steps.detail: A minor 'registration' amount may be taken to look genuine. The card is later used elsewhere, and the child's details help target other parents.

school-fees-text-scam.whyItWorks: Schools send a steady stream of payment requests and do change systems, so parents are used to acting on short messages from the office. No parent wants their child to be the one left off the coach because a form was missed.

realVsFake.real: Schools announce a new payment provider in newsletters and letters home, with login details issued per family.
realVsFake.fake: The change is revealed in one text with a link, and no teacher or newsletter has mentioned it.

realVsFake.real: Trip and dinner money is paid through the parent account you already log in to, which lists your child's items.
realVsFake.fake: The form knows nothing about your child and asks you to type their name and class.

realVsFake.real: The school office uses the same email domain and phone number shown on its website.
realVsFake.fake: The message comes from a mobile number or a free email address with the school's name in it.

steps.title: '1 new secure message'
steps.detail: A text says a secure message about your account is waiting and will expire, without saying whether it is from a bank, tax office or utility.

steps.title: Choose your provider
steps.detail: The link opens a page asking which bank or service you use, then loads a matching login screen, which is how one text suits everyone.

steps.title: Full login, piece by piece
steps.detail: It asks for customer number and password, then the whole memorable word instead of selected letters, then a card reader or text code.

steps.title: 'Message unavailable'
steps.detail: An error or spinning wheel appears and you may be sent to the real site. Meanwhile the thief uses the fresh login and code in your account.

secure-message-text-scam.whyItWorks: Banks and government services do keep sensitive letters in a logged-in inbox and send a short notice elsewhere, so the format is authentic. Not being told what the message says is the hook, since it could be about fraud, tax or a debt.

realVsFake.real: A real secure message stays in the inbox inside your banking app or online account until you read it.
realVsFake.fake: The text claims the message will expire unless you log in through its link.

realVsFake.real: Banks that use a memorable word ask for a few chosen characters, not the whole word.
realVsFake.fake: The copied login page wants every letter, plus a one-time code, before showing anything.

realVsFake.real: A genuine notice tells you to sign in the way you normally do. You can ignore any link and still find the message.
realVsFake.fake: The secure message cannot be found when you open the real app, because it never existed.

steps.title: You ask for help in public
steps.detail: You post on X, Reddit or Discord that your wallet will not sync. Within minutes, replies arrive from accounts named after MetaMask, Trust Wallet or Ledger support.

steps.title: The 'wallet validation' tool
steps.detail: The agent sends a link to a rectification page showing logos for dozens of wallets. You pick yours and it pretends to connect, then reports an error.

steps.title: Type your twelve words
steps.detail: A 'manual import' box appears with numbered fields for the recovery phrase, twelve or twenty-four words, described as the only way to resync.

steps.title: Restored on a stranger's phone
steps.detail: The criminal enters the phrase into their own wallet app and sends everything out. No password, device or two-step check stands in the way, because the phrase is the wallet.

seed-phrase-phishing-scam.whyItWorks: Crypto has no phone line to ring, so a person with a stuck wallet takes help where it appears. The fake agent arrives at the peak of worry, and 'validating' sounds like upkeep, not handing over keys.

realVsFake.real: Wallet makers say their staff will never ask for a recovery phrase. It is typed only into the wallet app when restoring.
realVsFake.fake: A web form, chat agent or email asks for the phrase to 'sync', 'validate' or 'migrate' your wallet.

realVsFake.real: Official support is reached from inside the app or the maker's help centre and works through tickets.
realVsFake.fake: 'Support' finds you by direct message seconds after your post and wants to continue on Telegram.

realVsFake.real: Wallet upgrades arrive as ordinary app updates from the official store or the maker's site.
realVsFake.fake: A notice says your wallet must be moved to 'version two' by a deadline or the funds vanish.

steps.title: An advert with a crest
