steps.detail: A sponsored post or website uses a police badge or customs crest and lists confiscated phones, watches and cars with starting bids of a few pounds.

steps.title: Registration and a bidder deposit
steps.detail: To bid you must register with your name, address and ID photo, then pay a 'refundable bidder deposit' by transfer, gift card or crypto.

steps.title: You always win
steps.detail: Whatever you bid, an email soon congratulates you on winning the lot and gives a deadline of a day or two to pay the balance.

steps.title: Release fees pile up
steps.detail: After the balance come a 'customs release' charge, storage and delivery insurance. Each is described as the last step, and nothing is ever dispatched.

seized-goods-auction-scam.whyItWorks: Police forces and customs really do sell confiscated property, and people expect it to go cheap because the state only wants rid of it. An official crest on the page makes a deposit feel like paperwork, not a purchase from a stranger.

realVsFake.real: Government bodies sell seized property through named auction houses or official portals that are linked from the agency's own website.
realVsFake.fake: The sale exists only on a social media page or a site with 'police' in the name and no link back from any force.

realVsFake.real: Real auctioneers publish viewing days, lot numbers and a physical saleroom, and take payment by card after the hammer falls.
realVsFake.fake: There is nowhere to view anything, and money is wanted before bidding opens, sent to an individual's account.

realVsFake.real: At a genuine sale, popular lots attract dealers and often fetch close to normal second-hand prices.
realVsFake.fake: A current flagship phone is 'won' for thirty pounds by every person who registers, each told they were the highest bidder.

steps.title: A recorded call about your listing
steps.detail: An automated voice or cold caller says your Google business listing is unverified or about to be marked closed, and asks you to press one.

steps.title: Borrowing Google's name
steps.detail: The agent introduces themselves as a 'Google specialist' or certified partner, and reads your address and opening hours back to you from the public listing.

steps.title: A guaranteed first-page package
steps.detail: They offer to fix the listing and put you top of search for a monthly fee, taken by card on the call under a twelve-month agreement.

steps.title: Junk links and a login handed over
steps.detail: The work is a batch of spam backlinks or nothing at all. Some ask for your listing login, then hold the profile hostage when you cancel.

seo-services-scam.whyItWorks: Most owners know their search listing brings in customers but not how ranking is decided, so a threat to remove it lands hard. A caller using Google's name and quoting the shop's own details sounds like the company that controls the listing.

realVsFake.real: A Google business listing is free to hold, and Google does not ring owners to sell ranking or threaten removal.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says a payment is needed today to keep the listing live or to 'renew verification'.

realVsFake.real: Honest search agencies explain that nobody can promise a position, and report on traffic and enquiries month by month.
realVsFake.fake: The pitch guarantees the number one spot within weeks, usually for a phrase nobody actually searches for.

realVsFake.real: A reputable agency works under your ownership of the listing and website, with access you can revoke.
realVsFake.fake: They ask for your password or to be made primary owner, which lets them lock you out of your own profile.

steps.title: An aparthotel at a long-stay rate
steps.detail: A serviced apartment in a business district is advertised for a stay of a few weeks, aimed at contractors, relocating staff and people between homes.

steps.title: The 'reservations manager'
steps.detail: The contact signs off as reservations manager for a building that really exists, attaching a rate sheet and floor plan with the genuine operator's branding.

steps.title: A 'direct rate' by transfer
steps.detail: They quote a 'direct' rate below the booking sites and ask for the whole stay or a large deposit by bank transfer, issuing a pro-forma invoice.

steps.title: No booking at the front desk
steps.detail: You arrive with luggage and the invoice. Reception finds no reservation under your name, and the account you paid has no link to the building.

serviced-apartment-scam.whyItWorks: Corporate stays in serviced apartments are often booked by email and invoice, so a PDF and a transfer look like standard practice. Because the building and its front desk are real, a quick search confirms everything except the person you paid.

realVsFake.real: Aparthotel operators take bookings through their own website or front desk and issue a reservation number reception can look up.
realVsFake.fake: The 'manager' writes from a free email address, and the booking exists only on their invoice.

realVsFake.real: A genuine operator accepts cards and usually takes just a pre-authorisation before arrival.
realVsFake.fake: The entire stay must be transferred in advance to qualify for the direct rate.

realVsFake.real: You can ring the building's published number and ask whether the named person works there.
realVsFake.fake: The contact gives only a mobile and claims the front desk does not handle long stays.

steps.title: You are a class member
steps.detail: You are told you are entitled to 740 from a settlement with a well-known company over a data breach or hidden fees. A 'claim ID' and a 'notice ID' are quoted.

steps.title: The claims website
steps.detail: A link opens a site with a court-style crest, a case caption and a claim form. It resembles a real settlement administrator's page and may copy text from an actual case.

steps.title: Choose how to be paid
steps.detail: The form asks for your full name, address, date of birth and Social Security or national insurance number, then bank account and routing number or sort code for 'direct deposit'.

steps.title: A fee before release
steps.detail: A final page asks for a small 'processing' or 'disbursement' fee by card before the 740 is released. The fee is taken, the card kept, and no payout arrives.

settlement-email-scam.whyItWorks: Real settlement notices do arrive by email out of the blue, from administrators nobody has heard of, about cases nobody remembers joining. A fake one is hard to tell apart, and a modest sum like 740 sounds more credible than a fortune.

realVsFake.real: Claiming from a real settlement is free. Legal fees and administration costs come out of the settlement fund by order of the court.
realVsFake.fake: You must pay a processing charge by card before your share can be 'disbursed'.

realVsFake.real: A real notice gives a case name and court you can look up, and a deadline that is typically months away.
realVsFake.fake: The case cannot be found in any court record or news report, and the claim window closes in days.

realVsFake.real: Administrators generally need a claim ID and a mailing address or payment choice, and rarely more identity detail than that.
realVsFake.fake: The form wants your full identity number and online banking details for a payment of a few hundred.

steps.title: A follow from an attractive stranger
steps.detail: A profile with model-quality photos follows you, likes several old posts and starts chatting. It has usually followed a few of your friends first to seem connected.

steps.title: Moving to disappearing messages
steps.detail: Within an hour or two they suggest Snapchat or a video call 'for privacy', send explicit pictures taken from elsewhere, and ask you to return the favour.

steps.title: The recording
steps.detail: Anything you send or do on camera is captured with a second device or screen recorder. The flirtation stops the instant they have enough.

steps.title: A collage and a countdown
steps.detail: They send your images beside a list of your relatives' and colleagues' accounts, then demand $500 in gift cards or crypto within the hour. Paying brings further demands.

sextortion-social-media-scam.whyItWorks: Shame keeps victims from telling anyone, which is exactly what the blackmailer needs. Seeing the names of your own mother or employer in the threat makes exposure feel minutes away, and paying looks like the only private way out.

realVsFake.real: Someone interested in you is willing to talk for weeks, video chat casually and meet in a public place.
realVsFake.fake: The stranger pushes for nudity on the first evening and has an excuse for never showing a live face.

realVsFake.real: A real person's profile has tagged photos, comments from friends and a history going back years.
realVsFake.fake: The account is weeks old, its pictures appear elsewhere under other names, and its followers are mostly people it is working on.

realVsFake.real: Platforms and police have reporting routes for intimate image threats, and they do not ask victims for money.
realVsFake.fake: The blackmailer promises to delete everything after one payment, then returns the next day wanting more.

steps.title: 'You qualify' for part-buy, part-rent
steps.detail: An advert or message says you are eligible for a shared ownership home in a new development, with a small share to buy and low rent on the rest.

steps.title: Brochure and plot numbers
steps.detail: You receive a glossy brochure with computer-generated images, plot numbers and a price list. The housing provider named on it is invented or impersonated.

steps.title: Eligibility fee, then reservation fee
steps.detail: An 'eligibility assessment' fee is requested first, then a reservation fee to take a plot off the market before allocations close on Friday.

steps.title: Paid to a person, not a provider
steps.detail: Payment is by transfer to an individual or an unrelated company. No solicitor appears, no mortgage is discussed, and the plots were never for sale.

shared-ownership-scam.whyItWorks: Shared ownership is a real government-backed route with real eligibility rules and reservation fees, and first-time buyers expect a process they do not fully understand. The scam borrows the vocabulary and adds a deadline.

realVsFake.real: Shared ownership homes are sold by housing associations and registered providers, which appear on the regulator's public list.
realVsFake.fake: The 'provider' is on no register and has no office or show home you can visit.

realVsFake.real: Eligibility is worked out through a financial assessment with a mortgage adviser, normally free, before any home is reserved.
realVsFake.fake: You are charged for an eligibility check and told within the hour that you passed.

realVsFake.real: A genuine reservation fee is paid to the provider after you view the plot, and solicitors handle the purchase money.
realVsFake.fake: Fees for the part-buy scheme go to a personal account and no solicitor is ever named.

steps.title: A buyer who cannot collect
steps.detail: Someone offers your full asking price straight away but says they are working away, so their own shipping agent will pick the item up from your home.

steps.title: The payment 'on hold' email
steps.detail: An email styled like a payment app or courier says the buyer's money, plus an extra 90, is held pending until you cover the insurance.

steps.title: Fronting the 90 yourself
steps.detail: The buyer apologises for the hassle and sends a link or account details for the insurance fee, stressing that it comes back to you with the item price.

steps.title: Then an 'account upgrade' charge
steps.detail: Once you pay, a new email asks for a 'customs' or 'account upgrade' fee before funds release. If the link took card details, those are used as well.

shipping-insurance-scam.whyItWorks: Sellers expect to be the ones receiving money, so they are not on guard for a request to pay. A fee of 90 looks small against a sale that seems already complete, especially with an email showing the payment waiting.

realVsFake.real: When a buyer arranges a courier, the buyer pays that courier directly, including any cover they want on the parcel.
realVsFake.fake: The courier's 'policy' somehow requires the person selling to send money first, to be refunded on top of the sale price.

realVsFake.real: A genuine payment shows as a balance when you open your banking or payment app yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The only evidence is an email saying funds are 'pending', sent from a free webmail address with a logo pasted in.

realVsFake.real: Real buyers ask about condition, haggle a little and are content to message inside the marketplace.
realVsFake.fake: This one asks nothing about the item, wants your email address at once and moves the chat to WhatsApp.

steps.title: Collecting your details
steps.detail: The fraudster gathers your name, address, date of birth and mobile number from earlier phishing forms, leaked data or what you post publicly.

steps.title: Posing as you to the carrier
steps.detail: They contact your network's support line or walk into a shop, say the phone was lost or damaged, and ask for the number to be moved to a new SIM.

steps.title: Your phone goes dead
steps.detail: Your handset drops to 'No Service' or emergency calls only. Calls and texts to your number now arrive on a device the fraudster holds.

steps.title: Password resets by text
steps.detail: They press 'forgot password' on your email, bank and crypto accounts, receive the reset codes, change the logins and move money out.

sim-swap-scam.whyItWorks: This one deceives the carrier's staff, not you, by sounding like an ordinary customer with a lost phone and the right personal details. Because so many accounts treat a texted code as proof of identity, the number alone opens the rest.

realVsFake.real: A network outage affects people around you and shows on the carrier's status page.
realVsFake.fake: Only your phone loses signal, in a place where it normally works, and restarting does not fix it.

realVsFake.real: A SIM change you requested involves a pack you ordered or a shop visit you made, with a confirmation you expected.
realVsFake.fake: A 'your SIM transfer is in progress' notice arrives when you asked for nothing.

realVsFake.real: Carriers let you add a port-out PIN or account password that must be given before a number is moved.
realVsFake.fake: The fraudster relies on staff accepting a date of birth and address as enough to move the number.

steps.title: A promo code from a stranger
steps.detail: Someone adds you on Steam or drops a code in a Discord server: free bonus credits on a jackpot site if you sign up today with your inventory.

steps.title: The sign-in box that isn't Steam
steps.detail: The 'Sign in through Steam' button opens a login window drawn inside the web page. It records your username, password and the Steam Guard code as you type.

steps.title: Early wins on a rigged wheel
steps.detail: Your bonus credits win several rounds in a row. To cash out, the site says you must first deposit skins of matching value into its trade bot.

steps.title: The withdrawal that stays pending
steps.detail: Once the knife or gloves leave your inventory, the balance freezes on 'processing'. Support stops replying, and stolen logins are used to redirect any later trades.

skin-gambling-scam.whyItWorks: Skins feel like game items even when one is worth a month's rent, so depositing them does not register as handing over cash. A run of early wins on free credits then makes the deposit look like the only thing standing between you and a payout.

realVsFake.real: Steam's real sign-in page loads on Steam's own address, and a true pop-up window can be dragged outside the browser.
realVsFake.fake: The fake box is only a picture of a window. Try to drag it past the edge of the page and it stops.

realVsFake.real: Licensed betting operators check your age, hold a gambling licence you can look up, and pay winnings to a bank account.
realVsFake.fake: The skin site names no licence or company, and your winnings exist only as a number on its own page.

realVsFake.real: In a fair trade, both sides of the offer window show items, and the other profile has years of history.
realVsFake.fake: A bot wearing your friend's name and avatar sends an offer with an empty side, from a private profile created that week.

steps.title: 'Your installation is overdue'
steps.detail: A call, text or visitor says your old meter is being switched off and a smart meter must be fitted by law, with a penalty for households that miss the cut-off.

steps.title: The installation fee
steps.detail: To secure an engineer slot they ask for an installation or admin charge, typically 30 to 100, by card over the phone or through a texted payment link.

steps.title: Billing details for the new meter
steps.detail: Next they want your sort code and account number to 'set up billing on the new meter', and ask who your current supplier is, which a real one would know.

steps.title: The same-day installer
steps.detail: In the doorstep version an 'installer' arrives within hours, asks for the meter cupboard and the fuse box, and is left alone indoors while you make tea.

smart-meter-scam.whyItWorks: Smart meter rollouts are heavily advertised and suppliers do chase customers to book, so being told yours is overdue sounds routine. Few people know the fitting is free, which lets a modest booking charge pass as normal.

realVsFake.real: Suppliers fit smart meters without an installation fee, and the appointment is made through your account or their main number.
realVsFake.fake: A charge is demanded before a date is offered, with talk of fines if you delay.

realVsFake.real: A real installer arrives on a day you agreed, and the supplier can confirm the name when you ring.
realVsFake.fake: Someone turns up within hours of a cold call, or with no warning, saying the job is scheduled.

realVsFake.real: Your supplier already bills you and does not need fresh bank details because the meter changes.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says the smart meter needs a 'new direct debit' and asks you to read out your account number.

steps.title: Your size, just after the drop
steps.detail: Soon after a limited release sells out, an Instagram or marketplace account posts the pair in a full size run, priced between retail and resale.

steps.title: Receipts and tagged pictures
steps.detail: In direct messages the seller sends a screenshot of an order confirmation and photos of a box label. Both are borrowed from other people's posts.

steps.title: Friends and family, to skip fees
steps.detail: They ask for 160 by e-transfer or as a 'friends and family' payment, saying the fee-free option keeps the price low and two other buyers are waiting.

steps.title: Blocked, or a bad pair
steps.detail: After payment the account blocks you. In the other version a box arrives with glue stains, the wrong font on the size tag and a strong chemical smell.

sneaker-resale-scam.whyItWorks: Anyone who lost the release-day raffle already believes the only route left is a stranger with a spare pair. Resale prices are so high that a figure a little above retail looks like a lucky break from a fellow collector.

realVsFake.real: Resale platforms that authenticate shoes hold your payment and inspect the pair before it is sent on to you.
realVsFake.fake: The scam seller refuses those platforms because of 'fees', and wants the deal finished in direct messages tonight.

realVsFake.real: A genuine reseller will photograph the shoes beside a handwritten note with your username and today's date.
realVsFake.fake: You are sent polished product shots and told a tagged photo is impossible because the pairs are 'at the warehouse'.

realVsFake.real: Someone holding a sold-out shoe usually has one or two pairs in odd sizes and knows what they resell for.
realVsFake.fake: This account claims every size from a child's four to an adult thirteen, all at the same price.

steps.title: A message request from nowhere
steps.detail: A stranger, or an account using a soldier's, widow's or minor celebrity's photos, writes that they are sorry to bother you but have nobody else.

steps.title: The crisis, with pictures
steps.detail: The story is a child in hospital, an eviction notice or being stranded abroad. It comes with photos of a ward or a bill lifted from elsewhere online.

steps.title: 'Anything helps'
steps.detail: They ask for a small sum by gift card code, payment app or crypto, explaining that their bank account is frozen so normal routes are closed.

steps.title: The next emergency
steps.detail: Gratitude arrives with blessings and a promise to repay. Days later the medicine costs more or the landlord returns, and guilt is applied if you hesitate.

sob-story-dm-scam.whyItWorks: Being singled out by someone in trouble makes a person feel responsible in a way a charity advert does not. The first request is small enough to give without checking, and having helped once makes it harder to refuse the second.

realVsFake.real: People in real hardship turn to family, local services or a public fundraiser where donors can see who is behind it.
realVsFake.fake: The plea goes privately to strangers one at a time, and the same text reaches many inboxes.

realVsFake.real: A hospital or landlord can be paid directly, and a genuine person in need will accept that offer.
realVsFake.fake: Offers to pay the bill itself are refused, and only gift card codes or a wallet address will do.

realVsFake.real: Registered charities give a registration number and a receipt, and they do not chase you after one donation.
realVsFake.fake: Each gift is followed by a worse turn of events and a hint that your earlier help will be wasted.

steps.title: A founder slides into your inbox
steps.detail: A 'small business owner' messages after seeing your profile or freelance listing and says they need someone to run their pages and paid adverts part time.

steps.title: No portfolio, no login
steps.detail: You are hired on the spot at a monthly retainer. They never ask to see past campaigns and never give you access to a single account.

steps.title: The ad budget cheque
steps.detail: A cheque for 2,500 arrives, described as the first month's advertising budget. Your 400 fee is inside it, and they ask for a photo of the deposit slip.

steps.title: Pay the 'ads vendor' today
steps.detail: They want 2,100 sent by e-transfer to an individual's name, said to be the agency booking the campaign. The cheque bounces after that money has left.

social-media-manager-job-scam.whyItWorks: Managing a client's ad spend is a normal part of the job, so holding their budget does not seem strange. A newcomer keen for a first client reads the instant hire as a compliment and the cheque as trust.

realVsFake.real: Real clients add you as an admin on their ad account, and their own card is billed by the platform.
realVsFake.fake: The budget is posted to you as a cheque, and you are asked to pass it to a third party.

realVsFake.real: A genuine client asks for past results, agrees a scope of work and signs a simple contract.
realVsFake.fake: You are 'perfect for the role' after three messages, with no brief, brand name or website to look at.

realVsFake.real: Freelancers invoice after the work is done and get paid the invoiced amount, nothing more.
realVsFake.fake: An overpayment arrives first, with a same-day deadline to forward the surplus by e-transfer, wire or gift card.

steps.title: A game in your feed
steps.detail: A bright image promises your stage name, elf name or royal title, built from your first pet plus the street you grew up on.

steps.title: Answers in the comments
steps.detail: You reply publicly with the result and tag three friends as instructed. The post is open to anyone, so each comment sits beside a name and profile.

steps.title: Scraped into a list
steps.detail: Whoever runs the page copies the replies and matches them with what your profile shows: full name, birthday, home town, and sometimes an email address.

steps.title: Used at a 'forgot password' screen
steps.detail: Months later someone opens the reset page for your email or bank and answers the security questions correctly, or uses the facts to sound convincing on a call.

social-media-quiz-scam.whyItWorks: No link is clicked and no money is requested, so nothing about the post feels like a scam. A pet's name seems trivial on its own, and friends are joining in, which makes answering a harmless bit of fun.

realVsFake.real: A harmless quiz asks about tastes and opinions, like a favourite film or how you take your tea.
realVsFake.fake: A harvesting post asks for fixed facts: first car, mother's maiden name, the school you attended, your birth month.

realVsFake.real: Quizzes from a known publisher show your result on the page and carry the publisher's name.
realVsFake.fake: The post comes from a page with no stated owner and only works if you type the answer where everyone can read it.

realVsFake.real: A quiz app from a reputable maker requests little beyond your public name.
realVsFake.fake: A data-grabbing quiz app wants permission to read your friends list, email address and birthday before showing a result.

steps.title: A scroll-stopping advert
steps.detail: Between friends' posts, a sponsored video shows a branded product, a designer coat or cordless vacuum, at a price that makes you stop scrolling.

steps.title: The in-app browser shop
steps.detail: Tapping opens a store inside the social app, where the address bar is easy to miss. It has a logo, a trust badge and a 'sold in the last hour' ticker.

steps.title: Card details or transfer
steps.detail: You pay quickly because stock is 'almost gone'. Some shops then email saying the card failed and ask for a transfer instead.

steps.title: Wrong item or no item
steps.detail: A cheap copy turns up, or an unrelated trinket posted purely to generate a 'delivered' tracking record. The advertiser's page has been renamed.

social-media-shopping-ad-scam.whyItWorks: An advert sitting in your feed beside posts from people you know inherits some of their credibility, and many assume the platform checks who it sells space to. Buying takes three taps, so there is no natural pause to look the shop up.

realVsFake.real: A genuine retailer's page has years of posts, tagged customers and comments left open.
realVsFake.fake: The advertiser's page was created this month, has changed name twice, and hides or deletes comments.

realVsFake.real: Real stores can be found by typing their name into a search engine, with results beyond their own site.
realVsFake.fake: The shop exists only through the advert; searching the name brings up nothing or complaints.

realVsFake.real: When something goes wrong, a proper seller offers a return label and refund.
realVsFake.fake: A 'delivered' tracking number for a different parcel is used to fight your claim.

steps.title: The robocall about your number
steps.detail: A recorded voice says your Social Security number has been suspended because of suspicious activity and tells you to press 1 to reach an officer before a warrant is issued.

steps.title: An 'officer' with a badge number
steps.detail: The person who picks up gives a name, a badge number and a case file, then describes a rented car found near the border with drugs and your number on the paperwork.

steps.title: Confirm the number, list your accounts
steps.detail: To 'clear your name' you are asked to read out the full number, then say which banks you use and roughly how much sits in each account.

steps.title: Money moved for 'protection'
steps.detail: They say your accounts will be frozen with the old number, so savings must go into a 'government safe account', gift cards or a Bitcoin machine until a new number is issued.

social-security-suspension-scam.whyItWorks: The number is tied to wages, benefits and credit, so hearing it has been 'suspended' sounds like losing access to everything at once. An official-sounding case file and the threat of arrest leave no room to wonder whether a number can be suspended at all.

realVsFake.real: The Social Security Administration does not suspend numbers. There is no such process, whatever has happened on your record.
realVsFake.fake: The recording treats suspension as routine and says only a call-back today can reverse it.

realVsFake.real: If the agency needs something from you, it normally writes a letter, and you can ring the number printed on its own website.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger phones first, keeps you on the line, and warns that hanging up will count as refusing to cooperate.

realVsFake.real: No government office takes payment in gift cards or cryptocurrency, or holds a citizen's savings in a 'safe' account.
realVsFake.fake: The 'officer' stays on the phone while you drive to a shop, and tells you to lie to the cashier about the cards.

steps.title: A grant that ends today
steps.detail: A caller, door-knocker or online form says a government scheme will pay for your panels, but funding closes tonight.

steps.title: The savings projection
steps.detail: A 'surveyor' spends an hour at your kitchen table with a tablet showing bills vanishing and the system paying for itself within a few years.

steps.title: Deposit and a finance form
steps.detail: You are asked for a deposit by transfer to 'lock in the grant' and to e-sign what turns out to be a long loan agreement.

steps.title: No install, or a poor one
steps.detail: The fitters never come, or panels go on a shaded roof and generate little. The loan repayments and the lost deposit remain.

solar-panel-scam.whyItWorks: Governments do run real energy grants with real closing dates, so a deadline sounds official. A long visit with charts builds a feeling of obligation, and the homeowner is shown savings in large print while the loan sits in a signature box.

realVsFake.real: Genuine grants are applied for through the government's or council's own site, and you can check eligibility yourself.
realVsFake.fake: A salesperson says only their firm can 'access' the funding and it expires tonight.

realVsFake.real: An accredited installer surveys the roof, gives a written generation estimate and leaves you to compare quotes.
realVsFake.fake: The figures assume perfect sunshine, and the rep will not leave the paperwork behind.

realVsFake.real: Reputable firms take a modest deposit by card after the survey, with the installation date in writing.
realVsFake.fake: A large upfront transfer is requested before anyone has looked at the roof or wiring.

steps.title: A text about a camera
steps.detail: The message says your vehicle was recorded over the limit and that you qualify for a speed awareness course in place of three points.

steps.title: No road, no speed
steps.detail: It names no road, date or recorded speed. The 'book now' link opens a page in police blue with a driver-retraining logo copied from the real scheme.

steps.title: Licence number and a course fee
steps.detail: The booking form takes your driving licence number, date of birth and registration plate, then a course fee of around ninety pounds by card.

steps.title: A booking that does not exist
steps.detail: You receive a confirmation with a date for an online session. No joining details follow, the card is charged again, and the licence details are reused.

speed-awareness-course-scam.whyItWorks: Cameras do not always flash and notices take a while to arrive, so few drivers can say for certain they were not caught last week. A course in place of points is a real and well-known offer, and it sounds like being let off lightly.

realVsFake.real: A speeding case opens with a Notice of Intended Prosecution posted to the registered keeper, stating the road, time and speed.
realVsFake.fake: The offer of a course arrives by text before any notice, and cannot say which camera caught you.

realVsFake.real: You must first return the notice naming the driver. Only then does the police force decide whether to offer a course.
realVsFake.fake: Nobody asks who was driving. The link goes straight from 'you are eligible' to a card payment form.

realVsFake.real: A genuine offer letter carries a reference number that you use to book with an approved course provider.
realVsFake.fake: The scam page will book anyone who types a licence number, because there is no record to check it against.

steps.title: Fine announced by text
steps.detail: A message says you have an unpaid speeding or traffic fine and 48 hours to settle it before prosecution, with no road, date or speed mentioned.

steps.title: A 'penalty portal'
steps.detail: The link shows a police-style crest and a notice number. It asks for driving licence number, date of birth and vehicle registration to 'retrieve the offence'.

steps.title: Points used as a threat
steps.detail: A summary screen shows a fine and warns that non-payment adds licence points and a court summons, with a discount for settling today.

steps.title: Card payment, licence data kept
steps.detail: You pay by card on the page. The thief leaves with the card details and enough licence information to attempt identity fraud.

speeding-fine-text-scam.whyItWorks: Speed cameras mean a fine can arrive weeks after a journey you barely remember, so drivers cannot rule it out. Court and penalty points threaten insurance costs and for some a job, which makes paying a modest amount feel like damage control.

realVsFake.real: A camera offence produces a posted notice to the vehicle's registered keeper, naming the road, time and recorded speed.
realVsFake.fake: The text gives no location or speed and reaches a phone number the police were never given.

realVsFake.real: A genuine notice first asks the keeper to name the driver, and explains how to contest it.
realVsFake.fake: The only choice presented is to pay immediately, with prosecution as the alternative.

realVsFake.real: Official fines are paid on the government or court payment site using the reference printed on the letter.
realVsFake.fake: Payment is taken on a page reached from a text, with a notice number you have never received on paper.

steps.title: Premium is about to end
steps.detail: A green-and-black email says Spotify could not collect your latest payment and Premium is on hold. Within 24 hours you will drop to the free tier, adverts and all.

steps.title: The 'Retry payment' button
steps.detail: The green button opens a login page on a lookalike address. Many people have used one Spotify password for years and share it with other sites, which is what the criminal wants.

steps.title: Card details for a tenner
steps.detail: A billing page then asks for card number, expiry, security code and the name on the card, to retry a charge of around ten pounds.

steps.title: Two things to sell
steps.detail: The card is tested with small purchases, then used or sold. The login is sold separately as a cheap 'Premium account', and tried against your email and shopping accounts.

spotify-payment-scam.whyItWorks: A music subscription renews so quietly that nobody remembers the billing date, which makes a failed payment entirely believable. Losing downloaded playlists before a commute or a gym session is a small, immediate irritation that invites a quick fix.

realVsFake.real: Spotify shows your plan, next billing date and payment method on your account page, reachable from the app's settings.
realVsFake.fake: The email hides those details and gives only a button, with no mention of when the payment was attempted.

realVsFake.real: If a real payment fails, the account quietly reverts to the free version. Your playlists and saved music stay where they are.
realVsFake.fake: The message warns that your library, playlists and followers will be permanently removed if you miss the deadline.

realVsFake.real: Updating a card on the real site happens after login, on one form, and never involves your banking password.
realVsFake.fake: The page asks for login and card together, and sometimes for a bank 'verification' password as a third step.

steps.title: Needs to go today
steps.detail: A listing offers an e-bike, power tools or a recent phone at half the usual price, with one or two photos taken indoors or in a car boot.

steps.title: Short answers about its past
steps.detail: Ask where it came from and the answers are short: an unwanted gift, a cousin's, an upgrade. The charger, keys or original packaging are missing.

steps.title: A street corner handover
steps.detail: The seller picks a street corner or station entrance, not a home address, takes cash only and walks off before you have checked the serial number.

steps.title: Blocked, traced and taken back
steps.detail: Later the phone is blocked by the networks, the bike's frame number matches a theft report, or police trace the item and take it back to its owner.

stolen-goods-sale-scam.whyItWorks: The goods are real and work when you test them, so nothing looks fake. Buyers tell themselves the seller simply needs money fast, and a cash bargain with no questions feels like luck until the item is identified.

realVsFake.real: An owner can usually produce something: an order email, the original box, a spare key or the phone still signed in to their account.
realVsFake.fake: A thief has the object and nothing else, and gets irritated when asked to show any link between it and themselves.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate seller will read out the IMEI or frame number in advance so you can run it through a stolen-property register.
realVsFake.fake: The number has been filed away, covered by a sticker, or the seller says they will show it when you arrive.

realVsFake.real: People selling their own belongings will often meet at their home and accept a bank payment that shows their name.
realVsFake.fake: Someone moving stolen stock wants notes only, changes the meeting point twice and uses a profile with no history.

steps.title: A half-price unit on a marketplace
steps.detail: A marketplace advert shows a large drive-up unit at about half the usual monthly rate, using photos taken from a real storage company's site.

steps.title: 'I manage it remotely'
steps.detail: The poster claims to be a private owner or remote manager. The facility is unstaffed, they say, and entry is by keypad so nobody needs to meet you.

steps.title: Deposit and first month for a code
steps.detail: You are asked to send a deposit plus the first month by transfer or gift card. In return they will text the gate code and unit number.

steps.title: A code that opens nothing
steps.detail: The code fails at the gate, or the address has no storage site. Some people are sent to a real facility whose staff say the unit is another customer's.

storage-rental-scam.whyItWorks: Modern storage sites really are run with keypads and few staff, so a manager you never meet sounds normal. People hunting for a unit are often mid-move and short of time, and a storage locker seems too mundane to fake.

realVsFake.real: Storage companies rent units through their office, website or kiosk, with a contract in the company's name and an ID check.
realVsFake.fake: A private individual rents you a unit by text with no agreement to sign.

realVsFake.real: A genuine facility lets you inspect the unit, and you fit your own padlock on move-in day.
realVsFake.fake: A gate code is promised after payment, and a visit beforehand is said to be impossible.

realVsFake.real: Real storage operators take card or direct debit and issue an invoice each month.
realVsFake.fake: The 'remote manager' wants a transfer to a personal account or gift card numbers.

steps.title: A peek through the roller door
steps.detail: A listing shows a photo through a half-open roller door: stacked boxes, a motorbike under a sheet, a safe. The caption says the tenant stopped paying rent.

steps.title: Bidding by message
steps.detail: You are invited to bid by direct message or on a one-page site. The 'auction manager' quickly replies that your offer is currently the highest.

steps.title: Deposit for the gate code
steps.detail: To reserve the win you must send a 200 deposit by payment app, crypto or gift card. In return you are promised the gate code and unit number.

steps.title: The facility knows nothing
steps.detail: The code never comes, or you are asked for a 'cleaning bond' first. Staff at the named facility, if it exists, have no record of the sale.

storage-unit-auction-scam.whyItWorks: Television shows about locker auctions have taught people that units are sold on a glance from the doorway and sometimes hide treasure. Not being allowed to look properly is part of the appeal, so it does not raise the alarm it would elsewhere.

realVsFake.real: Genuine lien sales are run by the storage facility itself, on site or through an auction platform the facility names publicly.
realVsFake.fake: The 'manager' is a private profile with no connection to the site, and ringing the front desk produces confusion.

realVsFake.real: The winner pays at the facility office when the auction closes, then clears the unit within a set number of days.
realVsFake.fake: Money is wanted before the auction has ended, described as a reservation on a bid that has not yet won.

realVsFake.real: Real units are mostly furniture, clothes and bin bags, and the photos show exactly that.
realVsFake.fake: The scam photo is staged or copied, with a tool chest, sealed electronics and a covered vehicle all conveniently in view.

steps.title: The declined-payment text
steps.detail: A text from an ordinary mobile number says your streaming subscription is on hold because the last payment was declined, and gives 24 hours to update billing.

steps.title: A sign-in page that looks right
steps.detail: The link opens a copy of the service's sign-in screen, logo and background included. Whatever email and password you type is saved, and the page lets you through regardless.

steps.title: The update-billing form
steps.detail: Next comes an 'update payment method' form asking for card number, expiry, security code and billing postcode, sometimes with date of birth added as an extra check.

steps.title: The bank code, then the real homepage
steps.detail: A final screen asks for the one-time code your bank has just texted. That code approves a purchase the criminals are making, and you are forwarded to the genuine homepage.

streaming-payment-text-scam.whyItWorks: Cards do expire and streaming payments do bounce, so the message describes something that has happened to most subscribers before. Losing tonight's viewing is a small, immediate annoyance, and fixing it through the link feels quicker than opening the app on the television.

realVsFake.real: A real billing problem shows inside the app or on the TV screen when you sign in, under your account settings.
realVsFake.fake: The only notice is a text from an unknown mobile number, carrying a shortened link.

realVsFake.real: The genuine service keeps you signed in and lets you change the card from the account page you already use.
realVsFake.fake: The linked page makes you sign in from scratch, then asks for the whole card again, security code included.

realVsFake.real: When a payment bounces, streaming companies usually retry the card over several days before pausing the plan.
realVsFake.fake: The text gives 24 hours before 'cancellation' and repeats the countdown at the top of every screen.

steps.title: Adverts timed to the start of term
steps.detail: In the weeks before term, listings for rooms near campus appear in university housing groups and on classifieds, after halls have filled and options are thin.

steps.title: Comfortable with tenants overseas
steps.detail: The landlord is relaxed about dealing with someone who cannot visit, and says the room was let to an international student last year without any trouble.

steps.title: One week's holding deposit
steps.detail: You are asked for a one-week holding deposit today, through a link or an international transfer. A tenancy agreement with a university-sounding letterhead follows.

steps.title: More to pay before the flight
steps.detail: Having paid once, you are asked for the first month and a full deposit before flying. The posted keys never arrive, and the address is a family home.

student-accommodation-scam.whyItWorks: A student holding a visa, a flight and a course start date but no bed will pay to remove the last uncertainty. International students cannot view in person and may not know how renting normally works in the country.

realVsFake.real: University accommodation offices and student unions keep lists of approved landlords and will read through a contract with you.
realVsFake.fake: The landlord says the university has no involvement and there is no time to ask.

realVsFake.real: Purpose-built student halls take bookings through their own portal, with a named building and a booking reference.
realVsFake.fake: The room is offered by a private individual who cannot say which other students live there.

realVsFake.real: A genuine landlord will walk through the room on a live video call, or let a friend visit for you.
realVsFake.fake: You get a handful of photos of the campus room and a promise that keys will be posted.

steps.title: 'Your file has been flagged'
steps.detail: A voicemail, text or social advert says you are pre-qualified under a new forgiveness programme and must call a 'processing centre' before enrolment closes.

steps.title: The eligibility check
steps.detail: A cheerful representative asks for your balance and servicer, then for your federal student aid username and password so they can 'pull up the loans'.

steps.title: A $199 enrolment charge
steps.detail: You pay $199 to start, plus a monthly 'maintenance' amount, and are advised to stop paying your servicer because the company will handle everything now.

steps.title: Locked out of your own loan
steps.detail: With your login they change the contact email so servicer notices reach them. Your loans slide into forbearance or default while their monthly fee keeps leaving.

student-loan-forgiveness-scam.whyItWorks: Forgiveness programmes do exist, and the rules have changed so often in the headlines that borrowers no longer know what they qualify for. A company offering to sort out the paperwork sounds as ordinary as paying someone to do your tax return.

realVsFake.real: Federal forgiveness and income-based repayment plans cost nothing to apply for, through your servicer or the government's student aid site.
realVsFake.fake: A 'relief company' charges to submit those same free forms, and bills monthly for 'monitoring' them.

realVsFake.real: Your servicer can already see your loans and will never need the password to your student aid account.
realVsFake.fake: The representative says they cannot check eligibility without logging in as you, and may ask you to sign a power of attorney.

realVsFake.real: Under any genuine plan your payments keep going to the servicer named on your loan statements.
realVsFake.fake: You are told to redirect your monthly payment to the company, which keeps it as fees while the loan goes unpaid.

steps.title: A sublet posted in a hurry
steps.detail: The post says the tenant moves abroad this week and needs someone for the remaining months, furniture included, at a rent below the neighbours'.

steps.title: Reasons the door stays shut
steps.detail: Packing, a flight, a sick relative: each explains why a viewing cannot happen. They may offer a video filmed earlier in place of a live call.

steps.title: Deposit and rent in one payment
steps.detail: You are told to pay the deposit and first month together through a payment link or transfer, with keys to follow in the post.

steps.title: Several tenants, one flat
steps.detail: On move-in day you may meet others with suitcases who paid for the same dates, or the actual resident, who never agreed to sublet anything.

sublet-scam.whyItWorks: Sublets are informal by nature, arranged between individuals with little paperwork, so the lack of an agent or contract does not look strange. A departure date days away makes the haste seem to be the lister's problem, not a tactic.

realVsFake.real: A tenant allowed to sublet can show the clause in their tenancy, or written permission from the landlord.
realVsFake.fake: Questions about permission are waved away with 'the landlord never checks'.

realVsFake.real: A genuine subletter hands over keys in person at the flat and shows you the meters and the bins.
realVsFake.fake: The keys are always about to be posted, once the money has arrived.

realVsFake.real: Real sublets tend to ask a modest deposit and then rent month by month.
realVsFake.fake: Deposit and rent are wanted together, urgently, before the lister 'leaves the country'.

steps.title: A renewal you never agreed to
steps.detail: A text announces that your membership renews today for 89.99. It never says which membership, so it could be antivirus, a gym, a shopping club or a forgotten free trial.

steps.title: The cancel button
steps.detail: The link leads to a page headed 'Manage subscription' with one large 'Cancel renewal' button. Pressing it opens a form instead of ending anything.

steps.title: Proving you are the member
steps.detail: To 'locate your account' the form wants your email, password and the card 'on file'. No membership number is shown, because there is no membership to find.

steps.title: Cancelled on screen, charged for real
steps.detail: A message confirms the renewal was stopped. Days later the card is used for purchases elsewhere, and the email and password are tried on your shopping and email accounts.

subscription-cancellation-text-scam.whyItWorks: Nearly everyone has signed up for a free trial and forgotten it, so an unnamed membership sounds plausible instead of invented. The amount is large enough to sting, and a cancel link looks like the responsible way to avoid paying it.

realVsFake.real: A genuine renewal notice names the service, the plan and the email address it is registered to, and usually arrives days ahead.
realVsFake.fake: The text says only 'your membership', gives today as the charge date and comes from a number you have never seen.

realVsFake.real: Cancelling a real subscription happens inside your account or app store settings and never needs the card number typed in again.
realVsFake.fake: The 'cancel' page asks for the long card number and security code, supposedly to match you to the subscription.

realVsFake.real: If a company bills you wrongly, the charge appears on your statement and your card provider can dispute it.
realVsFake.fake: Everything depends on acting before midnight, before any charge exists that you could look up or challenge.

steps.title: 'Find your forgotten subscriptions'
steps.detail: An advert or app listing promises to hunt down forgotten gym, streaming and app charges and cancel them for you in one tap.

steps.title: Connect your bank
steps.detail: Setup asks you to type your online banking username and password into the app itself, not through your bank's own approval screen.

steps.title: Email access as well
steps.detail: To 'find receipts', it requests full access to your inbox, where password resets and bank codes also arrive.

steps.title: Fees in, money out
steps.detail: A monthly 'premium' fee starts. With the logins, the operators can view balances, set up payments or sell the credentials, while few subscriptions are cancelled.

subscription-canceller-scam.whyItWorks: Nearly everyone suspects they are paying for something forgotten, and cancelling is tedious enough that handing it to an app is appealing. Legitimate budgeting tools do connect to bank accounts, so the request does not sound strange.

realVsFake.real: Regulated money apps connect through open banking: you are sent to your bank's own app to approve read-only access.
realVsFake.fake: The app has its own form for your banking password and memorable word.

realVsFake.real: You can cancel any subscription yourself in your bank app, app store settings or the provider's account page.
realVsFake.fake: The service charges a monthly fee and a cut of 'savings' for sending a template email.

realVsFake.real: A genuine provider is on the financial regulator's register under the name shown in the app.
realVsFake.fake: The developer name, the company in the terms and the name on your statement all differ.

steps.title: An allowance offer in your DMs
steps.detail: An account with photos of an older man in a suit, or a glamorous woman, says it wants to spoil someone with $800 a week, nothing expected.

steps.title: 'Which payment app do you use?'
steps.detail: They ask for your payment-app tag, email or bank login 'to set up the deposit', and move the chat to Telegram or a texting app.

steps.title: A screenshot of money on hold
steps.detail: An image shows $800 'pending'. A fake email from the payment service says the funds release once you pay a $50 activation or clearance charge.

steps.title: The reversal trick
steps.detail: In another version real money does land, from a stolen account or bad cheque. You are asked to forward part in gift cards before the bank claws it back.

sugar-daddy-scam.whyItWorks: It reaches students and people short of rent, for whom a weekly allowance would solve a real problem. Paying $50 to unlock $800 looks like simple arithmetic, and a balance that briefly shows in the account seems to settle any doubt.

realVsFake.real: Anyone who wants to give you money needs only your payment tag or account number, never a password.
realVsFake.fake: The benefactor asks for your online banking login or card PIN so they can 'deposit directly'.

realVsFake.real: Payment apps do not charge the recipient a fee to release an incoming transfer.
realVsFake.fake: An email styled like the app says your account must be 'upgraded' with a payment before the allowance clears.

realVsFake.real: A cleared payment from someone you know stays put, and nobody needs part of it sent back.
realVsFake.fake: Soon after the deposit shows, they ask you to buy gift cards for 'an orphanage' or a sick assistant.

steps.title: 'Two minutes of your time'
steps.detail: A caller from a research firm with a bland name says your household was selected for a short paid questionnaire on shopping or banking habits.

steps.title: Supermarkets first, then banks
steps.detail: It opens with where you shop and who supplies your energy. Then come which bank you use, whether you have savings and how you log in.

steps.title: 'Registering' you for the reward
steps.detail: To send payment they need your date of birth, mother's maiden name, first school or pet, and the sort code and account number to pay into.

steps.title: Your answers come back later
steps.detail: Those answers match your bank's security questions. A later caller posing as the bank already knows them, or a 'voucher delivery charge' is taken from your card.

survey-call-scam.whyItWorks: A questionnaire sets the rule that they ask and you answer, so by question ten few people stop to wonder why a researcher needs a mother's maiden name. The promised reward explains away the request for bank details.

realVsFake.real: Genuine market researchers ask for opinions and broad bands, such as an age range or region, and let you skip questions.
realVsFake.fake: The questions narrow to exact dates, account numbers and the answers banks use to reset passwords.

realVsFake.real: Real research agencies name the company, and you can verify the project with the industry body or a freephone line.
realVsFake.fake: The firm's name returns nothing in a search, and the interviewer will not say who commissioned the work.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate thank-you arrives as a voucher code by email or post, with nothing to pay.
realVsFake.fake: The survey reward needs your card number for a small processing charge first.

steps.title: A thank-you from a familiar brand
steps.detail: Borrowing the logo of a supermarket, pharmacy or parcel company, the message says you were picked to give feedback. Thirty seconds of questions earns a 90 reward.

steps.title: Five easy questions
steps.detail: The survey asks how often you shop and how you rate the staff. Whatever you answer, a spinning animation ends with 'Congratulations, you qualify'.

steps.title: Pick your prize
steps.detail: A page shows a tablet, headphones or gift card marked 'only 2 left', with invented comments underneath from happy winners. You choose one and are asked to cover 3.95 shipping.

steps.title: The small print
steps.detail: The card form sits above pale grey text enrolling you in a 'membership' billed every two weeks at a far higher amount, under a company name you will not recognise on the statement.

survey-reward-email-scam.whyItWorks: Answering the questions first makes the prize feel earned, so the shipping fee seems like a fair last step. A charge of 3.95 is small enough that people hand over a card number without reading what else it authorises.

realVsFake.real: Genuine brand surveys are linked from a till receipt or your account, and offer a prize-draw entry or a modest voucher.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger's email offers a 90 reward to everyone who clicks, for half a minute of multiple choice.

realVsFake.real: When a retailer gives a real reward, it is a code or points added to your loyalty account with nothing to pay.
realVsFake.fake: The 'free' gift needs a card payment for postage, taken by a company that is not the brand named in the email.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate subscription states its price beside the payment button and sends a confirmation with cancellation details.
realVsFake.fake: The recurring charge is disclosed only in faint text far down the page, and no confirmation email ever arrives.

steps.title: A real number, an invented person
steps.detail: A stolen Social Security or national ID number, often a child's because it has no history, is paired with a made-up name, birth date and a rented mailing address.

steps.title: A declined application creates a file
steps.detail: The first credit card application is refused, as expected. The refusal still prompts the credit bureaus to open a brand-new file for the invented person under that number.

steps.title: Months of good behaviour
steps.detail: The fraudster nurses the file with a low-limit card paid on time, or pays to be added as an authorised user on a stranger's old account, until the score looks healthy.

steps.title: The bust-out
steps.detail: Once limits are high, every card and loan is drawn down in a few days and the 'person' vanishes. What remains is unpaid debt attached to the real owner's number.

synthetic-identity-scam.whyItWorks: Lenders check whether a file exists and how it has behaved, and rarely confirm that the name belongs to the number. A child will not apply for credit for years, so nobody is looking while the false file matures.

realVsFake.real: A child under eighteen normally has no credit file, so a bureau search on their number comes back empty.
realVsFake.fake: A search on your ten-year-old's number returns open cards, a car loan and addresses in another state.

realVsFake.real: Your own report lists only the names you have used and the places you have lived.
realVsFake.fake: An unfamiliar name and a mail-drop address appear as an 'alias' on your report, sharing your ID number.

realVsFake.real: When a lender turns you down, the stated reason relates to borrowing you recognise.
realVsFake.fake: You are refused for 'too many recent accounts' or a default on a loan you have never heard of.

steps.title: 'I manage creators like you'
steps.detail: A DM or comment from an account with 'mgmt' or 'talent' in its name says your content has potential and lists famous brands it claims to work with.

steps.title: The discovery call
steps.detail: On a short voice or video chat they talk about campaigns waiting for the right face and say your account could earn a full-time income within months.

steps.title: Contract and onboarding fee
steps.detail: A PDF agreement arrives with an invoice for onboarding, a media kit design or a place on their roster. Payment is by transfer to an individual.

steps.title: Deals that stay 'in negotiation'
steps.detail: Weeks pass with updates about brands that are nearly ready to sign. More costs follow, for a photo shoot or profile audit, until replies stop.

talent-manager-scam.whyItWorks: Creators with a few thousand followers often believe a manager is the missing step between them and paid work. Being 'signed' is flattering, and a one-off onboarding cost sounds like the sort of business expense a professional would accept.

realVsFake.real: Real managers earn commission, a share of the deals they bring in, so they are paid only when you are.
realVsFake.fake: This 'manager' wants money from you before a single brand has been approached.

realVsFake.real: An actual agency has a registered company name, a website listing its roster, and creators who confirm they are represented.
realVsFake.fake: The agency exists only as a social profile, and the creators it names have never heard of it.

realVsFake.real: Reputable representation gives you days to read the contract and encourages you to get it checked.
realVsFake.fake: You are told two roster places remain this month and the paperwork must be signed and paid for tonight.

steps.title: 'Payment on hold'
steps.detail: Your tax credits payment has been paused, the text or email says, and will stop altogether unless you renew your claim and confirm where it is paid.

steps.title: A borrowed sign-in page
steps.detail: The link leads to a copy of the tax authority's sign-in screen. Your user ID and password are captured, then a 'renewal form' loads.

steps.title: Questions about the household
steps.detail: The form asks for your National Insurance number, your children's names and birth dates, and the bank account the credits were paid into.

steps.title: A fee to restart payments
steps.detail: Finally, a small 'reinstatement' charge is taken by card. The thieves leave with a card, a tax login and enough family detail to pass security checks elsewhere.

tax-credits-scam.whyItWorks: Families who relied on tax credits were used to renewing every summer against a fixed deadline, and a missed renewal really did stop the money. A 'payment on hold' message revives that yearly worry about rent and food, even for people whose claim has since moved.

realVsFake.real: In the UK, tax credits have closed. Former claimants were invited by posted letter to claim Universal Credit or Pension Credit instead.
realVsFake.fake: The message asks you to renew a benefit that no longer has a renewal process.

realVsFake.real: A tax authority already holds the account it pays into, and any change is made after you sign in yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The 'renewal' asks you to type the sort code and account number again, followed by the card linked to it.

realVsFake.real: No benefit or credit is restarted by paying a charge. Awards are paid out, never bought.
realVsFake.fake: A 'reinstatement fee' of a pound or two appears on the last screen, as a pretext for taking card details.

steps.title: Your year-end form is ready
steps.detail: In the weeks before the filing deadline, an email says your W-2, P60 or annual tax statement is available. It appears to come from 'Payroll' or a tax document service.

steps.title: A file called TaxForm.html
steps.detail: Instead of a PDF, the attachment is a web page file. Opened, it loads in your browser from your own computer and displays a login box over a blurred tax form.

steps.title: Sign in to unblur
steps.detail: The box asks for your work email password or payroll login 'to decrypt the document'. In the link version, the download is a zip holding a program disguised with a PDF icon.

steps.title: Used before you file
steps.detail: A stolen payroll login exposes your real tax form, with identity number, salary and address, which is enough to file a false return and claim the refund in your name.

tax-document-email-scam.whyItWorks: Timing does most of the work: in tax season, employers and banks really do email to say forms are ready, and people are waiting for them. An .html attachment looks like a harmless document to anyone who does not check file endings.

realVsFake.real: Employers usually tell staff in advance when year-end forms will be issued and where, typically inside the payroll system.
realVsFake.fake: The email arrives with no prior announcement and puts the 'form' in an attachment or behind its own download link.

realVsFake.real: A real tax form is a PDF or a page inside your payroll account. Once open, it does not ask for a password.
realVsFake.fake: The attachment ends in .html, .zip or .iso and shows a login prompt on top of an unreadable form.

realVsFake.real: Payslips and year-end forms come from the same sender and system as every previous one.
realVsFake.fake: The display name says 'Payroll Department', but the address behind it is a domain you have never seen.

steps.title: Your tax ID is obtained
steps.detail: The number comes from a breached payroll provider, a fake tax-preparer email asking for last season's documents, or a wage form taken from the post in January.

steps.title: A return filed before yours
steps.detail: As soon as the filing season opens, the criminal e-files under your number with invented wages and inflated withholding, designed to produce the biggest refund the system will pay.

steps.title: Refund sent to their card
steps.detail: The refund is directed to a prepaid debit card or a bank account opened days earlier, then withdrawn as cash before anyone compares the return with your employer's records.

steps.title: Your own filing bounces
steps.detail: Weeks later you submit your genuine return and the software rejects it as a duplicate, or a letter arrives about income and a refund you know nothing about.

tax-identity-theft-scam.whyItWorks: Tax systems accept the first return filed under a number and pay refunds quickly, often before employer wage reports are matched. The honest taxpayer files later, so the thief only has to be early.

realVsFake.real: Your own e-filed return is accepted once, and the acknowledgement arrives within a day or two.
realVsFake.fake: Your return is rejected with a duplicate-filing code because someone has already used your number this season.

realVsFake.real: The IRS raises a suspicious return by posting a letter that asks you to confirm whether you filed it.
realVsFake.fake: A caller or email claims to be fixing the 'duplicate return' and asks for your bank login or a fee.

realVsFake.real: The wage records on your tax account list only employers you actually worked for.
realVsFake.fake: Income from a company in a town you have never visited shows up, because someone is working under your number.

steps.title: A problem with your return
steps.detail: The sender poses as the tax-preparation service you filed with, or a popular one mailed to everyone. Your return was rejected, it says, or your refund is on hold pending verification.

steps.title: A clone of the software's login
steps.detail: The link opens a clone of the software's login page, down to the padlock artwork. You enter your user ID and password, then the code texted to your phone.

steps.title: 'Confirm your filing details'
steps.detail: A follow-up form asks for last year's income figure, your identity number, date of birth and the bank account for the refund, all 'to re-submit the return'.

steps.title: The refund is redirected
steps.detail: Signed in as you, the criminal downloads prior returns, files or amends this year's with his own bank details, and the tax refund is paid to him.

tax-software-email-scam.whyItWorks: People who file through software expect emails from it during tax season, including genuine rejection notices. A held refund is money you are already counting on, and the filing deadline makes any hitch feel like it must be fixed today.

realVsFake.real: A real rejection shows as a status when you open the software yourself, with the error code and the field to correct.
realVsFake.fake: The email gives no reason for the hold and no error code, only a button marked 'Verify account'.

realVsFake.real: Tax refunds are paid by the tax authority into the account named on your return. The software company does not hold them back.
realVsFake.fake: The message says the software firm itself is keeping your refund until you log in and re-verify.

realVsFake.real: Genuine services write to the address you registered and greet you by the name on the account.
realVsFake.fake: The same email reaches people who have never used that product, addressed to 'Dear taxpayer'.

steps.title: A teammate is trying to reach you
steps.detail: The email mimics a Teams activity notice: purple banner, a colleague's initials in a circle, the first words of a message, 'Hi, are you free for a quick...', and 'Reply in Teams'.

steps.title: A missed call from the boss
steps.detail: Other versions say a director tried to call you, or that you were added to a channel named after a real project. The names are scraped from the company website or LinkedIn.

steps.title: The work sign-in page
steps.detail: 'Reply in Teams' opens a Microsoft 365 login clone. It takes your work email and password, then relays the authenticator number or code and captures the session.

steps.title: Inside the company chat
steps.detail: Using your account, the criminal reads chats and shared files, then messages real colleagues from within Teams itself, where a link from you is trusted without question.

teams-notification-email-scam.whyItWorks: An unanswered message from a manager creates social pressure that an ordinary email does not. The truncated preview is designed so you cannot tell what is being asked without clicking, and replying fast feels like plain good manners.

realVsFake.real: A real Teams message is waiting in the app on your laptop or phone, with a red badge on the Chat icon.
realVsFake.fake: The app shows no unread chat and no missed call from that colleague. Only the email says otherwise.

realVsFake.real: Missed-activity emails are sent after you have been inactive in Teams for a while, and clicking normally opens the app you are already signed in to.
realVsFake.fake: The notice arrives while you are sitting in Teams, and its button asks for your password as if you were new.

realVsFake.real: Chat messages sit in the conversation history. They do not vanish because you were slow to read them.
realVsFake.fake: The email claims the two messages will 'expire' unless you sign in to read them today.

steps.title: Three viruses, one phone number
steps.detail: A text headed 'Security Alert' says three viruses were found on your device and your accounts are exposed. There is no link, only a freephone number to ring.

steps.title: The scripted diagnosis
steps.detail: The agent asks what phone you have and whether it has felt slow or warm lately. Any answer confirms 'the infection', which they say is reading your banking apps.

steps.title: An app that lets them watch
steps.detail: They talk you through installing a screen-sharing app from the official store and reading out its session code, after which they can see everything you open.

steps.title: The clean-up fee
steps.detail: A 'lifetime protection plan' is quoted at a few hundred, payable by card during the call or in gift cards. Some ask you to open your banking app while they watch.

tech-support-text-scam.whyItWorks: Phones do slow down and run hot, and almost nobody knows what a real infection looks like on a handset. Because you dial the number yourself, the call feels like something you chose, which lowers your guard with the stranger who answers.

realVsFake.real: Phone makers and mobile networks have no way of scanning your handset and texting you a virus count.
realVsFake.fake: The message quotes an exact number of viruses and says they were 'detected', without saying by whom.

realVsFake.real: Genuine support is reached through the manufacturer's own app or the number printed on your contract.
realVsFake.fake: The only route offered is a freephone number that appears nowhere except in that text.

realVsFake.real: A real repair shop or helpline bills through a receipt and a card terminal, or the store account you already hold.
realVsFake.fake: Payment is wanted mid-call, by reading card details aloud or by buying gift cards and sending the codes.

steps.title: Added to a group overnight
steps.detail: You find yourself in a Telegram or WhatsApp group of several hundred people, or an 'assistant' invites you after you click an advert using a famous investor's face.

steps.title: The professor and his helper
steps.detail: A mentor posts market commentary each morning while an assistant answers questions. Members share winning screenshots and thank the teacher, and most of those accounts are run by the organisers.

steps.title: Free signals, then the real ask
steps.detail: After a week of free tips, a coin is named with ten minutes' notice, or you are told to open an account on a 'partner platform' to copy trades.

steps.title: Profits you cannot withdraw
steps.detail: The platform shows your deposit growing. Cashing out requires a 'tax' or a VIP upgrade paid first, or the tipped coin collapses as insiders sell. Then the group disappears.

telegram-investment-group-scam.whyItWorks: Dozens of people appear to be making money in front of you, in real time, and none of them seems to be selling anything. Watching quietly for a week creates the feeling of having checked it yourself.

realVsFake.real: Licensed brokers sit on a public register and open accounts through identity checks and written risk warnings.
realVsFake.fake: An assistant sends a private sign-up link to a trading site that appears on no register anywhere.

realVsFake.real: Professional analysts publish their losing calls too, and none claims to time the market to the minute.
realVsFake.fake: Every posted trade wins, losing tips are deleted, and members who voice doubts are removed from the chat.

realVsFake.real: A regulated firm deducts its charges from your balance and pays withdrawals to your own bank account.
realVsFake.fake: You must send extra money, labelled tax or margin, before any withdrawal is released.

steps.title: Any prescription in minutes
steps.detail: An advert on social media or search promises antibiotics, weight-loss injections or anxiety medication online within minutes, with no appointment and no waiting room.

steps.title: A quiz in place of a doctor
steps.detail: The 'consultation' is a tick-box questionnaire. No clinician's name appears, nobody checks your identity, and every answer leads to the same approval screen.

steps.title: Payment by transfer or app
steps.detail: You pay a consultation fee and the medicine cost together, often steered towards a bank transfer or payment app, and upload ID and a health history.

steps.title: A plain envelope, or none
steps.detail: Nothing comes, or loose blister strips arrive from abroad with no label or leaflet. A request for a 'customs release' fee sometimes follows.

telehealth-scam.whyItWorks: Legitimate online clinics have made it normal to get a prescription through a phone screen, so a quick web consultation no longer seems strange. People after medicine that is hard to find or awkward to ask a family doctor about are ready to skip the checks.

realVsFake.real: A real service names the prescriber and gives a registration number you can look up on the regulator's register.
realVsFake.fake: The site shows stock photos of people in white coats and lists no names, numbers or clinic address.

realVsFake.real: A genuine clinician asks follow-up questions and sometimes declines to prescribe what you wanted.
realVsFake.fake: Approval is instant whatever you enter, including for medicines that normally need blood tests or monitoring.

realVsFake.real: Medicine from a licensed pharmacy arrives in a labelled pack showing your name, the dose and the dispensing pharmacy.
realVsFake.fake: Tablets come unboxed with foreign-language print, or the tracking number never moves after payment.

steps.title: A viewing the same evening
steps.detail: A buyer rings about your car advert, asks few questions and wants to view the same evening, sometimes arriving on foot or dropped off by a friend.

steps.title: Compliments on the driveway
steps.detail: They look round the car, compliment it and ask you to start the engine. Then they suggest a quick spin alone because their insurance 'covers any vehicle'.

steps.title: Something left as security
steps.detail: To reassure you they leave a set of keys, a rucksack or a photo of a licence. The keys fit nothing and the licence belongs to someone else.

steps.title: Five minutes becomes never
steps.detail: The car pulls away and does not return. In another version you step out to change seats and they drive off, or they hand back a dummy key and collect the car overnight.

test-drive-theft-scam.whyItWorks: A test drive is a normal part of selling a car, and refusing one feels rude when the buyer seems ready to pay. Sellers worry about losing the sale, so asking for a licence or insisting on riding along feels like an accusation.

realVsFake.real: A serious buyer expects you in the passenger seat and hands over their driving licence for you to photograph.
realVsFake.fake: The thief has left their licence at home and says a passenger would 'make it hard to hear the engine'.

realVsFake.real: Most genuine buyers arrive in a car of their own, which sits outside your house with its number plate visible.
realVsFake.fake: They were dropped at the corner, and the 'friend' who brought them is waiting out of sight.

realVsFake.real: An honest handover has both keys counted back into your hand before anyone talks about price.
realVsFake.fake: During the chat a second person asks to see the service book, and the key you get back no longer starts the car.

steps.title: Your number in the sender line
steps.detail: The message shows your own mobile number as the sender, or drops into the thread you use for notes to yourself. It opens with 'Free Msg' and thanks you for your loyalty.

steps.title: The loyalty reward
steps.detail: It says a gift is waiting on your account, such as a tablet, earbuds or a bill credit, and that the offer lapses within a day or two.

steps.title: A survey, then a delivery charge
steps.detail: The link opens a page in carrier colours with a short customer survey. You 'win' the gift and are asked to cover a small postage charge by card.

steps.title: The card was the prize
steps.detail: The form may also ask for your carrier account PIN. The small charge becomes a monthly one, and the PIN can be used to take over your mobile account.

text-from-your-own-number-scam.whyItWorks: People assume nobody else can send from their number, so the sender line feels like proof the message came from the network itself. A text from yourself is also odd enough that most people open it out of curiosity.

realVsFake.real: Mobile networks send service texts from a short code or their brand name, never from the customer's own number.
realVsFake.fake: The sender field is forged to show your number, a trick that needs no access to your phone or account.

realVsFake.real: Genuine loyalty perks appear in the carrier's app or on your bill, where you can see them after signing in.
realVsFake.fake: The reward exists only behind the link, and there is no trace of it in your account.

realVsFake.real: A real thank-you gift from your network does not need a card number before it can be posted.
