realVsFake.fake: A postage fee of a pound or two is requested, which quietly enrols the card in a recurring charge.

steps.title: Sold out, except here
steps.detail: The official sale ends in minutes. A search for the tour name brings up a site with the artist's artwork, a seat map and tickets still available.

steps.title: Choose your seats
steps.detail: You pick a block and row. A basket timer counts down from five minutes and a banner says dozens of others are viewing the same section.

steps.title: Transfer for 'instant e-tickets'
steps.detail: Card payment is 'temporarily unavailable', so the page gives bank details. An email follows with a PDF and a barcode.

steps.title: Rejected at the turnstile
steps.detail: On the night the scanner shows the barcode as invalid or already used, because the same PDF was sold to several buyers.

ticket-website-scam.whyItWorks: Fans who missed the official sale are upset and afraid of missing out a second time, so they search in a hurry. Genuine ticketing sites also use basket timers and seat maps, which makes the fake checkout feel like the real one.

realVsFake.real: The artist's or venue's own website links to its authorised ticket sellers.
realVsFake.fake: The site was found through an advert and is not named anywhere by the venue.

realVsFake.real: Many events now issue mobile tickets in the seller's app, with a barcode that refreshes.
realVsFake.fake: A static PDF or screenshot is emailed, which can be copied and sold repeatedly.

realVsFake.real: Authorised resale platforms hold the buyer's money until after the event or guarantee entry.
realVsFake.fake: Payment goes straight to a bank account, and the 'support' inbox stops replying before the date.

steps.title: A half-price recharge advert
steps.detail: A comment under a popular live, a video ad or a DM claims a reseller site offers 10,000 Coins at half the usual rate, or free with a promo.

steps.title: Type in your @username
steps.detail: The site asks for your handle and shows your real profile picture, pulled from public data, which makes it seem linked to TikTok itself.

steps.title: 'Log in to receive your Coins'
steps.detail: A copy of the TikTok sign-in appears, followed by a card form for the discounted bundle or a 'human verification' wall of surveys and app installs.

steps.title: An empty balance
steps.detail: No Coins are added. The card is charged or sold on, and the stolen login is used to drain any existing Coins or post scam videos.

tiktok-coins-scam.whyItWorks: Viewers who send gifts to streamers know Coins cost real money, and plenty of legitimate game currencies are sold at a discount by third parties. Seeing your own avatar load on the page seems to confirm an official connection.

realVsFake.real: Coins are bought on the recharge screen inside the TikTok app or on TikTok's own website while signed in.
realVsFake.fake: A third-party 'top-up store' with TikTok's logo sells bundles through its own card form.

realVsFake.real: Coins are a balance TikTok adds to your account after purchase. There is no stock for an outside seller to discount.
realVsFake.fake: The offer claims a bulk supply of Coins at half price, or a generator that creates them for nothing.

realVsFake.real: A purchase made in the app shows in your balance within moments and appears in your transaction history.
realVsFake.fake: The site says delivery takes up to a day and asks you to complete two sponsor offers while you wait.

steps.title: A viral product video
steps.detail: A clip shows a gadget, hair tool or branded trainers with a caption about a warehouse clearance. The account looks like a shop but has only a few uploads.

steps.title: 'Not available in-app'
steps.detail: The caption or a reply says the deal is website only and points to the link in bio, or asks you to message them on WhatsApp to order.

steps.title: A storefront built last week
steps.detail: The outside site has stolen product photos, a countdown and a stock bar that always reads 'only 3 left'. It takes card details or gives bank transfer instructions.

steps.title: A tracking number to nowhere
steps.detail: You may get a tracking code that never updates. The parcel is a flimsy imitation or never comes, and extra charges can appear on the card you used.

tiktok-shop-scam.whyItWorks: Shoppers are used to buying straight from short videos, and real sellers do sometimes run their own websites. The clip itself can be genuine footage copied from a real brand, so the product looks exactly as it should.

realVsFake.real: A TikTok Shop listing opens a product page inside the app, where you pay and the order is tracked under your profile.
realVsFake.fake: The seller insists the discount cannot go through the in-app basket and sends you out to a browser page.

realVsFake.real: Shops on the platform show a rating, a sold count and reviews with buyers' own photos.
realVsFake.fake: The profile has no shop tab, comments are switched off, and its praise is pasted into the video itself.

realVsFake.real: If an in-app order goes wrong, you raise a refund request with the platform from the order page.
realVsFake.fake: After an outside payment the only contact is a chat number that stops replying once the money has gone.

steps.title: The call with a buyer waiting
steps.detail: A 'resale broker' phones or emails, already knowing your resort and week, to say a corporate buyer has offered well above what you paid.

steps.title: Contracts that look right
steps.detail: A purchase agreement arrives with a buyer's name, a closing date and the letterhead of a title or escrow company, which is a clone of a real firm.

steps.title: The refundable closing fee
steps.detail: Before funds release you must wire a transfer fee or closing cost of a few hundred pounds, described as refundable and held in escrow.

steps.title: Taxes, then more taxes
steps.detail: The sale stalls. A foreign tax, a government permit or an 'anti-laundering bond' is now needed, payable to an overseas bank, and each new charge is larger than the last.

timeshare-resale-scam.whyItWorks: Owners paying maintenance fees every year for weeks they no longer use are desperate for an exit, and the resale market for timeshares is poor. A caller who already knows the resort and offers a profit sounds like rescue.

realVsFake.real: A reputable resale agent is generally paid from the sale proceeds at closing, after the buyer's money has arrived.
realVsFake.fake: The fraudulent broker needs your money to arrive first, and says the fee cannot be deducted from the buyer's payment 'for legal reasons'.

realVsFake.real: Your resort or its owners' association can tell you which resale routes it recognises and what transfers actually cost.
realVsFake.fake: The caller tells you not to contact the resort, claiming it would block the sale or demand a cut.

realVsFake.real: Used timeshares usually change hands for very little, and honest agents say so at the start.
realVsFake.fake: The offer is higher than the original purchase price, from a buyer you are never allowed to speak to.

steps.title: A call asking for the copier model
steps.detail: Someone rings reception sounding like your usual supplier and asks for the model number on the front of the printer 'to update our records'.

steps.title: The price-rise warning
steps.detail: A second call says toner prices rise next week, but they can ship at the old price today. They take the name of whoever answered as the authorising person.

steps.title: A box nobody remembers ordering
steps.detail: Cartridges arrive, often generic and poor quality, and get signed for and put in the stationery cupboard. The delivery note names the employee from the call.

steps.title: An invoice at several times the price
steps.detail: The bill is far above normal cost. Queries are met with a claimed call recording, a hefty restocking fee for returns, and threats of collections.

toner-scam.whyItWorks: Whoever answers the phone rarely knows who supplies the toner, so a confident caller is taken for the regular vendor. Once the box has been opened and the invoice names a real colleague, accounts assumes the order was genuine.

realVsFake.real: Your actual supplier already holds your printer model and account number, and has no reason to ask for either.
realVsFake.fake: The caller will not give a company name beyond 'the supply department' and hangs up when asked for one.

realVsFake.real: Genuine orders carry your purchase order number and match a quote someone in the business requested.
realVsFake.fake: The paperwork cites a verbal agreement with a receptionist or temp who has no authority to buy.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate vendor takes back goods sent in error at its own cost.
realVsFake.fake: Returns are refused or charged a steep fee, and each reminder adds interest and a firmer legal threat.

steps.title: A text with a download link
steps.detail: The message says your parcel is on its way and that you should install the courier's tracking app to follow it in real time.

steps.title: The download page
steps.detail: A page in courier colours offers a download button. On Android it delivers an APK file with instructions to allow installs from unknown sources.

steps.title: Permissions it should not need
steps.detail: On opening, the app asks to become your default SMS app, read your contacts and switch on accessibility access, which lets it see and tap the screen.

steps.title: A phone working for someone else
steps.detail: The malware reads banking codes from texts, lays fake login screens over real banking apps and sends the same parcel message to everyone in your contacts.

tracking-app-scam.whyItWorks: Every big courier does have an app, so being told to install one seems unremarkable. Android's warnings are easy to tap through when the page has already explained that they are normal for this download.

realVsFake.real: Genuine courier apps are installed from Google Play or the Apple App Store, found by searching the courier's name.
realVsFake.fake: The message links to a file and tells you to turn off a security setting first.

realVsFake.real: A real tracking app needs notifications and perhaps location to show the van on a map.
realVsFake.fake: This one demands to read and send texts and to control the screen through accessibility.

realVsFake.real: Any parcel can be followed on the courier's website with the tracking number, no app required.
realVsFake.fake: The text insists the delivery can be viewed only after installing.

steps.title: A straight swap offer
steps.detail: Someone replies to your listing, or posts their own, proposing to trade a newer boxed phone or console for yours, perhaps with a little cash on top.

steps.title: Proof sent in advance
steps.detail: They send photos of a genuine sealed box with matching stickers. What they bring to the meeting is a different box, shrink-wrapped at home with a hair dryer.

steps.title: Hurry at the handover
steps.detail: At the meeting they are double-parked or late for a train. They inspect your device carefully but say opening theirs would 'ruin the seal'.

steps.title: Opening the box at home
steps.detail: Inside is a clay block, a tile cut to weight, a dummy display handset or an older model in a new shell. Their number no longer connects.

trade-in-swap-scam.whyItWorks: A factory seal looks like the strongest proof there is, and breaking it feels like damaging the thing you are about to own. The swap also seems fair because no money moves, which lowers the guard people keep for a sale.

realVsFake.real: A genuine trader is happy to cut the seal, power the device on and let you check the serial number in settings against the box.
realVsFake.fake: The scammer argues an opened box loses value and offers to knock a little off if you take it sealed.

realVsFake.real: Honest swappers agree to meet inside a phone shop or at a police station exchange point, in daylight.
realVsFake.fake: The meeting point shifts at the last minute to a side street or a car window, with an engine running.

realVsFake.real: Both sides of a fair trade get the same time to test what they are receiving.
realVsFake.fake: They spend five minutes checking your phone, then pass over theirs while a companion asks you for directions.

steps.title: Your application goes public
steps.detail: When you file a trademark, your name, address and the mark itself are published in the official journal, where anyone can copy them.

steps.title: An invoice that looks governmental
steps.detail: A letter arrives from a 'Trademark Publication Register' or similar title, showing your logo, application number and filing date beside a barcode and payment slip.

steps.title: A four-figure 'registration' fee
steps.detail: The amount is often over a thousand, described as a registration, publication or monitoring fee, with a due date about two weeks away.

steps.title: Listed in a private database
steps.detail: The small print admits this is an offer to appear in a private catalogue with no legal effect. Payment goes to a foreign account and changes nothing about your rights.

trademark-scam.whyItWorks: The letter turns up just after filing, when an applicant expects official post and has already paid one fee. Seeing their own application number and logo printed on it, most assume only the intellectual property office could know those details.

realVsFake.real: The official intellectual property office takes its fee when you file and writes to you or your attorney from its own address.
realVsFake.fake: The sender has a grand title with 'Office', 'Agency' or 'World' in it and a return address in another country.

realVsFake.real: Trademark renewals fall due many years after registration, on a date shown in the official record.
realVsFake.fake: A 'renewal' or 'protection' bill arrives within weeks of filing, or years ahead of the real date, at an inflated price.

realVsFake.real: Official fees are paid through the office's own online account or by the attorney handling your filing.
realVsFake.fake: The slip asks for an international bank transfer and carries a disclaimer in tiny type saying it is not an invoice.

steps.title: A graded rookie, underpriced
steps.detail: A post in a collectors' group or marketplace shows a graded slab of a sought-after rookie or first-edition card, listed well under recent sold prices.

steps.title: Photos lifted from a past sale
steps.detail: The pictures were saved from a completed auction. Ask for a short video tilting the slab under a light and the seller says the card is already packed.

steps.title: 'Serious buyers only'
steps.detail: The seller refuses the platform checkout, asks for e-transfer or crypto, and promises to post the same day with tracking 'once payment clears'.

steps.title: An envelope that disappoints
steps.detail: Nothing comes, or a slab arrives with frosted edges where the case was cracked open and a lower-grade or reprinted card sealed back inside.

trading-card-scam.whyItWorks: A graded slab is meant to settle the question of authenticity, so buyers stop examining the card itself. The hobby also runs on fast deals between strangers in group chats, where hesitating usually means someone else gets the card.

realVsFake.real: A genuine slab has a crisp label, a certificate number that matches the grader's online record, and clean welded edges.
realVsFake.fake: The number is real but belongs to a cheaper card, or the label font and hologram sit slightly wrong.

realVsFake.real: Established card sellers have years of feedback and references in collector groups, and accept payment methods with buyer protection.
realVsFake.fake: The account joined the group last week, has no vouches, and calls protected payment 'a scam risk for sellers'.

realVsFake.real: High-value cards are sent insured and signed for, in a rigid mailer, with the tracking number shared on dispatch.
realVsFake.fake: You receive a tracking number for a letter delivered to a different postcode, or a plain envelope holding a common card.

steps.title: The per-page offer
steps.detail: An email says you have been selected as a remote translator at 35 a page. The sender uses a free email address and names an agency you cannot find.

steps.title: A sample text to translate
steps.detail: They send a short document to translate, often a generic article. You return it, they praise the quality, and nobody ever comments on the actual language.

steps.title: Certification and passport
steps.detail: To 'activate your account' you must pay 49 for certification and send a passport scan with bank details. The scan alone is enough to open accounts in your name.

steps.title: Forwarding the client payment
steps.detail: A cheque from a 'client' turns up for more than you earned. You are told to forward 400 of it to a software supplier before it fails.

translation-job-scam.whyItWorks: Bilingual people are told all their lives that their second language is worth money, and freelance translation genuinely is done remotely, per page, for clients you never meet. A praised test piece makes the agency feel real before the fees begin.

realVsFake.real: Real agencies test you with a short passage that is marked by another linguist, and many reject most applicants.
realVsFake.fake: Everyone passes, the rate is far above the market, and the 'project manager' cannot say which language pair they need.

realVsFake.real: Professional memberships and translation software are things you choose and buy yourself from the body or developer.
realVsFake.fake: The agency sells its own certificate for 49 and names one supplier you must pay for software.

realVsFake.real: A genuine agency pays your invoice by bank transfer, usually a month after delivery, for the exact amount.
realVsFake.fake: Payment comes early as an oversized cheque, with part of it to be passed on through a link.

steps.title: Cover for the price of a coffee
steps.detail: A social media advert or comparison-style page offers full worldwide cover for a few pounds, any destination, with 'no exclusions' in bold type.

steps.title: Insured in thirty seconds
steps.detail: The form asks only for a name, travel dates and card number. It skips age, medical conditions and destination, which a real insurer needs to price the risk.

steps.title: A certificate with no insurer
steps.detail: You receive a one-page certificate with a policy number and a shield logo. It names no underwriter, attaches no policy wording and lists a claims email only.

steps.title: The claim from abroad
steps.detail: When you fall ill or are robbed overseas, the emergency number does not connect and the claims address never replies. The hospital bill is yours.

travel-insurance-scam.whyItWorks: Travel insurance is bought in a hurry, often minutes after paying for flights, and almost nobody reads the policy until something goes wrong. A certificate in the inbox feels like protection, so the gap stays hidden until the first claim.

realVsFake.real: A genuine policy names the underwriting insurer, and that firm can be found on the financial regulator's register.
realVsFake.fake: The seller's name matches nothing on the register, or imitates a known brand with one word changed.

realVsFake.real: Real insurers ask about your age, health and route, then send the full policy wording with every exclusion listed.
realVsFake.fake: No medical questions are asked, and the paperwork promises cover for 'everything'.

realVsFake.real: Proper cover includes a staffed emergency assistance line that a hospital can ring to confirm payment.
realVsFake.fake: The only contact is a web form, or a mobile number that goes to voicemail.

steps.title: The visit is finally booked
steps.detail: After months of cancelled plans, your partner announces a date and sends a screenshot of a flight itinerary. You arrange time off and plan the airport pickup.

steps.title: A shortfall on the ticket
steps.detail: Days before, their card is declined or wages are late, so they ask you to top up the fare. The money goes by transfer, never to an airline.

steps.title: Stuck at the departure gate
steps.detail: On the day, a rushed message says officials have stopped them over excess baggage, a travel permit or undeclared valuables. Sometimes a stern 'officer' takes the phone.

steps.title: Rebooked, and stranded again
steps.detail: You pay to free them, the flight is 'missed', and a rebooking fee follows. The next attempt ends in a hospital stay or a stolen wallet.

travel-money-romance-scam.whyItWorks: The request lands when you are happiest and most invested: bags packed, spare room ready, friends told. Refusing a small fee at that point feels like cancelling the reunion yourself, and airports are places where odd charges seem possible.

realVsFake.real: A traveller short of the fare lets you book the seat yourself, on the airline's site, in their passport name.
realVsFake.fake: They refuse a ticket bought by you and want cash instead, saying a relative or travel agent gets a better price.

realVsFake.real: Airlines charge baggage fees at the desk by card, and border staff do not phone a passenger's partner for money.
realVsFake.fake: An 'airport official' demands a wire within the hour and says your partner will be detained otherwise.

realVsFake.real: A booking reference can be looked up on the airline's manage-booking page using the passenger's surname.
realVsFake.fake: The itinerary is only ever a cropped image, and the reference on it fails when you try it.

steps.title: A rate above the market
steps.detail: An advert or comparison-style page shows a holiday currency rate better than the mid-market figure banks themselves trade at.

steps.title: Lock it in now
steps.detail: You enter how many euros or dollars you want. A timer says the rate is held for fifteen minutes and offers free next-day home delivery.

steps.title: Transfer the full amount
steps.detail: Payment is by bank transfer to an account whose name does not match the brand, or in crypto, with a reference number to quote.

steps.title: The courier that never calls
steps.detail: A fake dispatch email gives a tracking code that goes nowhere. The envelope of cash or the prepaid card does not arrive before your trip.

travel-money-scam.whyItWorks: Travellers compare rates the week before leaving, when a few extra euros per hundred pounds look like free spending money. Ordering currency online for delivery is a normal service, so transferring a large sum to a stranger does not feel unusual.

realVsFake.real: Real bureaux make money on the spread, so their rate is always a little worse than the mid-market one.
realVsFake.fake: The quoted rate beats the interbank figure, meaning the firm would lose on every sale.

realVsFake.real: Authorised currency firms appear on the financial regulator's register and often let you collect in a branch.
realVsFake.fake: No registration is given and there is no counter anywhere you could walk into.

realVsFake.real: Established providers accept debit cards and send insured, tracked delivery with a named courier.
realVsFake.fake: Only transfer or crypto is taken, and the tracking link is a page on its own site.

steps.title: Drivers wanted, top pay
steps.detail: A social media advert or text offers a weekly rate well above what local hauliers pay, home every weekend, with new or lapsed licence holders welcome.

steps.title: A recruiter with no depot
steps.detail: The 'dispatcher' chats by app, asks for a photo of your licence and medical card, and confirms you are hired without a road test or a yard visit.

steps.title: The orientation and permit fee
steps.detail: Before your first load you must pay 300 for orientation, a permit, a drug screen or a uniform, sent by payment app to a personal account.

steps.title: A start date that slides
steps.detail: Orientation is postponed, then a second charge appears for a fuel card or tablet. Some send a cheque for 'equipment' instead and ask for part back.

truck-driver-job-scam.whyItWorks: Driving work comes with real paperwork: medicals, permits, drug tests, induction days. A new driver does not know which of those the carrier pays for, so one more fee before the first run sounds like the cost of getting on the road.

realVsFake.real: Haulage firms pay for induction and usually pay you for attending it, at a depot you can visit.
realVsFake.fake: Orientation costs 300 up front and takes place 'online', with no yard address given.

realVsFake.real: A real carrier checks your driving record and watches you handle a vehicle before handing over keys.
realVsFake.fake: You are approved from a licence photo alone, and the contract arrives as a chat message.

realVsFake.real: Licences and permits are issued by government licensing bodies, and you pay those bodies directly.
realVsFake.fake: The recruiter collects the permit fee personally and promises the document will be waiting in the cab.

steps.title: 'We couldn't take your payment'
steps.detail: An email or text says your latest Direct Debit was unsuccessful, the licence is no longer valid, and billing details must be updated within 48 hours.

steps.title: A convincing copy of the site
steps.detail: The link opens a close copy of the licensing site, with the familiar logo. Page one asks for your name, address, date of birth and phone number.

steps.title: Setting up a 'new Direct Debit'
steps.detail: Page two wants the sort code and account number, then the card number and security code, and sometimes your mother's maiden name 'for security'.

steps.title: The follow-up call from 'your bank'
steps.detail: A week or two later someone phones as your bank's fraud team. Knowing everything you typed, they say the account is at risk and must be emptied into a new one.

tv-licence-scam.whyItWorks: Most households have a licence and many pay it monthly, so a failed payment is an everyday possibility that few people would bother to question. Watching without a valid licence can mean prosecution, which gives 'no longer valid' more weight than a late bill.

realVsFake.real: You can check your licence's expiry date and payment status by signing in on the licensing site with your licence number.
realVsFake.fake: The email claims the licence has lapsed but never quotes the licence number or the address it covers.

realVsFake.real: A licence refund is something you apply for yourself, for example after moving in with someone who already has one.
realVsFake.fake: The scam announces a refund you never requested, for an overpayment it cannot explain or date.

realVsFake.real: When a payment is missed, the licensing body sends reminders, and you have time to put it right.
realVsFake.fake: The fake notice declares the licence dead after one missed payment and leaves two days before a penalty.

steps.title: A whisper during the stream
steps.detail: While the channel is live, a whisper arrives from an account named almost exactly like the streamer or their bot, saying you were drawn in tonight's giveaway.

steps.title: Moved to a claim page
steps.detail: The message links to a purple, Twitch-styled page, or invites you to a Discord server where a 'moderator' posts the same claim link.

steps.title: Login first, then a fee
steps.detail: The page asks for your Twitch password and authenticator code to 'verify the winner', then a small release or shipping fee paid by card or gift card.

steps.title: Your account joins the scam
steps.detail: No console or gift subs ever arrive. The criminals change your email, keep the fee, and use your account to whisper the same win notice to other viewers.

twitch-giveaway-scam.whyItWorks: Streamers do run giveaways and call out winners mid-broadcast, so a win message that lands while the stream is on screen fits what you were just watching. Being singled out by someone you follow every night is flattering enough to skip checking the sender's name letter by letter.

realVsFake.real: A streamer announces winners out loud or in channel chat, where the broadcaster and moderator badges are visible.
realVsFake.fake: The news comes privately from an account with no badge, a swapped letter in the name and no followers.

realVsFake.real: To send a real prize, a creator needs a delivery address or a gamer tag and nothing else.
realVsFake.fake: The claim page wants your Twitch password, the six-digit code from your authenticator, and a payment before 'release'.

realVsFake.real: Ask in the public chat and the channel's moderators can confirm within seconds whether a draw took place.
realVsFake.fake: The whisper gives you ten minutes, warns the prize will be redrawn, and tells you not to post about it.

steps.title: 'We love your profile'
steps.detail: A brand account you have never heard of comments on your video or sends a DM praising your content and inviting you to its paid creator programme.

steps.title: The rate card
steps.detail: They quote a fee per video, sometimes several hundred, and send a glossy brief template. You are asked to confirm your email, address and payout details.

steps.title: Buy the kit to start
steps.detail: Paid briefs unlock once you order the 60 starter kit from their shop link, supposedly so you film with the real product. A refund is promised with your first invoice.

steps.title: Videos delivered, silence follows
steps.detail: The kit is cheap or never arrives. If you film anyway, they take the clips, run them as adverts, and stop replying when you send the invoice.

ugc-creator-job-scam.whyItWorks: Small creators hear constantly that brands pay ordinary people for short videos, and a DM from a brand is what a first deal looks like. Buying the product to film with sounds reasonable when you have no portfolio and the cost is small.

realVsFake.real: Brands that commission creators ship the product free, because your video is worth more to them than the item.
realVsFake.fake: You must buy the item first from their own store, with a discount code to make it feel like a perk.

realVsFake.real: A real deal has a written agreement covering fee, deadline, number of edits and how long they may use the footage.
realVsFake.fake: Terms stay vague in chat, and usage rights are never mentioned until your clip appears in an ad.

realVsFake.real: Genuine brands contact you from a company email and can be found through their official site or a known creator platform.
realVsFake.fake: The account has few posts, copied product photos, and asks you to continue on a private messaging app.

steps.title: Your details reach the wrong hands
steps.detail: Sort code and account number are copied from a leaked database, a fake prize form, or the checkout of a 'free trial' that buried a subscription.

steps.title: A mandate set up in your name
steps.detail: Using only those two numbers and your name, someone signs you up online for a membership, a lottery syndicate or a service they can resell.

steps.title: Small sums under a vague name
steps.detail: A payment of 4.99 starts leaving each month. The statement reference is an abbreviation or trading name that could pass for an app or insurance add-on.

steps.title: Months pass before anyone looks
steps.detail: The amount stays low enough to sit among genuine bills. By the time a statement is read line by line, the same collector has taken many payments.

unauthorised-direct-debit-scam.whyItWorks: Setting up a direct debit takes only a sort code and account number, details people hand out freely to get paid. A few pounds a month under a bland reference looks like something you probably agreed to and forgot.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate company tells you the amount and date in advance of the first collection, by letter or email.
realVsFake.fake: The first you know of it is a line on your statement, with no welcome email, contract or account number to quote.

realVsFake.real: When you cancel a genuine subscription, the firm confirms in writing and the collections stop.
realVsFake.fake: A dishonest trial seller keeps charging after cancellation, sometimes under a new reference so the old block does not catch it.

realVsFake.real: Real collectors use a reference that matches their trading name and answer when you ring the number on their paperwork.
realVsFake.fake: Searching the reference turns up other people asking what it is, and no working customer service line.

steps.title: An advert or a held-parcel text
steps.detail: A social media advert shows pallets of sealed boxes sold as unclaimed courier stock, or a text says a parcel in your name is being held at a depot.

steps.title: A 1.99 fee and a countdown
steps.detail: The text wants 1.99 within 24 hours or the parcel goes back. The pallet advert runs a timer and claims only a few mystery lots remain.

steps.title: A checkout in courier colours
steps.detail: The link opens a page styled like a delivery firm, tracking number already filled in. It asks for your address, card number, expiry date and security code.

steps.title: Junk in the box, or nothing
steps.detail: Pallet buyers receive nothing, or a carton of cheap trinkets. People who paid the release fee later find bigger charges on the same card.

unclaimed-parcel-scam.whyItWorks: Plenty of people have a delivery on the way in any given week, so a held parcel sounds plausible and 1.99 seems too small to question. The pallet version borrows from genuine liquidation sales of returned stock.

realVsFake.real: A courier that misses you leaves a card or updates tracking for an order you can match to a retailer's confirmation email.
realVsFake.fake: The notice names no sender and no shop, only a parcel 'in your name' and a link to pay.

realVsFake.real: Genuine redelivery or customs charges are paid in the courier's own app, reached from the tracking number the retailer sent you.
realVsFake.fake: The release fee is taken on a page reached from the text itself, which then wants full card details.

realVsFake.real: Firms that sell returned stock in bulk publish a manifest of each lot and a business address buyers can visit.
realVsFake.fake: The pallet seller calls the contents a surprise and accepts only bank transfer or gift cards.

steps.title: Spam you never signed up for
steps.detail: A run of emails arrives advertising pills, loans or a 'final notice' about nothing. They are irritating by design, and each ends with a clear 'Unsubscribe' link.

steps.title: The click that confirms you
steps.detail: Clicking loads a page carrying a code unique to your address. The sender now knows the mailbox is live and read by someone who clicks, which raises its resale price.

steps.title: 'Enter your email to confirm'
steps.detail: The page may ask you to type your address, then your email password 'to verify ownership of the mailbox', or to tick boxes that feed a profile of your interests.

steps.title: More mail, not less
steps.detail: Your address moves to a list of confirmed responders and is sold on. Volume climbs within days, and some unsubscribe pages also push a 'spam blocker' download that is malware.

unsubscribe-phishing-scam.whyItWorks: Unsubscribing is the responsible thing to do with mail from real companies, and people have been told for years to use the link at the bottom. The scam hides inside that good habit, on mail where the habit should not be applied.

realVsFake.real: A real mailing list is one you can remember joining, from a shop, charity or newsletter with a name you recognise.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is a string of random letters or a brand you have never dealt with, and you gave them nothing.

realVsFake.real: Legitimate unsubscribe pages remove you in one or two clicks and already know which address to remove.
realVsFake.fake: The page wants you to type the address again, add a password, or 'log in to manage preferences'.

realVsFake.real: Your mail app's own Block and Report spam buttons deal with junk without contacting the sender at all.
realVsFake.fake: The spammer's link is offered as the only way to stop the messages, in large type at the foot of each one.

steps.title: The 60-minute final notice
steps.detail: A text or recorded call says your electricity will be cut within the hour over an overdue balance. Cafes and small shops often get it during their busiest hour.

steps.title: A crew already on its way
steps.detail: The link or callback number reaches a 'disconnections desk' that quotes an arrears figure and says a technician has been dispatched to switch off your supply.

steps.title: Why normal payment will not do
steps.detail: They claim card and bank payments take days to clear, so the only way to stop the technician is a prepaid card, a wire transfer or cryptocurrency.

steps.title: Reading out the card numbers
steps.detail: You are kept on the line while you buy prepaid cards at a shop and read out the numbers on the back. A second call often says the payment 'failed'.

utility-disconnection-scam.whyItWorks: Losing power means no heating, no fridge and, for a business, no trading, so the threat lands harder than an ordinary bill. Anyone who has ever paid late finds the arrears claim easy to believe, and an hour leaves no time to log in and check.

realVsFake.real: Energy and water companies send written notices over weeks before any disconnection, and the debt shows on your bill.
realVsFake.fake: The first you hear of any debt is a message giving you sixty minutes.

realVsFake.real: Your supplier takes payment through your online account, your bank or the methods printed on the bill.
realVsFake.fake: The caller insists on prepaid cards bought in a shop, a wire transfer or a crypto cash machine.

realVsFake.real: A genuine agent is content for you to hang up and ring the number on your bill.
realVsFake.fake: They say hanging up will lift the 'hold' on the technician and the power will go off.

steps.title: A villa free in peak week
steps.detail: A villa with a pool shows as available for school holidays or a festival week when everything nearby is booked, at a rate below its neighbours.

steps.title: Listing copied or account hijacked
steps.detail: The photos were lifted from a genuine owner's page, or a real owner's account or email was taken over, so the reviews and history look authentic.

steps.title: 'Finalise outside the site'
steps.detail: The 'owner' emails a rental contract and a link to a page resembling the booking site, saying a bank transfer deposit will secure your dates.

steps.title: Someone else is in the villa
steps.detail: You pay the balance weeks before travel. On arrival the real owner or other holidaymakers are in residence, and nobody has heard of your booking.

vacation-rental-scam.whyItWorks: Holiday dates are pinned down by school terms and flights, and the good places go early, so a suitable villa appearing late feels like a rescue. The loss is discovered only on arrival, long after the money moved.

realVsFake.real: Booking platforms hold your payment and pass it to the owner around check-in, so they can step in if something is wrong.
realVsFake.fake: The deposit goes straight to a bank account, often in a different country from the villa.

realVsFake.real: A genuine owner answers specific questions, such as how the pool heating works, and will video call from the terrace.
realVsFake.fake: Replies are generic and avoid any detail not already visible in the listing photos.

realVsFake.real: Real holiday lets keep the same photos, owner name and price across every site they appear on.
realVsFake.fake: A reverse image search finds the same villa under another name, town or owner.

steps.title: Searching 'register for VAT'
steps.detail: A new business owner searches online and clicks the first result, a sponsored advert for a site styled in the tax authority's colours and typeface.

steps.title: A long form on a third-party site
steps.detail: The page collects the company number, directors' names, home addresses, national insurance numbers and turnover, exactly the fields the official form would request.

steps.title: The fast-track charge at checkout
steps.detail: On the last screen a one-time fee appears for 'processing and compliance setup', payable by card, for a registration the tax authority provides free.

steps.title: Forwarded, delayed or never filed
steps.detail: Some sites simply retype your answers into the government portal. Others file nothing, and the director details are later used to open accounts or send convincing tax phishing.

vat-registration-scam.whyItWorks: First-time founders expect government paperwork to cost money and do not know that registering for VAT is free. A paid advert sitting above the official result, on a page with the right colours, looks like the front door.

realVsFake.real: The tax authority registers businesses through its own government web address and charges nothing for doing so.
realVsFake.fake: The site's address ends in an ordinary commercial suffix, and a disclaimer in the footer admits it is not affiliated with any government body.

realVsFake.real: An accountant who registers you is a named, qualified person who quotes for the work and signs an engagement letter.
realVsFake.fake: A caller from a 'business registration centre' says penalties begin this week unless you pay their fee by phone.

realVsFake.real: After a genuine application, the VAT number and certificate arrive from the tax authority, in your online tax account or by post.
realVsFake.fake: All you receive is a receipt from the website and an 'order number' that the tax office cannot find.

steps.title: The buyer with no questions
steps.detail: You list a car and a 'buyer' texts within the hour, calls it exactly what they want, and asks no questions about mileage or condition.

steps.title: One report, one website
steps.detail: They say they were burned before and only deal with sellers who provide a report from one particular site, then paste its link into the chat.

steps.title: Enter the plate, then the card
steps.detail: The site asks for your registration or VIN, shows a loading bar and a 'report ready' screen, then requests card details for a fee of around 20 or 30.

steps.title: The buyer evaporates
steps.detail: You send the PDF and never hear back. The card is later billed for a recurring 'membership', or its number is used elsewhere.

vehicle-history-report-scam.whyItWorks: History checks are a sensible part of buying a car, so a buyer who asks for one sounds careful, not criminal. The fee is small next to the sale price, and paying it seems the quickest way to keep a keen buyer.

realVsFake.real: A real buyer who wants a history check buys it themselves, using your registration number or VIN, from a provider they picked.
realVsFake.fake: The fake buyer wants you to pay, and rejects a report you already hold from a well-known provider.

realVsFake.real: Recognised history services are easy to find by name, list a company behind them and charge a one-off price shown up front.
realVsFake.fake: The linked site was registered recently, has no company details, and hides a monthly subscription in grey small print.

realVsFake.real: Someone serious about your car asks when they can see it and whether the service record is complete.
realVsFake.fake: The same scripted message goes to dozens of sellers, and the conversation ends the moment the report is paid for.

steps.title: The urgent recall alert
steps.detail: A text marked URGENT says your vehicle is under a safety recall and offers a free repair. It names no make, no model and no registration.

steps.title: Confirm your vehicle
steps.detail: The link opens a booking page with a dealership-style logo. It asks for your registration or VIN, name, home address and driving licence number.

steps.title: Choosing a workshop slot
steps.detail: A calendar lets you pick a date at a 'local authorised centre', which makes the booking feel real even though no garage has been told anything.

steps.title: The no-show deposit
steps.detail: To hold the appointment the page takes a small 'refundable deposit' or parts courier fee by card. The card and identity details are kept, and no repair exists.

vehicle-recall-text-scam.whyItWorks: Recalls are real, they concern brakes, airbags and fires, and most drivers have no idea whether one is outstanding on their car. A free repair costs nothing to accept, so typing in details feels harmless.

realVsFake.real: Manufacturers announce recalls by letter to the registered keeper, quoting the vehicle and the specific defect.
realVsFake.fake: A text mentions 'your vehicle' without saying which one or what is wrong with it.

realVsFake.real: You can look up open recalls yourself with your registration or VIN on the official government or manufacturer checker.
realVsFake.fake: The message steers you to its own link and warns that any delay puts you at risk.

realVsFake.real: Recall work is carried out free at a franchised dealer, with nothing to pay to book.
realVsFake.fake: A deposit, admin charge or parts fee appears at the last step of the booking form.

steps.title: The free webinar
steps.detail: A social media advert or 'business expo' stand invites you to a free webinar about owning snack machines or cash machines that earn while you sleep.

steps.title: A locator with sites ready
steps.detail: A sales rep sends a brochure with an income figure per machine per month and says a 'locator' has already secured hospitals, gyms and factories nearby.

steps.title: A package of ten
steps.detail: You are steered to a bundle of five or ten machines paid by wire in one sum, with a discount if the contract is signed this week.

steps.title: Machines with nowhere to go
steps.detail: Months later, cheap machines arrive at your garage, or none do. The promised sites turn out to be a launderette that never agreed, and the rep's line is disconnected.

vending-machine-scam.whyItWorks: Everyone has seen a busy vending machine and done the sum in their head, so the business feels simple and physical compared with online schemes. The hard part is winning good sites, and the seller claims to have done that already.

realVsFake.real: Working vending operators find their own sites, sign an agreement with each property owner and start with one or two machines.
realVsFake.fake: The promoter will not name a single location until after you have paid for the whole route.

realVsFake.real: A genuine business seller hands over written earnings records and lets you phone existing owners that you pick from a full list.
realVsFake.fake: You are given two 'references' who answer on the first ring and describe identical monthly takings.

realVsFake.real: Machines bought from a manufacturer or distributor have a list price you can compare, a warranty and a parts supply.
realVsFake.fake: The package price works out at several times the retail cost of the same machine, and the 'training and support' is a PDF.

steps.title: Money from a name you don't know
steps.detail: A stranger's payment of 400 lands in your Venmo feed, perhaps with a note like 'rent' or a house emoji. It was funded with a stolen card.

steps.title: The 'wrong person' message
steps.detail: Within minutes they message to say they mistyped a username and need it back for their landlord, asking you to pay it to a second profile.

steps.title: You return it from your balance
steps.detail: Feeling decent, you send 400. That payment comes from your own balance or linked bank, and is separate from the money they sent.

steps.title: The card owner disputes it
steps.detail: The stolen card's owner reports the charge and Venmo pulls the original 400 out of your account. Some victims then get a text from fake 'support' asking for a code.

venmo-scam.whyItWorks: The app is built around friends, emojis and quick taps, so payments feel casual and final. Seeing 400 sitting in your balance makes the stranger's story look true, and sending it back seems like the only decent response.

realVsFake.real: A mistaken payment can be reported through the app's help section, so the original is reversed without you paying anyone.
realVsFake.fake: The sender wants a brand new payment, usually to a different username or through a link they supply.

realVsFake.real: Venmo support answers inside the app or from its official help pages, and never needs your login code.
realVsFake.fake: A text from an ordinary mobile number says your account is frozen and asks you to reply with the six digits you just received.

realVsFake.real: Friends splitting a bill request the exact share and you recognise both the name and the photo.
realVsFake.fake: A 'cash flip' account promises to turn 50 into 500 and shows screenshots of other people's supposed payouts.

steps.title: A busy boss who is travelling
steps.detail: An executive, doctor or property investor replies to your application and says they are abroad on business, so everything will be handled by email or text.

steps.title: Small errands first
steps.detail: Early tasks are harmless: book a restaurant, compare flight prices, draft a letter. They thank you warmly and say your first week's funds are on the way.

steps.title: Starting funds appear
steps.detail: A cheque or bank deposit covers 'office supplies' plus your 200 pay. It shows as available, but it is a forged cheque or money from a hacked account.

steps.title: Three gift cards, codes by text
steps.detail: The urgent task is to buy three gift cards, scratch them and send photos of the codes. The cards are drained in minutes and the deposit is reversed.

virtual-assistant-job-scam.whyItWorks: An assistant's whole job is to run errands and spend the boss's money on their behalf, so buying cards for 'clients' or 'the office' feels like doing the role well. The easy first tasks build a working relationship before the costly one.

realVsFake.real: Real employers who need purchases made issue a company card or reimburse an expense claim with receipts.
realVsFake.fake: Personal funds are dropped into your own account, and you are told to spend them within the hour.

realVsFake.real: No business buys office supplies with gift card codes sent by text message.
realVsFake.fake: The cards are 'for supplies' or 'for clients', yet only the numbers on the back are wanted.

realVsFake.real: A genuine boss will speak to you on a call and tell you the company's registered name.
realVsFake.fake: They are always in a meeting or on a flight, and want your online banking login to 'set up payroll'.

steps.title: A last-minute search
steps.detail: Days before flying, you learn you need an ESTA or ETA and search for it. Adverts with flags and eagle crests sit above the government's own page.

steps.title: The same questions, retyped
steps.detail: The site asks what the official form asks: passport number, travel dates, parents' names, the yes or no security questions. It all feels correct.

steps.title: Extras at the till
steps.detail: The total appears only at the end, several times the official price once 'application review', 'priority handling' and travel insurance have been ticked for you.

steps.title: Found out at the check-in desk
steps.detail: Some sites file your answers using their own email, so official messages never reach you. Others send a home-made approval PDF the airline's system cannot find.

visa-application-scam.whyItWorks: Travel authorisations are a fairly new requirement that many passengers first hear about from their airline days before departure. They have never seen the official site or its price, and paying an agency for visa help is normal for longer-stay visas.

realVsFake.real: The issuing government's own site or app states one fixed fee before you begin the form.
realVsFake.fake: The lookalike keeps its price off every page until your passport details are already entered.

realVsFake.real: An approved authorisation is tied electronically to your passport and can be checked on the government's status page.
realVsFake.fake: You are emailed a decorative 'certificate' with a reference that the official status check does not recognise.

realVsFake.real: Honest visa agencies say plainly that they are private firms and list their charge separately from the government fee.
realVsFake.fake: The site puts 'official' in its name, uses national symbols, and confines its disclaimer to pale text below the fold.

steps.title: One ring, then a message
steps.detail: Your phone rings briefly or not at all. A voicemail appears from a number with an unfamiliar international or premium-rate prefix.

steps.title: A message that says almost nothing
steps.detail: A recorded voice mentions 'your account', 'a parcel' or 'legal action' without naming a company or you, then repeats a callback number twice, slowly.

steps.title: Kept on hold by design
steps.detail: Ringing back reaches hold music, a long menu or an operator who speaks slowly. On a premium-rate line, every minute of waiting is billed to you.

steps.title: Or handed to a fake 'agent'
steps.detail: On an ordinary line, whoever answers asks for your name, date of birth and card number to 'locate the account' or clear an invented charge.

voicemail-callback-scam.whyItWorks: A voicemail feels more official than a text, and a message with no detail leaves you to imagine the worst case yourself. Calling back to find out seems like the cautious thing to do.

realVsFake.real: A real company's voicemail names the business, gives a reason and a reference, and the number matches its website.
realVsFake.fake: The message could apply to anyone, and its callback number appears nowhere else.

realVsFake.real: Banks and couriers are happy for you to ignore a voicemail and reach them through their app or published line.
realVsFake.fake: The recording insists only this number will work and that action follows within hours.

realVsFake.real: Ordinary customer service lines cost the price of a standard call.
realVsFake.fake: The callback number carries a premium or overseas code, and the call is stretched to run up your bill.

steps.title: New voicemail, 42 seconds
steps.detail: A caller's partial number, a time and a duration of 0:42 are set out like a phone system's automatic notice. The subject may include your own name or company.

steps.title: A play button that is a picture
steps.detail: There is a grey audio bar with a play triangle. It is an image linked to a web page, or the 'recording' is an attachment named voicemail.html or VM_0042.htm.

steps.title: Sign in to listen
steps.detail: Pressing play brings up a login box over a blurred audio waveform, asking for the email password 'to authenticate playback'. The attachment version opens the same box from your own disk.

steps.title: No recording exists
steps.detail: After the password is sent, the page plays nothing or says 'playback error'. Some versions instead download a file posing as an audio player update, which installs malware.

voicemail-email-scam.whyItWorks: A voicemail is a person waiting for a call back, perhaps a client, a school or a hospital, and curiosity about who rang is hard to resist. Many office phone systems do email recordings, so the format is familiar.

realVsFake.real: Office phone systems that email voicemail attach an audio file, such as .wav or .mp3, that plays in your media player.
realVsFake.fake: The attachment is an .html page, or the play bar is a flat image that opens a website.

realVsFake.real: Mobile voicemail is retrieved by dialling your provider's short number or through the phone's own voicemail screen.
realVsFake.fake: A personal email address with no office phone system behind it receives a 'PBX voicemail' notice anyway.

realVsFake.real: Playing a real recording never needs your email password, since the message was delivered to that mailbox already.
realVsFake.fake: A login box appears between you and the recording, with your email address pre-filled and the password field blinking.

steps.title: A casting message
steps.detail: A 'producer' emails or messages through a freelance site about narrating an advert, audiobook or training video, quoting a flat fee for a few minutes of audio.

steps.title: You got the part
steps.detail: You record a short demo on your phone and are told you have the role within the hour. The script and a contract will follow 'after setup'.

steps.title: Studio-grade requirements
steps.detail: The client says the recording must be made with a particular microphone, booth or editing programme, available only from their supplier, so every voice on the project matches.

steps.title: Cheque in, balance out
steps.detail: Either you buy the software yourself, or a cheque for equipment arrives and you send the balance to the supplier. No script is ever delivered.

voiceover-job-scam.whyItWorks: Beginners in voice work expect to be judged on audio quality and assume professionals own specialist gear. Being cast straight away is flattering, and a technical requirement about matching sound is hard for a newcomer to question.

realVsFake.real: Real clients care about the finished file, usually a clean WAV or MP3, not which shop your microphone came from.
realVsFake.fake: The gig depends on one brand of software bought through a link the client supplies.

realVsFake.real: Casting directors hold auditions with the actual script and often ask for retakes with direction.
realVsFake.fake: Any recording is accepted, and the praise arrives before they could have listened to it.

realVsFake.real: Voice work is paid after delivery, or with a part payment in advance through the freelance site's own system.
realVsFake.fake: You receive a cheque larger than the fee and are asked to settle the supplier's bill from it.

steps.title: 'Your registration is incomplete'
steps.detail: In the weeks before an election, a text or call from the 'Election Commission' says your registration is incomplete or was removed from the roll.

steps.title: The flag-covered form
steps.detail: A link opens a page of flags and ballot-box icons asking for your full name, date of birth, address and driving licence or Social Security number.

steps.title: Twenty-five to stay on the roll
steps.detail: A $25 processing fee is requested by card to 'keep you eligible'. Phone versions offer to register you there and then if you read out the details.

steps.title: Still not registered
steps.detail: The card is charged and your identity details are kept. Nothing reaches a real election office, so anyone who truly needed to register still has not.

voter-registration-scam.whyItWorks: People do drop off the electoral roll after moving house, and the rules differ from place to place, so 'incomplete' is easy to believe. A real registration deadline is approaching, and nobody wants to be turned away at the polling station.

realVsFake.real: Registering to vote is free. No election office charges to add you, keep you or restore you to the roll.
realVsFake.fake: The page puts a price on eligibility and takes it by card alongside your ID number.

realVsFake.real: You register through the official election authority's form, online, on paper or in person, and you start the process yourself.
realVsFake.fake: A stranger rings and offers to complete it for you if you dictate your details down the phone.

realVsFake.real: Election offices confirm registration by post, with a card or letter sent to the address where you are registered.
realVsFake.fake: The warning comes as a text from an unknown number or a social media message naming no local office.

steps.title: The lifetime deal advert
steps.detail: A banner or sponsored post offers lifetime VPN access for $19 with unlimited devices, a logo you half recognise and a row of five-star badges.

steps.title: Checkout with no company behind it
steps.detail: The site lists no company name, address or staff. Its checkout takes your email and card, and often has you set a password you may reuse elsewhere.

steps.title: An app that asks for everything
steps.detail: You install an app or browser extension from a direct download. It requests broad permissions and sends all your browsing through servers the seller controls.

steps.title: It stops working, or it watches
steps.detail: Within weeks the servers refuse to connect and support emails bounce. In other cases the app keeps running and logs every site you visit to sell on.

vpn-subscription-scam.whyItWorks: Running VPN servers costs money every month, so a single $19 payment cannot fund a lifetime of service. Buyers seldom do that sum because a VPN is invisible when it works, and its privacy claims cannot be checked from outside.

realVsFake.real: Established VPN providers name the company behind them, publish independent audits of their no-logging claims and bill monthly or yearly.
realVsFake.fake: The seller is a logo and a checkout form, with a privacy policy that contradicts itself or was copied from elsewhere.

realVsFake.real: Reputable VPN apps sit in the official app stores under the provider's own developer name, with a long review history.
realVsFake.fake: You are handed a download file or an extension from a developer with no other apps.

realVsFake.real: A genuine provider gives you an account page where you can cancel, and a stated refund window.
realVsFake.fake: Once the one-time lifetime payment clears there is no account page, and the support address goes quiet.

steps.title: Cash before payday, no interest
steps.detail: An advert or sponsored app-store listing offers up to a few hundred against your next wage, with no credit check and a promise of zero interest.

steps.title: Permissions before any money
steps.detail: On first launch the app asks to read your contacts, text messages and photos, then to link the bank account your salary is paid into.

steps.title: A smaller advance than promised
steps.detail: The amount released is well below the headline figure. An 'express fee' is deducted and a suggested tip is already ticked on the confirmation screen.

steps.title: Payday grab, then the contact list
steps.detail: Repayment is taken the moment wages arrive, leaving you short enough to borrow again. Miss one and messages go to people in your address book.

wage-advance-scam.whyItWorks: Being a few days short before payday is common and embarrassing, and 'your own wages, early' does not sound like borrowing. Tips and fees are shown as small flat sums, which hides how expensive a two-week advance really is.

realVsFake.real: Earned wage access offered through an employer is tied to your payroll records and shows any fee before you confirm.
realVsFake.fake: The app has no link to your employer and reveals the charges only after the advance has landed.

realVsFake.real: A lender has no use for your contacts, photos or text messages, and reputable apps do not request them.
realVsFake.fake: Refusing the contacts permission closes the application, because the address book is what they use to shame late payers.

realVsFake.real: A responsible provider caps how much of a pay packet you can draw and lets you skip tipping without penalty.
realVsFake.fake: Declining the tip lowers your next limit, and a rollover offer appears each time a repayment is due.

steps.title: A 499 payment you never made
steps.detail: A text says 499.00 was paid to an online retailer through your mobile wallet, naming Apple Pay or Google Pay, with a link or number to dispute it.

steps.title: The disputes desk
steps.detail: Either route reaches a 'wallet fraud team', by web form or a calm voice on the phone, who agree the charge looks suspicious and offer to reverse it.

steps.title: Verifying the card to block it
steps.detail: For the reversal they want the card number, your wallet PIN or device passcode, and the six-digit code your bank is about to send by text.

steps.title: Your card on their handset
steps.detail: That code is the one a bank sends when a card is added to a new wallet. Once read out, your card sits on the criminal's phone, ready for contactless spending.

wallet-charge-text-scam.whyItWorks: A wallet payment feels like something that could happen without you noticing, from a lost phone or a stray tap at a till. The text offers exactly what a frightened person wants, a single button that undoes the charge.

realVsFake.real: Real wallet payments produce a notification from the wallet itself and show in your banking app within moments.
realVsFake.fake: Nothing appears in either app. The only trace of the charge is the text.

realVsFake.real: You dispute a card payment with your bank, through its app or the number on the back of the card.
realVsFake.fake: The dispute link or phone line belongs to nobody you hold an account with.

realVsFake.real: The message carrying a wallet set-up code normally warns you not to share it with anyone, bank staff included.
realVsFake.fake: The 'agent' says the code is needed to cancel the transaction and asks you to read it out at once.

steps.title: Card details already stolen
steps.detail: Your card number, expiry date and security code were captured earlier, typically by a fake parcel redelivery page or a breached online shop.

steps.title: Their phone asks to add it
steps.detail: The criminal enters those details into Apple Pay or Google Pay on their own handset. Your bank reacts by texting a one-time code to your number.

steps.title: A 'verification' call seconds later
steps.detail: Before you have read the text, someone rings as the bank's security desk and asks you to read out the code to confirm your card is still yours.

steps.title: Tap-to-pay on a stranger's handset
steps.detail: With the code entered, your card lives in their wallet. They buy gift cards and electronics in shops by contactless, with no PIN and no plastic.

wallet-provisioning-scam.whyItWorks: The code really does come from your bank's usual number, and it arrives at the exact second the caller says it will. Few people read past the digits to the line saying it is for adding a card to a mobile wallet.

realVsFake.real: Bank staff never need a one-time passcode read to them. The text itself usually says not to share it with anyone.
realVsFake.fake: The caller says the code proves you are the cardholder and that without it the card will be cancelled.

realVsFake.real: A wallet set-up code only arrives when you are adding the card on your own phone at that moment.
realVsFake.fake: A code turns up while your phone is in your pocket, followed by a call explaining it away as a routine check.

realVsFake.real: Many banking apps list the devices holding your card and let you remove any you do not recognise.
realVsFake.fake: After the call, an alert confirms your card was added to a phone model you have never owned.

steps.title: 'We are from the water board'
steps.detail: Two people in work jackets say there is a burst main or contamination in the road, and that they must test your water pressure and quality straight away.

steps.title: Kept busy at the sink
steps.detail: One asks you to run the kitchen tap at full pressure and keep watching the colour of the water, or to fill a jug and tell them when it clears.

steps.title: The second visitor upstairs
steps.detail: While the tap is roaring, the other goes 'to check the stopcock' or the bathroom, and searches bedrooms for cash, jewellery and bank cards.

steps.title: A filter fee, or simply gone
steps.detail: Some finish with a cash charge for a 'filter' or 'test certificate'. Others thank you and leave, and the theft goes unnoticed until the evening.

water-doorstep-scam.whyItWorks: A water problem sounds urgent and harmless at once, and the request is tiny: run a tap. Older residents who still say 'the water board' are picked on purpose, and the noise of running water covers footsteps on the stairs.

realVsFake.real: Water companies rarely need to come indoors, and planned visits are announced by letter or booked appointment.
realVsFake.fake: The visitors arrive unannounced and say there is no time to phone the company.

realVsFake.real: Genuine staff will wait outside with the door shut while you ring the number on your water bill.
realVsFake.fake: They offer a number from their own card to call, or one keeps you talking while the other edges inside.

realVsFake.real: Sampling tap water is part of the company's routine work and is never charged to the householder at the door.
realVsFake.fake: A cash fee is asked for a test kit, a tap filter or a 'safety certificate'.

steps.title: An income site on offer
steps.detail: A listing on a forum or broker marketplace offers a content site or online shop said to earn 5,000 a month, for roughly a year's profit.

steps.title: Screenshots as evidence
steps.detail: The seller shares screenshots of an analytics dashboard and payment processor payouts. Asked for read-only access to the live accounts, they send a screen recording.

steps.title: Skip escrow, save the fee
steps.detail: They suggest paying by bank transfer or crypto to avoid escrow charges, and promise to push the domain and hand over logins the same day.

steps.title: An empty shell changes hands
steps.detail: The domain never moves, or it does and the traffic vanishes within days because it was bought from bot networks. The 'revenue' was the seller paying themselves.

website-sale-scam.whyItWorks: An online business is only numbers on a dashboard, and dashboards can be edited in a browser in seconds. Buyers who dream of income without building anything accept screenshots because asking for more feels like questioning an owner's honesty.

realVsFake.real: A genuine owner adds you as a read-only user on the analytics and ad accounts so you can browse the history yourself.
realVsFake.fake: The scammer offers images and a spreadsheet, and says live access would 'breach the platform's terms'.

realVsFake.real: Reputable sales run through an escrow service that releases payment only after the domain and accounts sit under your control.
realVsFake.fake: You are asked to send the full sum directly, with the transfer of the domain promised for afterwards.

realVsFake.real: The real owner can prove control by placing a file you name on the site or changing a DNS record on request.
realVsFake.fake: The person selling is a 'broker for the owner', cannot make any change to the site, and blames the developer being on holiday.

steps.title: A portfolio that stops you scrolling
steps.detail: You find a photographer, florist or venue on social media or a wedding directory, with a gallery of beautiful work and a package price below the going rate.

steps.title: Your date is nearly gone
steps.detail: They reply fast, say another couple has enquired about the same Saturday, and send a one-page contract with no business address or registration details.

steps.title: Half now, off the platform
steps.detail: You are asked to transfer half the fee to a personal account, with a discount offered for skipping the directory's own booking and payment system.

steps.title: Silence as the day approaches
steps.detail: Messages are answered for a while, then slow down. A month before the wedding the profile is deleted, the number is dead and good suppliers are fully booked.

wedding-vendor-scam.whyItWorks: Couples book suppliers a year ahead and are told constantly that the good ones go quickly, so paying a deposit on the spot is normal behaviour. The long gap before the wedding means nobody expects to hear much for months.

realVsFake.real: A working photographer can show a complete gallery from one wedding, at a venue you can name, and put you in touch with that couple.
realVsFake.fake: The impostor has forty stunning single images in mixed styles, lifted from several real photographers' feeds.

realVsFake.real: Genuine vendors offer a video call or a meeting at the venue, and their contract names a business you can look up.
realVsFake.fake: Every attempt to speak live is put off because they are 'shooting abroad this month', but the invoice comes instantly.

realVsFake.real: A legitimate supplier's contract sets out staged payments, and the first instalment can be paid by card or through the directory.
realVsFake.fake: The payee name on the transfer does not match the business, and the rest falls due long before the wedding.

steps.title: The fake news article
steps.detail: A social advert opens what looks like a news site, where a TV presenter 'reveals' the fat-burner behind her weight loss, with before and after photos.

steps.title: Free bottle, pay postage
steps.detail: Every link on the page leads to one offer: a free trial bottle for 4.95 shipping, beside a countdown timer and a 'bottles left' counter.

steps.title: The terms nobody scrolls to
steps.detail: Pale text far below the order button says the trial lasts fourteen days from ordering, after which the full bottle price is charged and repeated monthly.

steps.title: Charges under other names
steps.detail: A charge near ninety appears, then another each month, under merchant names unlike the product's. Cancelling means a phone line that is rarely answered and returning opened bottles.

weight-loss-scam.whyItWorks: A familiar face telling a personal story persuades in a way an ordinary advert cannot, and the article format hides that it is an advert at all. Paying only postage feels like no commitment, especially to someone who has tried several diets already.

realVsFake.real: Celebrities announce paid partnerships on their own verified accounts, labelled as adverts.
realVsFake.fake: The endorsement exists only on the seller's page, in quotes the presenter never gave, under a borrowed news logo.

realVsFake.real: Prescription weight-loss medicines are supplied only after a clinician has checked your weight and medical history.
realVsFake.fake: A gummy, tea or capsule claims the same results with no prescription, no diet and no listed dose of anything.

realVsFake.real: An honest subscription shows the recurring price beside the pay button and sends a reminder before billing.
realVsFake.fake: Only the postage is visible at checkout. The monthly charge sits behind a 'terms' link in grey type.

steps.title: Someone sent you files
steps.detail: The layout is WeTransfer's: a sender's address, '1 file, 24 MB total', an expiry three days away, and a round blue 'Get your files' button.

steps.title: A download that stalls
steps.detail: The button opens a page showing a file name such as 'Scanned_Documents.pdf' and a progress ring that stops partway, replaced by 'Session timed out. Sign in to continue download.'

steps.title: Pick your email provider
steps.detail: A pop-up offers Office 365, Outlook, Gmail and 'Other mail' icons. Whichever you choose, the box that follows asks for that mailbox's password.

steps.title: Decoy file, live password
steps.detail: Some pages then hand over a harmless PDF so nothing seems wrong. Your password is tested within minutes, and work mailboxes are searched for invoices to tamper with.

wetransfer-file-scam.whyItWorks: Large files from designers, printers, accountants and clients arrive this way every week, often from addresses you only half recognise. The expiry date is a genuine feature of the service, so the built-in deadline raises no suspicion.

realVsFake.real: Collecting files from a genuine transfer needs no account. You press download and the browser saves them.
realVsFake.fake: The download refuses to start until you 'sign in', and it wants your email provider's password to do so.

realVsFake.real: A real transfer email shows the sender's address and usually a message they typed, about files you were expecting.
realVsFake.fake: The sender is 'noreply' or a contact who never mentioned sending anything, and the message field is blank.

realVsFake.real: The real service lists each file with its name and size before you download.
realVsFake.fake: The page shows one vaguely named document and a progress ring that always freezes at the same point.

steps.title: A profile shaped by loss
steps.detail: The profile describes a widowed engineer, nurse or army officer raising a child alone. The first message mentions the late spouse and how hard evenings have become.

steps.title: Grief as common ground
steps.detail: If you have lost someone too, they mirror your story back. Good-morning texts, prayers and talk of a second chance at happiness arrive every day for weeks.

steps.title: The estate that is frozen
steps.detail: Money trouble appears: funeral debts, a child's school fees, or a late spouse's insurance payout that a lawyer will only release after a tax or legal fee.

steps.title: You are the only one
steps.detail: They say they have no family left to ask and promise repayment from the inheritance. Hesitate, and the tone turns wounded: they thought you understood loss.

widow-romance-scam.whyItWorks: A widow or widower seems safe, with no ex-partner, no baggage and every reason to move slowly. Bereaved people recognise the loneliness described and feel protective, so a request for help reads as shared hardship, not a sales pitch.

realVsFake.real: Someone newly bereaved has a traceable life: relatives, colleagues, a funeral notice, old photos with other people in them.
realVsFake.fake: The persona has a handful of solo photos, no tagged friends, and a job that keeps them conveniently overseas.

realVsFake.real: Solicitors handling an estate take their costs from the estate or bill the family directly.
realVsFake.fake: A lawyer nobody can look up needs a fee from you, a new acquaintance, before an inheritance can be paid out.

realVsFake.real: A grieving person you meet online is usually cautious and glad to talk on live video at an agreed time.
realVsFake.fake: Love is declared within days, yet the camera is always broken or the signal on the rig too weak.

steps.title: A clean-looking bargain
steps.detail: A used car is advertised as accident-free with one careful owner, freshly valeted and priced a little under similar cars so it sells within days.

steps.title: Viewed at dusk, or in the rain
steps.detail: The seller prefers to meet in a car park in the evening. Wet or dim conditions hide mismatched paint, overspray on rubber seals and uneven panel gaps.

steps.title: Paperwork with gaps
steps.detail: The logbook is a recent duplicate, the service history stops abruptly, and the seller says they are selling for a relative and know little about it.

steps.title: The truth from a garage
steps.detail: You pay close to full market value. Later a history check, an insurer or a mechanic with the car on a ramp finds the write-off marker, welded chassis rails or missing airbags.

write-off-car-scam.whyItWorks: Fresh paint and a valet make a repaired wreck look better than an honest car with stone chips. Structural damage sits behind bumpers and under carpets, and most buyers judge a car by its shine and a short drive.

realVsFake.real: An honest seller of a repaired write-off states the category in the advert and prices the car well below clean examples.
realVsFake.fake: The advert says 'no accidents' and the price is only slightly low, enough to tempt without inviting suspicion.

realVsFake.real: Genuine owners give you the registration and VIN before you travel, and the VIN on the dashboard, door pillar and logbook all agree.
realVsFake.fake: The plate is blurred in photos, and on the car one VIN plate looks newly riveted or is missing.

realVsFake.real: A seller with nothing to hide agrees to an independent inspection at a garage of your choosing.
realVsFake.fake: An inspection is refused on the grounds that the car 'only just passed its test', though the certificate cannot be found.

steps.title: A notice about your badge
steps.detail: A DM or email headed 'X Support' or 'Verification Team' says your blue tick is under review, or that you have been pre-approved for one.

steps.title: A lookalike sender
steps.detail: The account uses the X logo and a handle padded with words like 'helpdesk' or 'verify'. Emails come from an address that only resembles the company's.

steps.title: 'Confirm your account details'
steps.detail: Following the link opens a black-and-white sign-in page matching X's design. It takes your username and password, then requests the login code sent to your phone.

steps.title: Your handle turns salesman
steps.detail: Once inside, the thieves change the email on the account and begin posting crypto giveaways or fake merchandise links to your followers, trading on the trust in your name.

x-verification-scam.whyItWorks: The rules around X's blue tick have changed several times, so most users are unsure how it is granted or removed. For journalists, businesses and creators the badge signals credibility, and a threat to it gets a fast reaction.

realVsFake.real: The blue tick comes with a paid subscription that you start and manage from the settings of your own account.
realVsFake.fake: A message says the badge can be granted or saved by filling in a form reached from a link.

realVsFake.real: X does not handle account reviews through DMs from other profiles. Anything affecting your account appears when you sign in normally.
realVsFake.fake: The warning comes from a recently created profile with a borrowed logo and a few hundred followers.

realVsFake.real: Subscription problems, such as a failed payment, are fixed in the app's billing section at your own pace.
realVsFake.fake: You are given 24 hours, and the page asks for your password plus the code that protects it.

steps.title: A sponsorship email to your business address
steps.detail: Someone claiming to be from a VPN, game studio or editing software firm writes to the contact address on your channel's About page, offering a four-figure integration.

steps.title: They agree to everything
steps.detail: You reply with your rates and they accept at once without negotiation. Then they send a link to a cloud folder or a password-protected archive.

steps.title: The 'contract' is a program
steps.detail: Inside is a file named like an agreement or a game demo but ending in .exe or .scr. Opening it shows nothing, or an error message.

steps.title: Cookies stolen, channel rebranded
steps.detail: The malware copies your browser's saved sessions, so attackers enter your Google account already signed in. They rename the channel and start a crypto live stream.

youtube-creator-scam.whyItWorks: Sponsorships are how most channels earn, and real brands do email creators out of nowhere with contracts and asset packs. A creator who has waited months for a first deal is primed to open whatever the sponsor sends.

realVsFake.real: A real sponsor's contract is a PDF or an e-signature link that opens in the browser and installs nothing.
realVsFake.fake: The paperwork arrives zipped with a password in the email, and one file inside must be run.

realVsFake.real: Brand partnership staff write from the company's domain and can be found on its site or professional profiles.
realVsFake.fake: The sender uses a free mailbox or a domain with an extra word, such as the brand name plus 'partners'.

realVsFake.real: Genuine sponsors ask for audience figures, discuss the talking points, and usually haggle over the fee.
realVsFake.fake: This sponsor has no questions about your viewers and only cares that you test their 'preview tool' today.
